posts.title: Bart Hess at Dutch Design Week: a studio, a latex cave and a location named after him
posts.subtitle: The photo archive holds four albums. Museum pages, press and Dutch Design Week's own listings show a wider record, and the 2026 listing at his address is another label's show.
posts.seoTitle: Bart Hess at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Bart Hess at Dutch Design Week, 2012 to 2026: a studio at NRE, a latex cave, a VR film and a location page that lists another label's show.

r: The 2026 Dutch Design Week page named Bart Hess | NRE lists one exhibition, and it belongs to a furniture label called OFFSITE.

This essay began with four albums of photographs and turned into a reading of a place. As a content strategist I watch what a name on a map promises, and a location that carries a designer's name promises that the designer is behind what is shown there. This essay checks how often the sources keep that promise. It draws on public sources only: Dutch Design Week's own program and location pages, the designer's pages, museum records, local and international press, a heritage-minded city page and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibits beyond what the published listings say.

blocks.x: The archive has four albums, and the record is wider than that

r: The official Flickr archive holds Bart Hess albums for 2016, 2017, 2019 and 2021, with 7, 7, 6 and 10 photos, which makes 30. The 2016 titles read 82_BART_HESS and credit Iris Rijskamp. The later titles begin NRE_BartHess and credit Nick Bookelaar. I read those albums in an earlier pass and did not reopen the account for this version, so every Flickr fact here is second-hand.

The written record shows a longer and odder pattern. It has a 2012 production line for visitors whose festival link I could not confirm, a 2016 open studio, a 2018 installation in a former dairy factory that no Hess-titled album covers, a 2019 virtual reality film at a different address, a 2024 dance project that DDW lists and its photo archive does not, and a 2026 location page that carries his name and someone else's show.

blocks.x: A designer who made his name early

r: Brabant Cultureel, a regional culture site, says Hess grew up in Geldrop, studied at the Design Academy in Eindhoven and graduated in 2007 from the Man and Identity department. After graduating he started a blog with Lucy McRae, who then worked for Philips Design, and each week one of them appeared in front of the camera dressed in everyday materials such as dish soap foam. In 2010 American Vogue approached the pair about doing something similar with the photographer Nick Knight, and in 2011 Lady Gaga approached them for a photo session for a new album.

The slime dress that came out of it was developed in his studio, then on the Kanaaldijk. The same article says he thickened the slime with flour so it would hold on the body during the shoot and took fifteen kilos of the mixture to New York on the plane. Omroep Brabant repeats the fifteen-kilo figure.

Hess's own account, in an interview on the design site WOTH, is that Lady Gaga's stylist picked his Slime Outfit for the cover of the album Born This Way while he was still at school. That is his recollection, and the two accounts differ on the order of events.
The Dutch Design Awards gallery lists him as the 2011 winner in the Young Designer category, and WOTH has him describing the prize as the Mini Young Designer Award.
Design Museum Den Bosch says the Slime Dress brought international fame barely four years after graduation.
The same WOTH interview has him saying he no longer calls himself a designer because he does not think in products.
That sentence matters for an archive that files him under "Bart Hess" and a place: the work he describes is a body of materials, films and installations, and a festival listing is a poor fit for it.

blocks.x: 2012: a production line that asked visitors to work

r: The earliest record I could open of Work With Me People is a research record at the University of the Arts London. It dates the installation and performance to 2012 through 2017 and describes visitors instructed through headphones to perform simple, repetitive acts, in that version dripping liquid latex onto a stretched latex surface. It says the piece is meant to highlight the beauty of the differences between each participant's workmanship, and that once the latex dries the sheet is released and shrinks so the drops draw together into a skin of rubber bubbles. It adds that the automated version came out of his appointment as a Creative Fellow at the London College of Fashion.
A trend service, LS:N Global, ran an item dated October 24, 2012 under the headline "Alien concept: Show visitors make future fabrics."

I could read only the headline and date, and I did not try to get around the wall in front of the text. Neither source I could open says the 2012 version ran during Dutch Design Week, so I treat that placement as a lead and not a fact. Hess's own site credits the Work With Me pop-up studio as a way he involved audiences in making.

blocks.x: 2016: back in Eindhoven with the studio door open

r: Hess left Eindhoven in 2012 for London, spent a year in different places abroad and came back in 2016, according to Brabant Cultureel. His first studio on return was on the Stratumsedijk, and since the spring he had been at the former NRE terrein.
A January 2016 interview on the Innovation Origins site has him saying the city had grown while he was away, calling it a drab-looking town with a lot going on beneath the surface.

Neon Moire's guide to the fifteenth Dutch Design Week lists "Bart Hess" at the NRE terrein from October 22 to 30, 2016, 10:00 to 18:00, as an exclusive look inside his new studio where he develops materials and installations. The same guide counts nine days, 100 locations and 2,500 designers for the festival.
This is the earliest program text I found that places him at NRE.

Two reports describe what visitors found. Visi's report says he opened his studio to show "a treasure trove of artificial hides," with the flesh-colored Royal Latex Bed getting under the viewer's skin.

Brabant Cultureel confirms he opened the studio to the public during Dutch Design Week and adds a detail from that visit: an intern was sewing sequins that looked like mussel shells onto a base for costumes for Khôra, another dance by the choreographer Nanine Linning, due in the Netherlands in 2017. It also says the pink latex he used for the strange creatures in Linning's Silver was the material he had used for the curtains of a canopy bed in his studio.

Those two reports disagree on color, flesh in one and pink in the other, and the 2016 album includes a photograph of a bed under pale pleated drapes whose title names no work. That is a lead and not a match, because a title is a source and a resemblance is not.

The place has its own history. The NRE terrein is a former gasworks site established in 1899, and it takes its name from the Nutsbedrijven Regio Eindhoven, the regional utilities that were there from 1989 to 2010. The municipality bought it afterward and turned it into a creative neighborhood.
In 2016 Hess said the mix of studios there worked for him, with a ceramics workshop on one side and a graphic atelier due on the other.

blocks.x: 2017: a museum survey, and photographs with no program page

r: In 2017 the written record sits in museums. Future Bodies: Bart Hess 2007 to 2017 ran from June 24 to October 1, 2017 and was billed as the first survey of ten years of his projects. Design Museum Den Bosch lists it under the Mondrian to Dutch Design year.

The accompanying book names the museum then as the Stedelijk Museum 's-Hertogenbosch, names Fredric Baas as curator, and describes Hess as a new type of designer who experiments with materials to develop concepts that can take many media.

Silver, the Linning production with his costumes, was scheduled for January 14, 2017 at the Parktheater in Eindhoven and January 17 in Den Bosch, and the TextielMuseum in Tilburg showed his new work in an exhibition running to May 28, 2017.
That Tilburg work came from a collection commission on the museum's braiding machine, which produced three new works that react to approaching visitors with small, irregular movements.
Brabant Cultureel describes the electronics hidden in braided cord or in a wrinkled pink silicone skin and responding to warmth and movement.

The studio that designed the Den Bosch survey, Studio Harm Rensink, says it turned the museum's 500 square meters into a landscape in which visitors moved from one world to the next through Hess's video works, soundscapes and material experiments, working closely with him.

For Dutch Design Week 2017 itself I found no program page. The Flickr album holds seven photographs by Nick Bookelaar titled NRE_BartHess that show performers in crumpled silver foil costumes under projected light.

A 2016 report says the robot-like dancers in Silver wore costumes of strips of reflective material, and that the Khôra costumes were in preparation, so a link is imaginable. No source I opened ties either production to these photographs, and I do not make the link.

blocks.x: 2018: a latex cave in a former dairy factory

r: Hess's 2018 Dutch Design Week appearance sits outside any album with his name. Robot Love, an exhibition running from September 15 to December 2, 2018 at the Campina Melkfabriek on the Kanaaldijk-Zuid, reported thousands of visitors during the festival and published a photo captioned as visitors in Hess's Grotto.
Core77 describes Grotto as a cave formed by enormous latex pillars in the center of the factory hall, made in 2015, and as one of his largest pieces.

Designboom adds the method. Pink latex sheets are stretched on six-meter wooden frames to double their size, a thick layer of liquid latex goes on, and Hess shapes vein-like lines with his fingers. When the sheet is released from the frame it springs back, and the surface distorts while the carved lines keep their size. The same article says Grotto grew out of a three-year process that began with his show at the 2015 design biennale in Saint-Etienne and presented it during Dutch Design Week as part of Robot Love.

As an anatomist I notice what that description borrows from tissue: a stretched sheet that recoils, with veins that hold their size while the skin around them puckers. That is the article's account of the method, and I cannot test it from a page. My narrower point is this. I did not find a 2018 album under his name in the archive, so anyone who searches the archive by name would miss a well-documented appearance.

blocks.x: 2019: Reveries, and an address that is not the studio

r: VPRO's tip number seven for Dutch Design Week 2019 is Bart Hess, Reveries. The tip describes a 360-degree film of about six minutes, watched through a VR headset on a swivel chair at Gasfabriek 18. It says he made the film from a long trend report for Première Vision, a textile fair in Paris, that the music is by Wouter de Belder, and that only five headsets were available. In the reviewer's account the viewer sits in a forest surrounded by objects that dancers climb out of, and the landscape keeps changing as the dancers appear in new outfits.
The address matters. Dutch Design Week's 2026 location page for The GASFAB gives Gasfabriek 18 and calls it a former industrial gasworks in the NRE district, in the Canal area.
The 2026 page for Bart Hess | NRE gives Gashouder 43A.

So the 2019 film was shown in a different building on the same site from the one DDW now names after him. The sources do not say where his studio stood in 2019, and the photo titles NRE_Bart_Hess record an area, not a building.

blocks.x: 2020 and 2021: a prize, a book and a gap

r: In 2020 Hess and Harm Rensink did the exhibition design for BodyDrift, Anatomies of the Future, at Design Museum Den Bosch, and the studio's page credits the photography to Hess.
Rensink also co-curated Modebelofte in 2016, according to Neon Moire, which is the kind of thread that makes the Eindhoven design world look small.

On June 19, 2021 the Cultural Fund of North Brabant gave Hess its Design Prize, which comes with 10,000 euros and alternates between an established designer and a breakthrough talent. Piet Hein Eek won it in 2017 and Simone Post in 2019.
Omroep Brabant quotes the jury on the alienation his work causes and mentions his body sculptures for the national opera and ballet.
He used the occasion to select three emerging talents for a presentation at the museum from June 19 to September 19, 2021.
None of this places him at the festival that October. The 2021 album holds ten photographs by Bookelaar that show projected lettering, drawings and printed fabric.

I found no program page for the year, and I could not open a printed 2021 festival map that a search summary suggested might list his entries, since the file returns an error. So for 2021 the evidence is photographs and a title.

blocks.x: 2024: Venus, and a festival that lists what the archive lacks

r: Dutch Design Week's program page for Venus names Bart Hess as presenter. It describes a collaboration between Hess and the choreographer and dancer Sedrig Verwoert that explores dance, multimedia and costume design, with costumes treated as an extension of the dancers' bodies. It also describes Woven Bodies, a textile project built around the human skin, using stitching, quilting and embroidery on a large digital print taken from a still of Verwoert's choreography on the intertwining of human bodies.
Hess's own site gives the credits: concept by Verwoert and Hess, choreography by Verwoert, costume design by Hess and music by Phantom Wizard, with six named dancers.
DDW's own area recap, dated October 25, 2024, calls the NRE site the first hotspot of the Canal area and names the Venus project among its attractions.
The NRE studio's own page lists a DDW 2024 presentation of Bart Hess.
Three sources agree that he presented there that year. None of the 2024 album titles I could list carried his name, and I could not recheck the archive.

blocks.x: 2025 and 2026: the address outlives the exhibit

r: The same Gashouder 43A has hosted other people's shows. DesignWeb's 2025 guide lists a solo show by the studio ZOWA, Details matter, at Bart Hess | NRE, Gashouder 43A, from October 18 to 26, 2025, 11:00 to 18:00, free.
The NRE studio page lists an Offsite Expo and a Zowa Expo next to the DDW 2024 note for Hess, and it also advertises the space as a rentable photo studio.
For 2026 the location page gives Gashouder 43A, October 17 to 25, daily 11:00 to 18:00, free entry. The Tuesday row prints the hours backwards as 18:00 to 11:00, which looks like an entry error.

The page lists a single item, Back and forth, and the program page names the presenter as OFFSITE. It is a pop-up café called Café ocho, where the furniture, lamps and vases are made from industrial waste streams, with material credited to Staco, Unilin, Palet, Volta Energy, Brainport Assemblers, Hydro and Befo. It shows a cabinet called Lamella by Nina van Bart and Willem van Doorn and work by Rik van Veen, Structural Aspect, Julius Esser, Rik Frans Jansen and Joris Wintgens, with curtains by Yvonne Mak.
Nothing on either page says Hess shows work in 2026. DDW lists the address as 5611CR, while the studio's own page gives 5613 CR.
A location name is a label that stays after the show changes, and anyone reading a map the way I do should read the exhibitor line, not the place name.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Whether Work With Me People ran during Dutch Design Week 2012. The two sources I could open do not say, and the others that might have said so (two design sites that returned HTTP 403 and 503, and a trend service whose text is walled) were not usable, and I stopped asking.
What the 2017 and 2021 albums show by name. No program page I opened names either body of work.
Whether the draped bed in the 2016 album is the Royal Latex Bed, and which color the bed was.
Where his studio stood in each year, and whether Gashouder 43A is the studio he moved into in 2016.
Whether a 2023 album exists. I did not find one.
Whether Venus was staged elsewhere before the festival, and what Back and forth has to do with Hess beyond sharing his address.
How Reveries came to be commissioned beyond VPRO's account of the trend report.

r: If a location carries a person's name, what would you check before crediting that person with what is inside?

posts.title: BioArt Laboratories hosts the work, and the record disagrees about where it lived
posts.subtitle: Ten Dutch Design Week shows by one Eindhoven organization, read through its own pages, local reporting, the 2026 listing and five albums in the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: BioArt Laboratories at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Ten Dutch Design Week shows by BioArt Laboratories, a forest bunker site and a disputed move date, set against five photo albums.

r: The photo archive knows who hosted the show and who took the picture, and it says very little about what stands in the frame or even which building the frame is in.

I like that gap because it gives a reader something to do. This essay draws on public sources only: BioArt Laboratories' own pages, a residency listing, a university excursion page, Dutch Design Week's program pages, regional reporting, a contractor's project page and the official DDW photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibits beyond what DDW's location page lists.

blocks.x: An organization that describes itself as a host

r: AIR Brabant lists BioArt Laboratories as a residency and gives its self-description: the National Development Institution for the Biological Arts, with programs aimed at practical development and production of work, up to presentation on platforms such as Dutch Design Week.

BioArt's About page calls it a foundation and a gateway where science, nature, technology and creativity meet, and it names the funders that have supported it, among them the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science, the Creative Industries Fund NL, the province of North Brabant and the municipality of Eindhoven.

The people who show work there change every year. BioArt's page for 2019 describes an annual open call for its Talent Pressure Cooker and a group of makers ranging from product developers to architects.

Its page for the 2020 digital edition says the talents get access to the working environment after submitting a project proposal and receive guidance on turning an idea or prototype into a concept or product.
An organization built like this has a program, and the program has many authors. That matters for a photo archive.

Regional reporting adds a public-policy fact. Brabant Cultureel reported on October 15, 2021 that BioArt Laboratories had been included in the national cultural basic infrastructure that year, on the condition that it could keep developing at its current site.

blocks.x: A founder with a record before the lab

r: The founder's own site says Jalila Essaïdi was born in 1980, is best known for the project 2.6g 329m/s, also called Bulletproof Skin, and founded BioArt Laboratories in 2011.
The Bio Art & Design Award says she won a BAD Award in 2010 for that project.
A 2017 excursion page from Burg Giebichenstein University of Art and Design agrees on 2011 and adds that the lab established a physical foothold in Eindhoven in 2012.
AIR Brabant lists the foundation as founded in 2012.
The sources are consistent if 2011 is the founder's start and 2012 the lab's first base, but I have not seen a company-register extract, so I do not state either year as the legal founding date.

Dutch Design Week named her one of its four ambassadors for 2019. In the DDW interview she says she prefers to work with young, not-yet-established talent, and she describes Dutch Design Week as a stage for makers who lack the network or the money to present in prominent places.
That is her account of her own approach, and it fits the shape of the annual open call.

blocks.x: More than an exhibition

r: The exhibitions are one visible output of a larger operation. BioArt's laboratory page describes a hybrid laboratory that is both a biochemical research station for analysis and cultivation of biomaterials and a traditional atelier for prototyping, and it describes a Materialenbank, a library of bio-based materials that includes slime mold and luminous bacteria.

In a 2017 interview with the materials library MaterialDriven, Essaïdi describes the same Materialenbank, and the interviewer's introduction names the public formats Open Stadslabs and Curiocity Labs. The interviewer's page shows photographs of the lab's Dutch Design Week exhibits for 2015 and 2016.
That interview also gives the lab's own account of why it sits in Eindhoven: Essaïdi credits the legacy of Philips and the supply of what she calls bright talents.

It is her explanation, and nothing in the other sources tests it. I mention it because the lab's later choice of a Second World War site in a forest is easy to read as symbolism, and no source says that was the intention.

blocks.x: The site: German Houses in a Strijp forest

r: The place has a documented history. BioArt's own Village page says the complex is the Duitse Woningen, or German Houses, a bunker complex originally built to house German military officers, five freestanding reinforced buildings disguised as a traditional farmstead in the Heimatstil, on a plot of about 1.5 hectares.

Brabant Cultureel adds that the occupier confiscated the neighboring Constant Rebecque barracks in 1940, that the complex kept a military function until 1996, and that it later served as a center for asylum seekers before it decayed and was looted.
A contractor that worked on the renovation estimate, bureau FRANKEN, gives the figures for five buildings with 3,089 square meters of floor area on 16,255 square meters of land.
That land area is 1.6 hectares, which matches DDW's 2024 page and is slightly more than BioArt's own 1.5.

BioArt's partner page shows what the renovation has needed: military engineers from the 13th Light Brigade for architectural counsel and landscape work, a firm that traces unexploded ordnance for a risk analysis of the site's history, and companies donating solar equipment, building materials and fire-safety advice.

Who owns the site is a separate question. Brabant Cultureel says the municipality owned the complex and offered it to BioArt in 2016, and that the municipality later agreed to transfer the land and buildings.
The contractor's page says the purchase was agreed in 2017 and the purchase agreement was signed in 2022, and it also lists the purchase under 2017 in its timeline, so it contradicts itself.
I have not found a municipal document, so I do not give a date for the transfer.

blocks.x: When did the lab move? The sources disagree

r: The question looks small and has a firm answer.
BioArt's Dutch Village page says that in 2016 BioArt moved from its 750 square meter lab in Strijp-T to the German Houses.
The English version of the same page contains the same paragraph twice, once with 2016 and once with 2017.
Brabant Cultureel and the contractor both say 2016.

A contemporary report says otherwise. On June 28, 2017, the IO+ archive wrote that the staff of BioArt Lab would soon be moving into the German Houses, after years of preparing the move from Strijp TQ, where the lab was still located, with an official opening planned for September.

BioArt's own page for Dutch Design Week 2017, titled Lost in Transformation, says that exhibition was the first occasion on which the public got insight into its plans for the new BioArt Village, and its page for 2018 says it had less than a year to refurbish the new location and welcomed the public at the brand new site.

I settle it this way. The municipality offered the site in 2016, as the regional report says. The move happened in 2017 and 2018, and the first Dutch Design Week show at the Village was in October 2018. The wording "moved in 2016" in BioArt's own pages reads best as the offer date. This matters for the photographs: a 2016 or 2017 album is unlikely to show the Village.

blocks.x: Year by year, with the claim each source supports

r: For 2015, BioArt's page says it ran Chilling in a Box at the Veemgebouw, Torenallee 80, between the food market and the Dutch Design Awards, after a half-year collaboration with ten young designers, scientists and local industries. It says the show drew more than 5,000 visitors and that the broadcaster VPRO listed it among ten tips. Those figures are BioArt's own.

For 2016 the Burg Giebichenstein page names the show The Essence of Things and describes nine projects, among them crystals grown from minerals by Isaac Monte, soap films by Simon Raffy, dissected fish gills by Mandy den Elzen, bone china made without bones by Marloes van Bennekom and Essaïdi's own manure project Mestic.
The page does not say where the show stood. The IO+ report places the lab at Strijp TQ in mid-2017, so the 2016 show was most likely there, but no page I opened states it.
The album of 21 photos by Iris Rijskamp shows a large hall with yellow columns and pink grow lights, which is not the forest.
For 2017, Lost in Transformation took the theme of metamorphosis, according to BioArt, with a tour through microorganisms and algae.
For 2018, Cybernetic Forest opened at the new Village.
Neither year has an album in the archive.

For 2019, BioArt's page says it was included in DDW's Bio Design route, with visitors reaching it by hop-on hop-off bus from Strijp-S, that the Symbiocene Forest opened on October 18 with speakers including a European Space Agency MELiSSA scientist and the water board's chief, and that the week included a debate on creative hubs and a storytelling session on water.
The album holds 18 photos by Nick Bookelaar.

For 2020, the first fully digital edition, the page says eleven artists showed work in a virtual exhibition, and it lists talents from South Africa, the Netherlands, Cyprus, Poland, Russia and Lithuania among them.

For 2021, BioArt's page gives October 16 to 24 and Brabant Cultureel counted work by more than twenty artists and designers, with talents from the Netherlands, the United States, Italy, Turkey, Poland, the Czech Republic and South Africa in its list, and guided tours all week.
For 2022, DDW's program page lists The Symbiocene Forest and says the participating talents' work varies from sculptures and experiments to product design.

For 2023, BioArt's page says the opening ceremony took place on October 20 with remarks by the North Brabant deputy for energy and culture and an Eindhoven alderman, and that activities ran October 21 to 29.
The archive may or may not hold a 2023 album; the listing I used was incomplete.
For 2024, DDW's page lists The Symbiocene Forest, Coexistence, in a 1.6-hectare forest with hidden bunkers.

BioArt's recap dated October 28, 2024 says more than 53 artists and designers took part, that visitors could enter the first floor of the main exhibition for the first time and that a willow weaving workshop made bracelets.

For 2026, DDW's location page lists BioArt Laboratories at Oirschotsedijk 14-10 with free access, opening hours of 11:00 to 18:00 for all nine days, and a list of exhibition projects that includes a book made from bacteria-derived bioplastic, a clay 3D-printed reef system and a lamp series about time in wood.

blocks.x: What a reader could test, and what no one has

r: Two details in the written record could be checked against the albums by someone who has them open. Brabant Cultureel describes a smoking room in the former officers' mess with its original parquet floor and wall paneling.
The 2019 album includes a wood-paneled room with framed botanical prints.
Nothing ties the two together, and the album title does not name a room, so I leave it as a question a visitor to the site could answer.
BioArt's 2024 recap lists a willow weaving workshop in which visitors made bracelets.
Four of the five photographs in the 2024 album show willow being woven.
The workshop and the photographs may be the same event, and the titles give no sign either way.
These two cases show how a single archive can be used in two ways.
A reader who stays inside the album can describe what is visible. A reader who brings a second document can propose a match, and the match is only as strong as the second document's wording.

blocks.x: A theme borrowed from a philosopher

r: The word Symbiocene runs through every program page from 2019 on. Glenn Albrecht, who wrote the 2019 Ecologist essay I read, uses it for a proposed new era in human-nature relations that he expects to emerge from the Anthropocene.

BioArt's 2019 page states its working principles as full circularity, the elimination of toxic substances, complete and safe biodegradability of materials and organic integration of technology with living systems.
DDW's 2022 page says the lab adopts key principles of the Symbiocene.

I cannot tell from these pages how much of Albrecht's argument BioArt adopts, because BioArt gives its own principles and does not cite him on the pages I read. I treat the term as borrowed and the list of principles as BioArt's.

blocks.x: What the titles carry

r: The archive holds BioArt albums for 2016, 2019, 2021, 2022 and 2024, with 21, 18, 25, 54 and 5 photos, a total of 123, and the photographers are named in the titles: Iris Rijskamp, Nick Bookelaar and Cleo Goossens.

A title reads like an inventory number: the organization's name, the photographer and a frame number. The 2022 and 2024 titles add a date and an area code, StrijpTQ and StrijpTR, which are DDW's codes.
DDW's 2026 page places BioArt under Strijp T+R.

As an anatomist, I am used to specimens that arrive with a tag, and I know how much a tag leaves out. A tag that says who prepared the specimen and when does not say what it is. The photo archive works the same way. It documents the host, the year and the photographer. The identity of the object needs a second document.

Suppose a reader wants to caption the 2022 photograph of an amber vessel in a lit display case. The scenario is hypothetical. The album title gives the organization and the photographer, and DDW's page gives a show name and a range of media. The maker, the title and the material are still missing, so any caption beyond "from BioArt Laboratories' 2022 album, photographed by Cleo Goossens" would be a guess.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know which work any photograph shows. I do not know where the 2016 show stood, though the lab's address in mid-2017 points to Strijp TQ.
I do not know the date the municipality transferred the site, or whether the 2022 purchase agreement the contractor mentions is the signed transfer.
I could not open the national advice document on which the 2021 inclusion in the basic infrastructure rests, so that fact stands on regional reporting alone.
I do not know whether other albums exist, because the album lists I read were incomplete.
The 2023 and 2024 numbers of artists come from BioArt's own recaps, and I have no independent count.
Dutch Design Week's 2026 page lists projects, and I do not know how many are by talents of the program and how many are guests.

Here is a concrete step for a reader: pick one project listed at BioArt Laboratories for 2026, and before reading its description, write the credit line you would need for a photograph of it. Maker, title, year, source. Which of those four could you fill in from the page alone?

posts.title: The Business Lounge at Dutch Design Week: a room for professionals, a studio behind it and a skate hall around it
posts.subtitle: The official photo archive files two Business Lounge albums, 2024 and 2025. Supplier pages, DDW's ticket page and local sources show who designed the room and what it was for.
posts.seoTitle: The Business Lounge at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: What DDW's Business Lounge at Area 51 is for, who designed it in 2023 and 2024, and what the photo archive shows for 2024 and 2025.

r: The Business Lounge is the one room at Dutch Design Week built for sitting down, and the photo archive files it under a name that says nothing about who made it.
The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds two albums titled Business Lounge, 4 photographs from 2024 and 73 from 2025, 77 in all.

The written record is thinner than for most places in this series, because the room is a service and not an exhibition, though it is not empty. DDW's ticket page says what the lounge is for, two supplier pages name the studio that designed it in 2023 and 2024, and a few local sources describe the building around it. This essay draws on those public sources only. It reports no visit and no conversation, and it says nothing about the 2026 program beyond what DDW lists.

blocks.x: What the room is for

r: DDW's PRO ticket page says the Business Lounge sits at Area 51 on Ketelhuisplein in Strijp-S and that PRO ticket holders can exchange their e-ticket there for a wristband and badge.
The page lists the lounge's facilities as unlimited barista coffee, tea, internet, personal support from DDW staff, and a comfortable place to work and network.

The same ticket includes other things the page lists: access to the Grand Opening, morning sessions in Natlab, a place on a Design Tour, two PRO networking events held in the lounge, an evening called Work in Progress with the Dutch Design Awards, and a bicycle for the nine days.
Tours are reserved in the lounge during the week, and tours that are not full can be joined on the spot.

So the lounge is a counter and a set of tables with three jobs: pick up credentials, book a tour, and sit down between appointments. That is a hospitality function, which helps explain why the archive photographs show curtains, lamps and chairs more than any single work.

blocks.x: Which year the ticket page describes

r: The PRO page carries a header for the October 17 to 25, 2026 edition, but its text describes an earlier one. It says the Grand Opening is on the evening of Friday, October 18, networking events fall on Tuesday, October 22 and Thursday, October 24, and the Design Tours begin on Sunday, October 20 and continue through the week.
Those weekdays fit 2024. October 18 was a Friday in 2024, a Saturday in 2025 and a Sunday in 2026, and DDW's own 2025 press release gives the 2025 edition as October 18 to 26.
The page also gives the last tour, on Friday, the same date it gives for Thursday, which reads like a typo in the source and is not something I can correct.
I therefore use the page for what the lounge offers and treat its dates as 2024's.

blocks.x: Who designed it, in 2023 and 2024

r: Two supplier pages name the design team.

For 2023, a case study by the laminate maker Formica says the Business Lounge was designed by the studio Daphna Laurens and Evelien Reich, with the supplier Blok Plaatmateriaal and photography by Ronald Smits. It describes a 12-meter bar in a laminate color called Earthenware that wound through the space and worked as a coffee point, a press and tours desk and a working station for the press. It says the goal was a warm, lively and optimistic room that avoided a black, white or gray palette, and it dates completion to October 2023.

For 2024, the furniture maker Artifort lists the project as DDW Business Lounge, in Eindhoven, completed October 2024. Its description says soft blues and yellows were balanced with raw metal and glossy earthenware, yellow curtains softened the daylight, and the seating combined customized Orange Slice armchairs with the modular Track sofa. It credits the design to Daphna Laurens in collaboration with Evelien Reich, with photography by Ronald Smits and Daphna Laurens.
Both pages are the suppliers' accounts of their own products, and neither is a DDW document. They agree with each other on the design team and on the photographer, which is a useful cross-check.

The studio behind the name is Daphna Laurens, a design duo that, according to a Domus profile of October 31, 2017, opened its firm in Eindhoven in 2008 as Design Academy graduates, joined the Dutch Invertuals collective in 2009, and in 2017 presented four projects at DDW.
A Dutch Design Awards announcement describes Evelien Reich as editor-in-chief of ELLE Decoration in the Netherlands and a member of the awards' main jury, in a version of the page I could not date.
An interview published by Collectible on April 20, 2021 also introduces her as editor-in-chief of ELLE Decoration Netherlands.
The DDW PRO page describes her as the host of the Work in Progress evening and as a former jury chair of the Dutch Design Awards and a former ELLE Decoration NL editor.
I did not find a source that reconciles those two descriptions of her role, so I give each with its source and make no claim about her current position.

blocks.x: What the archive shows

r: The 2024 album has 4 photographs, all titled October 23, 2024 and credited in the titles to Ronald Smits.
That matches the photographer Artifort names, so the album and the supplier page show the same room in the same week.

The 2025 album has 73 photographs, with titles that name Max Kneefel for 20, Ronald Smits for 21 and a date of October 24 and the name Cleo Goossens for 32 titled DesignTour. The titles do not say that Goossens is the photographer.

I read the albums at preview size on October 8, 2026 and did not reopen them for this version. In them I saw curtains, round tables, lamps, a checkerboard floor, rows of headsets on a curved table and signs reading TOURS, PRO and PRESS.
Those signs fit the Formica description of a press and tours desk in 2023, which suggests the lounge kept the same functions across years.
They do not show that the 2024 and 2025 rooms were built by the same team. I found no supplier or DDW page that names a designer for 2025, and without one I make no claim.
The DesignTour titles in the 2025 album are a reminder of the PRO ticket's tour booking, but no source links the two, so I leave that as an observation about naming.

blocks.x: The building around it

r: Area 51 is better known as a skate hall than a business space. A smow design blog of November 13, 2011 says the venue was established in 2002, covers 3,000 square meters of landscaped wood in an old industrial building on the former Philips estate, and that the blog's writers made a point of visiting it every year during Dutch Design Week.

This is a blog's description, and I have not found an official source for the 2002 date. This is Eindhoven describes Area 51 as the largest indoor skate park in the Benelux, in a building that was a former tool shop and one of the first to be reused after Philips left Strijp-S, an area once closed to everyone but Philips staff.

The hall changed in the early 2020s. A Brainport Eindhoven article of December 7, 2022 says the skate hall was renovated in 2020 and 2021 with support from the Region Deal Brainport Eindhoven, and quotes a regular skater saying the track is now bigger and that the former separate areas for skaters and for steppers and BMX riders were joined.
So the room hosting the lounge is not the same hall that the 2011 blog described.

DDW's own location page for Area 51 gives the address Ketelhuisplein 18, 5617 AE Eindhoven, daily opening from 11:00 to 18:00 from October 17 to 25, 2026, partial wheelchair access, a wheelchair-friendly toilet, Wi-Fi and dogs allowed.

That page does not mention the Business Lounge, and it offers a "Revisit DDW25" link, so I read it as a standing venue page and not as a 2026 program. Whether the lounge returns in 2026 is not something I can confirm.

blocks.x: Why a lounge is hard to photograph

r: The scale of the week explains why the room exists. DDW's 2025 press release expects around 350,000 visitors, more than 2,500 designers, design schools, ministries and brands, and 120 venues.
A professional who has to cover that many venues needs a base, and the PRO page offers the lounge as that base.

A base is hard to picture. A photograph of a lounge shows furniture and light, and the people who matter to the room's purpose are mostly outside the frame. That is a caption problem as much as a photo problem: the room's meaning lives in the PRO page's list, not in the images.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: Which edition the PRO page describes.
The header says 2026, the text dates fit 2024, and the 2025 edition opened on a Saturday. The weekday arithmetic settles it as 2024's text.
Formica (2023) and Artifort (2024) name the studio Daphna Laurens with Evelien Reich. For 2025 no source names anyone.
Whether the two albums show the same fitted space.

Artifort describes yellow curtains for 2024, while my own preview-size reading of the albums found pale blue and cream curtains in 2024 and violet and blue in 2025. Color at preview size is unreliable, so I do not rest anything on it, and the supplier's description is the stronger source for 2024.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know who designed or furnished the 2025 lounge, whether the 2023 lounge was also at Area 51, or how many PRO tickets were sold in any year. I do not know what the other 35 photographs of the 2025 album show, because only 38 of the 73 were viewed in the October 8 reading.
I found no DDW page for the lounge before 2023 and none that says when it began. I have no source for the lounge in 2026.
If a room exists to let professionals rest between rounds, what would you want its photographs to say about it: the furniture, the people, or the list of what it offered?

posts.title: The Design Academy Eindhoven Graduation Show at Dutch Design Week: five sites, one virtual year and a lease that ends in 2028
posts.subtitle: Ten albums in the official photo archive, the school's own pages for every year from 2012, and what they say about where the show was, how big it was and why one year has no album.
posts.seoTitle: Design Academy Eindhoven Graduation Show at DDW
posts.description: Where the Design Academy Eindhoven Graduation Show stood each Dutch Design Week from 2015 to 2026, why 2020 has no album and what comes after 2028.

r: A graduation show is a school's argument about design, made again each October by a new group of people, and for the Design Academy Eindhoven (DAE) the argument has been made in at least five different places.

As a medical educator I pay attention to how a school shows what its students can do, because the arrangement of a room teaches as much as the work in it. The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds albums for ten editions of the Graduation Show, 2015 to 2019 and 2021 to 2025, and the school's own website keeps a page for every year from 2012 to 2026. Read side by side, they answer questions the albums cannot: where the show stood each year, how many projects it held, why one year has no album, and where it is going next. This essay uses public sources only. It reports no visit and no interview, and it describes photographs only as far as the archive's titles and my earlier read of the albums allow.

blocks.x: What the school says the show is

r: DAE calls its Graduation Show one of the world's most influential exhibitions of work by new designers, staged annually in Eindhoven during Dutch Design Week, where bachelor and master students present final projects to thousands of visitors.

That is the organizer's own claim and I report it as one. The same page gives a short history. The show was originally staged in Amsterdam, and in 2001 Li Edelkoort, then creative director of DAE, moved it back to the academy building in Eindhoven when Dutch Design Week launched. DAE partnered with the Dutch Design Foundation, the organization behind the week.
The year in that history sits one year away from DDW's own count. In its 2016 press release the Dutch Design Foundation called DDW 2016 the 15th edition, which puts the first edition in 2002.

Both can be true if the show moved in 2001 ahead of the first week, or DAE's year may be a round figure. Neither page says which, so I give both and settle nothing. For scale, the same release counted 430 curated exhibitions and presentations at 100 locations in 2016 and an estimated 295,000 visitors over nine days, so the Graduation Show was one program item among hundreds.

blocks.x: The Witte Dame years, and a crowd that outgrew the building

r: Until 2017 the show was inside the academy's own building. DAE says the 2018 show was the first edition in almost two decades to take place outside the academy's walls.

The building is the Witte Dame, which DAE says was built in 1928 as Philips' first large-scale lighting factory and which the academy shares with a public library and other services, using 10,000 square meters.

The 2013 page shows what that meant in practice: visitors were invited to tour the 4th and 5th floors of the academy and talk to 126 graduate students, and a radio show broadcast sounds from the floors daily.
The school's yearly pages give a sense of scale. In 2012 the show was titled Up Close Wide Open, with 137 individual perspectives, curated by Strange Attractors.
In 2015, 141 graduates presented 153 projects, dealing with race, dematerialization, tactility and humanizing technology.
In 2016, 171 graduates presented 197 projects under the title In Need Of..., curated by Formafantasma.
In 2017 the overall theme was MINED, which the page ties to the fundamental research in the students' projects; it gives no total.
DAE's own history says the Arena, a live talks platform at the center of the show, began in 2016.
IO+ reported on the reason for leaving. Visitor numbers to the show had grown over recent years from 30,000 to 51,000, and the move to the Campina site was meant to give room for that growth.

Creative director Joseph Grima told IO+ that the move would double the available square meters, so that the students' work would be shown better, and that the academy would no longer have to relocate its teaching activities temporarily to make room.
I have the visitor figures from this one report, which is undated in the archive.

blocks.x: 2018 and 2019: a milk factory and eight worlds

r: DAE's 2018 page describes the move as the first outside the academy in almost two decades, to a venue on the site of the historic Campina milk factory, and says it reflected a major shift in the public's perception of design and the role of DAE. It counted 208 projects by 185 graduates, October 20 to 28, 2018.

IO+ places the site by the Kanaaldijk-Zuid and says DAE had signed an agreement with BPD, the site's owner, for the shows in 2018, 2019 and 2020. BPD had said at the end of 2017 that it wanted to build homes on the site eventually and would make it available for events such as DDW in the meantime.
In 2019 the show stayed for a second year at the Campina factory. DDW's own program entry and DAE's page both say so.
The change that year was curatorial. DAE's history says Grima replaced the old system, which arranged work under the title of each bachelor and master program, with projects gathered around themes.

The 2019 page gives the structure: from 120 bachelor projects came eight worlds, named Landscape Amnesia, Unknown Caller, Training Set, Seven Continents, One Ocean, The Scavengers, Hidden Publics, The Guests and Channel Eight, and 61 master projects modeled five characters of designer, Performer, Critical Observer, Material Appropriator, Situated Agent and Empath.
One of the worlds, The Scavengers, matches a banner that shows in a photograph in the 2019 album.

blocks.x: 2020: the year without a room

r: The archive has no 2020 album, and the school's own page says why. The 2020 page says that, because of the international nature of the graduates and the scale of the event, it became clear at the eleventh hour that a large-scale exhibition was no longer feasible. It presented the work of 184 graduates in other ways: 3D viewing rooms for each of the eight bachelor and four master departments as part of the virtual edition of Dutch Design Week, a website with a project page for each student, a printed graduation catalog, and the Arena broadcast live from DAE's Instagram twice a day.

The 2020 master's projects had a second life. DAE's Moving In Stasis page describes an exhibition of 60 master graduates of 2020 at Het Nieuwe Instituut in Rotterdam, March 8 to April 11, 2021, curated, designed and developed by the graduates themselves, with a mostly digital public because of continued Covid restrictions.
So the show that has no album in the archive does have a record, and part of it ended up in a museum six months later.

blocks.x: 2021 to 2025: a new building almost every year

r: In 2021 the show ran October 16 to 24 at the Beursgebouw, Lardinoisstraat 10, with 163 projects.

DAE framed it as an index, a navigational tool for the themes, keywords, materials and methodologies of the projects, and added The Stage, a digitally mediated platform alongside the physical exhibition, on which 25 of the 163 graduates presented.

In 2022 it ran October 22 to 30 in the Microtuin building, which DAE calls a former telecommunications center in the inner city, taking place there for the first time. The page says the show wound through the building's spaces on a single path and that The Stage grew out of a professorship in transdisciplinary design networks, combining scenography, theater, film and television techniques with extended reality and gaming technologies.
In 2023 the show moved to the top floor of the Heuvel shopping center, Heuvel Galerie 133, October 21 to 29.

DAE's opening-day news item counts 220 projects and quotes curators Nadine Botha and Martina Muzi in their opening speech: "Design is not just an object on a pedestal." It describes the choice as setting in-depth projects against the consumer-driven culture of the shopping center, and names three new kinds of space: a bookshop for theses and process books, a workshop area open to the public even without a DDW wristband, and a cinema.
In 2024 and 2025 the show was at Microstad, Professor Dr Dorgelolaan 2, October 19 to 27, 2024 and October 18 to 26, 2025, each time with 200 projects.
DDW's program entry for 2024 says that "since the last show in 2022" Microstad has been transformed.

DAE's own December 20, 2024 recap settles what the two names mean: it calls Microstad the former KPN telecoms building on the edge of the city center and puts the video works in the basement garage of the Microtuin, so Microtuin (2022) and Microstad (2024 to 2026) are one complex under two names.
The same recap says that 2024 was the last year in which the show included graduates whose studies had been affected by the pandemic.
The 2025 page names its spaces: an underground Space One for film and sound, a new Garden, Glass Rooms on the ground floor, a Gallery upstairs and a Bookshop.

blocks.x: A new organizing idea almost every year

r: Reading the school's pages in order, the way the projects were grouped changes nearly every year. In 2012 the show had a curator, Strange Attractors, and in 2016 another, Formafantasma.
In 2017 an overall theme, MINED, tied the projects together.
In 2019 the old arrangement by program gave way to eight worlds and five designer characters.
In 2022 it was a single path through the building.
In 2023 the concept was proximity, grouping projects so that neighbors complemented each other.

In 2024 a curatorial team led by Martina Muzi, head of the BA studio Technogeographies, organized the projects by typology, which the school's own recap says brought a much-needed clarity to the visitor's experience.
In 2025 the page describes distinct atmospheres, and in 2026 thematic pathways.
I read this as a school treating the layout of the show as part of its teaching, which is my interpretation and not a statement in any source.

DDW's own magazine described the 2019 show in similar terms. It called the set-up spacious, with projects that could be seen from all sides, a big difference from earlier presentations in the Witte Dame, and named two prize winners: Seok-hyeon Yoon, who won the René Smeets Award for a ceramic project using Korean lacquer, and Irakli Sabekia, who won the Melkweg Award for turning a barbed-wire fence in East Georgia into a radio antenna.
The annual Gijs Bakker, René Smeets and Melkweg Awards are presented at the show; the 2025 page lists a prize of 2,000 euros and a trophy designed by an alumnus.

blocks.x: 2026, and a correction about where it is

r: DDW lists the 2026 show as hosted by DAE at Professor Doctor Dorgelolaan 2, October 17 to 25, 2026, with over 200 projects and a DDW ticket required.
This is Eindhoven's September 29, 2026 tip puts it at Microstad, a five-minute walk from the central station.

DAE's page gives the same street address, 200 projects and a theme text about decisions that outlive the rooms they were made in. It says the Arena returns after several years away in an intimate format, and that the awards trophy was designed by DAE alumna Clara Schweers and produced with MAKE Eindhoven.
The 2026 show is therefore not at the academy building on Emmasingel 14.
Two dates need care. DAE's 2026 page lists opening times from October 18 to 26, a nine-day sequence that matches its 2025 page, while DDW and DAE's own header give October 17 to 25.
I use DDW's dates, and I cannot tell from the pages whether DAE's opening-times list is a leftover from 2025.

blocks.x: What comes after the Witte Dame

r: The school's April 7, 2025 news item says DAE extended its lease at the Witte Dame until 2028, with the city and the landlord, Profinn, arranging a phased handover while the new building is finished. It says the new rental building will stand in the Kanaalzone planning area at Kanaaldijk Zuid 3-5, right next to the former Campina factory site, in a tailor-made building, with 250 student homes in the plan area.
The factory where the show stood in 2018 and 2019 is therefore next door to where the school itself plans to move.
The sources do not say whether the Graduation Show will be held in the new building.

blocks.x: What the ten albums can and cannot show

r: The archive holds ten albums with 680 photos in all: 50 in 2015, 69 in 2016, 53 in 2017, 92 in 2018, 50 in 2019, 135 in 2021, 132 in 2022, 35 in 2023, 11 in 2024 and 53 in 2025.
Set against the school's project counts, coverage is uneven. The 2021 album has 135 photos for 163 projects, while the 2024 album has 11 photos for 200 projects, about one picture for every eighteen.
No album can be taken as a record of the show it names.

Photographer names come from photo titles. Sjoerd Eickmans and Cleo Goossens are credited in 2015, Goossens in 2016, Ruud Balk and Boudewijn Bollmann in 2017, Goossens in 2018 and 2021, Max Kneefel in 2019, Kneefel, Goossens and about.today in 2022, Goossens in 2023, Angelina Nikolayeva and Kneefel in 2024, and Kneefel in 2025.
DAE's own 2019 page captions its photographs with the spelling Sjoerd Eijkmans, where the archive titles say Eickmans.
I could not settle the spelling from the sources I opened, and I would check it with the photographer before a credit is printed.

blocks.x: Questions the sources settle

r: Five questions came up. Why there is no 2020 album: the show went virtual, and DAE's page says why.
Where the 2015 to 2017 shows were: inside the academy's building, since DAE says the 2018 move was the first outside its walls in almost two decades.
Where the 2019 show was: at Campina, according to both DAE and DDW.
Whether the 2026 show is at the academy: it is not, since the address is Dorgelolaan 2.
How many projects the 2023 show held: 220 by DAE's opening-day news item, and "more than 200" on its event page.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know why DAE and DDW differ by a year on the start of the partnership.
I do not know how many projects the 2017 show held, because its page gives none.
I do not know which photographs in each album show the Graduation Show hall itself and which show a neighboring DAE exhibition.
I did not find a source for the 2018 attendance after the move, and I did not find the terms of the new building beyond the April 2025 news item.
If you look at one of these ten albums, which page would you open to find out where the photograph was taken, the school's, DDW's or neither?

posts.title: DDW Music, 2015 to 2019: what the press archive counts, what the photo archive holds, and one number that did not hold
posts.subtitle: Dutch Design Week's own pages number four editions of its music program. Read against the photo archive, a venue listing and a 2019 news item, they show where the archive has gaps and where a summary went wrong.
posts.seoTitle: DDW Music at Dutch Design Week, 2015 to 2019
posts.description: DDW Music from 2015 to 2019: editions, venues, lineups, tickets and visitor counts from Dutch Design Week's own pages, checked against the photo archive.

r: Dutch Design Week's own press pages count the music program as a series of editions, and by their count the photo archive skips at least one.

I read the program that way because the pages are specific, and specific pages can be checked. This essay draws on public sources only: Dutch Design Week's press and news archive for 2015 to 2018, a venue listing, a festival-news item from 2019, a listing site for 2017 and the official photo archive on Flickr as I recorded it on October 8, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about a 2026 music program, because I found no page for one.

blocks.x: The program, edition by edition, by its own count

r: DDW Music was introduced in 2015. The press page of September 1, 2015 describes daily live performances at various locations in Eindhoven during Dutch Design Week, October 17 to 25, free on presentation of a DDW ticket, and calls it a collaboration between Dutch Design Week, the Effenaar and the booking agency Friendly Fire.
The press page of September 14, 2016 calls the next year the second edition.
The wrap-up of November 6, 2017 calls that year the third.
The page of September 4, 2018 calls the 2018 program the fourth edition.
By DDW's own count, then, there were four editions from 2015 to 2018, numbered consecutively, and the numbering is the strongest evidence that 2016 happened.
The program kept growing in the pages' own terms. The 2016 release says DDW Music drew more than 5,000 visitors in 2015.
The 2017 wrap-up says the third edition had more than 16,000 visitors in total and that three quarters of the performances sold out.
I find those two numbers useful and cannot compare them closely, because neither page says how a visitor was counted. I found no visitor figure for 2016 or 2018 in the pages I opened.
The 2018 page also carries a sentence that is easy to repeat and hard to date: with over 335,000 visitors, it says, the city's population will double for a week.
It is a pre-event description of Dutch Design Week as a whole, and it does not say which year the count belongs to.

blocks.x: One number that did not hold: 2015 had 29 named artists, not 37

r: My first-pass summary of the 2015 page, which came through a summarizing reader, gave a lineup of 37 artists. The page itself gives a complete line-up of 29 names, which include the two specials announced earlier, Two Gallants at the Effenaar on Thursday, October 22 and Rufus Wainwright at the Muziekgebouw on Sunday, October 25.

The page says twenty new names completed the line-up, and it separately lists two DJs for the Closing Party on Saturday, October 24 at the Effenaar, Kutmah from the United Kingdom and Zes from the Netherlands.
I counted the names myself, and I could find no DDW page that gives 37. The 2016 page, by contrast, speaks of more than 60 artists in 12 locations, and the 2017 page of more than 70 artists.
A fair reading is that the 2015 program was a program of a few dozen named acts that more than doubled within two years.

I cannot tell from the page whether the 29 names are all of the acts. The page says "to name but a few" about the venues, and it does not use that phrase about the artists, so I give 29 as the number of names the page prints and not as a total.

blocks.x: Who was booked

r: The lineups show a program that mixed names a design visitor might know with acts that had only just started. In 2015 the page lists Rufus Wainwright, Ryley Walker, Two Gallants, Charlie Cunningham, K.Flay and Elvis Perkins among its 29.
The first 2016 announcement, on August 3, names Jeremy Loops, Klyne, Benjamin Francis Leftwich and Baauer, and the September 14 page adds Loyle Carner, Palmbomen II, Dillon and Khruangbin.
The 2017 announcement lists Joep Beving, Lefto, Alex Vargas, Lapalux, Phoebe Bridgers, The Weather Station and Vagabon among more than 70.
For 2019 the festival-news item names Altin Gun, Rico & Sticks and Iris Hond as earlier announcements and Blanck Mass and Les Robots among the late additions.
I name these acts only as the pages do, and I did not hear any of them play at the festival.

blocks.x: Where the music went

r: Each press page lists venues, and the lists show a program that borrowed rooms from the rest of the week. In 2015 the page names the café Altstadt, the Van Abbemuseum, Tuchthuis, Stroomhuis, café Wilhelmina, Arcade, Nul Zes and the Ketelhuisplein, with the specials at the Effenaar and the Muziekgebouw.

In 2016 the list is longer, with twelve locations: the Effenaar, Nul Zes, the Gaslab, FIFTH | NRE, the Van Abbemuseum, Stroomhuis, Altstadt, De Oude Rechtbank, café Wilhelmina, the Muziekgebouw, Calypso and the Ketelhuisplein.

In 2017 it names the Effenaar, TAC, Altstadt, Stroomhuis, café Wilhelmina, The Student Hotel, Piet Hein Eek, FIFTH | NRE, De Oude Rechtbank and de Schuilplaats, and puts experiments on the Ketelhuisplein.

In 2018 the page says three new venues brought the total to eleven locations, "from music halls to bars and ateliers," for over 90 shows, and on October 10, 2018 DDW published an official timetable and a Spotify playlist for the festival.
Three things follow from reading the lists together. Altstadt, Stroomhuis and café Wilhelmina are on all three of the lists for 2015 to 2017, so a regular could plan a night around them.
Nul Zes is on the 2015 and 2016 lists and not on the 2017 list.
And Piet Hein Eek's complex is new in 2017: the wrap-up calls it a new concert location, with piano shows by Luke Howard and Matteo Myderwyk.
The same complex has its own entry in this series, as a venue with a long guest list.

A venue listing adds a detail for 2018. The Dynamo venue in Eindhoven lists a DDW Music evening on Saturday, October 27, 2018 with Caro and Sofie Winterson, doors at 19:30, and says it was the first time the festival visited Dynamo's basement.
The same listing describes the festival as having performances by 70 emerging acts over eleven venues, while DDW's own page says over 90 shows in eleven locations.

The two do not conflict if 70 counts acts and 90 counts performances, but neither page says so. The listing also says loose tickets cost 10 euros and were sold only at the door, which is higher than the 5 euros DDW's pages gave for earlier years.
It is a single venue's statement and I do not read it as the festival's price.

blocks.x: The design that stood on the stage

r: The press pages give the program a design layer that a plain gig listing would not. In 2016 the composer duo Strijbos & van Rijswijk presented a program of interactive installations at the DDW Music Lab on the Ketelhuisplein, open daily from 12:00 to 18:00 and, at weekends, a public workspace for guest musicians and designers, free to enter.
The page asks what it would be like to wander through a composition and what music based on body movement sounds like.

In 2017 the Lab returned, and the wrap-up credits it with interactive installations, lectures and workshops by Jeroen Strijbos, Rob van Rijswijk, the sound designer William Aikman and the producer and vocalist Chagall.

A listing site gives more detail: musical sculptures called Quiver#2 and Quiver#3 by Strijbos & van Rijswijk with Pierluigi Pompeï, Aikman's Self Portrait as a Musical Instrument, a performance by Vito Willems, the Mi.Mu gloves of the electronic performer Chagall, and a sound playground called Sound Scouts.
Also in 2017, the announcement says five designers made decor and stage design, and the wrap-up says that was a first.

The announcement names four of them, Joost van Bleiswijk, Elvis Wesley, Studio Big Mistake and Tijs Gilde, and the wrap-up names three, Joost van Bleiswijk, Thijs Gilde and Studio Big Mistake, spelling the last name differently.

No page I opened names a fifth designer. A designer of the same name is half of the pair Kiki & Joost, which has its own entry in this series. DDW's pages do not say whether the two are the same person, and TL Magazine's report of October 26, 2017 says the pair had an ongoing project at the Effenaar that week, which fits the music program's main venue without proving the link.
The same wrap-up reports a dance evening presented with the media partner Dezeen at the Effenaar, by the collective Omnipresent World of Wizkids, with Bart van de Sande, ZES and Polynation.

A listing from October 18, 2017 describes a DDW Music Keynote on Friday, October 27 at the Effenaar from 19:30 to 21:30, with presentations by two women pioneers of electronic music, Sophie Letitre and Chagall, and a demonstration of OWOW instruments.
I could not open the Dezeen page that would date the dance evening, because the site answered my request with an HTTP 403 and I stopped asking.
I therefore do not say the keynote and the dance evening were on the same night, only that both sat at the Effenaar and both involved OWOW.

blocks.x: One artist, three roles

r: Chagall appears in three places in the 2017 record. The September 2017 announcement lists Chagall among the artists.
The wrap-up names Chagall among the creators of the DDW Music Lab.
The listing places Chagall in the keynote on October 27.

I find that useful for a specific reason. The old dossier for this item recorded two photo titles for the artist, one for the keynote on Friday, October 27 and one for a performance on Wednesday, October 25, and could not say what the second one was.
The line-up supports it: Chagall was booked as an act, so a performance on a weekday evening fits the pattern of the other titles.
I still do not know what the performance was, because no page I opened describes it.

That one name shows what a program like this was trying to do. A performer who can be an act on Wednesday, a Lab demonstration on a weekend and a keynote speaker on Friday is a performer the program treats as a designer of musical situations, and the three roles are on three different pages.
That is my reading of the pages, and none of them says it.

blocks.x: What the ticket bought

r: The ticket rule stayed close to the same through the years, and its numbers moved. In 2015 the DDW ticket cost 16 euros online, excluding service costs, and a concert without it cost 5 euros at the door.
In 2016 the ticket was 17.50 euros excluding service costs, with the same 5 euros at the door and individual tickets for specials, with a 5 euro discount for DDW ticket holders.
In 2017 it was 19 euros including service costs, with 5 euros at the door and a free DDW Music Lab even without a ticket.
The three prices look like a rise from 16 to 17.50 to 19, but the first two exclude service costs and the third includes them, so the series is not comparable from the pages alone.
In 2018 the page says a DDW Festival ticket gives access to all DDW locations and to the DDW Music Festival.
The 2016 page also says the Lab's free admission was made possible by the Effenaar Poplab.
I read the structure as a cross-subsidy between a pop venue and a design festival, and the pages say nothing more about it.

blocks.x: 2019 and the end of the old dossier's window

r: The photo archive window I worked from ends in 2018, and the program did not. A festival-news item of October 3, 2019 says the program of the DDW Music Festival 2019 was complete, lists added acts including Blanck Mass, Kikok, Tim Dawn, Les Robots, Shaemless, Kléo, Meetsysteem and A Million Squeeks Will Do You No Harm, and says the festival is an initiative of the Effenaar and Friendly Fire in collaboration with Dutch Design Week, from October 19 to 27, 2019.
The wording differs from the 2018 page, which says the festival is organized by Dutch Design Week, the Effenaar and Friendly Fire.
It is a different publisher, and I do not know whether the change is a change of roles or only of phrasing.
I did not find a DDW page for any music program after 2019, and I did not find a DDW Music page for 2026. The sources I opened say nothing about what happened to the name.

blocks.x: What the photographs add

r: The old dossier counts three albums in the official archive: 84 photographs for 2015, 63 for 2017 and 112 for 2018, 259 in all, with no 2016 album in the list read on October 8, 2026.

I did not reopen Flickr for this version. The titles carry act, weekday and date, and the 2018 page on DDW's own site adds a credit trail for four 2017 concert photographs: Max Kneefel for Yung Nnelg, Lieke Vermeulen for Alex Vargas, Roos Pierson for Braz and Patrick Spruytenburg for Phoebe Bridgers.
That is a short list of named photographers against a program of 70 artists, and it is a reminder that a credit is a record too.

Two small mismatches belong here. The dossier lists a title naming Khruangbin among the 2018 photographs, while DDW's September 2016 page lists Khruangbin in the 2016 line-up and the 2018 pages I opened print no line-up.

If that photograph is dated 2018, the band played in both years, and if it is from 2016 it sits in the wrong album. I cannot tell which from the pages. The second mismatch is smaller: a 2017 title reads asiwyfa, and the 2017 announcement lists And So I Watch You From Afar.
The initials fit, and I read the title as that act, but the pages do not confirm it.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The photo archive list has no 2016 album, and DDW's pages of August 3 and September 14, 2016 describe the second edition, which the 2017 wrap-up and the 2018 page then count in their own numbering. The pages settle it: 2016 happened, and the gap is in the archive.
37 from a summarizing reader, 29 names on the page. The page settles it, and I use 29 as the number of names printed.
70 emerging acts on a venue's listing and over 90 shows on DDW's page. I attribute each, and I do not combine them.
Organized by three parties in 2018, an initiative of two in collaboration with DDW in 2019. Not settled.
Friday, October 27, 2017 from one listing and the old dossier's photo title. I did not find a second page.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know how visitors were counted in any year, and I found no figures for 2016, 2018 or 2019. I do not know what any act played, because titles and lineups name acts and not sets. I do not know who the fifth stage designer of 2017 was, or whether the dance evening and the keynote shared a night. I do not know whether Khruangbin played in 2018 as well as 2016, or what Chagall did on October 25, 2017. I did not open the Effenaar's own pages or Friendly Fire's, so the program's history from the organizers' side is missing here.
I did not reopen the photo archive for this version, so the album counts and titles come from the October 8, 2026 reading and need a recheck before posting.
DDW's pages for 2015 to 2018 give the program, and they stop at what was planned and announced, apart from the 2017 wrap-up. Nothing I opened is a review.
If you had one program page and one photo from the same night, which would you trust for what actually happened?
