posts.title: From Mind the Step to Drivers of Change: how one university exhibition split in two at Dutch Design Week
posts.subtitle: The archive files it from 2015. The organizers' own pages show it began in 2014, split in 2019 and kept showing up in years the archive has no album for.
posts.seoTitle: Mind the Step to Drivers of Change at DDW
posts.description: How TU/e, 3TU and 4TU Design United's Mind the Step began in 2014, split in 2019 and kept showing up at Dutch Design Week through 2026.

r: Mind the Step began in 2014, a year before the first album in the official Dutch Design Week photo archive, and by 2019 it had split into two exhibitions that now show up in different places.

As a content strategist I notice how a name can stay still while the thing it names moves. This essay follows one exhibition lineage through its own pages. It uses public sources only: the 4TU Design United edition pages, TU/e's event and news pages, a TU Delft research record, a University of Twente news item, Dutch Design Week's program pages, press reports and the photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibits beyond what the organizers' pages list.

blocks.x: The federation changed its number, and Design United changed its description

r: In the 2015 brochure, Design United is "the 3TU research institute of the design courses" of Delft, Eindhoven and Twente.
On May 27, 2016 the University of Twente announced that Wageningen University was joining the three technical universities and that the federation would be known as 4TU from then on.
Today Design United describes itself as the 4TU research center for design, "the leading platform for Design Research in the Netherlands," a claim I treat as its own.

So the same two words describe a three-university institute in one year and a four-university center in another. The edition pages on the 4TU site follow the change quietly: the 2015 brochure speaks of the 3TU institute, and the 2025 and 2026 pages speak of projects from the 4TU and the four Dutch universities of technology.

blocks.x: 2014: an experiment with 68 projects and 25 banners

r: The 4TU page for 2014 is the earliest edition page on the site. It places Mind the Step at the Klokgebouw from October 18 to 26, 2014 and describes 68 design research projects sorted into six themes: Care, Learn, Live, Make, Move and Sense.

The project leader, Dr. Lucas Asselbergs, writes that the show breaks with the tradition of barely showing the designers and users behind the designs: 25 banners carry their faces and a personal quote on design. He also says the three technical universities' solar-powered racing cars were shown together at Dutch Design Week for the first time.
The 2015 brochure confirms the order of events. It calls that edition a continuation of what began as an experiment in 2014, a collaboration between several TU/e faculties and Design United.
The photo archive I read holds no album for 2014.
That matters for any caption that says the show started in 2015.

blocks.x: 2015 to 2018: Mind the Step in the Klokgebouw

r: The 2015 edition ran from October 17 to 25 with eight themes: City, Future Mobility, Health, Wearables, Circular Economy, Design Conversations, Home and Material Innovations.
The brochure's welcome is signed by TU/e's vice-president, Jo van Ham, and Design United's science director, Daan van Eijk, and the same two sit on the 2015 steering committee.

Core77's gallery of that week says the design departments of the technical universities in Eindhoven, Delft and Twente teamed up for a group exhibition that took up most of one of the four main exhibition halls at the Klokgebouw.

The 2016 edition ran from October 22 to 30. Its page quotes the director of Dutch Design Week, Martijn Paulen, calling Mind the Step in just a few years an essential link for the festival, and it lists nine themes, among them Big Data, Design for Debate and Automotive.
The photo archive I read has no album for 2016.
The 4TU edition list jumps from 2016 to 2018 and has no page for 2017.

A TU Delft research record fills the gap. It calls Mind the Step 2017 the annual exhibition of the 4TU Design United community, shows a project titled Growing Seasons, and gives October 21 to 29, 2017.
The 2018 page gives October 20 to 28, 2018 and six themes, among them Design for Debate, Health and Wellbeing and The New Mobility.

Innovation Origins visited the hall the day before it opened and reported about 150 students and researchers from Eindhoven, Twente and Delft, with the show open through October 28. It describes a student team's electric car, Vision, meant for the 24 Hours of Le Mans, and conceptual projects such as a Delft machine that matches a family to a migrant, built to start an argument.
An earlier version of this essay gave the 2018 opening date as October 19. The reporter wrote on the eve of opening and the organizer's page says October 20, so the organizer's date stands.

blocks.x: 2019: one exhibition becomes two, and the dates disagree

r: TU/e's event page for 2019 says that after five successful years in the Klokgebouw, Mind the Step was merging into two exhibitions, TU/e Drivers of Change and Design United.
Five years fits the counting from 2014 to 2018.
The page places Drivers of Change at Strijp T, building TQ 6, from October 19 to 27, 2019.
A TU/e podcast page describes it as the university's exhibition at Dutch Design Week 2019, with Asselbergs as project leader of both Drivers of Change and Design United.
The Design United side called its 2019 edition TILT SHIFT, Reframing Futures, with four themes and three named directors. The 4TU page prints October 22 to 30, 2019.
Those dates do not match the festival: BEDA's announcement of September 26, 2019 gives October 19 to 27, 2019, with about 2,600 designers and 120 locations, and TU/e's page agrees.

I treat the 4TU dates as an error on a page that is otherwise reliable. The same page also names a curator and project lead who is not Asselbergs, so the two organizations describe the leadership of the 2019 shows differently.

blocks.x: 2020 and 2021: a talkshow and a campus

r: In 2020 Design United ran a talkshow format from October 19 to 23 around five themes, among them Hybrids and Crisis.

The edition page for 2021 describes five days at De Effenaar with five themes, from Entangled Ecologies to Evolving Methodologies, and prints the dates as October 18 to 22, 2022. The heading says 2021, and the 2022 edition has different dates and a different venue, so I read the printed year as a slip.

TU/e, meanwhile, held Drivers of Change on its own campus. Its news item of October 13, 2021 says Dutch Design Week would open officially on the campus that Friday, that the exhibition could be visited from October 15 to 24, and that it presented sixty showcases.
Its calendar entry gives October 16 to 24.
In the same item Asselbergs says that twenty years earlier the university was one of the founding fathers of the festival, then modestly called the Day of Design.

That is TU/e's own account, and I could not confirm it elsewhere. The Design Academy Eindhoven's history says the first Day of Design was organized in 1998 by the Vormgeversoverleg, a designers' collective, that it became a Week of Design in 2002 and took the name Dutch Design Week in 2005.
Neither date matches "twenty years" exactly, and neither source names TU/e among the founders.

The 2021 Flickr album titled TUe, dated October 18, 2021 in its titles, therefore belongs to the campus show. The earlier version of this essay said the 2021 titles named no venue. TU/e's own pages name one.

blocks.x: 2022 to 2024: a square, a lecture hall and a theme

r: TU/e's own news item for 2022 says Drivers of Change ran from October 22 to 30 at the Ketelhuisplein in Strijp-S, in glass containers, with 23 projects in five themes and a lecture series on campus from October 24 to 28.
The Dutch Design Week archive entry for 2022 names Eindhoven University of Technology as the presenter, and it too says the lectures were on campus.
An earlier note read that presenter line as a location. The exhibition itself stood on the square.
For 2023 Dutch Design Week's program entry puts Drivers of Change on the Ketelhuisplein, and TU/e's news item gives October 21 to 29 and twenty projects, free to enter.
Design United's 2023 edition ran themes including Politics of Design on Monday, October 23.

The 2024 record has one more surprise for anyone who works from the photo archive alone, because I found no 2024 album. TU/e's news item says Drivers of Change returned to the Ketelhuisplein from October 19 to 27, 2024, with about fifteen projects linked by the theme Semicon.
The 4TU page says its 2024 expo at the Klokgebouw, with 14 research projects, ran October 19 to 27 and that its dialogues ran October 21 to 25 at the Natlab.

blocks.x: 2025 and 2026: two containers, a joint show and a preview

r: TU/e's news item of October 13, 2025 describes Future by Design at the Ketelhuisplein, October 18 to 26, 2025: two transparent containers used as mini-labs by the Built Environment and Industrial Design departments. The containers were rented, and the university said it planned its own versions to stand on campus all year and move to Strijp-S for the festival.

The same item says the four universities jointly showed twelve projects at the Klokgebouw under the motto Less Hope, More Action, four of them by TU/e students, and that a festival ticket was needed to enter.
The photo archive holds four 2025 photos in a Design United album by Boudewijn Bollmann dated October 25, 2025, with banners carrying the same motto.
The containers, the TU/e show of 2025, are not in that album.

For 2026, TU/e's page lists the campus and the Ketelhuisplein, October 17 to 25, 2026. The Ketelhuisplein show is a preview of a larger anniversary exhibition in the Atlas building, where more than 70 projects mark 25 years of Industrial Design in Eindhoven, and the Built Environment department shows three projects on the square.
Dutch Design Week lists TU/e at Ketelhuisplein with free access and daily hours of 11:00 to 18:00.
Design United's 2026 edition is called Design Bridges, runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and its dialogue program begins on Monday, October 19.
Its call for 2026 projects, now closed, asked for work that fits five Dutch Design Week mission days: Living Environment, Thriving Planet, Digital Future, Health and Wellbeing, and Equal Society.

blocks.x: What was on the floor, as the organizers describe it

r: The organizers' pages let me list a few exhibits per year, and these are their descriptions, not my findings. In 2014 the exhibition showed an ambulance drone, clothing that holds a music collection and a way to generate wind power around buildings.
In 2015 the City theme included a project called The Twist, and a student project named Trashique presented a museum as a catalog for sustainable reuse.

In 2018 the Innovation Origins reporter found bacteria that produce pigment for coloring textile, a 3D-printed goalkeeper glove and a timber arch held together with about six hundred nuts and bolts, built by a TU/e student who wanted to bend wood without lamination or steaming.

TU/e's 2019 exhibition featured virtual acoustics, in which visitors hear their own voices in different simulated spaces, a research line on turning plastics into living heart valves, crowd dynamics measured at the train station and a light festival, and photonic chips.

In 2022 the projects included a 3D-printed beetle made of liquid-crystal ink that changes color when it meets moisture, and a spherical test chamber for measuring chip antennas for 6G. The university's Stella Vita solar camper stopped by for the opening.
In 2023 the list included a pavilion built from flax, wood waste and hemp, DNA as a data storage medium, and a hospital robot called CURA.

In 2024 the headline projects were an EEG-based brain-computer interface, a haptics group and Phoenix, a student-built electric car designed so that up to 75 percent of it can be reused for the next generation, against a closed-loop recycling rate of 21 percent that the page gives for existing cars in Europe.

In 2025 the TU/e containers held a flax-fiber structure tensioned by robotic arms, a study of composting clothing and 3D-printed clay vaults, and the joint Klokgebouw show held a ventilation hose that reacts to touch like a small creature.

In 2026 the university's Built Environment department shows an air-quality project, vibration in timber floors and a nature-inclusive building study at the Ketelhuisplein, and a student team's adaptive building system, MOD[us], is listed at The Body Building in Gashouder 41.

blocks.x: What the photo archive adds, and what it cannot

r: The Flickr listing I read holds eight albums and 147 photos for 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021 and 2025, with Boudewijn Bollmann credited on most of them. Two albums in 2015 and two in 2019 sit side by side, one for each organization. The album titles name the organization, the year and the photographer, and none names a work. I found no photo-level caption that says which organization a single picture belongs to.
The written record, taken together, shows the archive missing 2014, 2016, 2020, 2022, 2023 and 2024 under these names, even though the organizers' pages show exhibitions in every one of those years.
The gap reflects what was filed, and I have no source that says why. All Flickr facts in this essay are second-hand from my earlier reading, and I did not reopen the account.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Why the archive has no albums for years in which both organizers' pages show exhibitions.
The founding year of Design United. The pages I opened do not give it, and 2014 is only the start of its collaboration with TU/e at the festival.
Whether TU/e helped found the Day of Design, as its own account says.

Which dates are right where the organizers' pages contradict each other: the 4TU pages for 2019 and 2021 carry dates that conflict with other sources, and I settled both from other pages, not from the originals.
What most of the photographs show. Titles name an organization, a year and a photographer.
How the 2024 and 2025 TU/e shows appear in the archive. I found no album for either, and I could not reopen the account to look again.

r: When you meet a title that names a university or a research center in an archive, which year's organization does it mean, and which page says so?

posts.title: Designing Society put its own history on a wall, and the record shows how the exhibition was made
posts.subtitle: Two Dutch Design Week exhibitions by the Dutch Design Foundation, read through the organizer's own pages, DDW's archive and the text legible inside the official photographs
posts.seoTitle: Designing Society at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Two Dutch Design Week editions of Designing Society, a Dutch Design Foundation exhibition, read through DDF pages and photo-archive panels.

r: The clearest sentence about Designing Society in the photo archive is printed on a wall panel, and no photo title says anything like it.

I like evidence that carries its own label, because a label is the part of an archive I can check. This essay draws on public sources only: Dutch Design Week's press and news archive, pages from the Dutch Design Foundation and its public-sector program PONT, a tourism guide, a 2025 guide on Archipanic and the official photo archive on Flickr, including the text that is legible inside the photographs. It reports no visit and no interview, and for 2026 it repeats only what the organizer's published description says.

blocks.x: Who makes it: a foundation, not a venue

r: Designing Society is a Dutch Design Foundation exhibition. The foundation's own pages describe it as a non-profit that runs Dutch Design Week, the Dutch Design Awards and programs that bring designers together with companies, governments and scientists.

The 2024 edition was a consolidation. DDF's program PONT, the Dutch name of which is De Publieke Ontwerppraktijk, described it on September 18, 2024 as an umbrella exhibition of more than 600 square meters with about 40 projects, free to visit at the Ketelhuisplein, and made by four DDF programs: PONT, the World Design Embassies, What if Lab and Maakruimte voor Mooi NL.
DDW's press release of October 29, 2024 says all the World Design Embassies, Labs and PONT joined forces and presented together at Ketelhuisplein in the exhibition Designing Society.
The press release's "Labs" and PONT's "What if Lab" are the same program line in all likelihood, but the two pages do not say so in one sentence, and I treat that as a reading.

The 2024 dates need a note. Dutch Design Week 2024 ran from October 19 to 27, 2024: DDF's calendar entry for the Embassy of Digital Futures at the exhibition gives those dates, and the DDW press release speaks of the 2025 edition running October 18 to 26, 2025.
The 2024 photograph titles carry dates from October 19 to 25, which fits.

blocks.x: The square it stands on

r: DDW's own location page calls the Ketelhuisplein one of the festival's largest locations, at approximately 7,000 square meters, an outdoor square on Strijp-S between the Klokgebouw and Microlab Hall, open with free access from 11:00 to 18:00 on each of the nine days in 2026.
A tourism guide published on October 1, 2026 describes the square as a temporary open-air museum for large-scale installations, and lists Designing Society among its recommendations.

The 2026 location page itself lists installations such as Electric Grand, WETHOUSE and the Colonic Cleansing Clinic, and does not list Designing Society by name, so the exhibition's 2026 position on the square is not something I can state.

blocks.x: The year before: seven Embassies in seven places

r: The shape of 2024 is clearer against 2023. On October 10, 2023, DDW published a guide to seven themed Embassies of the World Design Embassies program: Circular and Biobased Building, Food, Health, Inclusive Society, Mobility, Safety and Water. Each sat in a different place. The Embassy of Circular and Biobased Building was at Ketelhuisplein, Food in the Evoluon, Health at Foundation We Are, Inclusive Society inside an exhibition at the Van Abbemuseum, Mobility at DONNA, Safety in the Klokgebouw and Water at Stadhuisplein.

In 2024 those embassies, with the Labs and PONT, came to one square. DDF's calendar entry for the Embassy of Digital Futures says it was part of the exhibition at Ketelhuisplein, and the same entry says the Embassy of Water was part of it too.

I read that as a move from a dispersed program to a single hall, and I mark it as my reading, because no source states the reason. The 2024 PONT page describes the exhibition as built around themes that connect design to the complex challenges of today and tomorrow, and says accessibility features included a physical model at the entrance for visitors with a visual impairment, project signs hung at wheelchair height and free hourly tours.

blocks.x: The archive: two albums, one photographer

r: The archive holds one album for each year. The 2024 album has 35 photographs and the 2025 album has 223, 258 in all, and every title I read credits Max Kneefel.
DDF's own pages use the same name in photo credits, including for a 2025 view of the exhibition at the Ketelhuisplein.

The 2024 photographs show a glass-roofed hall of white rooms, and the text inside them tells me more than the titles do. Flags on the square read Embassy of Safety, De Publieke Ontwerppraktijk and Maakruimte voor Mooi NL.
A wall panel reads Embassy of Inclusive Society and Dutch Design Foundation, with a tall blue school desk behind it holding a clock and a boxing glove.
A plywood board reads, "Good food should be a public service, instead of a commercial product."
Blue signs on the path read Loop nodig risico, Ongemak and Laat je kennen.
None of that says what each project did or who made it. It says which names stood in one place in October 2024, which fits the description of programs presenting together.
Many 2024 photographs also show visitors, and the carousel leaves those out because they show faces, not projects.

For the Embassy of Inclusive Society, a second document exists. DDF's case page says the embassy was a three-year program from 2023 to 2025 by the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport, the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science and DDF, that The Gym by Gabriel Fontana turned inclusion into something to practice, and that a campaign called Vraagje?! became an interactive installation during DDW24.
That does not identify the blue desk or the boxing glove in the photograph, and I do not say it does.

blocks.x: 2025: the same name with a new platform

r: In March 2025, DDF published a note titled "World Design Embassies and What if Lab continue as Coalitions," dated March 25, 2025. It describes Coalitions as a platform and structural approach for bringing together creative thinkers and doers with science, organizations and governments, built on the earlier programs, with PONT continuing alongside.
The 2025 exhibition therefore ran under a new umbrella.

The 2025 photographs are sharper about projects, because the exhibition printed large panels. One reads Co/Lab: Innovating our defense with society, and a made bed, a helmet and a camouflage backpack stand beside it.

DDF's page for that Co/Lab marks it as completed. It says the Ministry of Defence and DDF selected the design studio Muzus, whose concept Operatie Innovatie invited visitors during Dutch Design Week to contribute ideas to a current challenge of the Ministry.
The page does not mention a bed, helmet or backpack, so the connection between the objects and the page is mine to wonder about and not to state.
Steel letters read The future is fast food above a red menu board headed Geluk, Gemak and Geld, which are Dutch for happiness, ease and money.
A panel reads Sitdown Desk: Pay with time, meet inclusion.
Another is headed Design x Government and carries the PONT name.

The Archipanic guide of October 19, 2025 quotes DDF's description of Coalitions as a network where designers, governments, experts and challenge holders use the power of design to tackle societal challenges, and gives examples that include design solutions for elderly care professionals and a tattoo shop with an interactive machine.
I read that guide on October 8 and could not reopen it on October 10, because its robots file answered with an access error, so I rely on my earlier reading and treat the quotation as second-hand.

blocks.x: The wall that explains the change

r: One 2025 panel does something the 2024 material does not. It is titled What history are we making? and the text beside a long timeline of small illustrated ovals describes it as a historical timeline of the former World Design Embassies program, 2017 to 2024, now Coalitions.

That is the exhibition telling its visitors that the program behind the 2024 flags had changed its name and shape. DDF's March 2025 note says the same thing in prose, so the panel and the foundation agree.
The panel's 2017 start matches the year Baltan Laboratories' annual report gives for the first World Design Event, held October 21 to 29, 2017.

No source I opened says the embassies were created at that event, so I leave the link as a coincidence of dates. The panel is the organizers' account of themselves, and I treat it as their account and not as an independent finding.
One nuance: DDF's case page says the Embassy of Inclusive Society ran through 2025, a year after the panel's end date.
The panel dates the program, and the case page dates one embassy's three-year agreement with two ministries, which is a different unit.

blocks.x: 2026: what the organizer says, and what I have not seen

r: Dutch Design Week 2026 runs October 17 to 25, 2026, and I have not seen the exhibition. DDF's news item dated September 29, 2026 describes Designing Society as the foundation bringing designers and researchers together with citizens, public authorities and social organizations on issues that affect everyone, and says visitors may step into an experiment, join a conversation or share a story. It names projects in groups: care for life, with A Healthy Sense of Excitement, The Last Chapter and The First 1000 Days; life in a healthy environment, with Building for Wellbeing, a Building Happiness Score, Declaration of Dependence and Drinkable Nature; and opening up space for change, with a sustainable collective labor agreement experiment, a PONT workshop and the Un/School platform.
At least one 2026 item, Drinkable Nature, is labeled a Co/Lab, the same word that appears on the 2025 panel.
A tourism guide published on October 1, 2026 describes Designing Society at the Ketelhuisplein as a place to share thoughts on how people want to live, work and care for each other.
A DDF event page lists a Coalition for Safety conference on October 21, 2026 at Microlab, which sits outside the exhibition.
That is all I will say about 2026.

blocks.x: What a title cannot say

r: A photo title in this archive is a date, a photographer and a camera number. Nothing in it names a project, and I could only match images to projects when a panel or sign in the image did it for me. In anatomy teaching I learned to distrust a specimen without its label, and I read an unlabeled photograph the same way: it shows something real, and I still cannot say whose it is.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I viewed 75 of the 223 photographs in the 2025 album, so I cannot describe the other 148.
I found no visitor figure for the exhibition in either year; DDF's Coalitions page cites more than 300,000 visitors for Dutch Design Week as a whole, which is not a count for this exhibition.
I could not reopen the Archipanic guide, so the Coalitions quotation rests on my October 8 reading.

I do not know how DDF counts the 2024 and 2025 exhibitions together, whether as one series or two, and I do not know why the 2024 exhibition was consolidated. The sources do not say how many of the 2025 projects came from the earlier embassies.

If I were captioning this archive for a reader, I would write each caption from the panel in the picture, say which year and album it comes from, and leave a project's maker out unless a panel or a program page names one. That makes captions shorter, and a reader can check each one against the photograph in a few seconds.

If an exhibition prints its own history on a wall, should the archive count that wall as the record, or as one more exhibit? Next time you open a photo set from a show, read the panels in the pictures before you read the captions, and write down which of your sentences each panel supports.

posts.title: Driving Dutch Design: a business course for young designers, read through five years of photographs
posts.subtitle: The official photo archive files five albums, 2015 to 2019, under a program name. The partners' pages, DDW's archive and the press show when it began, who ran it and what the pictures leave out.
posts.seoTitle: Driving Dutch Design at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Driving Dutch Design, the business course for young designers shown at Dutch Design Week: start year, partners, yearly formats and the 2015 to 2019 albums.

r: The photo archive files five years of Dutch Design Week under the name Driving Dutch Design, and the name sounds like a motor show when it is the title of a business course.
The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds five Driving Dutch Design albums, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018 and 2019, 89 photographs in all.

The written record is rich enough to say what the program was, when it began, who ran it and how it changed, and it also shows how little of that a stage photograph can carry. This essay draws on public sources only: the program's partners, DDW's own news and magazine archive, a bank's press page, a regional news archive and a design academy's event page. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 edition beyond what DDW lists.

blocks.x: What the program is

r: Driving Dutch Design (DDD) is a program for young design studios that want to run a business. ABN AMRO's press page of October 8, 2015 describes it as an initiative of the bank, the Association of Dutch Designers (BNO) and the organizers of Dutch Design Week, in which each designer gets a personal coach and, over ten months, takes part in master classes and co-creation sessions.
DDW's own page for the bank says the program closes at DDW, where participants present designs and business plans to 150 potential customers, and that more than 120 designers had gone through it.
A DDW news item of 2020 lists the content of the monthly master classes: profiling, communication, financing, business operations and presentation.

The participants are called Drivers. They are not makers in the sense of one studio with one body of work, and that matters for the archive. A DDD album shows a stage, a hall and a crowd, and the studios appear as names on screens.

blocks.x: When it began

r: Three start years circulate, and the sources let me resolve them. A DDW page says the bank has supported DDW since 2009 and has been main sponsor since 2011.

That 2011 is the sponsorship, not the program. Innovation Origins, in a five-year look back published on May 24, 2017, says the program was created in 2012, and ABN AMRO's October 2015 page calls that year's group the third since the launch in 2012.

Counting the group of 2015 as the third puts the first class in 2013, and DDW's later edition numbers agree: the class of 2019 is the seventh edition, the class of 2020 the eighth and the class of 2022 the tenth.
The same October 2015 page says alumni of the 2013 and 2014 editions returned to DDW that year.

So the program was conceived and launched in 2012, and its first class of Drivers was the class of 2013. That reading uses the edition numbers from three different sources and contradicts none of them.

blocks.x: Why a bank and a trade body

r: The 2017 look back is the best source on motive, because it quotes the three organizers. Ilona Roolvink of ABN AMRO says entrepreneurship is in the bank's DNA and that young designers make beautiful products but struggle to market them. Martijn Paulen, director of the Dutch Design Foundation, says the three parties saw designers asking for support in professionalizing. Marsha Simon of BNO says the trade body has a large network of designers and of trainers and knowledge partners.
Roolvink also says the ultimate aim is for the program to become unnecessary, because academies would teach enough business.
Those are the organizers' own statements, made on the program's fifth anniversary.
The same piece says the program had 15 to 20 designers a year in an eleven-month workshop track, which differs from the ten months the bank's page uses.
I give each with its source and its date, because the program changed shape from year to year.

blocks.x: 2015: a pitch event and a hall in the Klokgebouw

r: The 2015 album, titled Drivers 2015, has 34 photographs by Jeroen van der Wielen.

The bank's page explains what that year consisted of. Participants showed their results in an exhibition called Momentum, a collaboration of young entrepreneurs, in Hall C of the Klokgebouw on Strijp-S, October 17 to 25, 2015, 11:00 to 18:00, and pitched to potential customers at the business event Drivers 2015 on October 20.

It lists fourteen Drivers: Alei Verspoor, Echter Ontwerp, Hats & Tales, Liat Azulay of Nudnik, Mark Vankan of Anidesign, Mianne de Vries, Pim Schachtschabel, Renate Nederpel, Rick Tegelaar, Studio Kars & Boom, Studio TOIMII, Thier&vanDaalen, Thomas Overweg of Glowbots and Tim van de Weerd.
Screens in the album carry the names Glowbots and Studio Mianne de Vries and the words Welcome to the ABN AMRO House.
I cannot tell from the album whether its stage photographs are of the Drivers 2015 pitch or of another session in the same hall.

blocks.x: 2016: signs on a dark stage

r: The 2016 album has 32 photographs, again by Jeroen van der Wielen, of a lit stage whose walls carry phrases such as THE MAKING OF, PERSISTENCE IS FRUITFUL, FOLLOW YOUR GUT and LOVE YOUR EXPERIMENTS.
I found no written source for DDD in 2016: no press page, no participant list, no venue. The 2016 album is therefore all picture and no text, and I leave it at what the signs say.

blocks.x: 2017: five years, shown in a loft

r: In 2017 the album is titled 5 Years Driving Dutch Design, has 4 photographs by Max Kneefel, and its titles name VEEM.

The Royal Academy of Art in The Hague lists, in its page on alumni at DDW 2017 (October 21 to 29), an exhibition called 5 years Driving Dutch Design & Hotspots, curated by Van Eijk & Van der Lubbe, at the Veem building, and lists works by its alumni in the Hotspots retrospective shown there.
The same page lists a second DDD show, Dating Dutch Design, with 21 selected designers, in the Klokgebouw.
The album's titles name VEEM, which fits the Veem exhibition, and nothing in the album points to the Klokgebouw show with the 21 designers.
Innovation Origins' five-year look back appeared in the same year, on May 24, 2017, five months before the festival.

blocks.x: 2018: a class in the Klokgebouw

r: The 2018 album has 14 photographs by Jeroen van der Wielen of a dark hall with white cloth walls. A wall text asks What's in it for you? The added value of design, and carries the logos of ABN AMRO, BNO and the Dutch Design Foundation, which is the clearest statement of who ran the program in the archive.
DDW's magazine profile of a Rotterdam trio, the studio Staalslagerij, says they presented with the rest of the DDD class of 2018 in the Klokgebouw during DDW, October 20 to 28, 2018.

The profile adds what the program gave them. A masterclass in storytelling by Paul Hughes taught them to talk about what a project does and not only what it is, and their personal coach pushed them to track which requests turn into paid commissions and why.
That is one studio's account in a partner-run magazine, and it is the kind of outcome the organizers claim.

blocks.x: 2019: the Driver, in a circular pavilion

r: The 2019 album has 5 photographs. Three are credited in their titles to Cleo Goossens and two carry no photographer.

DDW's magazine report on the seventh edition says it was held in Circl-E, the circular pavilion in the Klokgebouw designed by Overtreders W, that twenty designers were supervised over a year by coaches, and that the pitch, moderated by BNO's Marsha Simon, grouped presentations into nine "driving styles" from the Experiencer and the Conscious Driver to the Storyteller and the Futuristic Driver.
It names pitch speakers Onno Adriaanse, Julie Thissen, Mirl van Hoek, Billie van Katwijk, Katinka Versendaal of The Eatelier and Sander Lorier.
A DDW guide of October 21, 2019 lists Driving Dutch Design in Hall 2, Connecting Collaborations, with the Embassy of Health and the Renault concept cars, around ABN AMRO's Circl-E.

The class of 2019 also published a book, The Driver: Driving Dutch Design, in which the designers introduce themselves, show their studios, and in a chapter called Failing Forward describe their biggest setbacks. DDW reported it in 2020.
A sign in the 2019 album reads THE DRIVER, which is the book's title.

blocks.x: After the archive stops

r: The archive has no album after 2019, but the program kept going and DDW's own pages show it. The 2020 class, the eighth, had 26 designers including four duos, took monthly master classes and worked in a Bureau DDD toward an exhibition, a Drivers Pitch Event and a publication.
The 2021 class had 23 designers, started online for the first time, and showed in an exhibition titled I hear what you're seeing, with 17 studios at the Pullman hotel.

In 2022, the tenth anniversary by DDW's count, there was no large joint exhibition: each Driver presented in a way that suited the studio, with DDF support, 21 ABN AMRO coaches, BNO masterclasses and a new alumni club called Club DDD.
In 2024 DDW's program page for Driven by Purpose says 20 studios exhibited together and names BNO, the Dutch Design Foundation and the Stokroos Foundation as the organizers.
That page does not name ABN AMRO. I do not know whether the bank left the program or simply is not named on that page, so I do not claim either.

The change from a joint hall to individual presentations in 2022 and back to a joint exhibition in 2024 is the part the archive misses most. A reader of the 2015 to 2019 albums would conclude the program is a stage in a hall, and the written record says that was one format among several.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: 2011, 2012 and 2013 all circulate. 2011 is the bank's main-sponsor year, 2012 is the launch the organizers give, and 2013 is the first class by the edition numbers.
I use 2012 for launch and 2013 for the first class.
How many designers and how many months.
Fifteen to twenty and eleven months in 2017, about twenty and ten months in other years, 14 in 2015, 26 in 2020, 23 in 2021. These are consistent across years and I report each with its year.
The 2015 to 2021 pages name ABN AMRO, BNO and the Dutch Design Foundation. The 2024 page names BNO, the foundation and the Stokroos Foundation. Both are true for their year.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what the 2016 sessions consisted of, who the 2016 and 2017 Drivers were, or which album photographs belong to which session within a year. I did not read the program's own website, which answered with an error, and the Dutch Design Daily pages on the 2023 ten-year stage and the 2024 exhibition showed a bot-verification page, so I stopped requests to that site and did not use them. I found no DDW source for 2025. I have no source for the class of 2026.
If a program says its goal is to become unnecessary, what would you look for in its photographs to tell whether it was getting there?

posts.title: Dutch Invertuals at Dutch Design Week: a collective that became a studio, one theme at a time
posts.subtitle: From a Milan group show in 2009 to a listed DDW 2026 location on Fuutlaan. The studio's own pages, a 2018 business plan, trade press and DDW's archive, set against nine years of photo albums.
posts.seoTitle: Dutch Invertuals at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: How Dutch Invertuals grew from a 2009 Milan group show into a studio, foundation and academy, and what the DDW photo albums show of its yearly themes.

r: A name that stays the same for sixteen years can hide almost everything that changed behind it, and Dutch Invertuals is a good test of that, because its own pages describe a group show in Milan, a curator's side project, a registered company and a studio, foundation and academy, all under one name.

As a content strategist I look at how a name is used before I look at what it points to. This essay asks what Dutch Invertuals has been at each Dutch Design Week (DDW) it can be traced to, using the studio's own project pages, a business plan it wrote in 2018, trade press and DDW's program archive, and then asks what the official DDW photo albums can show of that history. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 program beyond what DDW's listing says.

blocks.x: The start: a hall in Milan, not a design studio

r: The studio's own history says that in 2009 its founder, Wendy Plomp, was invited to show a group of Dutch designers at the Salone del Mobile in Milan, and that this inaugural exhibition is where the collective began.

The 2018 business plan gives more detail: she was invited to exhibit in the Brera design district, the space was too large for her alone, and she asked other designers to present with her. It names Daphna Laurens, Edhv, Bart Hess, House of Origin, Lotty Lindeman, Pepe Heykoop and Raw Color among the first group.

Plomp told a city-marketing video in 2017 that founding it was almost an accident, that the success in Milan made a second show in Eindhoven during the next DDW obvious, and that from then on she organized and curated two exhibitions a year, one in Milan and one in Eindhoven.

The name has an explanation in the plan: Dutch refers to its roots in the Netherlands, and Invertuals is derived from inversion, a process of opposition and reversal, seeing the world upside down from radical new perspectives.
Interior Design gave a similar account in 2018, saying the name derives from inverse.

IO+ wrote in 2016 that Plomp had been the biggest motivation behind the group since the beginning of 2009, that she started as a fellow designer, that she took on a larger role as organizer and curator from 2010, and that it became her full-time job in 2015.

blocks.x: Before the photo archive begins

r: The official DDW albums for the group start in 2015, but the studio's pages list earlier DDW shows. Matter of Time, shown during DDW 2010, used 600-year-old oak wood excavated in 2007 at the Woenselse Poort in Eindhoven as its material.
Conflict was the group's exhibition for DDW 2012.
Cohesion, with 12 designers, was shown in 2014.
Transform, from 2013, carries the location line Milan, so it is a Salone show and not a DDW one.
I found no studio page that names a DDW show for 2011 or 2013. That does not mean there was none, only that I did not find it.

blocks.x: From collective to company

r: The business side arrives gradually. IO+ reported in October 2016 that Plomp had made the collective her full-time job the year before, and that the group worked from the edhv design agency on the Fuutlaan, which served as headquarters and as the venue of the annual DDW exhibition. Every two weeks the 13 members of that year's show met there, and for nine days the edhv workspaces were cleared for the exhibition.
In October 2017, Plomp said in the same city video that Dutch Invertuals had been registered as a company with the Chamber of Commerce two years earlier.
I did not look at a register, so the year rests on her statement as the video reports it.

The March 2018 business plan is the clearest document of what the group thought it was. It counts 18 exhibitions developed so far, with more than 100 new works, mostly made for the Salone and DDW and increasingly moved on to other places such as D'Days in Paris, Kazerne in Eindhoven and the London Design Fair. It counts more than 60 talents scouted and guided. It also says that, although the format was a proven success, the current activities were not yet viable as a business, which is why the plan sets out services under three headings, observe, manifest and create.

Today the About page describes a studio that does spatial and strategic design projects for clients, a foundation that initiates annual research projects, and an academy, an online program for young professionals.

blocks.x: 2015: No Static, and who made the room

r: The 2015 DDW exhibition was No Static, curated by Plomp, with exhibition design by Edhv. The studio's page names 11 participants: Aliki van der Kruijs, Alissa + Nienke, Arnout Meijer, Edhv, Jelle Mastenbroek, Jólan van der Wiel, Kirstie van Noort, Martina Lasinger, Noman, Odd Matter and Tijmen Smeulders.
It describes the show as an inquiry into movement, identity and digital life.
TL Magazine reported on it on November 11, 2015 and singled out NOMAN's sliding-door piece Welcome, Arnout Meijer's Feet of Twilight and Martina Lasinger's The Theory of Everything.
The DDW album for the year holds 29 photos, 21 of them credited by title to Boudewijn Bollmann and three to Ronald Smits.
The studio's page and TL Magazine both credit Smits for the exhibition photography, and the DDW album title carries the name of the show, which makes this the clearest album in the set.

blocks.x: 2016: Powerplay on the Fuutlaan

r: Powerplay, in 2016, looked at a society in which renewable energy has become abundant. The studio's page names thirteen designers and credits exhibition design to Remco van de Craats, Daniel de Bruin, Tijs Gilde and Carlo Lorenzetti, with Plomp as curator.
IO+ reported that the theme was energy overload, that the title was Powerplay and that some of the works would be developed further for Milan, which fits the group's twice-yearly rhythm.
The same report places the DDW exhibition at the edhv headquarters on the Fuutlaan.
There are two 2016 albums, both by Nick Bookelaar: Dutch Invertuals with 13 photos and Dutch Invertuals @ Veem with 9.

The first is most likely the Fuutlaan exhibition, because IO+ places it there, though no title says so. The second I cannot explain from 2016 sources. I found none that puts the group at VEEM that year, although DDW's 2019 magazine says that in 2019 the group held the art direction of VEEM, a Strijp-S warehouse used as a parking garage the rest of the year.

blocks.x: 2017: two shows in one October

r: In 2017 the group made two exhibitions. Enlighten, made with the window-covering brand Luxaflex, presented six designers experimenting with light and Luxaflex materials. The studio's page names works by Studio Mieke Meijer, by Jetske Visser and Michiel Martens and by Daniel De Bruin, with an exhibition setting by Tijmen Smeulders.
TL Magazine's DDW report, written when the festival was in its 16th edition, picked out Thomas Ballouhey's piece.
That count of editions matches a first edition in 2002.

Fundamentals, the second show, was made with the Eindhoven studio Raw Color. The studio's page says 45 Invertuals unearthed more than 800 objects from their studio archives, sorted into nine typologies, from The Workers and The Purists to The Brutalists. Each designer also made a container as a shared archetype.
Plomp told the city video that the participants showed objects normally hidden in their archives, with Raw Color as guest curator.
Interior Design reported that Daphna Laurens designed the exhibition, arranging the objects on a wooden ring 50 feet in diameter, and that Plomp had produced 18 shows in nine years.
Dezeen reported the show on October 27, 2017, a date I carry over from an earlier read because the site now blocks automated requests.
The 2017 album holds 19 photos by Boudewijn Bollmann, eight titled enlighten and eleven titled fundamentals, so this is the one year in which the photo titles themselves separate the two shows.

blocks.x: 2018: Take Away, and a Milan show that shares an album

r: Take Away asked how design can help to live with less. The studio's page lists ten participants or pairs, describes a circular arrangement with mirrored plinths as part of the exhibition design, and credits photography to Ronald Smits.

Its thanks list names Cultuur Eindhoven, Leeuwerik Plaatmateriaal, Mansveld expotech and Pyrasied. Two image captions on the page read Baars & Bloemhoff and Bone Interieurwerken, and the page does not say what part either company played.
Dezeen reported the show on October 30, 2018, again a date carried over.
The 2018 albums hold 12 photos for Take Away by Boudewijn Bollmann, and 8 by Max Kneefel in an album titled Mutant Matter whose photo titles say VEEM.
The studio's page for Mutant Matter, made with the research agency FranklinTill and ten designers, carries the location line Milan.

So the album and the page disagree, or the show traveled; no source says which. A third reading is that the VEEM titles reflect the group's role in organizing that building, as DDW's magazine describes for 2019, and not the show named in the album.
I keep the album and the Milan show apart.

blocks.x: 2019: The Circle, ten years in

r: The Circle marked ten years. The studio's page says the show was first exhibited in Milan during the Salone del Mobile in 2019 and then in Eindhoven during DDW, that it led to a book and a traveling exhibition series, and that it showed the work of over 40 designers who had played a significant role in the group's beginnings.
The studio's history page recalls it as the celebration of ten years.
Dezeen's report, carried over from the October 7 read, counted more than 20 designers and studios, so the two numbers differ. They may count different editions of the show; no source I opened says.
That same year DDW's magazine says the group's tenth anniversary coincided with its art direction of VEEM, which it transformed into an industrial exhibition space.

blocks.x: 2020 to 2023: a pause in the gallery, an academy in its place

r: There is no album for 2020, and the studio's pages name no 2020 exhibition. They do show what it did instead. The Dutch Invertuals Academy was launched in 2020, during the first wave of COVID-19, to keep the group connected to the global design community.
Its first intensive six-week program that year drew 22 designers from around the world.

In 2021 the group returned to the gallery with Objects for a New Kind of Society, made with the futures consultancy The Future Laboratory. The studio's page lists eleven participants, Daphna Laurens as exhibition designer, and support from Cultuur Eindhoven, the Dutch Design Foundation and Stichting Stokroo.
AnInteriorMag named it, in its report on DDW 2021, as perhaps the best in show, and said it was developed on the heels of the pandemic-born Academy.

In 2022 came Expedition Æqualis, with The Future Laboratory and Reon Brand of Philips. The page says the show exhibited during DDW 2022 featured eleven designers and used circular pedestals on a sand-covered floor of locally sourced sand, which visitors raked with special tools.
DDW's archive lists an Expedition Æqualis party on October 28 at Fuutlaan 12B.

That description lets me connect the 2022 album to the show with more confidence than before. The album's 21 photos, taken October 25, 2022 by Britt Roelse, show raked-sand islands with sculptures, according to the October 7 read.
The studio's description of a sand floor with works on circular pedestals matches that. I count it as a strong match, not a captioned one, since no photo title names the show.

In 2023 the group showed Flow with Béla Bezold, Ralf Gloudemans, Teresa Fernández-Pello and Edhv, an installation about a stream of water droplets that the studio says draws visitors away from their daily data flow.
The 2023 album has four photos by Almicheal Fraay of a long line of red and yellow elements on thin metal stands.
I cannot tell from the studio's text whether those four photographs show Flow, so I leave them without a show name.

blocks.x: 2024 and 2025: an anniversary chair and a New York exchange

r: Specimen, in 2024, marked the 15th anniversary. DDW's listing and the studio's page say 15 designers were each asked to redesign a chair that the studio had made for the 5TRACKS offices, and that the group has worked with over 90 designers.
Daphna Laurens, who took part in the 2009 Milan group, contributed the Di Mama Armchair.

The same year, Circles of Universal Language, commissioned by the municipality of Eindhoven, showed ten designers' proposals for objects in public space at Ketelhuisplein during DDW. The page adds that Queen Máxima visited it.
There is no 2024 album titled Dutch Invertuals. The 2024 Fuutlaan album has five photos, and one by Nick Bookelaar, dated October 27, 2024, shows many chairs; its title does not name Specimen.
The chair description fits, and I flag it as an inference. In 2025, DDW lists Objects of Exchange at Dutch Invertuals, Fuutlaan 12B, October 18 to 26, free with a DDW ticket or for 5 euros.

The studio's page describes six designers, three Dutch and three American, each given a pure metal to work with. DDW's listing places the project within Future 400, which it calls a long-term initiative strengthening Dutch-American partnerships.

blocks.x: 2026: a listed location again

r: DDW lists the Dutch Invertuals Studio at Fuutlaan 12B, in the Station area, October 17 to 25, 2026, from 11:00 to 18:00 daily, free with a DDW ticket or for 5 euros. DDW's location page says it is not wheelchair accessible.
A neighboring DDW location, the Design Perron at Fuutlaan 12, lists exhibits from Dutch Invertuals among others.
The sources do not say what the 2026 show is.

blocks.x: Why the studio's own dates need care

r: The studio's project pages are the richest list of what it showed, and they carry post dates that cannot all be show dates. The early pages read as contemporary: Matter of Time October 7, 2010, Conflict October 12, 2012, Cohesion October 12, 2014, Powerplay October 28, 2016.

But Enlightened, Fundamentals, Take Away and Mutant Matter all carry October 9, 2023, although the first of them says it was made for DDW 2017, and Circles of Universal Language carries July 25, 2026 for a DDW 2024 show.
My reading is that the later pages were re-published in a site rebuild, and no source says so. I used the pages for what was shown and the press and DDW for when.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know why the 2016 VEEM album exists, whether the 2018 Mutant Matter photographs show a DDW presentation, what the 2023 photographs show, or why there is no album for 2020, 2024 or 2025.
I do not know which DDW shows the group made in 2011 and 2013.
I did not see a company register, and I could not reopen the Dezeen reports.
When you meet a name that has lasted sixteen years, which line on the page tells you what it was in each of those years: the name, the date or the people credited beside it?

posts.title: ELLE Decoration at Dutch Design Week: a program page that names the show, and a Worklife album that no page explains
posts.subtitle: Two editions in the TQ building at Strijp-T. DDW's program archive, a trade-press post and two reports on the building say more than the photo titles do, and still not who made the rooms.
posts.seoTitle: ELLE Decoration at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: ELLE Decoration at Dutch Design Week 2018 and 2019 in the TQ building at Strijp-T: what DDW's program page, a trade-press post and the photo archive show.

r: Dutch Design Week's recap of October 25, 2019 names ELLE Decoration only as a link, and the page behind the link says more about the exhibition than any caption in the photo archive does.

That detail matters because this is a thin record, and in a thin record every page counts twice. This essay draws on public sources only: two pages from Dutch Design Week's own site, a trade-press article from November 2018, two reports about the building and the official photo archive on Flickr as I recorded it on October 8, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about a 2026 ELLE Decoration show, because I found no page for one.
The honest length of this essay is short. The sources about ELLE Decoration at Dutch Design Week run out after a handful of pages, and I have not padded them.

blocks.x: What the recap says, and what its link says

r: The recap is a short magazine item of October 25, 2019 in DDW's daily area tour. For Strijp-T and Strijp-R it says that Strijp-T is a popular place among high-tech makers, points visitors to the Innovation Powerhouse, the former Philips power plant, and says the TQ building behind it is also worth a visit, where "you will find the exhibition of ELLE Decoration and the research projects of TUe: Drivers of Change."
The words ELLE Decoration are a link, and the link goes to a page in DDW's program archive titled "ELLE Decoration presents... Fluid Forces."

That program page is the primary source for the 2019 show. It is marked as part of DDW 2019, presented by ELLE Decoration, in the category exhibitions, and carries the line "Concentrate - Cocreate - Celebrate."

It describes an immersive exhibit "from the world's leading interior magazine in collaboration with Tarkett," and says that, picking up from the previous year's exhibit and building on what was learned since, ELLE Decoration would work from the principle of zoning in the workspace.
The text breaks off mid-word in the archive page, in a sentence about trends, so I do not have the rest of the description.
The image on the page is credited as styling by F. Hofhuis and art direction by D. Westland, with a copyright line for Visual Citizens and Carlfried Verwaayen.
That credit belongs to the promotional image, and the page does not say those people made the exhibit.

An earlier reading of mine, through a summarizing reader, said the recap itself names "ELLE Decoration Presents Fluid Forces." The recap prints only ELLE Decoration, and the title comes from the program page it links to. The difference is small and it changes where the title should be credited.

blocks.x: What the 2019 page implies about 2018

r: The program page says the 2019 exhibit picks up from last year's.

That sentence ties the two editions together on DDW's own authority, and it gives the 2018 show a theme. A show that is followed by one about zoning in the workspace was probably also about the workspace, and the 2018 album is titled "ELLE Decoration: Worklife."
I read the two as one thread, and I label that as my inference, because the page does not call the 2018 show Worklife and no page I opened explains the album's title.

For 2018 itself the written source is thin. Italian Bark, a design blog, wrote on November 13, 2018 that among the exhibits at Strijp-T the author found the setting by Elle Decor NL most interesting, which took the very top of the Strijp-T building and recreated an apartment furnished with design pieces in a white and blue palette.
The same post names a second exhibit nearby, "Body of Work" by OS ∆ OOS, a minimalist setting with a series called Repeated Mirrors made of layers of colored glass.
The blog also writes the exhibitor's name as Elle Decor NL, where DDW writes ELLE Decoration.

I use the album's name, ELLE Decoration, and note that the blog's form is not necessarily a different organization. DDW's 2018 edition ran from October 20 to 28 and the 2019 edition from October 19 to 27.

blocks.x: The building

r: The photo titles for both years say TQ, and DDW's 2019 recap places the exhibition in the TQ building.

IO+ wrote in September 2015 that TQ was put up in the 1950s to keep pace with Philips' growth, that companies such as FEI, ASML and the European branch of Fluke trace their origins there, and that it held a Philips nuclear-war bunker from which the company would have been run and rebuilt.

A subsidy consultancy's reference page says TQ has more than 40,000 square meters of floor area, the largest building on Strijp-T, and that it was fully renovated into a shared building for companies with sustainability measures such as insulation and solar panels.

The two pages describe the same place at different moments: the 2015 article says its owner was a bankrupt company and that the bank which financed it had put it up for sale, and the later reference page describes it as renovated.
That is useful context for the photographs. The 2019 album, by the old dossier's description, shows raw concrete walls, and the 2018 album shows a window over the city.
Neither page tells me which part of TQ the show used, and the Italian Bark post says "the very top" in 2018 only.
I do not claim the 2018 and 2019 sets stood in the same rooms.

The other tenant of the building named in the recap is the Eindhoven University of Technology, whose exhibition Drivers of Change, according to its program page, showed more than 70 exhibits from departments, student teams and start-ups at Strijp-T, from very concrete to fairly speculative.
An interiors magazine and a technical university were in one building in the same week, and DDW's recap puts them in a single sentence.
I find that pairing more interesting than either exhibit's description, though no source says the two were planned together.

IO+ ran a photo gallery on October 23, 2019 whose caption lists Elle, Fontys and the Embassy of Sustainable Design as the Strijp-T, TQ and Innovation Powerhouse exhibitors, and the page has no text beyond the caption.
It confirms the company in one more place and adds no detail about the show.

blocks.x: What the albums add

r: The old dossier counts two albums, 9 photographs for 2018 and 14 for 2019, 23 in all, credited in the titles to Britt Roelse (20) and Max Kneefel (3), with the three Kneefel titles beginning 20191025.

I did not reopen Flickr for this version. The 2018 album shows a living room in white and blue with navy poufs, a swirled blue rug with mirrored panels and a gray wall with a yellow hexagon sign that reads qbe next to the ELLE DECORATION logo, and the 2019 album shows concrete walls, curved cream furniture, a gold arch lamp, a dark red room and a mirrored sculpture.
No title names a designer or a piece, and neither DDW page I opened names one.
The program page names Tarkett as the collaborator on the 2019 exhibit and does not say what Tarkett supplied.

I could not open Tarkett's own site, which refused my first request (robots.txt, HTTP 403), so I say nothing about the company. The yellow qbe sign in a 2018 photograph could belong to a sponsor, but no page I opened says what qbe refers to, and I make no guess.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The old draft credited the recap with the title. The recap links to the program page, and the program page carries the title. The program page settles it.
Italian Bark says Elle Decor NL, the photo titles and DDW say ELLE Decoration. Nothing I opened separates them, and I use ELLE Decoration.

Italian Bark calls Strijp-T an area with the former Philips headquarters building. IO+ and the renovation reference describe TQ as a company building from the 1950s with a bunker, and neither calls it a headquarters, so I do not repeat the headquarters label.
Not settled. The 2019 page suggests a workspace thread. The album title is the only source for the word.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know who designed or styled either show, which pieces were on display, or what Tarkett supplied. The program page for 2019 breaks off in the middle of its description, so I cannot say what trends it names. I found no DDW program page for the 2018 show and no page from the magazine itself, and I did not find the magazine's own account of either year.
I did not search for earlier or later ELLE Decoration appearances at Dutch Design Week, and my searches turned up none for 2017 or after 2019.
I do not know what the two shows cost to build or how many people saw them.
I did not reopen the photo archive, so the album counts, titles and photographers come from the October 8, 2026 reading.
Nothing here describes an ELLE Decoration show at Dutch Design Week 2026, which runs October 17 to 25, 2026.
If a magazine builds a room for a week and the label by the door gives only the magazine's name, who should the room be credited to?

posts.title: Envisions at Dutch Design Week: a collective built to show everything but the end product
posts.subtitle: From Products in Process in 2016 to a studio opening in 2026, what the organization says, what the press says and what a photo archive can hold.
posts.seoTitle: Envisions at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Envisions at Dutch Design Week, 2016 to 2026: Products in Process, a wood book, a retrospective and a new studio, read against what a photo archive holds.

r: Envisions says it began when its founders left the Milan design fair uninspired by finished products, and the sources show it taking that idea to Dutch Design Week from 2016 on.

I like a case where the subject's own idea runs against the format that records it. Envisions sets out to show the process and not the product, and a photo archive freezes whatever happens to be on the table the day the photographer comes. This essay uses public sources only: Envisions' own site, design and trade press, a designer's studio page, a university excursion page, Dutch Design Week's own listings and the official DDW photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibit beyond what the published listing says.

blocks.x: How Envisions tells its own beginning

r: Envisions' About page says it began in 2016 in Eindhoven, founded by Sanne Schuurman, Simone Post and Iwan Pol, all graduates of Design Academy Eindhoven. After attending Europe's largest design fair in Milan, the page says, they felt uninspired by the focus on finished products and the lack of diversity in design approaches, and the collective grew out of that: a group dedicated to celebrating the design process itself.
The page puts the aim this way: show everything but the final product, by working with designers known for experimental and colorful approaches.
Its present description is a multidisciplinary design agency that reimagines materials, with three services, Material, Content and Space.
The About page lists five people under Team, with Schuurman as founder and creative director, and a longer list of what it calls envisionaires, which includes Post and Pol.

The headcount has moved with the years and with the definition. It's Nice That pictured eight designers in 2016, the New Material Award described more than 20 designers in 2018, and the site today separates a small team from a wide circle of collaborators.
I read those as three different counts of three different things, not as a contradiction.
A claim that a show is about process rather than product is a statement of intent, and what the archive can add is limited to what was photographed.

blocks.x: 2016: Products in Process, in two parts

r: It's Nice That reported on August 24, 2016 that Envisions, a collective of Design Academy Eindhoven graduates, aimed to "showcase everything but the end product." The show, called Products in Process and also Envisions, had already been shown in New York and Milan and would join Dutch Design Week from October 22 to 30.
Helsinki Design Week, writing in November 2016, calls the Dutch Design Week show Part 2 and says Part 1 was at the Milan design festival in April.
The magazine names two pieces. Transsaddles by Adrianus Kundert looks at age in design, and Happy Concrete by Iwan Pol asks why the most widely used man-made material so often looks uninspired.
The Dutch Design Week photo archive holds a 2016 album of 23 photographs titled Envisions-DDW16, with the photographer Ronald Smits named in every title.
Two details about that credit matter. Smits appears on Envisions' own contributor list under photography, and WOTH credits him with the photographs in the 2017 Wood in Process book.

So the archive's 2016 and 2018 albums are credited to a photographer who also works with the subject. I cannot tell from the pages whether he shot those albums for Dutch Design Week or for Envisions, and the answer matters for how the pictures can be reused.

Where Part 2 stood in 2016 is not in the sources I could open. A page in a collaborator's portfolio and a magazine's venue listing might say, but the first returned a not-found error and the second blocked automated access, so I leave the place open. Envisions' archive also lists an installation called RGB Funfair for the Van Abbemuseum in 2016, with four envisionaires named, but the case page body is placeholder text and I cannot tell whether it belongs to Dutch Design Week.

blocks.x: 2017: a book, a hall and a mistaken launch

r: WOTH says Envisions launched the book Wood in Process, made with the Spanish wood manufacturer Finsa, during Dutch Design Week in Eindhoven, and a photo caption says the book launch was at VDMA during DDW 2017.
The same page says the research collected in the book had been on show at Dutch Design Week 2017, Salone del Mobile 2017, WantedDesign in New York in 2017 and the London Design Fair in 2017.
The photographer is Smits, and the book was designed by Studio Aandacht.
An earlier version of this essay, and the carousel built from it, said Wood in Process itself launched at VDMA. The page supports less than that: the book launched at VDMA, and the research traveled.
The 2017 album, titled Envisions_VDMA_2017, shows a large hall with many displays, some of which carry other names, so I cannot separate Envisions' objects from the rest by title.
The VDMA was still a Dutch Design Week location four years later: Salone del Mobile.Milano's 2021 report says it was transformed that year into a forest in its courtyard.

Envisions' home page describes Wood in Process as a laboratory exercise: it set out to find new uses for the full range of Finsa's materials, which it lists as chipboard, medium density fibreboard and high pressure laminates.

blocks.x: 2018: the second chapter, in an ice factory

r: Studio Simone Post, a founder's own studio, published a post on October 25, 2018 describing Wood in progress as the second chapter of the Finsa collaboration. It says six of the earlier researches were industrially tweaked in Finsa's factories in Spain, shown from October 20 to 28, 2018 at Campinaterrein De IJsfabriek on the Kanaaldijk Zuid, and that the display aimed to shift the viewer's perspective constantly.

The New Material Award, which also listed Wood in Progress for 2018, says six results of the collaboration were developed further in Finsa's factories, and that many of the designs use waste wood that is dyed or pulverized and glued or pressed into new boards.
The studio post adds that Wood in Progress was a nominee for the New Material Award 2018, with the nominees shown at the Veem building.

Envisions' own press release shows that Eindhoven was the second stop. Wood in progress opened in Milan first, at Officine Savona in Zona Tortona, April 17 to 22, 2018, with a press preview on April 16.

The release names six designers and six works: Aukje Fleur Janssen's Wrapping wood, in which patterned paper is laminated into board under a factory heat press; Elvis Wesley's Undertone, which turns wax finishes on black board into a decorative range of blacks and greys; Strips and stripes by Roos Gomperts and Wesley, which shows the strips that make up veneer; Sanne Schuurman's Open board, a play of repetition and structure that exposes the layers of the board; Simone Post's Wannabe wood, which uses CNC milling to uncover the fiber layers of the material; and Thomas Trum's Fossilised in fibre, dyed fibers pressed into sheets in a pressure press the release calls 500 meters long.

The release also describes the display as a diptych: a conceptual application of handcrafted materials now industrially altered, and a second part about the industrial developments and Finsa's manufacturing process.
These are Envisions' descriptions, and Finsa's own words in the same document say it has more than 12 factories serving 83 countries.
The 2018 album holds ten photographs titled envisions-wood in progress-ddw18, again with Smits named.

The earlier carousel said the show presented six experimental research projects developed with Finsa. The sources say six of the earlier researches, by six named designers, were reworked in industrial conditions, a narrower statement.

blocks.x: 2021: invitations at the Fuutlaan hall

r: The 2021 album holds nine photographs by Britt Roelse. One shows a printed curtain that reads envisions invites upcoming talents and says 12 upcoming designers are invited, though folds hide part of the text.
A Berlin art school's excursion plan lists Envisions at Fuutlaan 14i in October 2021, with a meeting with a founder and a participant.

Salone del Mobile.Milano's report says the Fuutlaan hall that year held Design Perron, Dutch Invertuals and Envisions and calls Envisions Italian, which is an error, since every source I opened places it in Eindhoven.
This shows how a large hall with several groups under one roof gets labeled by whoever writes the caption.

blocks.x: 2022: a retrospective and a municipality's cellar

r: For 2022, Envisions' archive lists More Than This as a self-initiated retrospective exhibition presented at DDW. The case page has placeholder text, so I use only its labels.

Two independent reports describe it. Design Insider Live calls it a 5 year retrospective of the collective's experiments, with work by Post, Schuurman, Studio Truly Truly and Robin Pleun Maas, and says many samples came from challenges by manufacturers such as Finsa and Levi's.
A German design magazine places it in a large tidy warehouse and calls it a five-year retrospective.
The 2022 album has 21 photographs by Roelse, banners that read Because there is more than this, and titles that begin FUUTLAAN_DESIGNPERRON.

The earlier carousel asked how the Envisions hall related to Design Perron. DDW's own location page for Design Perron gives its home as the Opvallers building at Fuutlaan 12 and lists exhibits from Dutch Invertuals, Envisions and others.
Design Perron's own site calls Opvallers its trusted base.

So Design Perron looks like the umbrella for the hall, and Envisions one of its exhibitors, which would explain the titles. That page describes 2026, though, so I do not know whether its wording about Envisions dates from an earlier year.

Envisions was also behind a second exhibition that year, which the album does not cover. Its archive lists De Volle Ondergrond, a 2022 exhibition for the municipality of Eindhoven, and Interior Design calls it one of the festival's highlights: organized by the municipality and designed by fffunction studios and Envisions, it examined the jam-packed underground of pipes, sewers, cables and garages.
An archive of albums called Envisions would miss it.

blocks.x: What a retrospective does to an archive

r: A retrospective gathers earlier work. If More Than This was one, then a 2022 photograph of an object could show something first made years before, and the album year would date the picture, not the object. That is reasoning, and I flag it as such. A caption that says 2022 is true about the photograph and silent about the work. The same logic runs backward: a photograph of a wall of samples dated 2016 does not say which samples were new that year.
My anatomy training has a parallel.

A dissection is taught layer by layer so that students see how the final structure was reached, and a student who sees only the finished specimen learns the name and misses the order. Envisions' stated idea belongs to that tradition, and a single photograph of a table of samples cannot carry it.

blocks.x: 2025: one trace in a craft council's list

r: For 2025 I found one trace, and it comes from another organization. Crafts Council Nederland's HOW&WOW page for Dutch Design Week 2025 lists 85 makers, and the last entry, [Re]value, spins, weaves and makes felt from local wool and hemp with scalable industrial techniques, with support from Interreg. The entry links to envisions.nl and an Envisions Instagram handle. The page does not say where the exhibit stood.
It is the only evidence in this record that Envisions took part in a Dutch Design Week after 2022, and it describes a material experiment in the way the About page promises.

blocks.x: 2026: a studio opens its door

r: Dutch Design Week's listing for October 17 to 25, 2026 puts Envisions' new studio at Hallenweg 1E, open daily from 11:00 to 18:00 with free access. It says Envisions works there all year on projects from material research and product design to interior design, and that it opens its doors to the public for the first time during the week, in more than 100 square meters.
The program entry, called Treasured, describes a daylit workspace full of treasures, projects, materials and try-outs, finished and in progress.

That is the first Envisions listing in this record that shows the process by its own description, in the place where it happens. The Crafts Council Nederland exhibition WOW NATURE is listed in the same Hallenweg area, at De Fabriek.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Where Products in Process Part 2 stood in 2016, and whether RGB Funfair was part of the festival.
Whether Smits photographed the 2016 and 2018 albums for Dutch Design Week or for Envisions.
Whether Envisions took part in 2019, 2020, 2023 or 2024. I found no album and no page, and a gap in an archive is not proof of absence. The only trace after 2022 is the 2025 craft-council entry.
Which objects the 2016, 2017 and 2021 photographs show by name, and who made them.
How much of More Than This was new in 2022.
Whether the Design Perron listing describes 2022 or only 2026.

r: When you open an album next to a listing, which does the sentence describe: the picture, the object in it or the organization that made it?
