posts.title: GEO-DESIGN left the museum in 2019, and its photographers were never the same people
posts.subtitle: Five Dutch Design Week chapters of a Design Academy Eindhoven series, read against what the school, the festival, a designer and the press wrote about each one
posts.seoTitle: GEO-DESIGN at Dutch Design Week, 2018 to 2021
posts.description: Five chapters of the Design Academy Eindhoven and Van Abbemuseum series GEO-DESIGN, set beside organizer pages and six photo albums.

r: GEO-DESIGN left the museum in 2019, and the photo archive recorded that move in the way it sorted its albums.

I like a series that changes its setting, because the setting is part of what an archive can and cannot prove. This essay draws on public sources only: pages from Design Academy Eindhoven, Dutch Design Week's own magazine articles, an e-flux announcement, the identity designer's project page, a review in Domus and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 festival.

blocks.x: A school and a museum, with a curator in the middle

r: Design Academy Eindhoven describes GEO-DESIGN as a platform that explores the social, economic, territorial and geopolitical forces shaping design today.
Its page says the platform transformed the annual exhibition of the Academy's alumni work, produced with the Van Abbemuseum, into an exhibition series.

Dutch Design Week's article on the second chapter calls the series an annual collaboration between the two institutions and says the Academy started it in response to a need for experimentation and support for young designers and researchers.
The people named around it are few and recur. Martina Muzi curated Sand and Budget Airlines, and DDW says she curated Junk with Joseph Grima, whom it calls director of the Academy.
Domus names the same pair for the first chapter.

Grima is quoted on the Academy's page calling the series emblematic of a shift toward design as systems, strategy and research, and saying it helps the Academy build long-term relationships with alumni.
I read that as a statement of purpose: the series is an alumni program as much as an exhibition.
The page for the platform is dated October 1, 2018 and was later revised, because it also announces the fourth episode, an online exhibition on COVID-19.
That is why the page reads as a running ledger, and it is the main reason I trust the order of the chapters: the Academy numbers the fourth, e-flux numbers the third, and DDW numbers the second.

blocks.x: One name, two things: an exhibition series and a master's program

r: The name GEO-DESIGN also belongs to a degree. On November 8, 2019, DesignDigger reported that Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin, who work together as Formafantasma, had been appointed head of a new two-year master's program called Geo Design at the Academy, to be added to the existing master's programs in Social Design, Contextual Design and Information Design.

The report calls the master a logical continuation of the exhibition series and quotes Joseph Grima describing the exhibitions as a breeding ground for ideas and technologies that seep ever further into the Academy's education.
The Academy's own page for the master says it was founded in 2020, calls it the youngest master's program at the Academy and lists Formafantasma as department heads for 2020 to 2023.

The two share a name and a school, and they are not the same thing: one is a series of shows with the Van Abbemuseum, the other is a course of study. A caption that says "GEO-DESIGN" without saying which one invites a mistake. The Onomatopee publisher's page for the Sand catalog describes the exhibition platform as launched in 2018 by the Academy, which is the clean way to say it.

blocks.x: 2018: Alibaba, in orange

r: The first outcome was GEO-DESIGN: Alibaba in October 2018, for which the Academy's page says nine graduates were invited to research Alibaba's operational model and its impact on the design field.
Domus, publishing on November 1, 2018, calls the exhibition at the Van Abbemuseum one of the most prominent events of Dutch Design Week 2018 and says it was curated by Muzi and Grima.
The identity designer Irene Stracuzzi gives the dates: October 13 to November 11, 2018 at the Van Abbemuseum, then Salone del Mobile in Milan from April 9 to 14, 2019.
The museum's own page for the show no longer opens, so those dates rest on the designer's page.

Stracuzzi's page adds a detail that explains what the photographs show. She describes appropriating the orange color recognizable across Alibaba's platforms for the identity, to evoke a new geography of global trade and e-commerce.

The 2018 album holds 17 photographs by Tommy Köhlbrugge, and they show white rooms, a bed with built-in controls, shoes laid out on a blue mat, screens playing video and a large orange globe printed with trade routes and place names.

The orange is the exhibition's identity, which means orange in a photograph is evidence of the setting and not of any one project. Her page credits Köhlbrugge among several photographers, one of them Peter Cox, whose pictures Domus used.

blocks.x: 2019: Junk moves into the city

r: Dutch Design Week calls Junk the second chapter and one of the most striking exhibitions of the 2019 edition.

The article says eighteen projects were selected, half shown in the museum and the rest across the center of Eindhoven in places such as De Bijenkorf, Sissyboy and De Witte Dame, and that spreading the show let the makers seek a connection with the city.

It describes two projects in detail: Shahar Livne's study of the plastic life forms of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, which it says visitors explored in videos and recordings, and Noud Sleumer's atlas of the illegal e-waste trade, which it says is built from satellite images.
The article credits its museum photographs to Oscar Vinck and its two city photographs, at De Bijenkorf and at Hutspot, to Köhlbrugge.

The archive answers that spread with three albums: 20 photographs at the Van Abbemuseum, 7 at Bijenkorf and 6 at Hutspot, 33 in all, every title carrying Köhlbrugge's name and dates between October 19 and 27, 2019.

In the Bijenkorf album a shop window holds a scroll and three green neon waves. In the Hutspot album, rows of pink translucent sheets fill a window, and a banner there carries the word JUNK and the words GEO DESIGN.
DDW's caption names Alissa+Nienke for the Hutspot work.

That banner is the clearest tie between a photograph and the series in the whole archive, because the picture names itself. Most other photographs depend on the album title and the venue in the file name.
The sorting is the interesting part. Venue albums exist for Bijenkorf and Hutspot, while Sissyboy and De Witte Dame, named in the article, have no album among those I opened.
A reader who builds a timeline from the albums alone would think two city locations took part, and the article says more did.

blocks.x: 2020: Sand, and an exhibition with no room

r: The 2020 chapter was Sand. An e-flux announcement from the Academy calls it the third chapter, subtitled The Building Block of Modernity, and says it opened on October 17 at the Van Abbemuseum and would stay until November 15, 2020, with nine research-based projects and one long-term research, curated by Muzi.

DDW's article on Sand names several of the projects. Landscope, by Romain Laval and Baiba Soma, looks at sand extraction in Morocco. Nine Dragons, by Bich Tran, concerns river-sand extraction in the Mekong delta. Mica-belt, by Matteo Dal Lago, concerns mineral mining in India.
The article closes with a tribute to Atelier NL's long-running sand research, shown as To See a World in a Grain of Sand, a collection of sand grains sent to the designers from all over the world.
The archive's album for Sand holds 10 photographs by Max Kneefel, and DDW's article credits its own Sand photographs to Max Kneefel too.
In the album are a cabinet of bottles and a photo wall with a long row of glass vessels.
The article's description of Atelier NL's sample collection makes a match plausible, but nothing ties those photographs to that project, so I do not say they are the same.

The same announcement presents the fourth chapter, GEO-DESIGN: COVID-19, as an online exhibition that interlinks eight original projects developed by alumni from June to September 2020, curated by Muzi.
It also announces an online archive of all earlier projects.
The Academy's page calls COVID-19 the fourth episode.
The archive has no album for it, which is what you would expect for something made for a screen. I tried to open the archive site, and its security certificate had expired, so I did not use it.

blocks.x: 2021: Budget Airlines

r: The 2021 edition, GEO-DESIGN: Budget Airlines, We Are All The Jet Set, ran from October 9 to November 14, 2021 at the Van Abbemuseum, according to the Academy. During Dutch Design Week it was open with a DDW ticket only, and afterwards with museum entry.
The Academy's page lists nine research projects, each with its alumni makers, and credits Muzi as curator and Cinzia Bongino with the graphic identity.
One of the nine, For FAQs Sake by The Ironing Board, is described as the exhibition's help center.

The archive's 2021 album has 8 photographs by Köhlbrugge, among them a lit poster that reads Budget Airlines, an All gates sign, an airplane lavatory and a sculpture with a sign that reads OVERSIZED BAGGAGE DO NOT FEED.
The Academy credits its own photographs to Peter Cox.
A caption that names the project behind the baggage sculpture would claim more than the titles support, because they do not link a photograph to a project.
The Academy's page does not number this edition. The chapter numbers I can document run from one to four, and 2021 would be the fifth, but no page I opened says so.

blocks.x: Whose photographs, and who credits them

r: Four editions yield six albums and 68 photographs.
The archive credits Köhlbrugge for 58 of the 68 and Kneefel for the 10 from 2020.

Meanwhile, the designer of the 2018 identity credits Cox, Marcel de Buck, Köhlbrugge and Nicole Marnati; DDW's Junk article credits Vinck and Köhlbrugge; the Academy's Budget Airlines page credits Cox.
A caption writer has to decide which credit belongs under which picture, and the sources rarely overlap, except where the same photographer appears in both the archive and the organizer's page.

blocks.x: What an album structure can say

r: The count is a record of what the archive chose to keep and how it sorted it. It does not tell me how many projects each year held, and it cannot show a digital edition.
The Academy's own count of projects is more complete: nine for Alibaba, eighteen for Junk, nine plus one for Sand, eight for COVID-19 and nine for Budget Airlines.
That sums to 54 projects across the five chapters, against 68 photographs in the archive, so the albums cover each chapter thinly.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know which project any photograph shows, apart from the Hutspot banner. I did not read the museum's own pages for Alibaba and Junk, because they no longer open.
I could not confirm the full list of 2019 city locations. I did not read the project-level archive for any chapter, and I do not know whether the 2021 chapter has a number.
Nothing I opened says what happened to the exhibition series after 2021, or how the master's program's own graduation work relates to it.

Nothing I opened gives the total number of alumni projects across the chapters. If a series can move into a shop window and then onto a screen, what should its archive record: the objects, the places or the question the series asked?
Next time you read a photo archive, check which of those three it is sorted by, and say so in your caption.

posts.title: The Grand Opening of Dutch Design Week: a ceremony that changes rooms, read through six photo albums
posts.subtitle: The official photo archive holds opening albums for 2015, 2016, 2017, 2022, 2023 and 2025. DDW's own pages, a ticket page and press fill in the venues, hosts and dates.
posts.seoTitle: The Grand Opening of Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Where Dutch Design Week opened in 2010, 2022, 2023 and 2025, what the PRO page says about 2024, and what the 2015 to 2025 photo albums leave out.

r: The Grand Opening is the one Dutch Design Week event that is a press moment, a party and a ceremony at once, and the official photo archive files it under three different names across ten years.
The Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds opening albums for 2015, 2016, 2017, 2022, 2023 and 2025: six editions and 181 photographs.

DDW's own news and press pages describe three of those evenings, a ticket page describes a fourth, and a few outside sources fill in the rest. This essay draws on public sources only. It reports no visit and no conversation, and it says nothing about the 2026 opening, which these sources do not describe.

blocks.x: An event that moves around

r: The first thing the record shows is that there is no fixed home. In 2010, when Core77 reported the opening of what it called the 9th edition, the official kick-off took place in the recently renovated Klokgebouw, a former Philips factory building, with guest speakers, premieres of new Dutch design, drinks and live music by a local rock band.
Twelve years later DDW's page puts the opening at MYLC, De Caai, and a year after that at the Area 51 skate park.

DomusDELA is a rebuilt complex of the Paterskerk, the Augustinianum and the Studentenkapel in Eindhoven, and Omroep Brabant reported in autumn 2020 that its brasserie, hotel and congress center had opened at the end of 2019.
The opening moved from a factory hall to a skate hall to a converted church complex. That is my reading of the sequence of sources, not a statement from any of them.

blocks.x: The ticket page also describes an opening

r: DDW's PRO ticket page, whose text describes the 2024 edition, lists access to the Grand Opening as a benefit. It says the Grand Opening takes place on the evening of Friday, October 18, and that after buying the ticket the holder receives an email with an RSVP link, because a place must be reserved in advance for the official part of the event.
October 18 was the day before the first public day, Saturday, October 19, 2024.
I found no DDW news item, press release or album describing that evening, so I know its date and its access rule and not its venue, hosts or program.

blocks.x: 2015 to 2017: parties and halls with no stated venue

r: The 2015 album is titled WHAT THE IF?! Official #DDW15 Opening Party and holds 20 photographs, eight credited to Nick Bookelaar and twelve to Max Kneefel in the titles, with dates of October 17 and 18, 2015.
ABN AMRO's page of that year gives exhibition dates of October 17 to 25, 2015, which fits a party on the first days of the week.
The album calls it a party, and I have no DDW page that calls it the Grand Opening, so I describe it as the opening party.
The 2016 album is titled Grand Opening DDW and has 16 photographs credited to Jeroen van der Wielen, with no date or venue in the titles.

DDW16 ran October 22 to 30, 2016, and DDW's press page says Queen Máxima visited the festival on Tuesday, October 25, 2016, touring the Klokgebouw and two exhibitions and talking with designers on the Ketelhuisplein.
That was a visit during the week, not the opening, and I do not match it to any album.
The 2017 album, again titled Grand Opening DDW, has 35 photographs by van der Wielen, and its titles read DDW Opening 2017_10_21.
Innovation Origins' announcement of the theme says the 16th Dutch Design Week took place from Saturday, October 21 to Sunday, October 29, 2017, and the theme was Stretch.
The titles' date is therefore the first day of the week.
Photographs in the album show a screen carrying the word STRETCH, which fits the theme.
I found no source that names the 2017 venue.

blocks.x: 2018 to 2021: the years without an album

r: The archive has no opening album for 2018, 2019, 2020 or 2021, and the written record explains little. For 2019, a DDW welcome item describes nine days, about 2,600 designers and more than 100 locations, and mentions no opening event.
The 2020 edition was a mostly online festival: Core77 reported on October 16, 2020 that it would open the next day, Saturday, October 17, with more than 500 3D viewing rooms, talks and a live studio.
For 2018 and 2021 I found no source about an opening at all. An absent album proves nothing about whether an event took place.

blocks.x: 2022: Get Set, a speech and a farewell

r: DDW's page titled DDW22 Grand Opening says the opening took place at MYLC, De Caai, hosted by Jess Øberlin of the collective PLASMA and the DDW chairman Jennifer Muntslag. It says the new Creative Head, Miriam van der Lubbe, explained the theme Get Set, and that Gunay Uslu, State Secretary of Education, Culture and Science, spoke about giving space to creativity, designers and makers.

The same page reports that van der Lubbe thanked Martijn Paulen for his dedication to DDW and the design field, that Øberlin talked with the ambassadors Marjan van Aubel and Formafantasma, and that a PLASMA afterparty followed.
Photographs on the page and in the album are credited to about.today.
The page is dated October 22, 2022 and begins by saying that the opening was "last night."

That puts the opening on the evening of Friday, October 21, 2022, the night before the first public day, and not on October 22 as a quick reading of the date would suggest. I have no second source for the date.

blocks.x: 2023: Picture This in a skate hall

r: The 2023 page says the Grand Opening was held "in the heart of the skate park at Area 51," hosted by Lynn Zebeda and Cesar Majorana, with a takeover by The New Originals and guests including Phantom Wizard, Fumez, Sokarekta and TNO Sound.

It records that van der Lubbe introduced the theme Picture This, that the year's DDW beacons were Stefan Diez, the founders of Muzus (Sanne and Neele Kistemaker) and Yinka Ilori, and that Cesar Majorana talked with Eindhoven's mayor, Jeroen Dijsselbloem.
Photographs are credited to Lotte Dale.
This page is dated October 21, 2023, the first public day, and says DDW23 "has officially begun." It does not say which evening the opening was held, so I cannot give the date of the event.
Area 51 is also where DDW's PRO ticket page puts the Business Lounge and the wristband exchange, which I cover in the Business Lounge essay.
Queen Máxima came to DDW during the 2023 week. HKU reported that she visited its Class of 23 exhibition on Thursday, October 26, 2023.
Omroep Brabant later wrote that 2023 was the last time before 2025 that she had attended.

blocks.x: 2025: a ribbon, a queen and a church-like hall

r: A DDW press release said Queen Máxima would open the 25th edition on Thursday evening, October 16, 2025. It says she would first visit the exhibition Bridging Minds at the Van Abbemuseum, then join Miriam van der Lubbe in conversation at DomusDELA on the value of Dutch design, and afterward officially open the festival.
DDW25 itself ran October 18 to 26, 2025, so the opening came two days before the public did.

Omroep Brabant reported that the queen first opened Philips' new headquarters in Amsterdam that Thursday afternoon, then traveled to Eindhoven and appeared on stage in a colorful outfit to open the 25th edition.
The 2025 album has 45 photographs credited in their titles to Bracket Studio, and the ones I viewed show a church-like hall with tall arches and chandeliers lit in blue, teal and magenta.
That fits DomusDELA's rebuilt Paterskerk, but no source says which hall of the complex the photographs show, so I leave it as a fit and not a finding.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The page is dated October 22 and says the opening was last night, so the event was on the evening of October 21. The page's own words settled it.
The page is dated October 21 and does not name the evening. Unsettled.

DDW's press archive calls the 2024 festival its 23rd edition, and its 2025 release calls the next one the 25th. Core77 called 2010 the 9th and Innovation Origins called 2017 the 16th, which fit a first edition in 2002.

The 2025 number, which fits a first edition in 2001, is the odd one out. Both 2024 and 2025 cannot be literally right if every year had one edition, and I could not find a DDW page that explains the count. I use the number each source gives and attribute it.

The 2015 album calls its event an official opening party, the 2016 and 2017 albums call theirs Grand Opening, and DDW's pages for 2022 to 2025 use "opening" or "Grand Opening." These may be the same kind of event under changing names, and I do not claim they are.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know the venue of the 2015, 2016 or 2017 openings, the date of the 2023 opening, or anything about openings in 2018, 2019, 2021 and 2024 beyond the PRO page's date for 2024. I do not know who attended any of them besides those the pages name. I found no source for what MYLC is. I could not read Eindhoven News' reports from 2018 because the site no longer serves them, and I could not read Dezeen's coverage because its server refused access. The album facts are from my reading of the Flickr account on October 7, 2026, which I did not repeat.
When a festival opens in a different room every year, which would you rather keep: the guest list, the room or the date?

posts.title: Guest academies at Dutch Design Week: four foreign schools in a former Philips warehouse
posts.subtitle: Nine albums from 2017 to 2019 and what the schools' own pages, DDW's magazine, a student interview and an architect's record say about who showed what in the Veem.
posts.seoTitle: Guest academies at Dutch Design Week, 2014 to 2021
posts.description: Burg Giebichenstein, Central Saint Martins, ECAL and Bauhaus-Universität Weimar at Dutch Design Week, and the Philips warehouse that hosted them.

r: Four foreign design schools turn up in the Dutch Design Week photo archive, and a closer look shows that each left a different kind of paper trail.

I like a guest because it shows what a host looks like from outside, and a school is a guest that returns with new students every year. This essay asks what the nine guest-academy albums from 2017 to 2019 can be matched to, using the schools' own pages, a DDW magazine article, a student interview, a university excursion program and an architect's record of the building. It reports no visit and no interview, and it names no student.

blocks.x: The building: a Philips warehouse that was a parking garage

r: The albums name a place as often as a school: the titles of the Burg and ECAL photos in 2017 and the Burg and Bauhaus photos in 2018 say VEEM.

DDW's own 2019 magazine piece calls VEEM one of the three main locations curated by DDW, with Klokgebouw and Ketelhuisplein, and describes a monumental building that is a parking garage for the rest of the year, entered by a long ramp.

The architects who rebuilt it, Caruso St John, describe the Veemgebouw as a former Philips factory building on Strijp-S, and quote the Architects Journal calling it a listed 1940s warehouse in the former Philips complex.
The rebuild, completed in 2022 according to the architects, gave the building workspaces on the upper floors, a car park and a food hall on the ground floor and 38 rooftop homes.

So the four schools showed in a building that was in its last years in the form DDW's magazine describes. The 2019 article adds that the Dutch Invertuals collective, which was celebrating its tenth anniversary, held the art direction for VEEM that year and turned it into an industrial exhibition space.

The guests were not alone in the building. A university excursion program for October 2017 lists, besides Weimar and Halle, Crafts Council Nederland, Plaatsmaken & Grind the Gap and the Dutch Design Awards at the Veem.
In 2018 the KABK alumni guide places Crafts Council Nederland's HOW&WOW studio there, with participants symbolically moving their workshops into the building.

In 2019 DDW's article names representatives of Dutch schools such as Creative Craftsman and KABK, and students from the Royal College of Art, Burg Giebichenstein, Aalto University and Central Saint Martins.
The Veem is still a DDW location in 2026: DDW lists VEEM floor 8, home of Manifestations, at Torenallee 100, October 17 to 25, fully wheelchair accessible.
DDW also tells readers that the week grows more international every year, with more foreign academies taking part.
That sentence is the organizer's claim about the whole festival, and the Veem is where it can be checked at the level of single schools.

blocks.x: Burg Giebichenstein: a diary of seven years

r: The school in Halle, Germany, has the longest written record. It announced that its students would make their premiere at DDW 2014 with Materials and Making at the Burg, ten selected projects at the Klokgebouw, October 18 to 26, 2014.
In 2016 almost 20 of its students took part through the Burg Roadshow in the 9 Days of Making exhibition, and a page about the trip carries a photo captioned Veemgebouw.
In 2017 nine projects were shown in a curated exhibition called Mastering the Material, from October 21 to 29, and the school describes DDW as one of the yearly stops of the Roadshow program.

The 2018 page says the school was at DDW for the fifth year in a row, which agrees with a first appearance in 2014. It names ten students and alumni at two locations, the theme Immaterial - Ultramaterial at the stand on the second floor of the Veem and the Rotor 3D light installation in the Area 51 basement, and lists the disciplines: industrial design, fashion design, textile design and interior architecture, plus ceramics and jewelry. It describes DDW 2018 as the largest design festival in northern Europe, with more than 2,600 designers and 335,000 visitors, under the title If not us, then who?, and says the festival has existed since 2002.

DDW's 2019 article describes the school's last archived show. Eight practical experiments explored how human civilization should reposition itself on the planet, through dialogues with animals, speculative scenarios, unstable matter and artworks looking for an identity, and a robot called Fiffy helped visitors take the first steps toward alternative solutions.
The 2019 album holds 17 photos, and a sign in one reads Meet the future ...and Fiffy the robot.

blocks.x: Central Saint Martins: a collective that returns every year

r: DDW's 2019 article says that in the VEEM, Central Saint Martins presented United Matters, a one-time collective named for the master's graduates of Material Futures who work at the edge of craft, science and technology.
The program entry says United Matters is a London-based collective of Central Saint Martins graduates from MA Material Futures.
A 2020 entry describes a collective of graduates from MA Material Futures 2020, and a 2021 entry says that for the fifth year United Matters would be part of DDW with the 2021 graduates.
Next Nature Network repeated that fifth year in a row.

Five years counted back from 2021 puts the first appearance in 2017, if every year counts, and 2020 was a virtual festival. That would make the archive's 2017 album titled Central Saint Martins and its 2018 album titled MA Material Futures the first two United Matters shows, although neither album names the collective.
I give that as an inference from the count, not as a caption. In the 2018 album a panel is headed Wine Matters, which no page I opened explains.

blocks.x: Bauhaus-Universität Weimar: a student show, found by a magazine

r: For the Weimar university I had only an album title and a sign until a German design site published an interview with the student group in 2017. Six students from a project called Design a sustainable value chain, supervised by a visiting researcher, Tjeerd Veenhoven, and a bachelor graduate, showed experimental material studies. They said the idea came at the end of the previous semester, that the exhibition was realized through student initiative, and that they were on floor 3 of the Veemgebouw.
A university excursion program for October 21 to 24, 2017 independently lists Bauhaus Uni Weimar and Burg Giebichenstein Uni Halle among the visits at the Veem.
The project names in that interview line up with what the 2017 album shows, which the October 8 read describes as fiber and sheet material samples, a helmet and jackets on stands.
The interview mentions a raincoat made from biodegradable paper, a fireproof jacket and gloves from basalt fiber, grown textiles made into two jackets and a dress, and a chitosan study.

I read the match as likely and not certain, since no photo title names a project. The 2018 album of 13 photos, titled with VEEM, has a sign for the Bachelor of Arts graduates of 2018 in Product Design and Visual Communication, and I found no page about that show.

blocks.x: ECAL: one page, one aisle

r: ECAL in Lausanne says that from October 21 to 29, 2017 it presented ECAL Graphic Design, an exhibition of projects by students of its Bachelor Graphic Design and its Master Art Direction.
The archive's ECAL album has five photos, dated October 24, 2017 in the titles and titled VEEM, showing printed posters on perforated panels along an aisle.
That is a page, a date and a place that agree, and nothing more than that.

blocks.x: What the nine albums can prove

r: The archive holds nine albums and 90 photos, all credited to Max Kneefel: four albums in 2017 with 7, 7, 9 and 5 photos, three in 2018 with 13, 7 and 13, and two in 2019 with 17 and 12.
The 2017 photo titles carry the date October 24, 2017, which settles two albums whose ids looked misfiled.
Set against the written record, the picture is uneven. Burg Giebichenstein has a page and an album for 2017, 2018 and 2019, and pages for 2014 and 2016 besides.
Central Saint Martins has an entry for 2019, a count that points back to 2017 and albums for 2017 and 2018.
Weimar has a magazine interview for 2017 and a sign for 2018.

A title can prove a date and a place. It cannot show the course, the brief or the people, and a school's page rarely lines up with a Flickr title. When I caption a photograph from a visiting school, I want the school's name, the year and the exhibit each to have its own source, and I want to say so when one is empty.

blocks.x: Questions the sources settle

r: Three earlier doubts have answers. Whether the Bauhaus albums belong to Weimar: the 2017 interview and the excursion program both name Weimar.
When Burg Giebichenstein started: its own 2014 page says 2014, which fits the fifth year in 2018.
Whether the archive's Central Saint Martins albums for 2017 and 2018 are the same collective as in 2019: a fifth-year count says they probably are.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what Bauhaus-Universität Weimar showed in 2018, what the Wine Matters panel belonged to, or whether any of these schools came back after 2019 under the same banner, apart from United Matters, which DDW lists in 2020 and 2021.

I did not find a record of why these four are the only guest schools with albums, since DDW's 2019 article lists others, including the Royal College of Art and Aalto University, that have none in this set.
I also do not know how the DDW art direction of VEEM, credited to Dutch Invertuals in 2019, worked in 2017 and 2018.
If you open one of these albums, which of the three lines, school, year or exhibit, would your own captions fail on first?

posts.title: HeyHeydeHaas and Biki90 at Dutch Design Week: a bamboo square, a bar with a new host each night, and a coin track in a studio
posts.subtitle: From a bamboo maze on the Ketelhuisplein in 2016 to a coin track at the studio in 2019, the pages give three kinds of place and the photo archive gives four albums of very different size.
posts.seoTitle: HeyHeydeHaas and Biki90 at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: HeyHeydeHaas and Biki90 at Dutch Design Week 2016 to 2019: the bamboo installation, the Inwisselbar, a museum commission and a coin track, read against the photo archive.

r: HeyHeydeHaas filled a square with bamboo in 2016, ran a bar in the middle of it for two Dutch Design Weeks, and by 2019 had moved its Dutch Design Week project into its own studio, and the photo archive records each of those years at a different size.

I like a project that changes scale from year to year, because it shows what an archive keeps and what it drops. This essay draws on public sources only: the agency's own pages, a profile from 2016, regional and local news, a bamboo studio, a heater maker, an Italian design magazine, DDW's own magazine pages and the official photo archive on Flickr as I recorded it on October 8, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about 2026 beyond what a tourism page lists for the square.

blocks.x: Who the two names are

r: HeyHeydeHaas calls itself a Dutch creative agency based in Eindhoven and operating worldwide, working on design, brand and identity development in both physical and digital work, and describes its approach as research-, insight- and instinct-driven.
In November 2016 a regional business site ran a profile in its Share the Vibe series under the line "three people, one agency," naming Erik Sjouerman, Elske van der Putten and Eric de Haas.
In the profile de Haas says Eindhoven leaves much room for randomness and that designers coming up from below had lifted the city in recent years.
That is his opinion, given to a journalist, and the same page is the only source I opened that gives the agency's size.

Biki90 is harder to place. A project page by the designer Guy Verbeek, one of its members, says Biki90 is an Eindhoven-based collective that "started off in 192005" as friends kicking local parties, that more people joined and the parties grew, and that the yellow illuminated letters that lit its venues were damaged, which led him to start a "partymachine project."
The page credits Labolleur for materials and frame-building, Maikel Engels for organizing and transport, De Vinyl Snijderij for last-minute milling, and Max Kneefel for the photography.
I cannot read "192005" as a date, and I do not guess one. I could not find a Biki90 page of its own, because its former website now shows something else.

The regional broadcaster Omroep Brabant joins the two names. Its tips for the 2016 festival, published on October 21, 2016, describe the Inwisselbar as a large bamboo promenade with a cafe at its glowing center and a different host every day, and call it a collaboration between the Eindhoven concept developers of HeyHeydeHaas and Biki90.
It is one outside source, and I would keep the wording as a report and not as a fact the two groups have confirmed.

The agency's home page lists other projects that show the range around the three at Dutch Design Week: a publication for MozFest called How to MozFest, an installation for the STRP festival 2019 made with Desirée Hammen and Pol Tijssen as part of the festival's identity, brand identity and research-based web archives for a pair of long-term partners, a script and copy project made with an animator, and entries labeled St. Joost School of Art & Design, AtelierNL, Het Zuidelijk Toneel, MU and Stedelijk Museum, which carry no description in the text I read.
I list them to show that a bar, a bamboo maze and a coin track are a small part of a long list, and that the page gives no dates for most of the others.

blocks.x: 2016: a bamboo maze on the festival's central square

r: DDW's own magazine calls the Ketelhuisplein the beating heart of the festival, one of three main locations curated by DDW, with Klokgebouw and VEEM.

That text was written for the 2019 edition. In 2016 the square's curated theme was sustainability: Omroep Brabant wrote on October 28, 2016 that the Ketelhuisplein had been turned into a large exhibition on that theme, with the main installation Agri meets Design bringing farmers and designers together in four installations, among them one about the egg economy called The EGGCHANCE.
The bamboo and the bar sat in the same square, and the broadcaster's text does not mention them.

The agency's site says its Bamboolala was an open-air installation within the art direction of the Ketelhuisplein during Dutch Design Week 2016, commissioned by the Dutch Design Foundation, and that the bamboo scaffolding connected the participants on the square and turned the open space into a maze of bamboo and design.

Neon Moire's festival guide of October 13, 2016 lists it as Bambooh Lala, October 22 to 30, 11:00 to 22:00, a "never finished" bamboo construction that would connect everything and everyone on the square, with the Inwisselbar at its center hosting a different party each night between 5 and 8 in the evening.

The bamboo was built by a partner. Studio Jeroen Wand writes that for the agency's Bamboohlala it filled the Ketelhuisplein with bamboo structures for a festival vibe, thanks its team of Daan Hesseling, Wouter Corvers, Ellis Holman and Roy de Regt, and opens with the words "Again we did an amazing project with HeyHeydeHaas," so the two had worked together before 2016.
The studio's page credits Sam Walravens for the photographs.
Jeroen Wand has his own entry in this series.
The installation has three spellings in three sources: Bamboolala on the agency's site, Bambooh Lala in the festival guide and Bamboohlala on the bamboo studio's page.
I use the agency's spelling because it is the maker's own, and I tell a reader about the others so they can search for them.

The archive has two albums for 2016. The old dossier counts 26 photographs in the one titled for the Inwisselbar and 9 in one titled Biki90: The making of a hangover, whose full title adds Official opening party, and says the 9 photographs show a silent disco in a decorated hall with colored headphones, DJs and a crowd, with no photographer named.
I found no page that describes that party, and DDW's pages I opened say nothing about it.

The Inwisselbar album shows bamboo scaffolding under a tent roof, signs reading Bambooh La La and DDW Music Lab, and a bar banner that reads "Iedere dag een andere party," every day another party, with a host listed for each day.
The music lab sign has an explanation in DDW's own words: its press page of September 14, 2016 says a special stage would be built on the Ketelhuisplein for the DDW Music Lab.

blocks.x: 2017: the bar without the bamboo

r: A heater maker's news item, published on October 23, 2017, says the company warmed the Ketelhuisplein during Dutch Design Week from October 21 to 29 in collaboration with the Inwisselbar, with wood stoves creating a cozy place and a lit fire.
It adds that at the end of each day the Inwisselbar would open the evening with music, a drink and a special guest, as the perfect lead-in to the DDW Music performances.
The page names neither the agency nor Biki90, and it does not mention bamboo.
The archive's 2017 album carries both names in its title and holds 34 photographs, the largest of the four.

The title is how I link the 2017 bar to the two groups, and I would say so in a caption. The photographs are dated October 23 and 27, 2017 and show a yellow umbrella tent with string lights, wood stoves, a food truck and a clock whose dial spells Inwisselbar, so the bar is confirmed for that year. Titles dated October 23 name OWOW x Hutspot, one of the nightly hosts.

OWOW, the Omnipresent World of Wizkids, is also named in DDW's 2017 wrap-up as the collective behind a dance evening at the Effenaar, which is the same week and the same collective name, though no page I opened ties the bar's night to that event.

blocks.x: 2018: a museum, a website and no album

r: The archive has no album for 2018, and the record is not empty for that year. The Italian magazine Domus reported on October 12, 2018 on A Balancing Act, a group exhibition at Kunsthal KAdE in Amersfoort that ran from September 15, 2018 to January 6, 2019, and its image captions list HeyHeydeHaas, 50/50, 2018 among the installations.
The agency's site says the 50/50 coin track was commissioned by Kunsthal KAdE in 2018.
Two sources, then, agree on a museum commission in 2018, and the museum show sits outside Dutch Design Week.

The agency also left a mark on another lab in this series. Baltan Laboratories' post of December 22, 2017 says its new website was developed by the team of Heyheydehaas, and the page for Baltan's Frankenstein Symposium on October 22, 2018 credits its header image to HeyHeydeHaas.
A design agency can be present at Dutch Design Week through other people's pages, and the archive's album titles will not show it.

blocks.x: 2019: a coin track in a studio

r: The agency's site describes 50/50 as an enormous coin track: 80 meters of custom-made, clear, recycled acrylic track whose only purpose is to carry 50 cent coins from one point to another. It says the piece was on display during Dutch Design Week 2019 at the HeyHeydeHaas studio, with free entrance and 50 cents as the price of taking part.
The studio's address on the same site is Gashouder 30 in Eindhoven.

The 2019 album titled HeyHeydeHaas holds only 6 photographs by Iris Rijskamp, and the old dossier says they show a track of clear acrylic tubes in a studio and a small sign reading 50 eurocent only, which matches the agency's description of the coin track, with visitors including children on a scaffold.
DDW's 2019 magazine page about the Ketelhuisplein does not mention the agency, and the 2019 square was devoted to sustainable architecture and society.
In 2019 the agency's Dutch Design Week project was not on the square at all.

blocks.x: What a small archive can carry

r: Four albums, 75 photographs and three kinds of place: a public square, the same square a year later and a private studio.
The sizes run from 6 photographs to 34, and the largest album belongs to the bar.
That fits a festival archive that follows crowds, but it also means the quietest project here, the coin track, has the fewest pictures.

A timeline built from the albums alone would say the work peaked in 2017. The text sources say something else. In 2016 the festival organizer commissioned the installation, in 2018 a museum commissioned a piece that never appeared at the festival, and in 2019 the same piece was shown at the agency's own studio.
The albums record a camera's attention and not the size of a commission.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: Omroep Brabant says HeyHeydeHaas and Biki90 together. The agency's own page claims the bamboo installation and does not mention the bar or Biki90. The albums' titles carry both names. I attribute the bar to the pair as a report and the bamboo to the agency.
Whether the 2017 bar was the same project.
The heater maker's page names only the Inwisselbar. The album title names both groups. I treat the link as the archive's, and I do not claim the 2017 bar was a new commission.

The agency's site says Kunsthal KAdE commissioned it in 2018, and Domus lists it in the 2018 show there. The agency says it stood at its studio in 2019. These are two showings of one piece, and they do not conflict.
Nothing first-party was found. The collective's start date is written as 192005 on one member's page, and I leave it unread.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what the 2016 Official DDW opening party was beyond its album title and photographs, who the hosts of each night's Inwisselbar were in 2016 or 2017, or whether Biki90 describes itself as a partner in the bamboo. I do not know whether the 2017 bar was a HeyHeydeHaas and Biki90 commission, because the one page about it names neither. I did not find a DDW program page for the bamboo, the bar or the opening party. The agency's own pages do not mention the bar at all.
I did not reopen the photo archive, so the album counts, dates, titles and what the photographs show come from the dossier's October 8, 2026 reading and should be checked again before posting.

I do not know why there is no 2018 album, and nothing I opened says what the agency will show in 2026. A tourism page of October 1, 2026 mentions a pop-up spot called The Bar on the Ketelhuisplein for this year's week, and no source ties it to the Inwisselbar.
When a project has two names on it, which source would you ask first about who made what, and which one would you trust last?

posts.title: HOW&WOW at Dutch Design Week: a craft council, a Philips warehouse and a plinth label
posts.subtitle: Crafts Council Nederland's own record from masterclasses in 2014 to WOW NATURE in 2026, read against what the Dutch Design Week photo archive holds.
posts.seoTitle: HOW&WOW at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Crafts Council Nederland at Dutch Design Week, 2014 to 2026: masterclasses, three HOW&WOW editions at VEEM, flax, baskets and WOW NATURE.

r: Crafts Council Nederland was at Dutch Design Week years before it had a show called HOW&WOW, and by its own list the show with that name began in 2017.

I like evidence that is small and checkable, because it shows how far a caption can honestly go, and the most useful evidence in the HOW&WOW photo archive is a white label on a teal plinth. This essay draws on public sources only: the pages Crafts Council Nederland keeps for each of its presentations, Dutch Design Week's own 2026 listing, a building page from Strijp-S, the national monument register and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibit beyond what the listings say.

blocks.x: A council for craft, founded in 2012

r: Crafts Council Nederland, which I will call CCNL, says on its About page that it was founded in 2012 and is the platform for creative craftsmanship. Its stated mission is to connect makers to socially urgent themes, and it lists five goals, from supporting makers to mapping and passing on craft knowledge, enabling research, offering a stage and encouraging crafts in other sectors.
The page adds that it follows the Cultural Governance, Diversity and Inclusion and Fair Practice codes.
Its presentation index says it presents excellent makers every year at Dutch Design Week, and lists items from 2014 to 2025, with WOW NATURE for 2026.
That index changes the starting point of this story.

blocks.x: Before HOW&WOW: masterclasses, a map and indigo

r: CCNL's 2014 page says masterclasses had already run during Dutch Design Week 2013 and that in 2014 (October 18 to 26) Etsy, CCNL and the Fonds voor Cultuurparticipatie, with the Center for Folklore and Intangible Heritage, offered nine daily masterclasses called Meet the Master. The masters taught laminating wood, painting Delftware, Staphorst dot painting, papermaking, gold embroidery, stained glass design, hat-making, weaving and felting.
The same page describes Dutch Darlings, a competition for contemporary souvenirs based on traditional Dutch techniques.
In 2015 the page says the online Craftsmap, a search engine for makers, was presented to the public for the first time at the festival, with an offline version on the theme of glass.
In 2016, CCNL sent four maker-designers to Kyushu, Japan, to study indigo dyeing with Japanese masters in September, and presented the results at Kazerne in Eindhoven from October 22 to 30, 2016.
One of the four, Adrianus Kundert, returns later in this story.
So CCNL's HOW&WOW had three earlier formats at the festival: a teaching program, a map and an exchange. None of them is in the photo archive under CCNL's name as far as I read it.

blocks.x: The building: a warehouse with a national monument number

r: CCNL's pages place HOW&WOW in 2017, 2018 and 2019 at Veem, or VEEM, on Strijp-S.

Strijp-S says the Veemgebouw was built during World War II as a Philips warehouse, that the developer Trudo acquired it in 2009, that several floors host pop-up exhibitions during Dutch Design Week, and that three layers with 39 homes were added in 2021.

The national monument register is more exact. It dates the Veemgebouw to 1942, to a design by the Philips engineering bureau with expressionist elements, and lists it as part of the Philips complex on Strijp-S.
A craft show about hands and materials therefore stood in a concrete industrial warehouse, and neither source comments on the contrast. I note it and leave it there.

blocks.x: 2017 to 2019: three editions at VEEM

r: The 2017 page says CCNL curated the show and that it presented exceptional making processes and current developments in creative craft. It lists no makers and credits photography to Theodoor Adriaans.

The 2018 page is titled HOW&WOW, Studio at VEEM. It names 25 makers and groups, among them Agustina Bottoni, Boris de Beijer, Sara Ricciardi and the weaving company De Ploeg, and credits photography to Adriaans and Max Kneefel.

The 2019 page gives the dates, October 19 to 27, 2019, and describes HOW&WOW as an initiative of CCNL in collaboration with Dutch Design Foundation, made possible in part by the Fonds voor Cultuurparticipatie and Forbo. It names 38 participants, including a museum, a flooring company that is also a funder and the exhibition design studio, Studio ZwartFrame, with graphic design by Daniël Maarleveld.
Its one-sentence description of the show runs from wood carving to polyurethane casting, from emerging makers to seasoned artisans.

The photo archive holds one album per edition, with 14, 25 and 25 photographs, 64 in all, and the photographer Kneefel named in every title. The 2017 titles start with 20171022 and the page for the first photograph gives October 22, 2017. I read the albums in an earlier pass and did not reopen the account for this version, so every Flickr fact here is second-hand.

CCNL credits Adriaans for 2017 and Adriaans with Kneefel for 2018, while the archive credits Kneefel for every photograph. Both can be true, since the organizer and the festival could each have had a photographer, and no page explains the difference.

blocks.x: Where a label closes the gap

r: In 2018 the plinths carry names. One photograph shows a teal plinth with a large raffia piece, a purple woven vase, a dark chair frame and two small hanging baskets, and white letters on the plinth read Agustina Bottoni and Sara Ricciardi. Both are on CCNL's 2018 list.
Another shows two round plinths, one green with colored glass bowls and one purple, each carrying the name Boris de Beijer, who is also on the list.

Anatomy teaching left me with one habit: read the label before you trust the specimen. Here the habit pays off and also sets a limit. A label sits beside several objects, and the photograph does not show which object belongs to which name. For the Bottoni and Ricciardi plinth I cannot say whether the raffia belongs to one name and the baskets to the other. For the de Beijer plinths I can say the name is there and that one plinth holds glass bowls. That is a smaller claim than a caption usually makes, and it is the one the photograph supports.

blocks.x: 2020 and 2021: flax, then baskets

r: For 2020, CCNL describes HOW&WOW Linen as a group exhibition about flax and linen. A video series called HOW follows the crop from blue flowers in the polder to processing, and in WOW a group of makers interprets what they learned. It names 15 participants, funders including the Bankgiro Loterij Fonds and the Province of Gelderland, and credits an exhibition designer, a text writer and film maker.
The festival was largely online that year, and CCNL's page calls its presentation a special online edition.

The flax work did not stop. The Linen Project, which CCNL says it started with the ArtEZ master's program Practice Held in Common and which is based in Arnhem, had thirty stewards growing and processing flax from 2020, and CCNL presented stewards' work at Dutch Design Week 2021 and again in a 2024 show titled The Linen Economy.
A Linen Project show ran at Museum Arnhem from May 22 to June 16, 2024, as part of State of Fashion.

HOW&WOW BASK IT! followed in 2021, an initiative of CCNL with Adrianus Kundert, designer and co-founder of Basketclub. CCNL describes Basketclub as an Instagram community that Kundert and Jamie Wolfond founded during the pandemic, with a monthly emoji challenge. The page lists more than 40 participants, among them Hella Jongerius, Bertjan Pot, Sebastian Herkner and Simone Post, and it includes loans from the national basketry museum in Noordwolde.
One exhibit is a funeral basket of willow, another a rattle woven from seven willow twigs holding seven stones, and another a machine meant to weave three-dimensional volumes.
The page does not name the venue.
Kundert is a thread across these pages. He is one of the four makers CCNL sent to Japan in 2016, and he led the 2021 basketry edition with CCNL.

blocks.x: 2022 to 2024: from a map of makers to a school

r: In 2022 CCNL presented iAtelier, NEW CRAFTS, which it describes as bringing artisans and digital makers together for knowledge exchange, with 18 makers named and funding from the Creative Industries Fund NL and the Creative Europe program.

In 2023 the Crafts Academy exhibition ran from October 21 to 29 at Sectie C, Daalakkersweg 16, for 36 young makers who had learned calligraphy and decorative painting, embroidery, basket weaving and kite making in three Wereldmuseum locations.
In 2024 the exhibition (w)aardewerk gathered twelve contributors around sustainable futures for ceramics, curated by three CCNL staff, with exhibition design by Elvis Wesley.
These pages do not name the HOW&WOW title, and they show CCNL moving from showing makers to teaching them.

blocks.x: 2025 and 2026: 85 makers, then 40 and a landscape

r: In 2025 CCNL used the HOW&WOW name again for a catalog of 85 numbered makers, from bronze casting to glassblowing, with Forbo, Artek and Iittala as partners.
The last entry, [Re]value, spins, weaves and felts local wool and hemp and is linked to the Eindhoven design agency Envisions.
The page does not name the venue.
For 2026 the listing is WOW NATURE: 40 craft experts, October 17 to 25, free, 11:00 to 18:00, at De Fabriek, Baarsstraat 38, in the Hallenweg area.
The exhibition design is by Scheltens & Abbenes, whose composed still lifes the page cites, and it describes an artificial landscape assembled from craft objects made from natural materials.
The page asks what can still be considered natural, given how much of the Dutch environment is managed by people.

blocks.x: Who comes back

r: CCNL's pages let me count recurring names. By my count of the printed lists, 20 names appear in more than one edition among 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025. Babs van den Thillart, Saar Scheerlings and Rik van Veen each appear in three, and Esmé Hofman in 2019, 2021 and 2022.

A show that returns the same weavers, ceramic artists and basket makers across eight years gives a photograph archive a practical problem, because a photograph of a woven object in 2025 may show a method first seen in 2018, and the caption year says only when the picture was taken.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Who made what in the 2017 photographs: CCNL lists no makers for that year.
Which object a plinth label refers to when it stands beside several.
Where the 2021 and 2025 HOW&WOW shows stood. CCNL's pages do not say.
Why the archive credits Kneefel for every HOW&WOW photograph while CCNL credits other photographers for some years.
Whether DDW's archive holds photographs of HOW&WOW or WOW NATURE after 2019. I did not find them and could not reopen the account.

r: If you caption a craft photograph from this archive, three lines can carry the claim: the label in the picture, the title in the archive and the organizer's list. Which will you let carry the sentence, and what will you leave out when none can?

posts.title: In No Particular Order left a factory for a white museum room, and the fund that made it kept its own count
posts.subtitle: Four editions of a talent exhibition by the Creative Industries Fund NL at Dutch Design Week, read through the fund's own pages, the press and three albums
posts.seoTitle: In No Particular Order at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Four editions of the Creative Industries Fund NL talent show In No Particular Order, 2014 to 2017, set beside three photo albums.

r: The Dutch Design Week photo archive shows In No Particular Order moving from a raw industrial hall to a white museum room, and the way the pictures look changes with the room.

I like to start from what the pictures can show before I trust any caption. This essay draws on public sources only: the Creative Industries Fund NL's own announcements and talent platform, a Dutch industry news site that republished the fund's text, a Core77 report, a 2017 preview and the official photo archive on Flickr, including text visible inside the photographs. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 festival.

blocks.x: Who made it, and how many editions there were

r: The organizer is stated plainly in the fund's own pages. The Creative Industries Fund NL, known in Dutch as the Stimuleringsfonds Creatieve Industrie, is named as the initiator of the exhibition on its 2015 and 2016 announcements, and its talent platform lists four editions of In No Particular Order.

The platform says the first edition took place in the Schellens Factory during Dutch Design Week 2014, built on the questions of what makes someone a talent and how talent is shaped, with curator Agata Jaworska.

The fund's own page for it says the show presented recent work by 21 young creatives in architecture, design and e-culture who had received a year of support in 2013/2014, with an exhibition and a publication, and quotes Jaworska, an alumna of Design Academy Eindhoven, saying that there is no uncontroversial standard for what counts as a talent.
The second edition, in 2015, was staged in the Veem Building.
Core77 calls the 2015 show the second edition of a showcase of promising young Dutch designers, curated by Jaworska, which agrees.
The fund's announcement of October 2016 calls that year's show the third edition, and the platform describes the fourth edition at the Van Abbemuseum in 2017.

So the photo archive's three albums cover editions two to four. The first edition, in 2014, has no album with this name in the archive that I know of, and I did not search for 2014 photographs elsewhere.

blocks.x: What the fund pays for

r: The exhibition is a showcase for a grant. The fund says talent development is one of its five objectives, that about 30 highly promising designers and makers are selected each year for a stipend, and that the program includes coaching toward entrepreneurship and professionalism.
The talent platform adds that grants run for twelve months and that participants must have graduated within the last four years.
The grants cover new work such as research, materials, equipment and projects at home or abroad.

That matters for reading the photographs, because the exhibition does not show a curator's choice of the best young designers. It shows the results of one cohort's grant year, selected by an independent committee, and the fund says so in 2016.

blocks.x: 2015: thirty-six designers and a wall of image archives

r: The fund's announcement, republished by CLICKNL on September 18, 2015, says the exhibition showed the newest work and ways of working of 36 promising designers, makers and architects, opening on Saturday, October 17 at 1:00 p.m. in the Veemgebouw.

It says Jaworska asked each designer to assemble a collection of images and photographs that reveal their artistic vision and the development of their practice, and that a media wall showed their personal image archives.

The credits list the fund as initiator, Jaworska as curator, Rana Ghavami as editor, Studio Remco van Bladel and Andrea Spikker for graphic design, three interaction designers and Bendewerk for production.

Core77's November 16, 2015 gallery names five works from the show, which the archive's titles never do: Ricky van Broekhoven's Solid Vibration, Marjan van Aubel's Current Window, Mark Sturkenboom's Ark (Volume 2): Paradigm Shift, Bora Hong's Cosmetic Surgery Kingdom and Maurizio Montalti's The Growing Lab, Mycelia.
Core77 also places the exhibition in the Veemgebouw with the Dutch Design Awards exhibition and Transnatural.
The 2015 album holds 10 photographs by Nick Bookelaar, each titled Veemgebouw_expositie.
They show small screens on poles across a bare hall, nine round lenses with images of sea and sky, a lamp before a round white projection and a rainbow-colored projection on a wall.

The fund's description of a media wall of image archives fits the screens, but no page ties the screens in the photographs to that wall, and I do not say they are the same. The lamp is a candidate for the Sturkenboom lighting object that Core77 describes, and again nothing connects them.
Two of the 2015 photographs show faces on screens, and the carousel leaves them out, because a face on a screen is still a person's face and no title says whose it is.

blocks.x: 2016: thirty-two designers on the eighth floor

r: The fund's announcement of October 12, 2016 gives more detail than any other source. It says the fund presents the work of 32 young designers in In No Particular Order, the third edition of the annual talent showcase, curated by Jaworska, on the eighth floor of the Veemgebouw from October 22 to 30, 2016.
The designers came from all disciplines of the creative industries and were selected by an independent committee, and each received a year-long grant.

The announcement names all 32. Among them are the architecture studio KNOL, Elejan van der Velde, the digital-culture makers Karel van Laere and Polina Medvedeva, the textile designer Marjanne van Helvert, the product designers Olivier van Herpt and Sabine Marcelis, the biodesigner Teresa van Dongen and the food designer Chloé Rutzerveld.

It describes three of their works: van Helvert launched a publication at a symposium, KNOL made a mirror piece about what it calls modern loneliness, and van Dongen showed a light installation powered by living micro-organisms.
Jaworska's question that year, in her words as the announcement quotes them, was how emerging designers organize their practice and what it means to have one.
The announcement links that question to the Dutch Design Week theme The Making Of.
The fund's platform says the designers answered with audio recordings and sketches.
A program of artist talks, tours, performances and workshops ran on a stage nearby, and the fund also presented two other exhibitions, Intensive Care and Making School, on the same floor.
That last fact is a caution for the albums. The 2016 album holds 12 photographs by Bookelaar, and the fund's own announcement says the floor held three exhibitions.
A bench-filled hall or a large printed face in the album could belong to any of them, and the titles do not say.
In one 2016 photograph a translucent screen hangs in the hall with white text that reads het stimuleringsfonds creatieve industrie is, and the same words appear reflected backward on the floor.
The announcement confirms the fund's role in plain words, which makes the screen's unfinished sentence part of the exhibition's own branding.

Other 2016 photographs show a cube lined in blue-green plaster with one visitor facing a small screen, a visitor pressing both hands against a white frame in a black wall and a blue torpedo-shaped craft with a round fan at its tip.
The announcement's list of works does not tell me which, if any, of these is by a named designer.

blocks.x: 2017: a curator who was also a participant, and a show in a basement

r: The fund's retrospective, dated October 30, 2017, calls the 2017 show the fourth exhibition on talent development, held in the Studio of the Van Abbemuseum during Dutch Design Week, October 21 to 29, 2017.
It says the fund received about 5,000 design professionals and led 230 students on tours.

The fund's platform describes it as a collective statement on the plurality of contemporary design practice, with nine installations on the themes of Position, Inspiration, Working Environment, Representation, Money, Happiness, Language, Discourse and Market.
The curator was Jules van den Langenberg, who was himself a participant in the talent program in 2017.
In 2014 to 2016 the curator was Jaworska; in 2017 the curator came from the cohort.
The retrospective quotes him saying that, instead of showing individual projects or end products, the exhibition showed the back side of design practice in the basement of the museum.
I do not know whether the change of curator was a deliberate shift and no source says.

The retrospective describes how the nine installations were made. Each of the 32 participants contributed to each theme through characteristic objects and fragments, from their own clothes and chairs to prototypes and books that inspired them, and Van den Langenberg then invited nine thinkers and makers to build an installation from those collections.
For Position, each participant packed a suitcase of things they would take to found a new society, and Jurgen Bey opened several suitcases each day to build a visual dictionary.
For Representation, each participant gave a garment to the fashion designer Duran Lantink, who made three composite portraits, and a performance artist wore one of the outfits during the week.

For Working Environment, participants described and drew their ideal workspace, and the architect Anne Dessing, herself an alumna of the program, presented an analysis on a curtain whose folds link the sketches.
For Discourse, daily talks were held on chairs the participants had brought, placed on a floor by the artist Simon Becks.

Set that beside the 2017 album, and the fit is striking. The album's eight photographs, credited to Tommy Köhlbrugge, show a white room with suitcases and chairs on a floor, coats and a red cap on a wall, a tall curtain printed with small drawings, shelves of small photographs and rolls of colored tape on a white table.
Suitcases, garments, chairs and a drawn curtain are the kinds of objects the fund's text assigns to the Position, Representation, Discourse and Working Environment installations.
That is a fit between a description and a picture, and not a documented match: no title names an installation, and the fund's text does not describe a red cap or rolls of tape.
I use the fit to say what kind of objects the room held and not to caption any frame as a particular installation.
The fund also credits its own retrospective photographs to Lonneke van der Palen and Hanneke Wetzer, not to Köhlbrugge, so the archive's pictures are a second set.
A preview of August 23, 2017 puts the show at the Van Abbemuseum with nine installations by talent stipend recipients, and it mentions that the festival that year included the new World Design Event.
The word to notice is "preview": it says the recipients will exhibit, and it is not a report on what happened.
The room in the 2017 pictures is white and bright, which is the opposite of the Veemgebouw.

blocks.x: After 2017: the name stops, the show continues under others

r: The platform shows what followed. In 2018 the fund presented 24 minute-long film portraits of the 2017/2018 grant recipients in an installation in the Veem Building, in 2019 portraits shown with performances at MU, in 2020 a program called Talent Tours and in 2021 and 2022 portrait installations at the Klokgebouw and MU.
None of those pages uses the name In No Particular Order.

I read that as the series ending in 2017 under that name, while the fund's yearly presence at Dutch Design Week continued in a different form. That is my reading of a list of titles, and no page says the name was retired.

blocks.x: What the change of room does to the evidence

r: The darker Veemgebouw photographs let a reader see the work as light, screens and shapes. The 2017 photographs show it as objects against white walls. A reader comparing the albums is comparing two photographers and two rooms as well as three exhibitions, and I do not think the archive lets me separate them.
In my own field I learned that a specimen photographed on a dark cloth and the same specimen on a white tray look like different specimens, and I treat these albums the same way.
The titles stay steady in one respect: each names a place. The Veemgebouw appears in 2015 and 2016 and the Van Abbemuseum in 2017, which agrees with the fund's pages.

If I had to caption these albums for a reader, I would write the year, the place from the title and the credit, and describe what is visible and nothing about who made it, unless a named page or a legible label does the matching.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know which designer any photograph shows. Core77 names five 2015 works and the fund names 32 designers for 2016, but neither connects a work to a frame in the archive.
I did not read the fund's talent pages for individual designers. I could not open Metropolis M's review, because the site answered with an access error (403), and I did not retry.
I do not know which installation any 2017 photograph shows.
I do not know whether the 2014 edition left photographs in the archive. The fund's retrospective lists 32 participants for 2017, and I have not matched any of them to a photograph.

When a show changes rooms from one year to the next, should its archive stay faithful to the room or to the work? Next time you open a multi-year album, look at the first and last photograph of each year, and write down what changed in the setting before you decide what changed in the exhibition.
