posts.title: Jelle Mastenbroek asked for your data twice: a card swipe in a living room and an ID chip in a forest
posts.subtitle: The official photo archive holds two albums, 2017 and 2019, with no work named. His own site, DDW's interview, museum and press pages fill in 2015 to 2022.
posts.seoTitle: Jelle Mastenbroek at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Jelle Mastenbroek's Data Orchestra and The Robin Who Wondered If He Was a Nightingale, and what the DDW photo albums for 2017 and 2019 leave out.

r: Jelle Mastenbroek built a piece that plays music from your bank card and, three years later, one that makes mechanical birds sing from the chip in your ID, and the photo archive holds two small albums that show neither process.

The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds two albums under his name: 2017, titled Jelle Mastenbroek/MIR, with 6 photographs credited to Ronald Smits, and 2019, with 16 photographs credited to Max Kneefel.

That is 22 photographs, and none of the titles names a work. The written record is much fuller, and it also shows he was at DDW in 2015 and 2016, years the archive does not cover. This essay draws on public sources only: his own site, DDW's interview series, museum and press pages, and a broadcaster's festival guide. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about 2026.
In anatomy teaching, consent is the first document on file, so I notice how little a card swipe records of it. That is a perspective, not a claim about his work.

blocks.x: Who he is, from the record

r: Jelle Mastenbroek is an artist and designer who works from Eindhoven. A 2015 profile on the Creative Industries Fund NL's talent site says he graduated from the Design Academy Eindhoven in 2012, is a member of the studio collective Collaboration O, takes a humorous and playful approach and uses storytelling to reflect on society, often through interactive installations made with musicians, composers and programmers.
VPRO's festival guide in 2019 places the Collaboration O studio at Sectie-C, the former factory site on Daalakkersweg that opens its studios during DDW.
His own site lists dozens of works, grouped by theme, with money, porcelain and sound recurring.

blocks.x: 2015: a cuckoo clock named Frank

r: In 2015 the Creative Industries Fund NL presented 36 emerging designers under the title In No Particular Order.

Mastenbroek's entry was Frank, a cuckoo clock with an animated character who is, according to Mastenbroek, an expert on time and being punctual, made in collaboration with the artist Niels Hoebers. The profile says it offers a playful view of the nine-to-five routine.
The page I read does not give the exhibition's venue, so I cannot say where in Eindhoven it stood. There is no album for 2015 in the archive under his name.

blocks.x: 2016: the card, the living room and an award

r: Data Orchestra is the work that made his name. VPRO Medialab describes it as an installation in which visitors swipe a credit card, or another card with data, through a reader and receive a composition played on everyday objects such as cutlery, plates, pens and glasses, so that personal data are exchanged for a piece of music.

Designboom, in a May 5, 2016 post that its editors say came from reader submissions, adds that the work was made with the agency OWOW and sets itself against how influential companies collect data and trade it.

In April 2016 the installation was shown in Milan. The Dutch technology site Bright reported it as part of a group of Dutch designers presenting in the Lambrate district, with Data Orchestra at Via Massimiano 23 from April 11 to 17, and quoted Mastenbroek saying personal data is a new kind of currency.
His site and VPRO Medialab both say the jury of the Milano Design Award rewarded it with the prize for Best Technology among 1,600 exhibitors.
The award is the organizer's claim on the artist's site and the broadcaster's page, and I did not find the award organizer's own page.

The first Dutch showing came on Saturday, May 14, 2016, at the Klokgebouw on Strijp-S, in a free evening called Klokgebouw viert de toekomst, connected to the 125th anniversary of Philips, according to VPRO Medialab. IO+ reported the same evening.
That event was not part of DDW.

At DDW 2016, theme The Making Of, DDW published an interview with him. He said Data Orchestra began as a design for a music festival, that the sound side came from OWOW's software and electronics and the acoustics from him, and that the Creative Industries Fund helped him present it in Milan.

He said the scanner can read bank and credit cards and also the chips of driving licenses and passports, that he does not store the data though in principle it could be stored, and that people react very differently: some swipe at once, some realize afterward what they handed over, and some refuse for privacy reasons, which he reads as a sign of awareness.
He also said that he was showing work at Ketelhuisplein and in his studio at Sectie-C, where mirrors hang.
The page is dated November 3, 2016, but its text says DDW would be over next week, so the interview was written during the festival and the date on the page is probably a later republication.
There is no DDW album for him in 2016. The DDW interview and the Sectie-C studio are the evidence that he took part.

blocks.x: 2017: a museum show, a competition and a second DDW

r: Between March 24 and October 9, 2017, his site says, Music Box No.1 and Data Orchestra were on show in New Icons: Rietveld Now at Kazerne in Eindhoven.

IO+ describes the side room at Kazerne where Data Orchestra could be activated with any chip card, and lists Mastenbroek and OWOW among the New Icons participants, with Atelier NL, Maarten Baas, Studio Drift and others.

On May 16, 2017, IO+ reported that he had won the What if Lab: Marathon Eindhoven, an initiative of Marathon Eindhoven and the Dutch Design Foundation in which five studios pitched ideas for the finish of the 34th Eindhoven Marathon. His idea put runners' own motivations on banners and on boards along the route, with boards at the toughest points that recognize a runner by a chip and show a personal message. Jury member Arne Hendriks said the jury was moved by experiencing the marathon as a collective.
I found no source that says the design was built as pitched.
His site lists Dutch Design Week 2017 as October 21 to 29.

Interior Design's roundup of November 2, 2017 described Sectie C as four former factory buildings turned into studios and wrote that he showed musical crockery vending cabinets, Data Orchestra and new pieces, including a lightbox with a twirling dancer, all coin-operated. It credits its photograph of the vending cabinets to Ronald Smits, the same photographer the 2017 album's titles name.
The archive's 2017 photographs show a wall panel headed Data Orchestra, wooden cabinets, lit frames and a model, with no people.
The album title ends in MIR, which no page I opened explains.

blocks.x: 2019: a forest that sings from your ID

r: The 2019 album shows a yard with young trees and ferns on wood chips, small domes on poles and visitors reading stands.

VPRO's DDW tips of 2019 identify the work behind that setting as The Robin Who Wondered If He Was A Nightingale: a miniature forest with mechanical birds that sing according to the data on your ID card, passport or OV-chip, at Sectie-C, Daalakkersweg 16.

His own page describes improvisations by an orchestra based on your identity and the natural environment, with woodpeckers delivering percussive rhythms and the forest's acoustics playing a large role. It lists the musicians, from nightingale and cuckoo to four species of woodpecker, and says the work was commissioned by Oerol and curated by Marin de Boer and Atelier NL.
Atelier NL is the Eindhoven studio of Nadine Sterk and Lonny van Ryswyck, and the credit shows how small the circle is: a festival commission curated by a studio that had been a DDW ambassador.
I could not find which Oerol edition the piece first appeared in, so I do not date the commission.
The piece traveled. His site says it was on show from June 20 to August 20, 2022 at the Crossrail Place Roof Garden in Canary Wharf, London.

blocks.x: What came after the archive

r: Much of what is known about his later work is on his own site and in museum news. On January 14, 2026, Museum Speelklok announced it had bought his Porcelain Piano, a piece that combines a china cabinet and a piano and whose 48 porcelain plates each have their own tone. The museum said it was the first work by a contemporary artist to enter its permanent collection.
His site also lists Shell Symphony for Oerol 2024.
I found no DDW album or program page for him after 2019.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: When the DDW interview was published.
The page carries November 3, 2016, and its text says DDW would be over next week. The text settled it: it was written during the festival.
Whether the 2017 pieces were at Kazerne or Sectie C.

Both. His site lists Data Orchestra at Kazerne from March 24 to October 9, 2017, and Interior Design places Data Orchestra at Sectie C during DDW, October 21 to 29. A work can be shown in two places in one year, though I cannot say if there were two copies.
VPRO places The Robin at Sectie-C. The album does not name a place. I read the match from the trees and domes only.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what MIR means, which photographs in the 2017 album belong to which work, where the 2015 exhibition stood, or which Oerol edition commissioned The Robin. I could not read the Vimeo page for The Robin because the site showed a bot-verification page, and I could not read the Canary Wharf press release because its robots file excludes my request. I did not find the Milano Design Award organizer's own page.
The works ask for your data in exchange for pleasure. When you swipe a card for a song, what do you think you are giving, and what do you think you are getting?

posts.title: Jeroen Wand at Dutch Design Week: a Hallenweg workshop, five objects in a museum and albums that never name a work
posts.subtitle: A studio that opened its doors on the Hallenweg in 2015, the Boijmans records and presentation that followed, a move in 2019, DDW pages from 2023 to 2026 and what the three archive albums can and cannot show.
posts.seoTitle: Jeroen Wand at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Designer Jeroen Wand's Hallenweg studio at DDW, the five objects Boijmans holds, the DDW pages through 2026 and what the official photo albums can show.

r: In 2015 a designer on the Hallenweg in Eindhoven described his workspace as a small free state, and by 2018 the Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive had three albums for it, none of which names a single work.

I like a studio that opens its doors, because a visit leaves a record that finished objects cannot. This essay asks what the sources say about Studio Jeroen Wand at DDW, from a 2015 article, a 2017 trade-magazine profile and the museum's own records to the studio's news and DDW's program pages for 2023 to 2026, and then asks how far the three archive albums can be tied to that story. It reports no visit and no interview, and it names no one who appears in a photograph.

blocks.x: The place: a post-war industrial street

r: This is Eindhoven writes that the Hallenweg came into being after the Second World War as an economic recovery project, that metal and welding companies were its first tenants, that the buildings follow the Delft School style and are hidden behind the Hoogstraat, and that the street now holds studios and ateliers including Vij5, HeyHeydeHaas and the church of Atelier NL.
Eindhovens Dagblad, via De Erfgoedstem, reported on January 9, 2016 that the business halls at Hallenweg 1 to 7c were among seven postwar buildings newly designated as municipal monuments.
That is the setting for the 2015 to 2018 albums, a protected row of working halls and not a gallery district.

A June 28, 2017 profile in the trade magazine ArchitectuurNL gives a picture of the workshop itself without naming the street: a large workshop on a site full of creative activity, chickens outside, a trainee cutting veneer inside, racks of sorted wood and veneer, and a wall of small labeled bins of screws and bolts with the word GAMMA, in the writer's phrase a wink, over the hardware cabinet. Upstairs is what Wand calls his memory, a cabinet arranged like a candy shop and filled with material tests, from plaster and glass to porcelain and PVC pipe.
The chickens match the 2015 description of the Hallenweg workspace, so I read the two as the same place, though the 2017 article does not say so.

blocks.x: The designer and the studio

r: The studio's own page says it was founded by Jeroen Wand in 2007, that it specializes in interior design, furniture and products, and that it alters traditional combinations of materials and techniques, for example with paper laminating and plaster rotation molding. It gives his birth year as 1985, a product design education at the academy in Maastricht and a master's degree at the Sandberg Institute in Amsterdam in 2008.
The Boijmans record gives Heerlen as his birthplace.

ArchitectuurNL adds that he graduated in Maastricht in 2006, finished at Sandberg in 2008 and also holds a welding diploma, and that he applied to the academy at 16, a year early, with a portfolio of clothing, jewelry, lamps and furniture.

The graduation piece was the Paper Chair. The museum's text says Wand made it in 2006 as his graduation project from many layers of 160 gram paper, strong enough to sit on, and that the museum bought it in 2008.
A Vij5 interview from 2023 says he ended up in Eindhoven by chance: a friend found a studio too big for one person, and Wand was working in Geldrop at the time.

He describes the studio as three pillars, free work made in-house, commissions, and executive work for other designers, says the workshop runs on solar power and that the veneer used for its products is a residual stream, and says the 's-Chair that Vij5 sells has been tested to NEN-EN 16139, level 2.
Those are his statements as an interviewer for his publisher recorded them.
One number does not line up. The studio says it was founded in 2007.
DDW's program text for 2023 says the studio had existed for 15 years, which counted back from 2023 gives 2008.
A studio can be counted from the year it was registered or the year it began to show work, and neither page explains its count, so I do not choose between them.

blocks.x: 2015: Same place, New stuff

r: The e52 program and Dutch Design Daily chose Wand as one of nine hidden gems of DDW 2015, in an article that the IO+ archive carries. The article, by Renske Mehra, calls his workspace on the Hallenweg a small free state, with a large outdoor area, a few chickens, a radio playing and a lot of hard work going on. His newest work would be exhibited in his own studio under the title Same place, New stuff.

The show was to include new Phases vases, which he had shown at the Milan design fair that year. According to the article, each vase's basic shape comes from one mold; after the first version hardens it is immersed in liquid plaster, giving an irregular, uncontrolled outer layer, and the process is repeated several times, so that the inside stays sleek while the outside gets rougher. A second new piece was a laminated table, made in part during a stay with an Italian furniture maker in South Tyrol as an artist in residence. Other designers, among them Jo Sijen and Wouter Corvers, were invited to show experiments in ceramics and construction, and Wand would explain the exhibition himself at a meet and greet on Wednesday, October 21, 2015, at 16:00.

ArchitectuurNL tells the residency story differently. It places the artist residency in what it calls Swiss Bolzano (translated from the Dutch), says he learned there something with paper that he then translated to veneer, using the discarded offcuts of a nearby factory, and says he presented the first products of this collection at the Milan design fair in 2015. It adds that he built his own vacuum bag to press the layers together.
The two accounts differ on the country, and I use IO+'s version, which was written during the 2015 festival and names a region. The Milan 2015 date agrees in both.
The official archive's 2015 Hallenweg album, with 18 photos credited by title to Ralph Roelse, shows a courtyard with signs for Studio Jeroen Wand, according to my October 8 read.
So the 2015 show is in the archive, filed under the area and not under his name.

blocks.x: Five objects in one museum

r: Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen holds five Wand objects, not two. The artist page in its online collection lists a Paper Chair, a Paper stool, two vases titled Phases and a Laminated Table.

The Paper Chair (V 2506, made 2006, laminated and pressed paper, 75.5 centimeters high) and the Paper stool (V 2507, made 2006, 40.5 centimeters high) were both bought in 2008 with the support of the Mondriaan Fund.
The first Phases vase (V 3106, made 2013, plaster with a polyurethane coating, 44.5 centimeters high) was purchased in 2016.
The second (V 3107, made 2015, plaster and polyurethane coating, 45 centimeters high) came to the museum as a gift from Jeroen Wand in 2016.
The Laminated Table (V 3193, made 2015, veneer and glue, 50 centimeters high, 121 wide and 70 deep) was bought in 2017 with the support of the Mondriaan Fund.
The Montreal Museum of Fine Arts holds a further vase, from the series Phases IV, dated 2015, bought as the Suzanne Caouette Bequest purchase and inventoried 2016.2.
One of the two Boijmans vases is therefore a gift from the maker and not a purchase, and the museum's purchases are the chair and stool (2008), one vase (2016) and the table (2017).
All five Boijmans records list the same exhibition, Studio Jeroen Wand. Een gelaagde collectie (2017), which can be read as A layered collection.

The records label it an internal exhibition and do not say where it was held. The museum's own exhibition page, which I read through an Internet Archive capture of July 16, 2019 because the live address now redirects, answers that: the presentation was shown in the Paviljoen, and the page says the plaster vases in it were built layer by layer, two of them acquired in 2016, and that the Laminated Table and the Sarentino Chair from 2016 are the result of his latest experiment with laminating wood and integrating the legs into the gluing.
ArchitectuurNL, in its issue 03/2017, says the exhibition could be seen until and including August 27, 2017.

A second source disagrees about the year. The Meer arts calendar, in an entry dated August 23, 2018, gives the dates of the presentation as August 1, 2018 to January 13, 2019 and repeats the museum's text word for word.
The records and the trade magazine say 2017, and Meer says 2018 to 2019. The museum's page, as captured in 2019, carries no dates, so it settles the place but not the year.

I take 2017 as the documented date, because two sources and the museum's own records agree on it, and I list the 2018 to 2019 entry as unexplained: it may be a second showing, an extension or an error in the calendar.
The table has a date problem of its own. Boijmans dates it to 2015, and IO+ called a laminated table new in October 2015.
The museum's exhibition text dates the Laminated Table and the Sarentino Chair to 2016.
Kazerne, the Eindhoven exhibition house, writes in 2020 that a table in its show is a reinterpretation of Wand's first Laminated Table, presented in 2012.
I cannot tell from these pages which iteration the museum owns, and I cannot connect the Sarentino Chair to a place or a source beyond the museum's text.

blocks.x: 2016 to 2018: three albums and one dated recap

r: The archive's Wand albums are Hallenweg: Jeroen Wand for 2016 with 7 photos and for 2017 with 9, and Jeroen Wand for 2018 with 12, 28 in all, every title crediting Iris Rijskamp.

The photos show a cluttered workshop with glaze jars, a moped and a hand press and a workbench covered in rows of small vases in 2016, pendant lamps, a white cabinet with bottles and white vases beside black candlesticks in 2017, and a bright hall with a long table of vases, wooden chairs and screens in 2018.

A Berlin art university's program for its DDW trip of October 21 to 24, 2017 lists a visit to the Hallenweg for Vij5 and friends and Jeroen Wand, which puts the studio on a visitor's route in the year of the 2017 album, though a program is a plan and not a report.

Only 2018 has a DDW page that names him. DDW's recap of Day 3, October 23, 2018, says that during the week the designers of the Hallenweg welcome visitors into their studios and that Jeroen Wand and Maarten Baptist were also exhibiting, one of eight design areas of the festival.

Wallpaper*'s 2018 guide places Wand's veneer, PVC, porcelain and paper creations in The Young Collectors II, a three-story 1960s house of the studio Thier&vanDaalen on Populierenweg, not on the Hallenweg.
So in 2018 his work was in at least two places, and the album does not say which one it shows.

The same year he showed abroad. A July 3, 2018 note from the London agency Zetteler lists Eindhoven's Studio Jeroen Wand, which it describes as known for raw and unpolished pieces that challenge conventions of beauty, among the highlights of that year's Dutch Stuff selection at London Design Fair, held at the Old Truman Brewery.
Kazerne's designer page lists him in its exhibitions Open World (2014 to 2015), with a vase of PVC pipe, two small pieces of round timber and a hand-molded reservoir, and Fundamentals (2018 to 2019).

blocks.x: After 2018: a move, a prize and a different address

r: The studio's news says it moved to a new address, Bayeuxlaan 7, on March 14, 2019, which ends the Hallenweg workshop of the album years.
On June 26, 2019 it posted that COS was showing its work in the retailer's Coal Drops Yard store in London.
That September it took part in Dutch Design in NYC, shown from September 12 to December 20, 2019 by Ventura Projects with the designers' co-op Colony in SoHo.

Design Milk lists it as one of seven designers in a show curated by Jean Lin of Colony and Margriet Vollenberg of Ventura Projects, at 324 Canal Street, and Interior Design adds that the project was supported by Dutch Culture USA, a program of the Dutch consulate general in New York.
The studio's Laminated Coffee Table won the ARC19 Award for best piece of furniture on a post dated November 14, 2019.
The collection page confirms the prize and describes the table as part of the Re-veneer collection, in which leftover veneer is pressed together.
MaterialDistrict, which published an entry for Re-veneer on May 26, 2021, says the pieces are industry leftovers pressed with a vacuum technique that needs no complicated molds.
The 2020s pages show a studio that works in several directions. Kazerne showed a Wand Laminated Table in its exhibition The Circle in 2020 and lists him in New Melancholy for 2020 to 2021.

A post from November 2020 describes a vase experiment a day during the first lockdown, a post of April 2021 announces the Design Open route in Eindhoven from June 13 to 17, a post of April 16, 2021 shows a custom interior for Design Museum Helmond made with HeyHeydeHaas, and a post of November 1, 2021 reports a new shop interior for the Haags Historisch Museum.
In 2023 Vij5 described the 's-Chair and 's-Table, designed for the education space of the Stedelijk Museum 's-Hertogenbosch, now the Design Museum Den Bosch, as part of its collection.

blocks.x: What DDW's own pages list from 2023 to 2026

r: DDW's program has pages that bear on the studio in 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026, though only the 2024 recap and the 2026 location page state their edition.

The 2023 entry is Making, 15 years. It says the studio exists 15 years and shows its way of making in a retrospective of works with new interpretations added, that the outcome of 15 years includes a paper chair and glazed constructions, that visitors can browse a sample sale, and that the studio and workspace, in an old garage building hidden behind a gas station, are open to look into the workshop. It credits a plate made in collaboration with Cor Unum.
The page prints no year. The image files attached to it carry upload dates of August 29, 2023, which is why I place it in DDW 2023.

The 2024 entry is Stacking. Multiple shapes are immersed in liquid plaster that unites them almost like a weld; the position of the shapes must be decided instantly while the plaster sets, and the page calls Stackings a continuation of the Phases project.

The year again comes from the page's image upload date, September 27, 2024, and from DDW's own DDW24 area recap, which tells visitors in the Hallenweg area not to miss Studio Jeroen Wand for unconventional designs such as Stacking and EXO.
I found no program page for EXO.

For 2025 the program names Wand among the Dutch designers invited to make coat racks for To Come and to Go at Design Daily's gallery at Gestelsestraat 234, October 18 to 26, 2025. DDW lists that project under the Hallenweg area, but the address is not the studio's.
DDW lists Studio Jeroen Wand for 2026 in the Hallenweg area, D8, at Bayeuxlaan 7, October 17 to 25, free to enter, 11:00 to 18:00 daily and fully wheelchair accessible.
The Hallenweg is therefore an area label and not a street address for his studio today.

blocks.x: What the albums can and cannot prove

r: A title in these albums can prove a year, a photographer and a place. It cannot show a work. The 2016 vase with a layered band tempts a caption, since the Boijmans records describe plaster vases with a coating, but no photo title names Phases, so I do not join them.
The 2017 album coincides in year with the museum presentation, and nothing connects the two.

There is also a data question. Flickr album ids rise with creation time, and the series plan's list of 493 albums shows that the ids of the 2017 album (72157662464553208) and the 2018 album (72157675404555828) sit among ids of albums created in late 2015 and autumn 2016.
That pattern appears in dozens of albums, including guest-academy albums whose photo titles carry the 2017 date, so it may reflect how DDW created and filled albums and not a wrong year.
I cannot check the photographs' taken dates without contacting Flickr, so I treat it as a flag for checking and not as a finding.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know which work any photograph in the three Wand albums shows, what the 2016 and 2017 shows were called, or whether the studio exhibited at DDW 2019 to 2022 under its own name; I found no program page for those years that I could open.
A search summary pointed to a studio post about a 2022 show, but it sits on a professional-network site that I did not open, so I use nothing from it.
I did not open the studio's downloadable CV, a Word file, because it was a file download, and the About page's list of exhibitions appears to live there.
I do not know which Boijmans year is right for the presentation in the Paviljoen, 2017 or 2018 to 2019, or which version of the Laminated Table the museum holds.
I do not know how the studio counts its 15 years.
Dezeen and Archello, which carry coverage of the 2019 New York show and a studio profile, refused automated requests, and I stopped there.
When you meet a studio through an archive of its open days, which would you rather have next to the picture, the year or the name of the piece?

posts.title: Manifestations at Dutch Design Week: eleven editions that count themselves, and five that the photo archive keeps
posts.subtitle: A media art festival publishes a site for every year and numbers its own editions. Read against its funder, an academy and the official albums, the sites settle some questions and open others.
posts.seoTitle: Manifestations at Dutch Design Week, 2016 to 2026
posts.description: Manifestations, the media art festival at Dutch Design Week: eleven editions by its own count, edition sites, themes, venues and what the photo archive holds.

r: Manifestations counts its own editions, and the count settles a question its edition sites leave open: Dutch Design Week's 2025 listing calls that year the tenth in a row and the 2026 listing the eleventh, which puts the first edition in 2016.

That kind of self-counting is why this festival is easy to read and hard to check. The organizers publish a website for every edition, with themes, dates, floors, artist lists and sometimes visitor numbers, and the official photo archive holds albums for only five of the years. This essay reads the two against each other. It draws on public sources only: the festival's edition sites, its organizer's own site, a curator statement, a 2017 news item, two Royal Academy of Art pages, DDW's program listings, the funder's 2026 announcement and the photo archive as I recorded it on October 7 and 8, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 show beyond what those pages state.

blocks.x: What the festival says it is

r: Manifestations calls itself a media art festival with an expo during Dutch Design Week, under the tagline Art, Tech & Fun.
Its 2026 about page says it is an initiative of Stichting Art & Technology and its creative director and curator, Viola van Alphen, and that it is free for everyone.

The organizer's own site gives the foundation's name as ViolaVirus, Stichting Art & Technology, in Nijmegen, and says ViolaVirus is a split from PLANETART that arose in 2008 and is known for the projects GOGBOT, the Twente Biennale and TEC ART.
Every edition site from 2018 to 2024 closes with the line "a production of ViolaVirus."

The festival describes its method on the 2026 page: each year the curators go through the graduation shows of Dutch art and design academies looking for promising talent, which, the page says, makes the festival a springboard for beginning makers who are then noticed by scouts from festivals and museums.
The same page lists a 2026 team of staff, floor managers, volunteers and guest curators and scouts, among them former exhibitors, and credits exhibition design to St Lucas College.
That is the organizer's account of itself, and it fits what the edition sites show: lists of mostly young makers, with a Young Talent Award each year.

Curator statements are the other place to hear the festival's voice. In a statement for the ISEA2020 symposium, van Alphen writes that during Dutch Design Week, which she puts at 350,000 visitors, the festival presents 50 to 100 artists, that it works with a pool of more than 5,000 international artists, and that its focus is art with a human dimension, "always critical, playful, recognizable and awe-inspiring."

In the same statement she lists four artists with the year each work was shown: Tim Dekkers' The Parasitic Humanity in 2018, Maartje Dijkstra's four works in 2019, Jip van Leeuwenstein's A Diverse Monoculture in 2017 and Daniëlle Ooms' Apple-based Material in 2019.
Those are the only dated work titles in the sources that tie to a year outside the edition sites themselves.

De Caai, the former Campina Melkfabriek, plus virtual worlds
not stated in the page text
Vision, Think Bigger, Make Smarter Choices

r: Three cells need a note. The 2016 place is not in the page text I could read, because the 2016 site refused my request twice with an HTTP 403 on its robots.txt, the second time after a 10-minute wait, and I made no further request to that host.
The 2017 dates are those of Dutch Design Week 2017 in DDW's own music announcement, because the 2017 site itself is a blog without a date range in the text I read.
And the 2019 theme name rests on the Royal Academy's listing, not on the festival's own 2019 page.
The 2018 page also carries a number that does not hold still. It prints 4,500 square meters in one block and 6,000 in two other blocks, with the same wording around them.

I report both and do not choose. Other sources give other sizes: the organizer's site describes the 2017 festival as three locations, 5,000 square meters and 50,000 visitors, and DDW's 2025 listing says Manifestations is 3,000 square meters.
None of the sources says how floor area was measured, and the numbers are a reminder that the festival's size varied with the floors it used.

blocks.x: What the early years looked like

r: The first public account of 2017 I found is a news item of September 27, 2017. It says the exhibition in the Veemgebouw shows the work of more than a hundred designers, fills the eighth and ninth floors with cyberpunk, brain-controlled robots, virtual reality, fashion-tech and a Museum of the Future, and includes smart nails, fantasy organs, an electronic house doctor, a robot that eats oak processionary caterpillars and interactive stick-on tattoos.

It also reports a satellite exhibition in the Eindhoven library, The Internet of Women Things, where technology with a feminine edge is the subject, and quotes van Alphen saying that internet and technology are too often made by men for men.

The festival's 2017 site is a blog of about 95 program posts with categories such as Young Talent (35 posts), High Tech Presentations (30) and Internet of Women Things (30), and a December 15, 2017 post says pictures and videos were online and that the site would not be updated to 2018 yet, to prevent copycats.

For 2016 the organizer's own site says the exhibition Manifestations: Will the Future Design Us? won the title Best of Dutch Design Week 2016 and lists press mentions it attributes to RTL-Z, de Volkskrant, De Telegraaf, Dezeen's best tips, a High Tech Campus tip and E52 as the most critical event of the week.
The 2018 edition site repeats that the 2016 edition won Best of DDW, and the 2019 to 2024 sites close with "Manifestations was Winner Best of DDW."
The 2026 about page gives the award without a year, and the 2016 date comes from the 2018 and organizer pages.
I could not open any of the press items themselves, so these are the organizer's list.
The question Will the Future Design Us? was the title in 2016 and 2017 and again the 2018 site's frame.
An essay that treats it as the 2018 theme alone would be wrong, and a caption should say the question was a standing heading across three editions.

blocks.x: 2018 and 2019: works with names

r: The 2018 page lists works with their makers, among them Tim Dekkers' The Parasitic Humanity, Annemiek Höcker's The Search for Submission, Pelle Schilling's Incandescence, Esmee Kiewiet's OBJECTS, Pia Walter's AWE, Caio Vita's Imprecisely Human, Freerk Wieringa's Exoskeleton, Alexandra Ehrlich Speiser's USELESS WEAPONS, Jeanine Verloop's Reawaken, Dan Chen's End of Life Care Machine and Nicole Spit's NeoBio, and it names the 2018 Young Talent Award winners: Diego Grandry, Marie Cantenys and Sissel Tolaas from the Royal Academy of Art in The Hague took the award given with the sponsors GBO and Sioux, and Alexander van Bakel of the Rietveld Academy came second.
The page's header text has been updated to advertise 2019, so the works list may mix years; Dekkers' 2018 date is confirmed by the curator statement.

The Royal Academy's own page for Dutch Design Week 2018 says curator Viola van Alphen selected works showing the interaction between man and technology from different perspectives, lists alumni and students on floor 9 of the Veem, and names among them works such as Peer to Peer, Home in a Bag, Airphone, Responsive Tactility: 4D Printed Skins, George.io and The Undesirables.

For 2019 the same academy lists the show as Manifestations - Superpowers on the ninth floor, with work by young talents and recent graduates, calls out the newest fashion and wearables, "botox," human mutations and post-apocalyptic design, and says two of its alumni were nominated for the Young Talent Award.
The 2019 site gives the Young Talent Award winners as Pia-Marie Stute and Katja Trinkwalder for Accessories for the Paranoid, from the Köln International School of Design.

This is the best match between the festival's text and the photo archive. The old dossier read the 2018 and 2019 albums as 19 and 21 photographs by Tommy Köhlbrugge showing glass sculptures, mannequins in garments, a robotic arm and a person in a headset.
The titles name none of the works, so I do not pair a photograph with a name from the lists above, and a caption should not either.

blocks.x: 2020 to 2022: virtual worlds and a cap on visitors

r: The 2020 site says the edition would take place virtually on manifestations.nl, on ddw.nl and in several virtual worlds, naming Second Life, Sansar and Mozilla Hubs, and that the festival hoped to be physical again at a later time at Sectie-C.

That sentence resolves the puzzle in the old notes, which read the page as both virtual and located at Sectie-C. The address was a hoped-for later location. The page also gives the theme as Monsters on the 2019 page's header and asks visitors whether they might be the monster themselves.
The 2020 page is no longer a 2020 page: its text says the exhibition runs October 16 to 24 and that the 2021 site was coming.
For 2021 the site says the edition would take place in the Melkhal De Caai, the former Campina Melkfabriek, and online in the same virtual worlds, with entry free from 11:00 to 18:30.
It sets a limit of 250 visitors inside at once, in a space the page says was calculated for many more, with constant ventilation and a tip to come between 11 and 13 hours.
On masks the page says visitors could choose, and it names the World Health Organization and the German national institute's guidance instead of the Dutch national institute's.
I report that as the organizers' statement and take no position on it.
In 2022 the festival returned to the Veem, on floor 8, with the same 250 cap and the theme Bubbles.

The 2022 page sorts roughly 35 projects into four sections: Known Circles or Different Worlds?, Masks & Uniform, Conflict & Confidence, and Soap Bubble & Transience, and tags 21 projects as nominated for the Young Talent Award by named academies.

It names the French collective RYBN's The Great Offshore, a research project on offshore finance co-produced with several French and European institutions, as one work, and notes that a design and art shop was being set up next door with Emmaus Eindhoven where artists could sell without charge.
A visitor looking at the 2022 album would meet a staged bedroom with a retro computer, according to the old dossier, and the page does not say which project that was.

blocks.x: 2023 and 2024: the same floor, different questions

r: The 2023 page gives the theme as Vision, Think Bigger, Make Smarter Choices and groups its works under headings including Mens? and Duurzaam.
The 2024 page gives Invisible Enemies, with headings on the human as creator and destroyer, social injustice and victim blaming, and technological influences and alternative realities.
Both pages list between 30 and 40 projects with short texts, and both say the festival was on floor 8 and in virtual worlds, with entry free.

Names recur across the three years from 2022 to 2024. Viola Renate appears in 2022 and again in 2023, Nonna Hoogland and Agnes van Dijk appear in 2023 and 2024, and the Emmaus Eindhoven design shop is on both the 2023 and 2024 pages.
The 2026 team page lists Agnes van Dijk as supervision and a guide, and names Abel Kamps, Tom Haakman and Aïsha Dingemans among guest curators and scouts, so exhibitors turn into curators.
I draw one conclusion from this: the festival keeps its own alumni near it. I do not know how many of the roughly 35 projects a year are new, because the pages do not say.

blocks.x: 2025 and 2026: counted by DDW

r: DDW's own program listings are the plainest source for the last two years. The 2025 listing says Manifestations is 3,000 square meters, with 50 artists of the future, robots, e-fashion and kids, at VEEM on Strijp-S, with free entrance.

The 2026 listing says it is hosted by Manifestations, Art & Technology, on floor 8 of the VEEM building, with free access, open daily from 11:00 to 18:30, and describes more than 50 works by mostly young, recently graduated artists, tours that open three days earlier for tours and press, and wheelchair access at the back.
The 2026 listing also says it is the largest art and tech event during Dutch Design Week, and I treat that as the organizer's claim.

The funder describes the 2026 festival too. The Creative Industries Fund NL's announcement of January 14, 2026 says the fund considered 31 proposals in a festival grant scheme, selected 21, and lists Manifestations 2026 among them as a 10-day free festival with some 50 works whose theme MUTE touches on silence, censorship and self-censorship.
That description says ten days where the festival's own dates give nine, October 17 to 25, and the difference may count an earlier opening for tours.
The 2026 edition is covered by its own piece in this series, and this essay stops there.

blocks.x: What the albums keep

r: The old dossier counts five albums for 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022 and 2024, with 19, 21, 83, 100 and 8 photographs, 231 in all, credited in the titles to Tommy Köhlbrugge, about.today and Cleo Goossens.
I did not reopen Flickr for this version. What the albums show is mostly mood: lit glass, mannequins, a staged bedroom, visitors reading paper scrolls.
The festival's own sites hold what the albums lack, which is the names of works, makers and themes.
The albums miss 2016, 2017, 2020, 2023 and 2025 by the dossier's reading.
Between them, the festival's sites show that Manifestations took place in each of those years, so a timeline built from the archive alone would skip five of the eleven editions.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The edition archive on the sites runs back to 2016, and the DDW listings count the 2025 edition as the tenth and the 2026 edition as the eleventh. The count settles 2016, including the virtual 2020 edition.
The 2026 page gives it without a year. The 2018 site and the organizer's site say the 2016 edition won it.
Online, in virtual worlds, with a physical edition at Sectie-C only hoped for later.
The 2018 page prints both 4,500 and 6,000 square meters. Not settled.
Whether the question was a 2018 theme.
It was the title in 2016 and 2017 as well.
Nine days by its own dates, ten by the funder's summary. Not settled.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know where the 2016 edition stood, what it showed or how many visited, because the 2016 site was not open to me. I do not know how many visitors any edition drew apart from the organizer's own 50,000 for 2017, which sits on its site without a method.

I do not know which works the photographs in the albums show, or whether the albums include works from the lists above. I did not find independent reviews of any edition, and the press items the organizer lists were not opened.
The photo archive counts and titles come from the October 7 and 8 readings, not from this pass.

If a festival numbers its own editions, keeps a website for each and then moves on to the next year's site, which of those pages would you trust to tell you what happened in a year you did not attend?

posts.title: Modebelofte, then New Order of Fashion: a graduate platform that kept changing its organizer, its name and its building
posts.subtitle: What the curators' pages, the trade press and Dutch Design Week's listings say about one fashion platform, 2014 to 2026, and what the photo archive can hold.
posts.seoTitle: Modebelofte to New Order of Fashion
posts.description: One fashion platform at Dutch Design Week, 2014 to 2026: two names, changing organizers and buildings, and what a photo archive can hold.

r: Modebelofte's own curators credit one organizer for its first three Dutch Design Weeks and another for the next three, and a photo archive that files every year under one name cannot show either change.

As a content strategist I read a rename as a content problem: the thing keeps moving and the label has to keep up. This essay follows one fashion platform through its own curators' pages, trade and design press, Dutch Design Week's listings and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibit beyond what the published listings say.

blocks.x: Two names, and a start date that depends on who is counting

r: Modebelofte is Dutch for fashion promise. Studio Harm Rensink, the studio that designed and curated it, calls it an international platform for fashion talents that presents graduates of international bachelor and master courses.

FashionUnited reported on October 26, 2018 that Modebelofte would continue after that edition as New Order of Fashion, and a year later said 2019 was the first edition under the new name, chosen to make the international character of the platform clear.

The curator's own page for 2018 is already titled New Order of Fashion, while FashionUnited and the photo archive call the 2018 edition Modebelofte, so the name changed inside a window and not on a single day.
Start dates disagree in a useful way. Studio Harm Rensink says it has worked on the creative direction and exhibition design since 2014.
FashionUnited wrote in 2017 that the platform was founded five years earlier as part of Dutch Design Week, and in 2018 that it had been part of the festival for six years.
Both counts point to 2012. Dezeen's 2025 report, which I read in an earlier pass and could not reopen, also gives 2012 as the year Ellen Albers started it.
I read these as one story told by different people: the platform began around 2012, and this studio has shaped it since 2014. The trade counts are loose, so I say around 2012 and not 2012.

blocks.x: 2014 to 2016: the retailer years

r: For the first three editions in the studio's records, the credit lines name a local retailer. The pages for 2014, 2015 and 2016 say the show was initiated and organized by You Are Here, with the exhibition design by Studio Harm Rensink and HeyNiek.
The 2017 and 2018 pages instead say initiated by Ellen Albers.
No page I opened explains the handover, and FashionUnited calls Albers the initiator of Modebelofte in 2017.
That leaves the earlier years of her role open.

The 2014 edition was called Seductive Precursors and filled an abandoned, slightly notorious disco club with floating mannequins, black walls, directional light and white dust on a granulated floor. The studio describes the mood as Tim Burton's Corpse Bride going clubbing.
The 2015 edition, Performing Advancers, took its sports theme to the home of PSV, the Philips football stadium.
Dezeen counted 42 designers from 15 courses and gave the dates as October 14 to 25, 2015.
The photo archive holds 42 photographs for 2015 too, and I treat the match as coincidence, since a count of photographs is a count of what was posted.

In 2016, under the theme Adaptive Travelers, the platform took over de Bijenkorf, one minute from Eindhoven Central Station, using the shop windows, part of the first and third floors and the roof for about 30 graduates.
Neon Moire's guide to the fifteenth Dutch Design Week listed it at the Bijenkorf roof, October 22 to 30, 2016, 10:00 to 18:00, entrance 2 euros, with a talk show at the Van Abbemuseum on October 23.
Visi, reporting from the festival, wrote that fashion students showed how clothes might become resources for shelter, safety and energy in an apocalyptic world.

blocks.x: 2017: a department store with the lights half off

r: Digital Realists in 2017 showed 18 international designers in what the studio calls an abandoned V&D warehouse and FashionUnited calls the former V&D store on the Vrijstraat.

FashionUnited gives the size as 2,500 square meters, made available by the owner of the building to Albers, and says the ground floor also held a small coffee shop, a design hair salon and a robot space, and that Vlisco showed creations on the floor where clothing collections used to hang.
The curators were Rensink and Lisanne Fransen, and the reporter noticed that they left out mannequin silhouettes, so gender did not show, and let masks, headwear and shoes carry the human presence.

The studio's credits show how many hands a platform like this has. Production was by Fabian Briels, artwork and animation by Leeza Pritychenko and music by a Gothenburg electronic duo, with photography by Barbara Medo.

blocks.x: 2018 and 2019: the rename year, then the new name

r: The 2018 edition, Shape Shifters, ran to October 28 with a 2 euro ticket. FashionUnited names 21 participants, one of them a studio, among them Sinéad O'Dwyer, Kota Okuda, Pierre-Louis Auvray, Emma Wessel and Paolo Carzana, and two collaborations with New Order of Fellowships, a concept it says was introduced in 2017: Ecco Leather and Kobe with Kira Goodney, and with the duo AnoukxVera.
The studio's text asks what fashion does with our shape and with our concept of self.
An earlier version of this essay said FashionUnited counted twenty individual designers. The page lists 21 names and states no count.
In 2019 the exhibition moved to a vacant former V&D store at Rechtestraat 8, open through October 27, under the theme The End is Near, Time for New Beginnings.
The studio describes a tilted world where walls were about to collapse, airbrushed artwork provided by the graduates, and a Talks program at the center of the exhibition.
FashionUnited quotes Rensink saying the dark entrance hall signals a world at a tipping point.

The report lists a coat made of used tea bags by Benedetta Marcucci, a dress of old plastic car parts strung on metal chains by Valentine Tinchant, and a graduation project by Laura Frandsen that was a cart of discarded clothes instead of a collection.

FashionUnited notes the earlier venues, the old V&D building several times, the Bijenkorf roof and the Philips stadium, and that earlier partnerships included Ecco and Vlisco. In 2019 the partners were instead textile-innovation parties: Unseam, which makes seamless fabric from digital 3D shapes and researches a leather alternative from jellyfish, and Sunbrella with the designer Wendy Andreu.

The studio's 2019 page thanks Albers, Emma Wessel, Frank Verkade, Grietje Schepers and Jelle Smidt as the team that supports the exhibitions through the year, and credits the photography to Ronald Smits.

blocks.x: 2020 to 2023: a lab, a school and a theme

r: I found no written source for 2020, when the festival was largely online. The archive's 2020 album has nine photographs of a New Order Fashion Store, as I read it earlier, and nothing in the pages I opened describes that show.

For 2021, FashionUnited reported the show, Do It, A joint Catalyst for Change, at Strijp S from October 16 to 24, with 16 entries in its list of graduates (Jessica Guzman appears twice, so the list holds 15 names). The graduates were mentored by Rensink as creative head, Pauline van Dongen as artistic research mentor, Matthew Needham and Stina Randestad, and their work would stay in the platform's circular lab and fashion atelier.

The report names the supporters as Cultuur Eindhoven, Het Nieuwe Instituut, the Prins Bernhard Cultuurfonds, Regiodeal Brainport Eindhoven and the Stimulation Fund Creative Industries, and lists partners that include Aalto University, Fashion for Good, Kniterate and The Student Hotel.

By 2022 the FashionUnited route for fashion fans placed a New Order of Fashion Lab on the Torenallee, with recent graduates' work and material and artistic research by the makers around the lab, and an embroidery atelier at The Student Hotel near the station with workshops by Martine van 't Hul and Woo Jin Joo.

Design Milk's report on the 2023 exhibition, Regeneration: Fashion From The Ground Up, says it explored regeneration through three lenses, Earth Care, People Care and Fair Share, and describes projects such as a needle-lace dress of lavender seeds grown over two summers and a garment woven as a whole.
The photo archive I read has no 2023 album.

blocks.x: 2024 to 2026: the lab with a wool theme

r: For 2024 the only source I have is the archive's five-photograph album titled with the lab, as I read it earlier, and nothing describes the show.

For 2025, Dezeen reported a wool exhibition, Wool (Re)discovered, in the platform's makerspace at Strijp-S, noting that 1.5 million kilograms of wool are discarded each year in the Netherlands, and named Haiko Huvenaars as director. I read that article in the earlier pass and could not reopen it.
For 2026, Dutch Design Week lists the New Order of Fashion LAB at Torenallee 22-06, daily from 11:00 to 18:00, October 17 to 25, with the exhibition Regeneration: Fashion from the Source.

The program entry Flock, Folk, Field is a wool exhibition in three parts, Flock, Folk and Field, that follows wool from animals and landscapes to the people who shape it. The entry describes the organization as a talent development and knowledge platform with three pillars, Explore, Educate and Activate.
A second item at the same address, With Reflection, shows ten textile veils by the Brussels designer Antoine Guitou.

blocks.x: The curator's other work

r: The same studio that curates the platform designed the Bart Hess retrospective Future Bodies at the Stedelijk Museum in 's-Hertogenbosch in 2017, transforming 500 square meters of exhibition space, and shared the exhibition design credit with Hess for BodyDrift in 2020.
That is the kind of fact an archive of fashion albums cannot hold.

blocks.x: What an archive can and cannot do for a platform like this

r: The photo archive holds ten albums, with 42, 23, 18, 17, 19, 9, 23, 51, 5 and 21 photographs, 228 in all. I read them in an earlier pass and did not reopen the account for this version, so the Flickr facts are second-hand.

The photographer credits in the archive titles differ from the credits on the curator's pages. The studio credits Barbara Medo for 2014, 2015, 2017 and 2018, Gert Jan van Rooij for 2016 and Ronald Smits for 2019, while the archive's titles name other photographers. Festival and studio photographers can differ, and the pages do not say.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Whether Albers was part of the organization in 2014 to 2016, when the credit line names You Are Here.
Details of the 2025 show beyond one article I could not reopen.
Why the archive has no 2023 album although a 2023 show is documented.
Where the 2018 and 2022 shows stood; no page I opened names the 2018 venue.

r: When you read a timeline of a moving platform, which line tells you who was organizing it in a given year, and which only tells you where?

posts.title: MVRDV built a hotel in 2017 and a walk-through in 2018, and the city kept the argument
posts.subtitle: Two Dutch Design Week editions of an architecture office whose founder was also the city's supervisor, read through MVRDV's pages, the press, the municipality and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: MVRDV at Dutch Design Week, 2017 and 2018
posts.description: MVRDV at Dutch Design Week 2017 and 2018: a nine-room folly, a city-center pavilion and the supervisor role behind them.

r: In 2017 MVRDV put a nine-meter hotel on a town square, and in 2018 it asked visitors to walk through a city center that did not exist yet.

I like an architecture office that shows its argument at full size, because the photographs then have something to prove. This essay draws on public sources only: MVRDV's own news posts and project pages, a VPRO interview, two Dutch architecture-news reports, the municipality of Eindhoven's own policy page and the official Dutch Design Week photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about what MVRDV shows at the 2026 festival.

blocks.x: An office, a festival role and a city job

r: MVRDV says it was founded in 1993 by Winy Maas, Jacob van Rijs and Nathalie de Vries, works from Rotterdam, Shanghai, Paris, Berlin and New York, and has a team of over 300.
The Dutch Design Week archive holds four MVRDV albums, two for 2017 and two for 2018, 53 photographs in all, 43 for 2017 and 10 for 2018.

The photographs show the work of an office, and the sources show that Maas wore two other hats in these years. MVRDV's post of October 18, 2017 begins with his role as ambassador of Dutch Design Week 2017, in which he, The Why Factory, the municipality of Eindhoven, the Eindhoven University of Technology and the festival curated four interventions on what he called future city products.

In the VPRO's interview of the same day he says he first came to the festival four years earlier and has not missed an edition since, and the interviewer notes that the municipality had recently named him supervisor of the city center.
Architectenweb later put the start of that supervisor job in 2017, and MVRDV's own announcement of February 25, 2022 describes almost five years in the role.

The exhibitions of 2017 and 2018 therefore sit at the start of a municipal appointment. I could not open the municipality's own announcement of it, because the city's website refused the request, so the appointment date rests on the two news items.

blocks.x: 2017: four interventions, not two

r: MVRDV's project page for the same week lists a slightly longer partner line than the post does: MVRDV, The Why Factory, the municipality, the Eindhoven University of Technology, IIT Chicago and Dutch Design Week.
MVRDV's post names four interventions, and the shorthand of a hotel and a masterclass leaves two out.
The Future City is Wide was a film at the entrance of the Klokgebouw exhibition center, sorted by agenda point, showing hundreds of ideas from students of The Why Factory.

The Future City has Memories was a presentation and book launch of the Why Factory's Copy Paste: A Badass Copy Guide at the Klokgebouw, which the post says treats works of architecture as if they were science, so that a famous bridge could become a hospital.
The VPRO adds a datingbank for designers and plants in the Veemgebouw, a board with a thousand packets of seed, as a prelude to the Floriade 2022 in Almere, which it says MVRDV would design.
The two interventions the archive photographed are the other two: (W)ego and ICI Eindhoven.

blocks.x: (W)ego: a hotel of nine wishes

r: The post calls (W)ego The Future City is Flexible, an installation on the Markt square with nine rooms made from an idealistic but egoistic perspective, including a panorama room, a stair room and a sky room.
A second post dated October 20, 2017 gives the opening dates, October 21 to 29, 2017, and quotes Maas on the hypothesis that the maximum density could equal the maximum of desires.

It adds that the installation represents a frozen moment of a living, flexible vision from The Why Factory, in which future dwellings adapt in real time to their users, and that a film in one of the rooms details that vision.
The first post describes it as a walkable folly nine meters high with nine hotel rooms.
The idea is a negotiation. Users share a limited space and must deal with the dream rooms of others, so that ego becomes wego.

The VPRO quotes Maas describing a labyrinth of small rooms, some vertical and some horizontal, a puzzle in which you feel close to the neighbor and still have privacy, and it says the intention was that the public could really sleep a night there.
MVRDV's own posts do not mention overnight stays, so I cannot say whether anyone slept in it.
The archive's (W)ego album holds 21 photographs, 16 credited in the titles to Ossip van Duivenbode and 5 to Ruud Balk.

In one view, rooms in green, orange, pink and blue glow on a black platform at dusk, with café umbrellas and old buildings behind. In another, a single red room has slatted shutters, a round basin and a toilet.

Titles name no rooms. That is the problem with photographing a building made of wishes: the whole facade can stand for the project, while what each room was for goes unrecorded. I can say the archive shows the rooms, and I cannot say which wish belongs to which.

The idea did not end with the week. The Why Factory's own news page lists a Wego exhibition at the TU Delft on October 7, 2021, as part of the Together! exposition, describing the research as a desire-based design process that brings residents' wishes into the construction and adaptation of housing, with a book in its Future Cities series planned with NAi010 Publishers.
The same page announces a launch of the Why Factory's book (w)Ego, with a lecture by Maas, dated May 18, 2022.
The folly on the Markt was, on that evidence, one stage of a research project that ran at least four and a half years.

blocks.x: ICI Eindhoven: the kick-off

r: The fourth intervention, The Future City is Eindhoven, was the presentation on Stadhuisplein of a masterclass on the intensification of uses in the city center, in which students from several universities showed a wide variety of towers that could one day be built there.
MVRDV's post says the event was the kick-off for Maas's supervisory role for Eindhoven's inner city and that he began by asking citizens and discussing the future of their city.
The archive's album for it holds 22 photographs, all credited to Ruud Balk.

A gray pavilion carries cut-out letters that spell COME beneath the words Future Downtown Eindhoven, and inside, a round table is covered with an aerial photograph and a white block model of the city center.
At night a panel on the pavilion reads WE ARE HERE BECAUSE OF and lists logos, among them Eindhoven, Dutch Design Week Eindhoven, TU/e, MVRDV, TU Delft and De Meeuw.
The post names several of the same partners among the sponsors: De Meeuw, Dutch Design Week, the municipality, Van Beek Art Supplies, TU Delft, TU Eindhoven and Keeper Development.

Here the photographs do more than the titles. Lettering and a partner panel are text a reader can check, and they tie the pictures to the project in the project's own words. A city-scale argument needs more than one author, and the sponsor list says so in plain terms.

blocks.x: 2018: Future Downtown, with the job already running

r: MVRDV's post of October 19, 2018 dates the week October 20 to 28 and lists three things. A talk by Winy Maas was set for Wednesday, October 24 at 14:00 at the VDMA complex, supported by Architectuur Centrum Eindhoven and the municipality. An exhibition ran there all week, and Virtual Future Downtown, an augmented reality walk, stood in a large glass greenhouse on Stadhuisplein, made with the municipality and Dutch Rose Media as Future040.

The post says that in his role as supervisor of the city center Maas was asked to guide the vision and planning of the inner city, and that the exhibition's pavilion shows the work on upgrading the center, on radical greenification and on intensifying urban life, with an invitation to add more and talk about your Future Downtown Eindhoven.
An MVRDV event page gives the talk's address as 31T Vestdijk and says tickets sold out and the lecture was live-streamed.
The archive answers with two albums, 6 photographs by Tommy Köhlbrugge and 4 by Ruud Balk.

A window sign reads Future Downtown Eindhoven and the words intense, accessible, green, for everybody and wonderful. A white block model carries small green trees. A greenhouse of glass pavilions carries the words Virtual Downtown Eindhoven on its panes.

It is tempting to put the greenhouse and the walk in the foreground, but the post puts the exhibition and the talk at the VDMA first, and the six-photograph album most likely belongs there, given its title.
One caution on names: the album is titled Virtual Future Downtown, while its four photo titles read Near Future Downtown.
MVRDV's own post uses Virtual Future Downtown, so I use that name and note the difference.
The augmented reality walk itself cannot appear in a photograph of a greenhouse, so the archive shows the container and not the experience.

blocks.x: What came of it

r: The exhibitions were not self-contained. MVRDV's announcement of Maas stepping down describes the Inner City Densification Vision, adopted by the city council at the end of 2020, as an important achievement of the supervision, with two layers, an Eindhoven layer capped at 17 meters at ground level and a Brainport layer on top that reaches 45, 75, 105 or even 160 meters for individual buildings.

The municipality's own page for the vision confirms that the council adopted it on December 15, 2020, unchanged, and that the council embraced two motions, to keep the green wedges free of housing and to evaluate every large building project completed in the center.
Architectenweb reported that 39 of the 45 council members voted for it.
The numbers differ. MVRDV writes that the vision shows tens of thousands of additional homes can be created through densification alone.
Architectenweb wrote that up to 10,000 new homes could be realized.

The municipality's page says a tactical study found room for at most 21,000 homes within the ring road, provided that conditions on mobility, green space and water are met, against a regional agreement to build 35,000 to 40,000 homes in Eindhoven by 2040.
I take the municipality's 21,000 as the best-sourced ceiling and note that neither "tens of thousands" nor 10,000 matches it exactly.

The ending was contested. Architectenweb reported that the contract with Maas as supervisor was not extended and ended on December 31, 2021, that the municipality said the decision was taken in good consultation, and that local politicians had criticized a double role as supervisor and architect, after which a new supervisor would not be allowed to combine the two.
MVRDV said the new conditions made a proper fulfillment of the role impossible, and Maas said he wanted to do things himself and would focus on projects such as De Heuvel and the city office.
The municipality said the area visions had been adopted and the phase had moved from plan to development.

I mention this because the 2017 and 2018 photographs can look like architecture alone. They are also a record of a public role being introduced to the public at a festival, and the role's later dispute is part of what those exhibitions were for. The sources say that Maas's DDW work was framed as the start of the supervisory role. They do not say whether the dispute affected how the festival later treated MVRDV.

blocks.x: What an archive count cannot tell us

r: I would not read 43 photographs against 10 as a measure of how big each year was. An archive count records what was photographed and kept. MVRDV's posts give no visitor counts for its own projects, and the 2018 post's total refers to the whole of Dutch Design Week, with a figure of more than 335,000 visitors that matches the number Baltan Laboratories gives for the 2017 edition, so I do not use it for 2018.
Credits show the same partial record: three photographers cover the four albums, and no title names a designer at MVRDV.
Two editions are enough to compare and not enough to call a trend. The archive may also hold more MVRDV photographs under other album titles, and I did not search for them.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know whether anyone slept in (W)ego. I could not open the municipality's announcement of the supervisor appointment, or the festival's own programme pages for the 2018 events, which no longer open at the old addresses. I do not know which of the 2018 photographs were taken at the VDMA and which on Stadhuisplein.
If a project asks you to imagine a city, is the model the exhibit or the evidence? Next time you photograph a model, photograph its label too.

posts.title: Next Nature went from a job agency for robots to a museum in a landed spacecraft
posts.subtitle: Four Dutch Design Week editions of Next Nature, 2017 to 2025, read from Next Nature's own pages, DDW's program archive and the photo archive.
posts.seoTitle: Next Nature at Dutch Design Week, 2017 to 2025
posts.description: Next Nature's HUBOT job agency in 2017, RetroFuture in the Evoluon in 2022, and the 2024 and 2025 museum shows, against the DDW photo albums.

r: Next Nature began its Dutch Design Week story in this archive as a job agency for people and robots in an electronics store, and it appears in the later albums as the museum inside a building that looks like a landed spacecraft.
The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds four Next Nature albums, 2017, 2022, 2024 and 2025, 62 photographs in all.

Next Nature's own pages are unusually detailed about what it was doing in each of those years, and DDW's program pages let me test them. This essay draws on public sources only. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about what the museum will show in the 2026 edition beyond what its pages list.
I like a maker whose projects grow in size while the question stays the same, because it lets me test whether an archive can follow.

blocks.x: An organization that describes itself as a radar

r: Next Nature's about page calls it a non-profit of creatives, thinkers, educators and supporters, with members in 44 countries and a museum in the Netherlands, and says it explores how technology becomes so omnipresent, complex, intimate and autonomous that it becomes a nature of its own.

Its colophon lists Koert van Mensvoort as founder and CEO, a core team based in Eindhoven, and a set of named ambassadors that includes the astronaut André Kuipers, the philosopher Jos de Mul and the biotechnologist Mark Post.
I found no founding year on those pages, so I give none.

Next Nature's project pages describe earlier work in the same register. One is the NANO Supermarket, a mobile exhibition disguised as a shop that presents 50 speculative nanotech products, which its page says had received more than 75,000 visitors in cities including Eindhoven, Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Pamplona, Milan and Stavanger.
That page gives no dates and does not mention DDW, so I treat it as background and not as a DDW presentation.

blocks.x: 2017: HUBOT, in a store window

r: In a story dated October 4, 2017, Next Nature introduced HUBOT as the job agency for people and robots. It said the virtual office would open on October 12, and that HUBOT could be found at the MediaMarkt in Eindhoven from October 21, during Dutch Design Week 2017, and would travel the world afterward. It named three partners: Next Nature Network, Start Foundation and Gemeente Eindhoven.

The story describes 16 professions, "jobs from the future," in which technology lets people do work they could not otherwise do, and offers examples such as a mover in a robotic suit, a gaming farm manager and a six-armed masseur.

The project page adds an air traffic security worker who flies an eagle drone to keep birds away from planes, and a home healthcare professional whose cleaning drone leaves time to talk with patients.
It also says the exhibition could be hired for events, with two self-driving robots, a career test and four trained agency workers.
The 2017 album is titled HUBOT | Next Nature Network and holds 19 photographs by Ralph Roelse. Its photo titles name MediaMarkt and the dates October 21 to 29, 2017, which matches the story.

The photographs show a store with displays set among the shelves: a clear robot torso with white tube arms beside a screen reading Uitzendbureau voor mens en robot, a robotic suit on a plinth, and a wooden sign headed HUBOT - The job agency for people and robots.
The suit and the torso fit the jobs the pages list, but no sign I could read names the six-armed masseur, so I do not say that is what the torso is.

blocks.x: The building Next Nature took on

r: Next Nature's New Evoluon page says the Evoluon was built in 1966 as a technology and science museum on behalf of Frits Philips, to celebrate the 75th anniversary of Philips; that it drew over 500,000 visitors by 1970 with interactive exhibits; and that it was withdrawn from operation in 1989 despite many protests.

The page says the building's design reminds one of a spacecraft that landed in Eindhoven, announces a collaboration between Next Nature and the Evoluon Foundation, and proposes a plan in four rings: geosphere, biosphere, technosphere and mindsphere.
It says that in the fall of 2021 the building became a VR Time Machine, and that the first major exhibition, RetroFuture, would debut on September 24, 2022.
These are Next Nature's own statements, and they carry its enthusiasm. I did not find an independent source for the visitor count or the closure date.

blocks.x: 2022: RetroFuture

r: DDW's program lists RetroFuture as a DDW 2022 project presented by Next Nature, in the Evoluon, with ten tunnels across 3,000 square meters and work by Studio Drift, Maison de Faux with Esmay Wagemans, Driessens & Verstappen, Audrey Large, Tabita Rezaire, Michael Mandiberg and Studio Smack.

It describes a fairground area with ten ideas on contemporary topics, among them the Microbial Vending Machine by Emma van der Leest, a converted snack machine with products made from algae and enzymes in place of croquettes, a VR Time Machine, a haunted house and a slot machine about the future of money.
Next Nature's own project page gives a figure of over 50,000 tickets sold and says visitors could create a deepfake of themselves in the funfair.
The ticket figure is Next Nature's claim, and the page gives no date for the count.
The 2022 album is titled Evoluon and holds 22 photographs: 16 by Tommy Köhlbrugge titled RetroFuture and dated October 22 and 23, 2022, and six by about.today titled with the spelling VRPO.
They show a glass tunnel of robots, a wall of historic photographs, an atrium with a spiral stair, banners reading Inclusion in many languages and a DeLorean with an Evoluon plate.
The spelling VRPO is probably a typo for VPRO, but no page I opened says so.

blocks.x: 2024: a recap with names and no dates

r: The DDW24 area recap, dated October 24, 2024, says the West area is home to the Evoluon, which it calls the Next Nature Museum, and names projects such as Microbial Oasis, A House of Salt and Meet Meat: Rourou's Adventure, and a Breathing Session with Geoffrey Lillemon.
It prints no dates for them.

The 2024 album is the smallest in the set, with 7 photographs dated October 19, 20 and 23 that show a yellow dome with hand-drawn walls, a dome of seed images and visitors lying on mats in a dark dome.

blocks.x: 2025: fifty talents under one dome

r: Next Nature's page for Digital Futures says the museum presented it in collaboration with DDW, with the works of 50 pioneering talents and makers in the Dome from October 18 to 26, 2025, free to visit as part of the DDW program, while a museum ticket was needed for RetroFuture and the Digital Wellness Center.

It describes Econario by Woven Studio as a 5-meter-high robotic plant driven by predictions from the Natural History Museum's Biodiversity Intactness Index, and Apathos by Studio Falkland as a human-sized phone from the front and a server from the back that shows how scrolling and liking lead to recommendations.
It describes Bloomlight S by Justus Bruns as a lamp whose stem bends toward someone who approaches, an example of slow tech.

Those are the museum's descriptions of works. The 2025 album holds 14 photographs, several with visitors in headsets gesturing in the air, and no title names a work, so I cannot match a photograph to any project above.

blocks.x: The plan that changed

r: In 2022 the New Evoluon page said the aim was a fully reopened Evoluon from 2025.

The museum's current "on show" page says something different: it lists Once Upon a Time… the Earth as the first chapter of Enter Spaceship Earth, the permanent exhibition being developed at the Evoluon, alongside a Quantum Escape Room, a Facebook Museum, the Digital Wellness Center and RetroFuture.
So by October 2026 the permanent exhibition is under development and has not fully opened, and the 2025 date in the old plan has passed.

I do not know why the schedule moved, and no source I opened says. DDW's location page lists the Next Nature Museum at Noord Brabantlaan 1A with opening hours of 11:00 to 18:00 daily during October 17 to 25, 2026.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: An earlier timeline could not place the album at the Evoluon. Next Nature's story and the photo titles agree on the MediaMarkt, which settles it.
The 2022 page promises a full reopening from 2025, and the current page describes a permanent exhibition in development. The current page is the later statement.
Over 500,000 by 1970 (the Evoluon) and over 50,000 tickets (RetroFuture) are Next Nature's figures, undated and with no outside source.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know the founding year of Next Nature, the dates of the 2024 projects, what any 2024 or 2025 photograph shows beyond its description, or what the Evoluon's 2023 album adds, since it belongs to the Evoluon venue timeline. I did not find a DDW program page for HUBOT. Next Nature's press page lists a media kit titled Eindhoven viert 60 jaar Evoluon, and I did not find its text.
The album facts are from my reading of the Flickr account on October 8, 2026, which I did not repeat.
If an organization's address changes from a store to a spaceship, what would you ask a photograph to prove before you let it tell you the story?
