posts.title: NUL ZES at Dutch Design Week: a gasworks site, a collective of studios and the makers the archive files under three names
posts.subtitle: The NRE terrein, the studios of Lotte de Raadt, Kirstie van Noort and Alissa+Nienke, and what five albums from 2018 to 2025 can and cannot show of them.
posts.seoTitle: NUL ZES at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: The NRE terrein, the NUL ZES collective since 2013, the studios of Lotte de Raadt, Kirstie van Noort and Alissa+Nienke, and what the DDW albums show.

r: One corner of Eindhoven, a former gasworks, appears in the Dutch Design Week photo archive under a collective's name, under the names of two sets of makers, and under a show title that a 2018 review ties to a third maker.

I like an archive that makes me sort names before I write a caption. This essay uses the places' own pages, a city guide, a municipal planning document, DDW interviews and program pages, the founders' and makers' own accounts, regional and trade press from 2017 to 2023, and the DDW photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and it does not call the makers young, because no source I opened does.

blocks.x: The place: a gasworks that became a utility, then a neighborhood

r: This is Eindhoven says the NRE-terrein has been a gasworks site since 1899, owes its name to the Nutsbedrijven Regio Eindhoven (the utilities of the Eindhoven region) that were there from 1989 to 2010, and was then bought by the municipality and turned into a creative neighborhood where working, living and culture come together.

A concept appendix of justifications for the municipality's plan, dated September 10, 2015, shows the idea in its working form. It identifies the site as a possible breeding ground (broedplaats) for the creative industry, plans up to 10,000 square meters of housing and up to 11,500 square meters for offices, businesses and community uses, and lists a 1,000 square meter event location called FIFTH among the leisure uses, adding that the current users together occupy 1,700 square meters.

The 2019 IO+ article describes the change from the inside: new residents such as the jazz club Fifth and the cycling cafe Cyklist, apartments rising on the site, and a group of people over 50 who converted monumental building number 2 into housing.

Omroep Brabant, writing in late 2021 when the NRE-terrein was a finalist for the Brabantse Stijlprijs, adds that one of the first initiative groups saw the empty utility buildings as a place for a housing group for people over 55, that eleven former factory buildings now hold residents of all ages, designers and craftspeople among them, and that the municipality helped the initiators develop their plans themselves without a developer in between.
Both are local accounts, and both fit the city guide's picture of empty utility buildings turned into a mixed neighborhood of housing and creative use.

blocks.x: NUL ZES in its own words, and in others'

r: DDW's location page for 2026 says NUL ZES is the home of more than 18 creatives, from designers to architects and form researchers to illustrators, in two redeveloped buildings on the industrial NRE terrain, at Gasfabriek 3A. It is open October 17 to 25, 2026, from 11:00 to 20:00, and the page says it is not wheelchair accessible.
This is Eindhoven describes a multidisciplinary collective of individual companies whose motto is that their work is their mission.

The collective's start has a date in its founder's own words. In an IO+ hidden-gem profile published on October 14, 2017, Renee Scheepers, a designer who graduated from the Design Academy Eindhoven and the founder of NUL ZES, says she started it after graduating because she had wanted a place of her own in Eindhoven for a long time, with different people under one roof, and that "in 2013, we started on the NRE-area." She says empty sites in a city are often filled temporarily with creatives, who are then pushed out for bigger companies, and that when the land on the NRE terrain went up for sale the group decided it wanted to be that established order itself and planned to buy its own space with an investor.

That is the founder's account, published four years after the start. The profile settles a question the earlier version of this essay left open, the year the collective began: 2013, according to the person who started it.

The next account comes from the people who rented there. In a DDW interview with Alissa+Nienke, NUL ZES arose out of necessity: after their studies at Design Academy Eindhoven they wanted an affordable workspace with shared facilities, knowledge and networks, wrote a ten-year proposal to the municipality as a group and found someone willing to invest.

The 2019 article counts seventeen members at that point and describes separate workspaces, brainstorming places and their own ceramics, wood and metal workshop, where the first layout of one large open space had stopped working as the group grew.

An undated VPRO Dorst page about Dutch Design Week, which gives the festival dates as October 19 to 27, describes ten people who turned an old building on the NRE terrain into a workshop and hangout, from studio to stage and bar to office, and it counts the group as ten.
The counts differ because the accounts date from different years, and none of them gives a registered founding date for the collective.

An official visit puts a date on the standing of the place. On February 16, 2023 Queen Máxima made a working visit to designers in Eindhoven, and the Dutch Design Foundation, reporting it on February 17, 2023, says she went first to NUL ZES, which it describes as a designer collective and creative laboratory for designers, architects and researchers, where she met its founder Renee Scheepers and designers Alissa van Asseldonk and Nienke Bongers of Alissa+Nienke, and talked about their preparation for Milan Design Week 2023.
A royal-house social media post, as quoted by a fan blog, says the same.

blocks.x: Lotte de Raadt and Kirstie van Noort: iron sludge as pigment

r: The two ceramic designers have separate studios and share a ceramics workshop in the collective.

Lotte de Raadt told Vij5 that she applied to the Design Academy at sixteen, started her studio straight after her studies, graduated on tap water with three drinking-water carafes inspired by the three kinds of Dutch water source, and turned to ceramics in an anti-squatting studio, where she found she loved it. The Water Research Knowledge Center KWR then asked her for a commission, and she remade her carafe in terracotta, which cools water by evaporation.

Kirstie van Noort's own page says she graduated from the Design Academy's department Man and Well-Being in 2011, has run her own studio in Eindhoven since 2012, received the Material Award in 2012 for design research in Cornwall and did a two-month residency on porcelain in Arita, Japan, in 2014.

The OER project, whose name is the Dutch word for iron sludge, has been in development since 2016, according to Vij5, which says KWR asked them to find uses for the residual stream of tap-water production that would otherwise go back into the sewer.

Van Noort's own page describes the sludge as a residual waste product from water production, deep red, usable as a source of ceramic pigment, and says the work produced a pink-to-red coloring on ceramics and a line of wall tiles.

The tiles are the long project. DDW's program page for Van slib naar tegel, From sludge to tile, says Inbo designed a new circular groundwater production plant for Brabant Water in Eindhoven, that more than a thousand liters of iron sludge would be processed into 10,000 tiles for one wall, that the design refers to the reflecting character of water, and that Koninklijk Tichelaar was producing the tiles with the plant's realization planned for 2023. It invites visitors to the designers' studio at Nul Zes to see the first results.

The page prints no year. A MaterialDistrict entry dated February 21, 2023 repeats the same sentences, with the plant still described as planned for 2023, and I found no source that says whether the wall was installed.

The tableware is the other branch. Vij5 describes porcelain mixed with iron sludge, drawn from the buffer pond of the water production company, dried, ground and sifted into a rust-colored powder, poured into plaster molds, glazed on the inside and fired at 1250 degrees Celsius, so that the pigment turns beige with dark brown specks, and says it has been in its collection since 2023.

Vij5's interview adds how the link to the shop came about: Lotte de Raadt says she met Vij5's founders through her colleagues Alissa and Nienke, and that her products have been in the Vij5 collection since 2017.

The DDW record for them is older than the 2018 album. Van Noort's own exhibition list says OER was shown at DDW 2017 in the Crafts Council exhibition HOW&WOW, and that she took part in the Dutch Invertuals shows No Static in 2015 and Fundamentals in 2017.
A 2018 review says the duo presented OER at NRE as ceramics decorated with oxidized iron, spelling her first name Kristie, as the archive's 2018 and 2021 album titles do.
I use the spelling on her own site.

blocks.x: Alissa+Nienke: A+N Studio, from porcelain to woven walls

r: A+N Studio's own page says it is a material research and design studio founded in 2014 by Alissa van Asseldonk and Nienke Bongers, who met at Design Academy Eindhoven, with its studio at Gasfabriek 3A on the NRE terrein, and it names Dior, Fendi and the Municipality of Eindhoven among the organizations it has worked for.

In a January 3, 2018 interview Alissa van Asseldonk says they met at the academy during internships, started with a "material get-together" that became their porcelain line Pigments & Porcelain, and later widened the studio to manipulating flat materials so that they pop up, move or elevate.
Vij5 sells Pigments & Porcelain as cups made of colored porcelain in limited series.
The DDW program listing for 2026 describes A+N Studio as founded by the same two people, so the album titles Alissa_Nienke and the 2026 listing refer to one studio.

The October 9, 2019 article describes what they brought to DDW that year. They had spent months exploring 3D weaving with EE Exclusive, a family business in Heeze that makes jacquard fabrics, supported by the Creative Industries Fund NL, and had run at least 300 tests for woven textiles that can serve as wall coverings, room dividers or acoustic coverings. The Fringes & Floats textile collection was shown in a smaller building behind their studio, and The Sun Show, a materials vision on awnings, in the studio itself. The article also mentions paneled drapes they developed for the office of the Minister of Education, Culture and Science.
DDW's own program page for Fringes & Floats, credited to Alissa+Nienke x EE Exclusives, describes it as a total overview of the research, from samples to large surface applications.

The DDW interview adds their view of the festival: they say they take part because the studio is in Eindhoven, because guests and business relations from abroad come, and because DDW allows more research-oriented presentations than the sales-oriented one they had at the Salone del Mobile in 2018.

For 2026 DDW lists Weave / Weld, in which A+N and EE Exclusives test what happens when woven recycled PET is welded instead of sewn. It says the exhibition ranges from tiny weld points to large-scale structures and a process wall of sketches, tests and samples, and that it is not wheelchair accessible.

blocks.x: The third name in 2018: Crush on Nature

r: The 2018 album carries a title the earlier sources did not explain, CrushOnNature. The Italian blogger whose 2018 round-up places Lotte de Raadt and Kristie van Noort at NRE also writes that, always at NRE, Fabrique Céramique showed in an exhibit together with Liesbeth Bulk, who with Crush on Nature makes objects from glass and synthetic resin, and mentions the ceramics of Hester de Wolff.
That is one blog, and the album title is the only other place the name appears, so I read it as a lead and not a record.
It does show that the NRE terrain in 2018 held more makers than the three names in the album, and that the album's single CrushOnNature photograph probably belongs to a fourth presentation.

blocks.x: Five albums, four years

r: The archive holds five albums for these names: 2018 with 13 photos, titled for Lotte and Kristie, Alissa+Nienke and NulZes; 2019 with 12, for Alissa+Nienke; 2021 with 12 for Lotte & Kristie and 9 for Alissa & Nienke; and 2025 with 68 for NUL ZES, 114 photos in all.
Nick Bookelaar is credited by title for 2018 to 2021, and the 2025 titles name no photographer.
The 2018 album mixes presentations: of its 13 photos, 5 are titled Alissa_Nienke, 4 Lotte_Kristie, 3 NulZes and 1 CrushOnNature.
The review and Van Noort's list explain the Lotte and Kristie part, because OER was shown at NRE that year, and the review explains the CrushOnNature photo.
For 2019 the article names two shows, and the 12 photos name neither.

For 2021 the albums show pink and orange tiles and discs, and freestanding panel walls in blue, pink and gray. The DDW program page for From sludge to tile is the closest match for the first album, since the tiles are pink to red, but the page prints no year and the album titles name no work, so I treat the match as a lead.
The 2025 album's titles name Friend & Friends of Friends, Rematerialised and Oori Apparel by Cleo Goossens, with the date October 19, 2025. None names the four makers.

DDW's 2026 location page lists four exhibitions at NUL ZES: Touch On Connection by Plura Studio, Workroom in progress by Tessa van der Wey and Oori Apparel, Atlas by Cleo Goossens and Oori Apparel, and Weave / Weld by A+N Studio.
So the collective is a venue for several makers' shows, not a single exhibitor.

blocks.x: Questions the sources settle

r: Does the A+N name in the 2026 listing mean the Alissa+Nienke of the albums? Yes: A+N Studio's page and the DDW listing give the same founders, and the studio's 2019 DDW interview names the same pair.
Did Lotte and Kirstie show only at NRE? No: Van Noort's list puts OER at DDW 2017 in HOW&WOW as well.
Is the OER project old or new? It has been in development since 2016, and its tiles were planned for a plant due in 2023.
When did NUL ZES start? In 2013 on the NRE-area, per its founder.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what the 2021 photographs show by name, whether any 2025 photograph shows work by these makers, who took the 2025 photographs, or when each maker joined the collective.

I could not open the municipal EU ROCK document on the NRE site, because its host's robots.txt returned 403, and Eindhoven's monument register PDF for the gasworks answered with a rejection page, so the site's dates after 1899 rest on the city guide, the planning appendix and the press.
The collective's own website redirected to an empty page, so I have no statement from NUL ZES about itself beyond DDW's page and its founder's interview.
I do not know whether the Brabant Water wall was installed, how the collective financed its own building, or whether it bought it.
When you sort an album's titles into collective, studio and show, which of the three has a source in front of you, and which is a guess?

posts.title: NUL ZES at Dutch Design Week: a collective that predates its two photo albums by nine years
posts.subtitle: A 2013 broadcaster's post, DDW's music pages, a 2019 news story and a royal visit show a collective on the NRE terrain long before the archive's first album.
posts.seoTitle: NUL ZES at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: NUL ZES, the collective on the NRE terrain in Eindhoven: a 2013 pop-up office, DDW music venue, member shows, the 2022 Ambassadors Dinner and a 2023 royal visit.

r: The photo archive's first NUL ZES album is from 2022, and a public broadcaster's site was already reporting from a pop-up office inside the collective during Dutch Design Week 2013.

That nine-year gap is the main finding of this essay. The archive makes NUL ZES look like a place that appeared in the past few years, and the written record says it was part of the week long before. This essay draws on public sources only: a 2013 blog post, DDW's own pages for several years, two city listings, a regional news report, a report on a royal visit, Baltan Laboratories' 2025 report and the official photo archive as I recorded it on October 8, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 week beyond what DDW's location page states.

blocks.x: The earliest account: ten people and a pop-up office in 2013

r: On October 21, 2013 the VPRO's Dorst site wrote that it was reporting on Dutch Design Week from a pop-up office at the collective Nul Zes on the NRE terrain in Eindhoven.

The post says ten people, listed by first name, had turned an old building on the terrain into a workshop and hangout "from studio to stage, from bar to office and everything in between," that together they make more than objects, since they also make image and sound, launch ideas, build spaces and organize events, and that they call the place Nul Zes.

Two of the ten first names, Alissa and Nienke, are also the first names of the designers of the studio Alissa+Nienke, which Innovation Origins calls part of the NUL ZES designer collective in October 2019, but the 2013 post gives no surnames, so I do not say they are the same people.
That one post moves the collective's start back at least to 2013. No page I opened gives a founding date, and the later descriptions do not say how many of the original ten remain.

Six years later, Innovation Origins wrote on October 9, 2019 that NUL ZES had expanded to seventeen members, that the group had kept its own building among the newer neighbors, the jazz club Fifth and the cycling cafe Cyklist, and that it had refitted the interior from one large open space into separate workspaces, with its own ceramics, wood and metal workshop.

The same article says the Alissa+Nienke studio showed two projects during Dutch Design Week 2019, a textile collection called Fringes & Floats in a smaller building behind the studio and The Sun Show, a materials vision on awnings, inside the main building.

So there was a NUL ZES presence at the 2019 week, even though the photo archive has no NUL ZES album for that year. DDW's 2026 page says NUL ZES is the home base of more than 18 creatives, from designers and architects to researchers and illustrators, in two redeveloped buildings on the industrial NRE terrain in the center of Eindhoven that serve as workspace, community and creative laboratory.

The city's tourism listing adds that the members are all individual companies with one thing in common, "our work is our mission," and that they aim to work and meet in complete freedom, openness and tolerance.

blocks.x: The terrain: a gasworks that became a neighborhood

r: The tourism guide's page on the NRE terrain says it has a long history as a former gasworks site, that the area has changed shape several times since its establishment in 1899, and that the name comes from the Nutsbedrijven Regio Eindhoven, the public utilities that were based there from 1989 to 2010, after which the municipality bought the site and turned it into a creative city neighborhood.

A regional news report of December 2, 2021 adds the residents' side. It describes a group of initiators who, almost ten years earlier, had spotted the empty utility buildings and wanted a housing group for people over 55, who got one, and says the other former factory buildings, eleven in all, now hold younger residents, designers and craft businesses, a ceramics workshop, a bicycle repairer, a bike cafe and a restaurant with live music.
It says the initiative group developed its own plans with the municipality's help and no developer in between, and that the terrain was a finalist for the Brabant style prize 2021.
The NUL ZES address on DDW's page and on the listing is Gasfabriek 3A in Eindhoven.

DDW's page for the 2026 week lists daily opening hours of 11:00 to 20:00 from October 17 to 25 and says the location is not wheelchair accessible, while the tourism listing gives 11:00 to 18:00 every day, which is probably its ordinary schedule.
The two hour sets are different statements for different weeks, and I do not treat them as a conflict.

blocks.x: The music years: a venue in 2015 and 2016

r: NUL ZES appears in DDW's own pages as a music venue before it appears in the photo archive. The press page of September 1, 2015 lists Nul Zes among the places for the first DDW Music, and the page of September 14, 2016 lists it again among twelve locations for the second.
The 2017 announcement lists ten venues and does not include it, although another NRE-terrain venue, FIFTH | NRE, is on that list.
DDW's pages say nothing about what the collective did on those nights, and the archive's DDW Music albums of 2015 and 2017 were read in the music item of this series, not here.
So the collective shows up in 2013 as a workplace, in 2015 and 2016 as a stage and in 2022 as a host.

blocks.x: 2019 and 2022: where the Ambassadors' Dinner sits

r: DDW's report on its 2022 edition, published October 30, 2022, shows a photograph with the caption "DDW22 Ambassadors Dinner hosted by Nul Zes," credited to about.today.

The same report gives the theme as Get Set... We're on a mission, quotes Miriam van der Lubbe on a new generation of designers, and says visitor numbers were on the level of the peak year 2019, which is DDW's own claim and carries no figure.
It also quotes the ambassadors, the Formafantasma duo Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin and the solar designer Marjan van Aubel.
It does not say who sat at the dinner.

The host changes from year to year. DDW's page for the 2019 Ambassadors' Dinner, published December 19, 2019, says Studio Drift, in their role as DDW Ambassador, organized the dinner in the Paterskerk, a church built in 1890 that was still being refurbished, with guests at three long tables lit in green, the theme color of the eighteenth edition.
The 2019 page does not mention NUL ZES, and no page I opened says the 2019 dinner and the 2022 dinner belong to a series with a fixed rule about who hosts.
I read the pairing as a pattern, a different ambassador and a different place each time, and I label that as my reading.
The archive's 2022 album holds 59 photographs, every title reading DDW2022 Ambassadors Dinner, with no photographer named.
The old dossier describes a hall and a yard at night with red neon digits, a performer in a silver suit on a cable, an open kitchen under a tent, a lit FOOD sign and a crowd.
None of those has a name attached, and I do not give one.

blocks.x: 2023: a royal visit

r: On February 16, 2023, Queen Máxima visited NUL ZES first on a working visit to Eindhoven designers, according to the Royal House's own social posts as quoted by the design blog UFO No More: she first visited NUL ZES, a designer collective and creative laboratory for designers, architects and researchers, and afterward the Home of Design Kazerne.

The Royal House's news page of March 15, 2023 says her visit to Milan Design Week follows an earlier meeting with designers during her visit to Eindhoven on February 16, where she will meet some of them again.
The visit is the strongest evidence of the collective's standing outside the festival. It also places the collective in the same trip as Kazerne, which has its own entry in this series.

blocks.x: 2025: events at the collective, and one named week

r: Baltan Laboratories' year report for 2025 lists two NUL ZES events. On May 31, 2025 a meet-up organized by DES.ENG.AGE took place at Nulzes, the second quarterly networking event of a platform connecting Eindhoven designers and artists with ASML engineers, with an in-person test of an app called Skibly, organized with Skibly, Nulzes and Baltan.

From October 23 to 26, 2025, during Dutch Design Week, the report lists Silicon Souls at NulZES, a series of open dialogues organized by DES.ENG.AGE with Baltan Laboratories on the transformation of raw materials such as sand into silicon-based technologies.
That is the first written account I found of anything the collective hosted in 2025, and it covers four days of the nine.

The archive's 2025 album holds 68 photographs, and the old dossier counts titles in sets: Friend&Friendsoffriends, Rematerialised and OoriApparel_CleoGoossens on October 19, nine titles by Max Kneefel dated October 22 and 32 titles ending CleoGoossens_24okt.
The photographs show busts, hanging tiles, pleated cloth, posters and lamps, and in two a window and a chalkboard that name A+N x Kraftmann, Friends of Friends and Oori Apparel.
None of those events is the same as Silicon Souls, and no title or page ties the albums to it, so I do not link them.

blocks.x: What the credits say

r: The old draft treated the name Cleo Goossens in the 2025 titles as a maker's until a source said otherwise. A source now leans the other way. DDW's own magazine page of October 27, 2019 on the Ketelhuisplein is credited to Cleo Goossens as its author and carries the photograph credit "© Cleo Goossens" on its images.
The album titles in the archive follow a pattern of subject plus photographer's name, as in titles that read Strijp-S_VEEM_Manifestations_TommyKöhlbrugge.
So a title ending CleoGoossens_24okt is more likely a photographer's file label than a maker's name.
Against that, DDW's 2026 page for NUL ZES, as the old dossier read it, lists an exhibition by Cleo Goossens and Oori Apparel, which could be the same person in another role.
I cannot settle it from the pages, and a credit line for those photographs should be confirmed with DDW.

In my own field, a specimen without a label teaches me less than a labeled one, and I read an archive the same way. The 2022 album records an evening well and says almost nothing it can be held to, and the 2025 album carries more labels and gains from them.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: DDW and the city listing give no date. The VPRO post of October 21, 2013 shows it operating then, so the start was 2013 or earlier.
What NUL ZES did at Dutch Design Week before 2022.
The old draft found nothing for other years. DDW's 2015 and 2016 music pages list it as a venue, and Innovation Origins describes member shows there in 2019.
Studio Drift in the Paterskerk in 2019 and the collective in 2022 per DDW's captions. No rule is stated.
DDW's magazine credits a photographer of that name, and the 2026 exhibition list may name a maker. Not settled.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know when the collective formed, who its members are now, or whether the 2013 ten still work together. The count of seventeen in 2019 and the "more than 18" in 2026 are the only membership numbers I found.

I do not know what NUL ZES showed in 2025 beyond the Baltan-related events, because the album's sets and the report's two events do not overlap in any source I opened. I do not know who photographed the 2022 dinner, since DDW credits about.today for one image only. I did not open the collective's own website, which returned an empty page, and I did not open the municipal monument register, which refused my request.
I did not reopen the photo archive for this version, so the album counts, titles and what the photographs show come from the dossier's October 8, 2026 reading.
Nothing here describes NUL ZES's 2026 program.
If an archive can show you a collective for the first time in 2022, and a broadcaster's post can show you the same collective in 2013, which one do you believe about when it began?

posts.title: OS ∆ OOS at Dutch Design Week: a name you can type, two albums and a hidden gem
posts.subtitle: A Strijp-T studio read through its own words, two 2016 profiles, a museum page and the Dutch Design Week photo archive.
posts.seoTitle: OS and OOS at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: OS and OOS, a Strijp-T design studio: its name, its materials, a hidden gem show in 2018 and two photo albums read against their sources.

r: OS ∆ OOS chose a name that a gallery could type without asking for a logo, and the photo archive that files the studio once with an ampersand and once with the triangle shows how far a typed name travels.

I like work you can look through. This essay draws on public sources only: a Dutch Design Week magazine page, the Innovation Origins article behind it, two profiles from 2016, the Design Museum's page for an exhibition and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about what the studio shows at Dutch Design Week 2026.

blocks.x: A name you can type

r: Sight Unseen's 2016 studio visit explains the name. Sophie Mensen says Os comes from Oskar, and Oos is a family nickname from her childhood: when Oskar Peet met her family they said, hey Os and Oos, before the studio existed. The distinctive triangle can be made on a keyboard by pressing Alt and J, and Peet says that way a gallery asking for the logo can type it themselves.

So the triangle was chosen to travel. The Flickr archive I read in an earlier pass files the 2017 album as OS&OOS and the 2018 album as OS ∆ OOS, which means a keyword search for one spelling finds one year.
In plain text I write OS and OOS.

blocks.x: How the studio began, in three accounts

r: WOTH's July 2016 profile says Peet studied engineering in Canada before entering the Design Academy Eindhoven, where he met Mensen at a party during their third year. After graduating he worked at Scholten & Baijings, she worked as a trainee for Pieke Bergmans and started her own studio, and the two studios merged in 2011 to form OS ∆ OOS.
A Sight Unseen teaser dated January 9, 2012 says the studio was founded "this fall," meaning fall 2011, and launched with a trio of lamps.

The lamps were Syzygy, named after the alignment of three celestial bodies. WOTH describes three filters with film between them that manipulate the light, with a light source that stays on, and a rotating disc that can block it.
Sight Unseen describes the same thing as three lamps whose intensity depends on the rotation of three light-filtering discs.
DDW's page adds that the Syzygy lamps were later put into production by the Italian brand FontanaArte.
Because the sources describe the same lamp in three different ways, I take the common core: light that can be dimmed or blocked by turning discs by hand.

blocks.x: A catalog built on materials

r: The profiles list a run of objects with one thing in common: each starts from a material. The Keystone chair is a pile of geometric blocks that WOTH calls Memphis-like, made first in concrete, with a version weighing 450 kilograms, then in ceramic and then upholstered in fabric by Raf Simons for Kvadrat. Sight Unseen says the first version had no connections, with only weight and gravity holding the blocks of concrete, rubber and ceramic together.
The Mono-Lights combine tubes that look like fluorescent tubes but contain LEDs with flexible links of extruded silicone foam.
The Design Museum lists Mono-Lights by OS ∆ OOS among the entries of Beazley Designs of the Year 2016, an exhibition that ran from November 24, 2016 to February 19, 2017.
WOTH adds that the Vitra Design Museum acquired the studio's Concrete Colouring Table, which balances on a single concrete leg.

Peet says in the Sight Unseen visit that the two try not to make things that could have been made 50 or 100 years ago, and WOTH says the designers love sheets of glass, metal and brass and hardly ever use wood.
Mensen describes a process that begins at a moment when they do not know what the thing will be.
These are the studio's own accounts of its method, and I report them as that.

blocks.x: A workshop at the edge of Strijp-T

r: WOTH describes a blue door marked OS∆OOS at Strijp-T, the studio behind it and a workshop shared with the designer Daphna Laurens and Studio Mieke Meijer. Each designer bought an expensive machine, so together they have what they need.

Sight Unseen visited during Dutch Design Week in the fall of 2015 and describes the workshop as a former industrial building shared with those two Design Academy graduates, noting that rent in Eindhoven is cheap compared with Amsterdam and Rotterdam.
That visit is the earliest link between the studio and the festival that I found, two years before the first album in the archive.
Peet says in the same piece that Eindhoven feels a bit rough, that it is constantly developing, and that every year they think of moving and the city gets better.

In 2018 he said the city is slowly moving toward them. In the Innovation Origins profile the studio sits at the edge of Strijp-T opposite the renovated TQ building, next to the recently opened office of Additive Industries, and not far from the large Innovation Powerhouse, which had opened the year before.

blocks.x: 2017: Tunnel Vision, as far as a file title goes

r: The 2017 album holds 11 photographs by Tommy Köhlbrugge, and its file titles read OS&OOS_TunnelVision. They show a white room with an orange perforated panel, black cylinder benches and an aluminum tube on thin rods, a white U of light on a ceiling track, and a round wall lamp over glass shelves. I read the album in an earlier pass and did not reopen the account for this version, so every Flickr fact here is second-hand.
No page I opened describes a 2017 show or says where it was held, and none of my sources, including the 2018 profiles, mentions Tunnel Vision.
The phrase may name an exhibition, a room or a photographer's shorthand, and I cannot choose among them.
One thing can be set beside another without being joined. The photographs include a round wall lamp with a dark disc on its face, and the studio's Syzygy lamps use rotating discs.
Nothing in a title or a page ties the two together.

blocks.x: 2018: Body of Work, a hidden gem

r: The 2018 exhibition has the best documentation of any year. Dutch Design Week's magazine page and the Innovation Origins article both name it Body of Work, in building TQ 1 at Strijp-T, opposite the studio.
The studio called it a dream location, a large, empty space, and Mensen says it was a wonderful place to show their work.

The two pages are really one text. The Innovation Origins article of October 18, 2018 says the studio wishes to present its Body of Work at this DDW, and marks the fifth year it has worked in Eindhoven. The DDW page repeats the piece in the past tense, as presented at last DDW, and its page date reads January 1, 2019.
An earlier note called that date impossible. The wording shows the page was written or revised after the festival, so the date is plausible.

The profile was part of the Hidden Gems series. Every year Dutch Design Daily, Innovation Origins and Dutch Design Week's program manager Katja Lucas pick nine designers they consider the year's hidden gems, and the studio was number eight. A daily bike route let visitors meet the selected designers.

In the profile the studio describes its method: designs are launched in limited editions and most products are made only once they are sold. Peet says their handwriting is layered, that they play with transparency and optical effects, and that they work a lot with glass and aluminum, though the combination of materials defines their style.

The same profile says the first thing they made as OS ∆ OOS was Syzygy, and that the large room dividers Perspectives no. 1 and no. 2, supported by the Zurich gallery Roehrs & Boetsch, are Mensen's choice for their most autonomous piece.
WOTH names the dividers' three variants: Reflection, a brass sheet bent at 90 degrees, Color-Bleeding, and Distortion, made of three polished steel surfaces.

The profile ends on interiors. Eyewear brand Ace & Tate opened a flagship store in Eindhoven and wanted local designers. It first asked for the lamps, then for the entire interior, and the studio says it had no experience with traffic flows in shops. Ace & Tate then commissioned the new offices in Groningen, Dublin and Brussels.
An earlier version of this essay, following a summary of the DDW page, said the interiors were for shops in four cities. The page text says the other three are offices.

blocks.x: What the 2018 photographs can say

r: The 2018 album holds 11 photographs by Nick Bookelaar, and DDW's own page credits him for its Body of Work pictures.

The photographs step back from objects: a tunnel lined with red grid ribs, a wall of square glass blocks lit from behind, a skylit white hall with glass pendants, a net of gold rods across a pale floor and a round lamp on stacked concrete slabs, and a glass desk before a coral wall.

A grid that looks like a room divider might be one of the Perspectives pieces, and the tunnel might not be a divider at all. DDW's page names the Syzygy lamps, the dividers and the shop interiors as notable work, and no photo title names any of them.
I would rather leave the question open than write a caption that sounds sure.

blocks.x: What a thin record can still teach

r: Two albums show how a studio reaches an archive. The 2017 photographer worked from objects and visitors, the 2018 photographer from the hall and the light. The two albums have different photographers, so I would not credit the difference to the studio.

A studio whose process starts with sketches, texts, scale models and 3D images, and whose materials are glass, metal and brass, invites photographs of surface and light. The photographs fit that, and a fit is all it is.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: What the 2017 show was, where it stood and on which dates.
Whether the round wall lamp in the 2017 photographs is a Syzygy lamp.
Whether the archive holds more of the studio's photographs under other titles. I did not search for them and could not reopen the account.
What the studio shows in any other year, or in 2026.
How much of the studio's catalog was on show in 2018. The profile calls it a body of work, and no source lists the pieces.

r: If a piece is made to bend light, what would you want written beside it?

posts.title: Piet Hein Eek at Dutch Design Week: a workshop, a former Philips building and a long guest list
posts.subtitle: The official photo archive files nine years under one name. Pages from the designer, the redevelopment record, museums and the press show who was in the building, and when.
posts.seoTitle: Piet Hein Eek at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Piet Hein Eek, a former Philips ceramics workshop on Strijp-R and the guests who filled it during Dutch Design Week, 2015 to 2026.

r: The archive files nine years of Dutch Design Week under one name, Piet Hein Eek, and the sources describe a building with many hands in it.

As a content strategist I read titles for what they promise, and an album title that carries a person's name promises authorship. This essay asks how much of that promise the record keeps. It draws on public sources only: the enterprise's own pages, DDW's pages, a heritage site, a cultural magazine, a handful of news reports, museum and festival listings, and the official DDW photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibits beyond what DDW's pages list.

blocks.x: The designer, from several hands

r: Piet Hein Eek was born in Purmerend in 1967, according to a profile by Petri Leijdekkers in The Low Countries, and graduated in 1990 from the Eindhoven academy that is now the Design Academy, where his teachers included Ed Annink and Gijs Bakker. His graduation piece was a cupboard of reclaimed wood.
The enterprise's own press page, a biography from the Louis Kalff Institute and a 2017 news item all give the same year and the same cupboard.
The profile ties the choice of material to the memory of his father repairing a garden shed with scrap planks, which is the author's account and not a document.

The business history is less tidy. The Louis Kalff Institute biography, which cites a 1993 article in the design magazine Items, says the success of his early cabinets led to a small independent factory with Norbert (Nob) Ruijgrok in 1993, and that he received an incentive prize for design from the Amsterdam Fund for the Arts in 1993.
The Low Countries profile says Eek en Ruijgrok BV, the company's official name, was set up in Geldrop in 1996.

I read 1993 as the start of the partnership and the factory, and 1996 as the date this later article gives for the company, but I have not seen a company register, so I cannot say which date is the legal one. The enterprise's own About page, as the Internet Archive captured it in December 2015, gives no founding year. It says the series production and the assignments are carried out by Eek en Ruijgrok B.V., the company of Eek and Nob Ruijgrok, and that the self-initiated work is done by the one-man business Piet Hein Eek.
Two legal forms under one name would fit a partnership first and a company later, and that is my reading of the page and not a statement in it.

The profile also records that in autumn 1995 Eek took part in the Dutch Design Café at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, supplying aluminum tables, chairs and stools for the museum's garden café during a Mondrian retrospective.

In 2017 the Culture fund of North Brabant gave him the first of its design prizes. The news item reporting this quotes the jury chair, Jan Post, calling him a successful designer and entrepreneur of great importance to the design climate in Brabant, and says that since 2015 Eek has also designed for IKEA, with a prize of 10,000 euros.

The same news item says Eek also designs buildings and interiors, among them the Verkade factory conversion in 's-Hertogenbosch, interiors for the Van Abbemuseum and Schiphol, and that he is a co-founder of Piet Hein Eek Architecture.

The IKEA line connects to Dutch Design Week. On October 16, 2017 Innovation Origins reported that Eek had not intended a big show that year but was preparing thermal-bottle vases, furniture from New York water-tower wood and several prototypes of the collection he made for IKEA, to be introduced the following spring under the theme of handmade, serial-produced objects.

IKEA's own page for the resulting Industriell collection quotes Eek and an IKEA creative leader about keeping knots and changes in the grain and about giving ceramic vases a variety of shapes. The page carries no date.

blocks.x: A designer who was finding Philips material before he moved in

r: The Low Countries profile traces a habit that predates the building. It says Eek made a metal storage unit based on the rectangular glass doors of a lab cupboard he found on a Philips dump, and it dates the resulting Philips cabinet to 1994, calling it one of his most successful designs.

After the move, the profile says, he built the restaurant's bar from gas, water, air-conditioning and heating pipes reclaimed from the Philips factory, and made tube chairs and benches from pipes he found there.
A man who built his name on reused material now works inside a reused factory, and that fit is easy to find in the sources.

The record supports a narrower statement than the tidy story. Eek was already using Philips discards in the 1990s, and the building supplied more of the same after 2010. Whether he chose the building for that reason is not something any source I opened says.

blocks.x: The building: a 1950s ceramics workshop that some call a factory

r: The enterprise's press page says its factory, shop, showroom, hotel and restaurant sit under one roof in the former ceramic workshop of Philips.
DDW's 2026 location page calls the same place a former Philips ceramics factory at Halvemaanstraat 30.

Herbestemming.nl, a heritage-reuse site, gives the most detail. It describes Strijp R as a post-war terrain where Philips produced picture tubes on a large scale, the third business park Philips developed after Strijp-S and Strijp-T. It lists the building as "Keramische werkplaats (RK)," a ceramic workshop where parts for radios and televisions were made, in a building from the 1950s that Eek transformed and delivered in 2010.
The redevelopment record names it a workshop, as the enterprise does, so I use that word and treat "factory" as DDW's looser term.
What the building made is less settled. The Low Countries profile says it was originally a ceramics workshop for the lighting industry.
Herbestemming says radio and television parts.
Both could be partly right, and neither names a document. I leave the product open.
The same profile gives the factory an area of 10,000 square meters in five large halls, in two blocks connected by a transport corridor, and says the company had moved there in 2010.
A Michelangelo Foundation craft page confirms the move, saying Eek relocated his workshop from Geldrop to the former Strijp-R area of Eindhoven in 2010.

Herbestemming adds that the site's owner since a 2005 bid was the developer Amvest, that demolition of most of the other Philips buildings began in 2009 for about 500 homes, and that the ceramic workshop was the first development of the new Strijp R.
It also offers a caution about the venture, wondering whether the project had made itself very dependent on Eek's place-making.
The staff numbers move with the years. The profile, written around 2012 since it calls 2011 "last year," says the company employed fifty people and had an annual turnover of 4 to 5 million euros.
In 2021 an Austrian trade-promotion page said the enterprise employed sixty.

The enterprise's press page now lists a design hotel with 13 rooms and a studio at the Beeldbuisring, each furnished by Eek and holding art by a different artist, next to the factory and the restaurants.

blocks.x: How a workshop became a DDW venue

r: The building's own account ties its start to the festival. The hotel's About page, as captured in 2022, says that the enterprise first opened its doors on the first day of Dutch Design Week in October 2010, with a shop, showroom, gallery, restaurant and event space part of the plan from the start.
That agrees with the other sources' 2010 and adds that the opening coincided with the festival.
The 2015 About page adds that the enterprise rents out studios in the building.

The best statement of the arrangement is Eek's own, from the October 2017 news item. He says that although he almost always says Dutch Design Week is not leading and should not be exaggerated, "we are kind of trapped by DDW every year." That year he had also begun renting out ateliers at the front of the building on the Halvemaanstraat, in space that had been a storeroom and had become a dump for valuable items. The tenants wanted to use Dutch Design Week to present themselves to the public, and he understood why.

The enterprise's press page describes the practice as standing policy: every year during Dutch Design Week it opens its doors to a wide range of exhibitors, so that visitors can see the work of Eek and of dozens of other designers.

Eek's account to Omroep Brabant in 2021 adds the commercial logic. He says Dutch Design Week lets him show his work to hundreds of thousands of people, and that department stores, gallery owners and IKEA come to see which young designers present for the first time.
That is his reading of the week, and it explains why a maker's workshop would want guests.

The guest tradition is older than the week. The profile describes a large exhibition floor above the shop where Eek shows artists and designers he feels an affinity with, and says the Van Abbemuseum used a display case designed by Eek in the middle of that space to present small works by El Lissitzky, René Daniels, Henk Visch and JCJ Vanderheyden.

Food and events grew alongside. The enterprise's page for Dutch Design Week 2019, October 19 to 27, announces a Sergio Herman dinner titled WASTE ART FOOD DESIGN, "just like last year," so a similar dinner took place in 2018 as well, and it announces a new fry shop, FRIET (Piet Hein Eek), opening that week. It also says the organizers were looking for sponsors for the dinner.
DDW's 2021 area preview names FRIET at the restaurant and a food project called Bricknic at the location.

The hotel came later than planned. A post on the enterprise's site dated December 11, 2020 said Hotel Piet Hein Eek would open its doors in the first quarter of 2021 and offered gift vouchers that were not valid during Dutch Design Week.

Omroep Brabant, in a report published on October 17, 2021, says the first guests would sleep there during the week, that the hotel has thirteen rooms furnished by different artists, and quotes Eek saying the team made 95 percent of the hotel themselves.
That figure is the designer's own claim.

blocks.x: Year by year, and what each source lets me say

r: The photo archive and the written sources each cover different years, so the honest picture is a patchwork. The album facts below are from my October 7, 2026 reading of the official DDW Flickr account. I did not reopen that account for this version.

The archive holds Piet Hein Eek albums for 2015 to 2022 and 2024, with 21, 14, 14, 17, 17, 33, 37, 66 and 9 photos, which adds to 228. Credit sits in the photo titles: Nick Bookelaar in 2015, 2016 and 2021, Max Kneefel in 2017 and 2020, Britt Roelse in 2018, 2019 and 2022 with Kneefel also in 2018, and Jeroen van der Wielen and Cleo Goossens in 2024.
In 2015 every title reads sfeerimpressie, the Dutch word for atmosphere impression, and none names a work.
In 2016 a window sign in one photo is headed IK BEN WAT IK MAAK beside a notice that lists a pop-up and the name Social Label.
The 2017 titles name IKEA and New Collection, which fits the news report of IKEA prototypes that October.
On October 28, 2017, the design prize was reported awarded to Eek at Design Center Kazerne, not at his own building.

For 2018, TL Magazine's look back says Dutch Design Week had 355,000 visitors, 2,600 designers and 120 locations, and that Social Label, a platform pairing designers with people with disabilities, had a solo exhibition at Piet Hein Eek.
The 2018 album titles read Piet Hein Eek Collection and Piet Hein Eek.
In 2019 the enterprise's own page supplies the program: the second Herman dinner, a new fry shop, and designer exhibitions open from 10:00 to 20:00.
The 2019 album has 17 photos credited to Britt Roelse, and no title names the dinner.
For 2020 there is a 33-photo album credited to Max Kneefel and no written source that I found.

In 2021, the enterprise's own post of September 20, 2021 lists the designer exhibitions for October 16 to 24, among them Postapocalyptic Kaffeehaus by Advantage Austria, A Simple Machine and Easy Green Living by House of Thol.

The Austrian exhibition used the building as its location, according to the Austrian trade-promotion page, which says the stand showed twelve products, ran for nine days from October 16 and drew more than 7,000 visitors.
The same year had the hotel opening, a 37-photo album credited to Bookelaar, and the area preview.
The 2022 album is the largest, 66 photos credited to Roelse with titles that carry the date October 25, 2022.

That same year, from October 8 to November 6, the Van Abbemuseum's Edelkoort collection show listed Piet Hein Eek among its prominent pieces, so his name was on a museum wall at the same moment his own building was a venue.
For 2023 I found nothing: the listing I used on October 7 showed no album, and it is known to be incomplete.
For 2024 the album has nine photos, and a wall text in one reads I MAKE OBJECTS by Dirk Duif.

Dutch Design Daily's area preview, which I read on October 7 and did not reopen for this version, names Dirk Duif, Snackbar Esthetica, Scheublin & Lindeman Studio, WhiteNoiseDada and Studio RENS in the Piet Hein Eek area.

The enterprise's press page adds exhibitor notes, two of which are explicitly dated to Dutch Design Week 2024: Giorgio Bena's Lockwerk collection and an electric bus camper. Other notes on that page, such as the label Hul le Kes and the Rotterdam gallery Untitled, carry no year.

The 2025 edition, October 18 to 26, is also in the press page, which carries notes from exhibitors presenting at Piet Hein Eek that year, including cardboard work by Wijnand Driessen, ceramics by Sam Linders and the first lighting collection of OBJETFORMT.
The press page shows the event took place at the location. Whether the archive holds a 2025 album is unknown to me.
For 2026 DDW's location page lists 39 projects, 38 exhibitions and one seminar on October 23, from studios and schools in several countries, with free access.

The enterprise's own page for the 2026 designer exhibition, posted September 4, 2026, lists participants by name in five zones, Office, Workshop, Showroom, Platform and Studios, which I count at 80 names, with the designer exhibition, shop and showroom open from 10:00 to 19:30 from October 17 to 24 and until 18:00 on October 25.

The two lists count different things, projects on one side and names on the other, and I did not reconcile them. Neither says how many participants are guests and how many belong to the enterprise. A local tourism page published October 1, 2026 describes the location as a design hotspot all year with designers from around the globe showing work in the showroom during the week.

blocks.x: Where Eek and Kazerne meet

r: Kazerne, the Eindhoven design venue, appears three times in Eek's story. Its opening exhibition, Open Mind, which ran from winter 2014 to summer 2015, listed a group called ICE that includes Jeanine Eek Keijzer and Piet Hein Eek.
The 2017 design prize was presented at Kazerne.
And the 2022 Edelkoort collection show, which had a second showing at Kazerne, named Eek among its prominent pieces.

I draw one conclusion from these three: the same small circle of institutions keeps appearing across Eindhoven's design year. I do not draw a conclusion about who influenced whom, because no source says so.

blocks.x: Guests, hosts and what a photograph can show

r: A photograph from a Piet Hein Eek album can show a guest's work, the host's own work or the building itself, and the title usually will not say which.

The record shows how often it was a guest: Social Label from 2016 to 2018, the Austrian exhibition in 2021, five named exhibitors in 2024, a long run of exhibitor notes for 2025 and 39 listed projects in 2026.
That is why I read the albums as records of a place first and of a maker second.

The arrangement also has a commercial side that the sources show without hiding. Eek names the buyers who come to scout young designers, the enterprise seeks sponsors for its dinner, and the redevelopment record notes how much the project leans on his place-making.
None of that makes the guest work less real. It means the venue and the maker are two roles under one name, and a caption that merges them claims more than the record supports.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: Workshop, factory, ceramics workshop for the lighting industry, radio and television parts. The redevelopment record's building name settles the word, "workshop." It does not settle the product.
The full Herbestemming page says the 1950s. Herbestemming's full page says the 1950s for the ceramic workshop, and no second source dates it. I use the 1950s and attribute it.
1993 for the partnership and factory in a biography citing a 1993 article, 1996 for the BV in a later profile. The enterprise's own page gives no year. Not settled without a register.
Fifty around 2012 and sixty in 2021 are consistent with growth, and I give each with its year.

The news item is dated July 3, 2017 and narrates a ceremony on October 28 in the past tense. The page's own metadata give July 3, 2017 for both publication and last modification, so it was written before the festival, and I read its past tense as an announced plan and not as a report of the evening. I found no post-ceremony source, so I report the ceremony as announced.
Planned for the first quarter of 2021 on December 11, 2020, and reported with first guests during Dutch Design Week on October 17, 2021. The hotel's own site gives no opening date.
2010 in three sources, and the first day of Dutch Design Week in October 2010 in the hotel's own account.
The enterprise's press page shows the event took place at the location. Whether the archive holds an album is open.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what most photographs in the archive show, because most titles carry a name, a photographer and a number. I do not know whether the 2019 dinner appears in that year's album. I do not know whether albums exist for 2023 and 2025. I did not read a company register that would fix the date and form of the company, and the enterprise's own pages do not state them, and I did not open a museum catalog entry for the scrap-wood cupboard.
I cannot say how the building's earlier life as a Philips ceramic workshop relates to what is made there now, beyond the enterprise's statement that it makes its products in house.
The sources do not say how many of the 39 projects on the 2026 page are new this year.
When you open any album titled with a maker's name, which question comes first: whose work is on the table, or whose building is it in?

posts.title: Plan B holds more than 200 designers, and the archive shows 26 photographs
posts.subtitle: Two Dutch Design Week albums, 2018 and 2019, of an Eindhoven design hub, read with its own pages, DDW's recaps and the designers' sites.
posts.seoTitle: Plan B at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Plan-B, the former Philips laboratory at Hurksestraat 19, and what DDW's 2018 recap, its 2023 and 2026 pages and two photo albums show.

r: A building that houses more than 200 designers shows up in the Dutch Design Week archive as 26 photographs.
The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds two albums for Plan-B, 2018 with 9 photographs and 2019 with 17, all credited in their titles to Iris Rijskamp.

Plan-B is a venue, not a maker, so the record that matters is split between the building's own pages and the guests who rented its rooms for a week. This essay draws on public sources only: Plan-B's own site, DDW's location and recap pages, a news caption, a studio's page and a ceramics studio's page. It reports no visit and no interview, and it describes the 2026 program only as the organizers list it.
I like a venue that holds many small studios, because the archive has to decide whose name goes on the file.

blocks.x: A laboratory that became a home for makers

r: Plan-B's own story page calls it the Eindhoven home base for makers, housed in the former Philips laboratory. Its history section says the building was originally built by Philips, which used the former laboratory to produce radio tubes and to endurance-test products, a function it kept until the end of the last century.
DDW's location page and Plan-B's 2026 page call the same place a former Philips factory, and DDW's 2018 recap called it a former Philips lab at De Hurk.
Plan-B's own history is specific, and it uses the word laboratory, so I use laboratory for the building's original use and treat "factory" as the looser word in the festival texts.
Today Plan-B describes itself as the home of creative entrepreneurs, designers, artists and musicians, with a restaurant, meeting rooms, a loading dock and a freight lift among its services.
DDW's location page says the hub is home to more than 200 designers, artists and makers, and in the festival week opens a 500 square meter exhibition area with studios open to the public.
It also has an alumni program for graduates of SintLucas and the Design Academy Eindhoven, who start on a 20 square meter work area in a shared room and grow into a studio of their own.
The address on DDW's page is Hurksestraat 19, 5652 AH Eindhoven.

blocks.x: 2018: three names and thirty more

r: DDW's recap of October 25, 2018 says the festival consisted of eight design areas and took its readers to Plan-B that day. It describes the former Philips lab at De Hurk as a creative hotspot, and names three exhibitors: Kiki & Joost with Alter Ego, Cor Unum with Future History, and Klaas Kuiken with his latest work, among some thirty other designers.
It adds that the hub is a 45-minute walk from the city center, and that a free Renault taxi would take visitors there in ten minutes from four stands, with rental bikes at three other places.
A place that needs its own transport plan is a destination, and an archive of it records a trip as much as a building.
The 2018 album holds 9 photographs, and none of the titles names a designer.

The photographs show a white hall with a sculptural seat and hanging fabrics, a wire sculpture on a round plinth, a gridded tile wall with a clothes rack lettered ARCH HOOK, a studio sign reading studio erik stehmann, a hand-lettered sign reading REBLEND Collective, and a star-shaped table.
Those words come from signs in the pictures, so they are the exhibitors' own labels, and I cannot match them to the three names the recap gives.

blocks.x: 2019: six names in the titles

r: In 2019 DDW's welcome item counted nine design areas, with Plan-B one of them.

The 2019 album holds 17 photographs, and this time the titles name the designer: Annabet Philips in three, Cor Unum in three, Erik Stehmann in one, Jordan Artisan in three, Klaas Kuiken in five and Studio Roex in two.
Annabet Philips is a designer's name and has no connection to the company that once occupied the building.
An IO+ caption of October 22, 2019 puts a visit at Plan-B at Hurksestraat, which it calls the home of Kiki & Joost.
Kiki & Joost is the design studio of Kiki van Eijk and Joost van Bleiswijk.

Their own news page for 2025 gives the studio's address as Gabriël Metsulaan 1 in Eindhoven, a 1,200 square meter studio, gallery and workshop that they say turned 25 in 2025, the same year the festival did.
I found no source that explains how Hurksestraat 19 and Gabriël Metsulaan 1 relate, and I do not claim the studio moved.

blocks.x: 2023: Fluid Threads, from the fifth floor down

r: The album stops after 2019, but Plan-B's site documents 2023. Its program page says the Fluid Threads exhibition ran from October 21 to 29, 2023 through the building from the fifth floor to the ground floor, with eight designers, some Plan-B residents and some external DDW participants, plus talks on October 22, 24 and 25 at 2 p.m. and lunch at Subbar on the ground floor.

After the week, a recap in Dutch says nine designers had shown, that the route began on the fifth floor, and that themes included gender fluidity, reuse of fashion, natural pigments and AI. It credits its photographs to Willeke Machiels.
The two pages disagree on eight versus nine designers, and I report each with its date.

blocks.x: 2026: the program as listed

r: DDW's location page for Plan-B lists a 2026 program of exhibitions at the same address, with opening hours from October 17 to 25, 2026, in the West area.

Plan-B's own page for DDW 2026 lists 17 exhibitors under the title Look Closer, with a text about the stories behind extraordinary design, three evening music sessions on October 22, 23 and 24, and the DDW theme as RAW.
Among its entries are Cor Unum with a residency by Ralf Gloudemans and Atelier Jordan Artisan with ReConstruction.

Plan-B's text describes Cor Unum as a ceramic studio in 's-Hertogenbosch that for over 70 years has brought together designers, craftspeople, students, volunteers and people distanced from the labor market.
These pages are the organizers' announcements, and I describe what they say.
Two names therefore cross the years: Cor Unum, named in the 2018 recap, three 2019 titles and the 2026 page, and Jordan Artisan, named in three 2019 titles and the 2026 page.
Erik Stehmann crosses between 2018 and 2019 by a sign and a title.
Three of those threads rest on a page and a title, and the Stehmann thread rests on a sign and a title. I trust all of them and would not call them equal evidence.

blocks.x: A venue is also a curator

r: A hub that hosts many studios chooses its tenants and arranges them for a week, so it behaves a little like a maker with a body of work. The work belongs to the designers, and what belongs to the hub is the setting, the building, the 500 square meter open area and the week's arrangement.
A caption that gives the hub credit for a lamp would claim too much, and a caption that leaves the hub out of a photograph of its own rooms would claim too little.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: Plan-B's own history says laboratory, with radio tubes and endurance testing. The festival texts say lab in 2018 and factory in 2026. Plan-B's own history page settled it.
Plan-B's program page says eight and its recap says nine. Unsettled.
DDW's 2018 recap says eight and its 2019 welcome item says nine. They are different years.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know who the other thirty designers of 2018 were, which of the 2018 photographs show the three named exhibitors, or what the 2019 titled rooms contained beyond what the photographs show. I did not read Plan-B's pages for 2018 or 2019, which the site does not carry, and I did not search for Plan-B photographs filed under other album titles. The album facts come from my reading of the Flickr account on October 8, 2026, which I did not repeat.
If a building holds 200 studios and an archive keeps six names, who decides which six?

posts.title: Precious Plastic at Dutch Design Week: an open-source recycling project, three Octobers and a donated warehouse, 2017 to 2019
posts.subtitle: From a Design Academy graduation project in 2013 to Version 4 in 2020: the project's own timeline, its posts about three Eindhoven weeks, press and program records, and the two photo albums.
posts.seoTitle: Precious Plastic at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Precious Plastic at DDW: the 2017 launch exhibition, the donated VDMA workspace in 2018, the Version 4 show in 2019 and what the two photo albums can show.

r: A recycling project that publishes every machine as an open design can only be photographed at a design festival by its tables, boards and test strips, and the two Dutch Design Week (DDW) albums for Precious Plastic show exactly that.

As an anatomist I trust a labeled specimen more than a polished figure, and the same instinct makes me read a test strip before a finished bench. This essay uses the project's own timeline and its posts about three Octobers in Eindhoven, 2017, 2018 and 2019, together with a university excursion program, a public-broadcaster series, two Dutch articles from 2018, an architecture firm's note and the official photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview.

blocks.x: A graduation project that became an organization

r: The project's own history page starts in 2012, when Dave Hakkens began working on Precious Plastic as part of his studies at the Design Academy in Eindhoven. In 2013 he put Version 1 online during his graduation show. In 2014 three people independently replicated the machines, which the page calls enough motivation to continue. In 2015 the project won a 10,000-euro award and used it to hire a machine builder. Version 2 followed in early 2016, and Version 3, with a workspace inside a shipping container, in late 2017.

A Dutch engineering magazine's report from DDW 2018 says the project began in 2014, which differs from the project's own 2012 and 2013, and I use the project's account because the article gives no basis for its year.

The Version 3 team page adds how that version was made: a team of 12 over 2017, a campaign to find people and money that drew about 200 applicants and raised 20,000 euros, a workspace in Helmond, and a recycling container that was shipped to the Maldives for a pilot.
The page does not say whether the container in the October 2017 invitation is the one that was shipped.

The history page says that in mid-2018 the project won an award of 300,000 euros, which it calls the Famae award, and spent the entire budget on a new version, and that from September 2018 a team of 40 to 50 volunteers worked for a year and a half on Version 4.
The project's own post of May 28, 2018 is titled for the 300,000 euros, and its post of July 23, 2018 thanks FAMAE and says the team was in Portugal planning how to spend the money.
A Raspberry Pi magazine article dates the award to May 26, 2018 and names the FAMAE Foundation as the giver.
The January 7, 2020 release post gives other numbers for the same effort: 16 months, 300,000 euros, more than 100 volunteers and 35,000 vegan meals.

The pages count different things, the core team in one and everyone who took part in the other, and a third figure, 39 people working in Eindhoven in November 2018, comes from the project's own post about its gifts.
I do not choose between them.

The name One Army is newer than all three DDW weeks. A post of December 4, 2020 says the group's projects, Phonebloks, Precious Plastic, Story Hopper and Project Kamp, fall from that day under the One Army Foundation, and the project's history page says it set up its own legal structure, a non-profit in the Netherlands, only in 2023.
The 2017, 2018 and 2019 posts about DDW carry a line saying they are part of Precious Plastic, a One Army project, which reflects the site as it is now and not the name used at the time.

blocks.x: 2017: a launch week and a container

r: The first DDW trace outside the albums is a plan to visit. A Berlin art university's itinerary for its trip of October 21 to 24, 2017 lists a Dezeen talk during DDW on pollution, with Dave Hakkens, Bernhard Lenger and Eline Strijkers, and a visit to Sectie C that names Dave Hakkens among others. It is a program and not a report of what happened.

The project's own posts show what the visit would have found. On August 21, 2017 it announced an online release of Version 3 on October 16 and, from October 21, the offline version, a full exhibition during DDW devoted to Precious Plastic with its experiments, container and creations and the whole team present all week.

An invitation of October 5, 2017 gave the festival dates as October 21 to 29 and promised new products, experiments, installations, art objects, machines, community members and "the mighty container."

The report of October 22, 2017 says the team camped out on Sectie-C in a big empty building, showed machines, blocks of waste, experiments and products by the worldwide community, introduced art pieces it calls artifacts, had community members at the opening from nine countries, and would run the exhibition until October 29.
The post, signed Dave, says he had never felt the urge to set up an exhibition before, because his projects were documented online for everyone.

A public-broadcaster series covered Hakkens in the same week. VPRO's De toekomstbouwers 2017 lists him, aged 29, among the designers presenting at DDW, with the latest version of Precious Plastic, and says the machines were running in Cambodia, Australia, Morocco and nearly 80 other places.

TL Magazine's report of October 23, 2017 says Hakkens and Precious Plastic were present at Sectie-C, De Bijenkorf, the Van Abbemuseum, Kazerne and the VDMA, and jokes that the festival should be renamed for him.
The DDW photo archive has no 2017 album for the project, so the first year of its presence in Eindhoven during the festival exists in the project's posts and in the press and not in the pictures.

blocks.x: 2018: a workspace for nine days

r: One Army's post of September 12, 2018 says that from October 20 to 28 the team would open the doors of its new workspace at the VDMA building, kindly donated by the city of Eindhoven, with the full team at work, and that visitors could come every day from 10:00 to 19:00. It promised shared vegan lunches and a kick-off event for Version 4 on Saturday, October 20.

The workspace itself was new. Omroep Brabant, on October 17, 2018, wrote that Hakkens had used the prize money to bring dozens of creatives from around the world to Eindhoven and that the VDMA building was bubbling with ideas.
The Dutch engineering magazine De Ingenieur, on October 29, 2018, wrote that the team had moved onto the VDMA terrain in the city center six weeks earlier.

The project's own post of November 21, 2018 says the city donated a huge warehouse in the center of town for one and a half years, free of charge, that eight houses were made available for the crew, and that 39 people were then working there.

The project reported on the week afterward. Its post of November 1, 2018 calls the exhibition A day in the workspace and says visitors came from as far as Canada and China. It names guests in the workspace and talks in its Colosseum by Van Plestik, Plastic Odyssey, Café de Ceuvel and Polimeer, and it says the team had entered the space only a few weeks before, so it chose to show its process and early experiments on Version 4 rather than finished work. It ends with a promise to unveil Version 4 at DDW in 2019.
That report counts the week as eight days of open workspace, while the announcement gives October 20 to 28, nine calendar days, and I do not know why the two differ.

An architecture firm that wrote up its four favorite DDW 2018 stops chose the project too, describing it as run by Dave Hakkens at the VDMA complex and as speaking to sustainability and innovation, with a focus on re-using plastic rather than dumping it.
That is a visitor's note, one step removed from the project's own account.
The archive's album for the year, Precious Plastic at Work, has 15 photos, 14 credited by title to Tommy Köhlbrugge and one to Max Kneefel.

My October 8 read describes a steel-roofed hall with tall white signs headed AT WORK, THE TEAM and VERSION 4, a line of colored objects on a taped floor strip, a strip of shredded plastic, and handwritten cards giving minutes from 1 to 15 and temperatures of 180 and 170 degrees Celsius beside pale plastic strips. A sign counts a team of more than 40 volunteers in the workspace.
That count sits close to the 40 to 50 on the project's history page and to the 39 in its November post, and each is the project's own figure.

blocks.x: 2019: an exhibition of the finished version

r: The November 20, 2019 post says the team put together an exhibition of Version 4 at DDW 2019 in the VDMA warehouse, which it calls its home for the past year, with machines, products and the year-long research. It describes five workspaces to walk through, collection, shredder, injection, sheet press and extruder, a Bazar area with printed images of workspaces around the world, and three research projects, robotics, Beyond Plastic and fashion, in a cube three meters by four. It adds workshops by the Version 4 designers, from a plastic carabiner to a bowl of wheat bran and coffee grounds, and presentations by other sustainability designers in what it calls its colosseum. About 80 people were there at one point, it says.
It gives no dates for the exhibition, and DDW 2019 ran October 19 to 27.

The Version 4 team page credits two people with the exhibition: Charlotte Allen, who developed the visual identity and curated both DDW exhibitions, and Adrienn Veres, who designed and organized it with her.
I read both Dutch Design Week exhibitions as 2018 and 2019, because the Version 4 team worked from September 2018.

MaterialDistrict's preview of October 18, 2019 says that at DDW the project would launch Version 4 and show the work of over 100 designers, engineers, developers, activists and chefs. The project's own post says the full release was set for January 7, 2020, so the preview's word launch means a first showing.

The post also explains how the exhibition was kept cheap: the information boards were made from recycled polystyrene that had been old CD cases, built to be completely reused afterward without screws or holes, and the team says it was close to the end of its budget.

The release post two months later says the whole of Version 4 was online on January 7, 2020 with starter kits for each kind of recycling space and three new semi-industrial machines, the Shredder Pro, Extruder Pro and Sheetpress.
The 2019 album holds 28 photos, with the 24 titles shown crediting Köhlbrugge.

The earlier read describes tables and plinths of small recycled objects and tiles, a machine with a hopper, motor and screw barrel, a pink slatted bench, a geodesic dome frame, pendants and earrings, and a dark bowl whose paper band says it is a mixture of coffee grounds, tea leaves and stale bread.
The band does not mention wheat bran, so I do not equate that bowl with the workshop the post names.

blocks.x: After 2019: a release and an eviction

r: The Eindhoven workspace did not last long after the exhibition. On April 24, 2020 the project posted that the municipality of Eindhoven, after testing in March, had found chromium 6 in the paint covering its workspace, which it captions as its Eindhoven HQ, and had asked it to vacate the building and empty it within 30 days during the Covid-19 lockdown. The project said it would sell everything, including machines, tools and one-off plastic pieces, to cover Version 4 expenses.
The post does not name the VDMA building. The same city donated the VDMA space, and I read the two as one place without being able to confirm it.
I found no Precious Plastic entry in DDW's program for 2020 to 2026, and no new Eindhoven workspace for the project.

blocks.x: What the project says it became

r: The first global impact survey, published June 28, 2020, had answers from more than 1,000 people; workspaces recycled over 540,000 kilograms of plastic a year, the average team was five people, and 10 percent of workspaces were profitable.
The project's home page today says 1,100 workspaces in 56 countries recycle 1,400,000 kilograms a year, based on 2024 data.
Its timeline ends with trouble in 2024, a Version 5 crowdfund in 2025 and a membership program in 2026.
These are the project's own figures, and I have no independent measure of them.

blocks.x: Questions the sources settle

r: Who was behind the project in 2017, 2018 and 2019? Dave Hakkens and the Precious Plastic team, with the One Army foundation created in December 2020 and not before.
Where was the workspace? On Sectie-C for the October 2017 exhibition, at the VDMA building in 2018, a donation from the city of Eindhoven, and in the VDMA warehouse in 2019.
When did Version 4 appear? The kick-off was on October 20, 2018, the exhibition in October 2019, the release on January 7, 2020.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know which work any photograph in the albums shows, because the titles name none.

I do not know whether the project took part in DDW before 2017, because the 2013 graduation-show coverage I found sits on a site that refused automated requests, and I do not know what, if anything, it shows in 2026.
The Famae award's giver is named only as a foundation, and I found no page about it.
I do not know where the container stood in 2017, since the project's posts mention it without a location, or whether the Sectie-C building and the VDMA building were ever connected.
I could not open the videos behind the timeline's award links, so the name and organizer of the 2015 award come from the project's text only.
If a project shows its working one year and its results the next, which would you rather find in the archive?
