posts.title: Sander Wassink at Dutch Design Week: a designer who hardly makes anything new, seen from 2012 to the Sectie-C of today
posts.subtitle: One interview in his own words, a 2015 lamp show, a 2012 news report and two photo albums. The sources are few, and each one carries weight.
posts.seoTitle: Sander Wassink at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Sander Wassink, the Sectie-C designer who works from leftover materials: his 2020 interview, a 2015 lamp series at DDW and two photo albums from 2019 and 2021.

r: Sander Wassink's work was at Dutch Design Week at least four years before the photo archive's first album for him, and he describes his method in his own words in one interview that Dutch Design Week published in 2020.

That is why this is a short essay with a longer reach than the old draft. The sources are few, and I have not padded them. This essay draws on public sources only: DDW's interview of September 1, 2020, a design-trade report from 2015, a news report from 2012, the Sectie-C site and its newsletter-style articles, and the official photo archive as I recorded it on October 8, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview of my own, and its sentences about 2026 say only what a published page lists.

blocks.x: An interview between two classmates

r: The DDW piece is not a profile written about a designer. It is a conversation between two people who know each other's work. DDW introduces it as an interview from BLANK SPACE MAGAZINE, a magazine started by creatives at Sectie-C that portrays creative makers in their workplaces while they are interviewed by colleagues, edited for ddw.nl.
The interviewer opens by saying they have followed Wassink as a designer since their graduation show at the Design Academy Eindhoven in 2012.
The text is credited to Mats Horbach and the photographs to Britt Roelse.
That setup matters for how to read what follows: the questions come from someone inside the same community, and the answers are Wassink's own account of his work.

blocks.x: What he says about his method

r: Wassink says his work is a personal research into who he is in the world and how he fits in it as a designer, and that existing materials bind all his projects together: "you could say that I hardly make anything new."

Even in interior projects with many identical pieces, he says, he looks for ways to make them from leftover material, and he is always searching for what is no longer in use, such as the foam blocks in his studio that would normally be thrown away.

The interview gives three concrete projects. He says he was making sofas for the interior of a hotel and bought a foam saw to cut shapes that someone else would upholster, doing most of the production himself.
He says a charity that collects and ships sporting goods, Sport for Children, asked him to design a product it could sell, and that he was making large foam dolls for it.

And he describes keeping the leftover forms in the studio for weeks, thinking of turning them into furniture with different sitting or lying functions and then photographing them to send to design labels.
On where the habit comes from, he gives two answers. One is money: he did not have much when he started. The other is a childhood among the materials lying around his grandfather's farm.

He says that ten years before the interview, when he arrived at Sectie-C with Collaboration-O to create their own universe, they also had no money and worked with whatever material they found or were given, and that he believes the best kind of creativity lies within restrictions.
He adds that he saw people in China make very practical objects from anything at hand.
The old draft summarized these positions. The new reading adds that he ties the method to a place and a collective, not only to a material.

blocks.x: The politics in the interview

r: The second half of the conversation is about production, and it is more pointed than the first. Wassink describes his project the Dashilar Flagship Store, in which he created a fictional shoe brand with a temporary store in the Dashilar neighborhood of Beijing, and says the project is about using creativity to make your own products and gain social status from it, while questioning the globalization of social status that makes young people everywhere want big Western shoe brands.

He argues that outsourcing production to low-wage countries has a massive effect on how things are made and that ordinary daily products such as shoes or toothbrushes can no longer be produced in the Netherlands.

He calls the production industry a modern form of slavery, says the Netherlands will never forbid such a system and that Europe and the Western world should take a stand, and adds that he has stopped fighting the system and has accepted the world as it is.
He ends by saying he would like to repeat the Dashilar project with a big Western brand, so that such companies might see the value of the people, materials and techniques in low-wage countries.
I report these as his opinions. They are strong ones, they were given in an interview that DDW chose to publish, and a caption that quotes any of them should name him as the speaker.
The interview is dated 2020, and nothing I opened tells me whether his views or his projects have changed since.

blocks.x: Before the albums: 2012 and 2015

r: The record before the photo archive's 2019 album has two dated items. On October 26, 2012 the site Bright wrote that the biggest surprise of that Dutch Design Week was the new location Sectie C, east of the city center, reached by free design rides, behind a large gate with yellow letters, with a jumble of buildings and a chaos of design studios, a five-meter lamp and a swimming pool in a container.
That is the first mention of the site in the sources I opened, and it comes in the same year Wassink says he graduated.

On November 16, 2015, Core77's photo gallery of Dutch Design Week included a group exhibition called OXI at Club-C on Sectie-C, curated by Justine Kontou, and one caption says the lamps in the foreground are from the Stacked "Geographic Production" series by Sander Wassink and Luuk van den Broek.
That puts a Wassink work at Dutch Design Week in 2015, four years before the 2019 album.
The Core77 page does not describe the lamps further, and I do not know whether the Stacked series relates to the reused materials he describes in 2020.
I did not check whether the archive's 2015 Sectie-C album includes those lamps.

blocks.x: 2019 and 2021: two albums, two photographers

r: The archive's two albums titled Sander Wassink hold 16 photographs from 2019 by Max Kneefel and 9 from 2021 by Boudewijn Bollmann.

The old dossier describes the 2019 set as a white room with a rug of gray and cream shapes, round mirrors reflecting blue sky with boots, shoes, slippers and a bucket set on them, and a tall assemblage of found chair frames, rods and a monitor beside a red plastic chair, and the 2021 set as four large paintings of folding chairs on a white wall, a long shelf of small colored objects and a bright blue lounger being worked on.
No title names a work, and no page I opened describes what he showed in either year.
I leave the match between the interview's foam and those photographs open, because the pairing would be a guess.

For the weeks around the 2021 festival, Sectie-C's own site adds that it was one of the main locations of DDW 2021, open October 16 to 23 from 11:00 to 20:00 and October 24 from 11:00 to 18:00, with the studios of more than 100 designers, artists and other creatives and, in the organizer's words, more than 25,000 visitors a year.
The same page lists Sander Wassink among the studios open to visitors during the #designopen days from June 13 to 17, 2021, an initiative of the Eindhoven design community.

It also lists him among current and former residents taking part in an exhibition titled A Home of Many Addresses, which the page dates October 17 to 25, 2026 and describes as a show in which residents give their view of the mailbox.

blocks.x: The place he works in

r: Sectie-C is the setting for all of this. A Sectie-C article by Niels Hoebers, a stop-motion animator whose studio has been there for 16 years, says his group had been in a hall on the Heezerweg with a creative entrepreneur, saw possibilities in the forgotten site of the former Stork Nolte, and began there as a collective called Collaboration O.
The name is the same as the collective Wassink mentions in 2020, and the Sectie-C site also lists Collaboration-O among its studios.

The article asks what will stay when the site is developed, mentions the question of 1,300 homes being added, and quotes Hoebers saying the place always worked through a mix of young wild and established old.
I treat that as one resident's account, and it explains why Wassink talks about working with limits: the site he describes was one where you made things with little.

blocks.x: What the albums and the page cannot say

r: I cannot say how his reuse method relates to the objects in the photographs, because the titles never name a work.
The interview is the only source for the method, and the albums are the only source for the objects.
A caption would have to join them, and the person who could do that is the maker.
The credits are simple. The interview's photographs are credited to Britt Roelse, the 2019 album to Max Kneefel and the 2021 album to Boudewijn Bollmann.
The 2019 album's description asks that the photographer and Dutch Design Week be named whenever a photograph is used.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: How long he has been at Sectie-C.
The interview says ten years before 2020, and Hoebers's undated article says his studio has been there 16 years, which fits an arrival around 2010 if the article is from 2026. I do not know its date.
When Sectie-C joined Dutch Design Week.
Bright's report of October 26, 2012 calls it new, and the tenants had been there before. The two are consistent.
The old draft's albums began in 2019. Core77 shows a Wassink and van den Broek lamp series at DDW 2015.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what he showed in 2019 or 2021, which work any photograph shows, or whether the Stacked series is related to his reuse method. His own website did not load for me, because the name did not resolve and the secure connection failed, so it is not used. The Dashilar Flagship Store is known to me only through his own description. I did not find a DDW program page for him in 2019 or 2021.
I did not reopen the photo archive for this version, so the album counts, titles and descriptions come from the dossier's October 8, 2026 reading.
Nothing here describes what he shows at Dutch Design Week 2026, which runs October 17 to 25, 2026, beyond the Sectie-C exhibition listing named above.
If a designer tells you he hardly makes anything new, which question would you ask him first: where a thing came from, or who it was for?

posts.title: Social Label at Dutch Design Week: thirteen years of borrowed addresses, and the four the photo archive caught
posts.subtitle: A Den Bosch foundation's own posts, the Dutch Design Awards and Dutch Design Week's listings, set against four albums.
posts.seoTitle: Social Label at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Social Label, a Den Bosch design foundation, at Dutch Design Week 2014 to 2026: Piet Hein Eek's factory, the Kazerne, The Social Hub and four photo albums.

r: Social Label's own news archive documents a Dutch Design Week presence in every year from 2014 to 2026, and the official photo archive holds four albums of it.

I like a record that forces me to separate an organization from the places that hosted it. Social Label is a Den Bosch foundation with a lab in Den Bosch, and its festival story is one of borrowed addresses in Eindhoven. This essay draws on public sources only: the label's own news posts, the Dutch Design Awards, Dutch Design Week's magazine and program pages, a design magazine and the photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibit beyond what the published program says.

blocks.x: A label whose lab is in another city

r: Dutch Design Week's own interview of April 7, 2020 has Simone Kramer and Petra Janssen saying they founded Social Label in 2014. Kramer runs C-mone, a culture and communication business, and Janssen runs Studio Boot, a visual communication studio, and the two describe a shared aim of making the world more social and beautiful and changing systems.

The label says it works with designers, workshops and makers at the edge of society, listing people with a disability, psychological problems, homeless people and school leavers, and designs work around what each person can do.

Its home is the Social label Lab on the Tramkade in Den Bosch. The label's post on the opening says Queen Máxima opened it, that the site was once the De Heus cattle-feed factory, and that the architecture was by Piet Hein Eek and Iggie Dekkers. The post is dated May 15, 2018.
The foundation's 10th anniversary in 2024 counts from 2014.

One design magazine gives 2011 instead. Designwanted wrote in May 2025 that the label was founded in 2011 and ties that year to its first product, the wooden furniture collection HOUT by Piet Hein Eek, made with the Woodworks workshop at the 2011 Huttenfestival De Vlek.
I read the two years as an origin and a launch, 2011 for the first product and 2014 for the label and platform, but I did not find the label saying so, and I use 2014 on the label's own authority.

blocks.x: 2014 to 2019: a guest of the factory floor

r: For six years in a row the label's posts put it in or beside Piet Hein Eek's factory on Strijp-R, and the photo archive sees only three of those years.
In 2014, from October 18 to 26, the label says it was a guest again in Eek's workshop, with the collection on stage for ten days and, in its words, more than a thousand retellings of the story.
The post mentions first sales and an online Werkwarenhuis, and that makers made television appearances.

On October 22, 2014 the label also hosted a round table of 24 social entrepreneurs, experts, administrators, scientists and designers at the Wonderkamer, which it calls an annual part of the platform.
The prototype of a broom called >VEEG, designed by Dick van Hoff with the neighborhood-management company Cambio in Deventer from old bicycle frames, was presented that week.
In 2015, from October 17 to 25, the label was selected to present on the stage of the festival's official opening at the Klokgebouw, and its main location was Eek's factory.
Its look back quotes the festival director, Martijn Paulen, and counts more than 30,000 visitors.

In 2016 the label presented two new product lines on Sunday, October 23 in the middle of Eek's workshop: LICHT with the designer Kiki van Eijk and the workshops of RIBW Brabant in Tilburg, and WARM with the designer Edward van Vliet and the foundation Vrolijk Werk in The Hague.

It ran four exhibitions in the festival: a pop-up Werkwarenhuis at Eek's factory for nine days, an exhibition of the Dutch Design Awards at the Veemgebouw, The Making of Your World at the Klokgebouw and Making School by Jurgen Bey on the eighth floor of the Veemgebouw.
The label counts 50,000 visitors to its pop-up Werkwarenhuis that week, a figure that is its own.

The label's post also records that Queen Máxima spent time at the festival's fifteenth anniversary edition talking with about ten designers and the organizers on the status of Dutch design, and that Petra Janssen described design applied in and with society.

In the lab-opening post of 2018 Janssen says that after a good conversation about the future of design at the festival, the dream of the lab came true two years later, and the opening speech thanks the queen.

The 2016 Dutch Design Awards listed >VEEG as a nominee in Service & Systems, and the committee praised the way the relationships among the parties and the production process had been designed along with the broom.
DDW's 2020 interview says the nomination came in 2017. The awards site and the label's June 2016 post say 2016, so I use 2016 and treat the interview as a slip.

In 2017, October 21 to 29, the label was again in Eek's workshop, launching a new label on Sunday, October 22 with the design duo Kranen/Gille and the work company WeenerXL in 's-Hertogenbosch, and announcing partnerships in Helmond and Tilburg.
The same post says >VEEG was also shown in an exhibition of Dutch bicycles by Yksi and that products appeared at an exhibition in the Klokgebouw.
In 2018, October 20 to 28, the label moved from the workshop to the first-floor exhibition space of the same building, under a banner of positivity.

The Dutch Design Awards named it the winner in Best Commissioning that year. The jury's text says the work lacks the usual customer-designer relationship, because the brief is set by what the people who will produce it can do.

In 2019, October 19 to 27, the label presented on the platform at Piet Hein Eek, within the festival's Social Design Route. It called the year its fifth in a row, introduced a new label with the municipality of Breda and showed an update with Amarant Groep.
The label's own count of years sits next to its own posts from 2014, so either it counts from 2015 or counts a year differently. I mention it and leave it.

blocks.x: 2020: the first year off the map

r: Social Label says that in 2020 it was absent from the festival's physical program for the first time in all those years. It had planned to be a guest at the studio of Kiki van Eijk and Joost van Bleiswijk.

The physical festival was canceled, and the label offered tours, a Radio Social label to break the isolation of makers and an exhibition at its Den Bosch lab, and hosted a webinar for the World Hope Forum, in which Janssen served as the Netherlands ambassador.
The program shows 19 designers in the collection and 15 workshops.

blocks.x: 2021 to 2023: a pink house, a factory and a hall

r: In 2021 the label showed The Pink House at the Kazerne on Paradijslaan, October 16 to 24, as part of the festival's Greater Number theme, with an entrance fee of 5 euros and a daily schedule from 12:00 to 18:00.
It describes a house where people sew aprons and gloves from old tents and tell stories, and presented education pilots, updates and a dance pilot.

In 2022, October 22 to 30, it was at the Schellens factory at the corner of Vestdijk and Bleekweg, free, with daily hours of 11:00 to 18:00, and opened on October 25 together with Isola. It showed the labels JAS, KOM and KLUIS.

In 2023, October 21 to 29, it was a guest at Fuutlaan 12c with Isola's Tools & Crafts show, a wood worker and The Visionary Lab with Vitra and Levi's, under the title Joy of Work, and launched the labels MIRROR, JOY and WORK.
The Fuutlaan hall is the same complex where the Envisions and Design Perron show stood.

blocks.x: 2024 to 2026: a hotel lobby and a museum

r: For its tenth anniversary in 2024 the label showed at several places: a joint exhibition with Isola Design called Forms unfolding at Area 51 on Strijp-S, and an installation called Too Big to Fix at The Social Hub Eindhoven.

In 2025 it was a guest at The Social Hub for the second time, with LABland, a tribute to its lab, open October 18 to 26 from 11:00 to 18:00, a short performance film premiering on October 19 and a Changemakers lecture on October 20.
The Cookie Club showed a world cookie, made with women from refugee centers in Den Bosch and a chef, at the Redbox exhibition at Area 51 on the Ketelhuisplein.
And the Van Abbemuseum's design exhibition Bridging Minds, running from October 4, 2025 to January 18, 2026 under guest curator Miriam van der Lubbe, included the label's workwear.

For 2026 the label says it is a guest at The Social Hub for the third time. Dutch Design Week lists FUTURE Proof!, hosted by Social label foundation, at Stationsweg 1, October 17 to 25, free, 11:00 to 18:00, and the label's program adds a presentation on October 18 at 11:00, a talk on October 20 at 10:00 and a workshop called Among strangers.

blocks.x: The archive and the years in between

r: The photo archive I read holds Social Label albums for 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2025, with 8, 11, 6 and 8 photographs, 33 in all. The 2017 titles name Piet Hein Eek and the date 20171026, and the 2018 and 2019 titles credit Britt Roelse. The 2025 titles name The Social Hub and the date October 20 but no photographer. I read the albums in an earlier pass and did not reopen the account, so every Flickr fact here is second-hand.
Set against the label's posts, the albums catch 4 of 13 festival years, and the photo titles agree with the label on the places for 2017 and 2025.

The label's own posts add nine more years, with places the archive's titles do not name: Eek's workshop in 2014 to 2016, the Kazerne in 2021, the Schellens factory in 2022, Fuutlaan in 2023 and Isola's hall in 2024.
The listing I read earlier also held a 2024 album titled The Social Hub with no count, which I never opened, and the label's 2024 post places part of its anniversary there.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: Which product any photograph shows. The titles name a label, a photographer and a number.
What the archive holds for the years in which the label's posts show a presence, and whether a 2024 album is the label's.
Whether 2011 or 2014 is the better start. The label chose 2014.
What the people who make the products think of the festival. This essay uses organizational sources and leaves the makers' own stories to the label's lab and shop.

r: If a design label appears in your archive under four years, how would you check that the other nine are missing from the archive and not from the label?

posts.title: Studio RENS puts its partners' names on the wall next to its own, and its own pages keep the dates
posts.subtitle: Five years of the official Dutch Design Week photo archive, 2017 to 2021, read against the studio's project pages, the press and the festival's listings
posts.seoTitle: Studio RENS at Dutch Design Week, 2017 to 2021
posts.description: Studio RENS and its partners at Dutch Design Week, 2017 to 2021, read against the studio's own project pages and five photo albums.

r: Look closely at the wall labels in the Studio RENS photographs from Dutch Design Week, and a partner's name often sits next to the studio's.

The 2017 window reads auping x RENS. In 2018 a label reads RENS x Desso beside a rug panel, and another reads Black, RENS x Baars & Bloemhoff. In 2019 three walls carry the names Auping, Baars & Bloemhoff and Desso next to the studio's.

I like a pattern that I can check against the pictures, because it lets me test a story instead of repeating it. This essay draws on public sources only: the studio's own project pages, Dutch Design Week's listings, trade and design press, and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and for 2026 it repeats only what the festival's listings say.

blocks.x: A pair of designers who formed a studio by accident

r: Studio RENS describes itself as a design research studio specialized in the applied investigation of colors and materials, based in Eindhoven, run by Renee Mennen and Stefanie van Keijsteren.

In a December 2018 interview with Sight Unseen the two say they met at the AKV St. Joost academy in Breda, worked together a lot during their studies and, after graduating, "just got on with things" and realized after a few months that they had subconsciously formed a studio.
That account is theirs, and I have no second source for it.
The founding year is where sources part. The studio's own About page says RENS was founded in 2008.
Wolf-Gordon's designer page says the studio was founded in 2009, and IO+ described a tenth anniversary at Dutch Design Week 2019, which agrees with 2009.
A studio that forms by accident may not have a clean birthday, and I leave the question open: 2008 is the studio's statement, and 2009 is what two outside sources say.

blocks.x: Where it works

r: DDW's location page gives the studio's address as Halvemaanstraat 24 on Strijp T+R and says the studio occupies a former building of Philips.
The enterprise of Piet Hein Eek is at Halvemaanstraat 30 in the same street.

The two are more than neighbors. The studio's project page for Piet Hein Eek says that in 2020 Eek asked RENS to research the colors that run through 30 years of his work, with the result a paint collection of 40 hues made with the paint maker Lacq, divided into four themes: hotel, site, projects and objects.
The page names a hotel room gray, a restaurant floor pink, a crisis-collection orange and a bakery green.
A year later, the studio's page says, the same research led to a color scheme for every room of Eek's hotel, with bold bathroom colors taken from the Lacq chart and custom Colour Traces tiles.
A page of the Piet Hein Eek enterprise, posted September 4, 2026, lists Studio RENS among the participants in the building's studios zone for Dutch Design Week 2026.

blocks.x: The method, in the studio's own pages

r: The studio's pages give its method a long history in red. The page for its Re-vive rugs says the designers began experiments in the early 2000s that applied only red pigments to textiles, wood, metals and plastics.
In the IO+ profile of 2019, van Keijsteren dates the exploration of red to 2012 and says it began with the question of what happens if you paint everything red.
The Cor Unum Ceramics page says the collaboration began in 2013 with an exploration of red in ceramics.

The Re-vive rugs date from 2014, the same year as the studio's study of chromatography on textiles called True Colours and its study of mourning dress for the Zuiderzeemuseum, in which tapestries were dyed to show stages of grief.
In 2015 Fade to Stay used sunlight to study how colors fade, with help from Canon and Philips Innovation Services.

The accounts differ on when the red began, and none is a document. I take the broadest reading as correct: red was a long interest, and the collaborations of 2013 and 2014 are where it becomes visible in the record.

blocks.x: 2016 to 2017: black, then the colors people buy

r: The studio's page for Black dates it to 2016: nine objects from nine materials in a single color, made for Baars & Bloemhoff's exhibition Transitions II, with the studio noting that the items are no longer in regular production and exist for demonstration on request.

The Auping project is the 2017 piece. The studio's page says RENS used consumer-preference data in Auping's order history to visualize which colors are bought most and least, and the differences between countries, and it calls the exhibition part of Dutch Design Week 2017.
IO+ confirms that RENS staged an exhibition for Auping in 2017.
Auping's own designers page says the color study was presented during Dutch Design Week in 2018 as the exhibition Nighty Night Colours.
Three sources therefore point to 2017: the studio, IO+ and the 2017 photo titles dated October 26, 2017.
Auping's page is the outlier, and I treat it as a mistake until the company says otherwise.
The 2017 album has six photos by Max Kneefel. One shows pink lettering on window glass that reads auping x RENS, and another shows wall text reading Nighty Night Colours.

blocks.x: 2018: partners one by one

r: The studio's pages give the 2018 year to Finissage with Pode, side tables made after research into the paint technology of the design label, and to Table Top, ceramic side tables with Cor Unum.

Sight Unseen's December 17, 2018 profile described the show with Pode as a series of layered panels in wood, metal, glass and textile that served as a visual archive of the color research, and lists the year's other work as Working Glass, Unfoiled and RE:re-vive rugs with Desso.

The 2018 album has 27 photos, and the 24 I could read mostly credit Britt Roelse in their titles. The labels in them read RE:re-vive RENS x Desso, Working Glass, Black RENS x Baars & Bloemhoff, RENS x Social Label and RENS x Pode.
Those labels match the studio's pages, with one apparent exception: the studio dates Black to 2016, and a Black label stands in a 2018 photograph.

The simplest reading is that an earlier work was shown again, which the studio's note about demonstration pieces would allow. I could not confirm that, because no source describes the 2018 display of Black.

blocks.x: 2019: ten years, and the pattern as the point

r: Dutch Design Week 2019 ran from October 19 to 27, and Stylepark, writing on August 23, 2019, said the studio would give an overview of its research and collaborations over ten years, in time for its anniversary.
IO+ named the show RENS Marks the Spot, at the studio on Halvemaanstraat, and listed the partners as Auping, Pode, Desso, Baars & Bloemhoff, Cor Unum, Best Wool and the Zuiderzeemuseum.
The IO+ interview quotes van Keijsteren on why the show used a multiplication sign: because the letter is used to point out where you are, and because it means ten.
Stylepark also traces the Table Top work to the Reddish collection of 2013, in which pigment was applied as a liquid to unglazed ceramic and slowly permeated it.
The 2019 album shows a tall red panel with the show's title and walls labeled RENS x Auping, RENS x Baars & Bloemhoff and RENS x Desso.
In this year the text in the press and the labels in the pictures say the same thing. That agreement is the reason I trust the 2019 reading more than the others.

blocks.x: 2020 and 2021: Eek's colors, and tiles

r: DDW 2020 was a digital edition. The studio's pages give 2020 to the Lacq and Piet Hein Eek research and 2021 to the hotel colors and to the Re-glow tiles made with Cor Unum Ceramics, hand-painted and glazed wall tiles built on existing stock.
The studio's Re-vive tile line followed in 2021, extending the partnership with Desso, a division of Tarkett, that started in 2014.
The 2020 album has 20 photos by Max Kneefel. They show plates with colored discs, tall pale vessels, glass sheets and carpet squares, and none of them carries a partner label I could read.

The titles do not mention Lacq, so I do not connect the two. The 2021 album has 13 photos credited to Nick Bookelaar in the file titles. They show red boxes, rugs with triangle patterns, curtains and a block of glazed tiles.
Red boxes and carpet squares fit the Re-vive description, and glazed tiles fit Re-glow, but the album does not name either, so these are fits and not matches.

blocks.x: Away from the week: data as a design material

r: The Auping study of 2017 turns out to be a method and not a one-off. The studio's page for Tally Up, made with the wallcovering maker Wolf-Gordon, says RENS studied Wolf-Gordon's Scuffmaster order and sales data for 2021 and 2022 and built a ten-by-ten color chart that combines all-time favorites with overlooked colors, noting an oversupply of whites, grays and blacks and of metallic "material colors."
Wolf-Gordon's designer page lists the Auping sales analysis among the studio's projects and lists wallcovering designs by the studio.

The studio's own services page says it develops color concepts and CMF directions for interiors, products and brands, and that it translates its findings into color cards, working palettes and sample sets for architects and design labels.

That places the Dutch Design Week shows in a larger practice. The labels on the walls name the brands the studio works with, and the studio's pages show that the work for them is often an analysis of the brand's own numbers before it is an object.
The exhibitions are one place where that analysis becomes visible to a public. They are not the whole of it.

blocks.x: What the festival lists for 2026

r: DDW's program lists two Studio RENS items for October 17 to 25, 2026, both at Halvemaanstraat 24. Studio RENS ON DISPLAY is a studio presentation of recent work and color studies, which the listing describes as an open studio. CANVAS Surface of Sleep describes hand-screenprinted color studies translated into bedding textiles for Auping.

I have not seen either. The Auping partnership that opened this essay's labels in 2017 is therefore still running, and the listing says nothing about whether the 2026 bedding relates to the 2017 color study.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know which object any photograph shows beyond what a label says. I do not know whether Black was shown in both 2016 and 2018, or why the Auping page gives 2018. I could not open Dutch Design Daily's 2019 report, because the site answered with a verification page, so the 2019 partner list rests on IO+ and Stylepark.

I do not know whether the archive holds RENS photographs after 2021 in albums that do not carry its name. The five albums hold 83 photos in all, and the studio's own pages credit other photographers, among them Ronald Smits, Lisa Klappe and Hugo Thomassen, so the archive and the studio each hold a different set of pictures of the same work.
When you read the two 2026 listings, look for the x between two names and ask who chose the color. Which name answers that, and where does the label say so?

posts.title: The Bar appears in the DDW photo archive twice, and its own page describes a third year
posts.subtitle: The Dutch Design Week pop-up bar at Ketelhuisplein, read through the 2021 and 2025 albums, signs in the photographs and the program page.
posts.seoTitle: The Bar at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: The Dutch Design Week pop-up bar on Ketelhuisplein: why DDW's page for it describes 2024, what the 2021 and 2025 albums show, and what the signs say.

r: The page that describes The Bar at Dutch Design Week lists opening days that fit neither year the photo archive holds for it, and that mismatch turns out to be the most useful fact about it.
The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds albums named The Bar for 2021, with 32 photographs, and 2025, with two albums of 14 and 84.

This essay draws on public sources only: DDW's own page for the bar, two festival summaries, a city guide and a district page, plus the signs legible inside the photographs. It reports no visit and no interview, and it describes 2026 only as a listing.
I find a record that disagrees with itself a good place to start, because it shows me where to look.

blocks.x: What the page says, and which year it is

r: DDW's food and drinks page for The Bar calls it the official pop-up bar of Dutch Design Week, at Ketelhuisplein, 5617 AE, for drinks, music and design meet-ups, fueled by SUBBAR, with DJs every day from 17:00. It types it as a pop-up food truck, lists an Instagram handle, and gives wheelchair access as partial.
Its opening hours run from Saturday, October 19, 11:00 to 22:00, through Sunday, October 27, 11:00 to 19:00, with the latest closing, 23:00, on Saturday, October 26.
Those weekdays fit 2024: October 19, 2024 was a Saturday. They do not fit 2021, when DDW ran October 16 to 24, or 2025, when it ran October 18 to 26.
So the page is the program entry of an edition for which the archive holds no album, and it shows that The Bar was part of the program in 2024.

blocks.x: 2021: an album with a place missing

r: CLICKNL's note of October 16, 2021 gives the setting: after a completely virtual DDW20, the twentieth edition ran in person from October 16 to 24, 2021 under the theme The Greater Number, with more than 2,600 designers and more than 110 locations.
The 2021 album holds 32 photographs credited in the titles to Max Kneefel, 18 dated October 19 and 14 dated October 21, 2021.

They show a round tent roof lit in blue, pink and green, a DJ desk with a screen reading VEDETT, a wood stove with benches, a lit sign reading MOZEM above stacked crates and a crowd on a raised round floor.
No title names a place, and I could not find a page that places the 2021 bar. The photographs make a bar easy to recognize and a location hard to prove.

Most of the 2021 photographs show guests' faces at close range, so the carousel uses the wide ones, the sign, the stove and the tent. That narrows the selection to places and objects, and it means the people who made the evening are mostly absent from this record.

blocks.x: 2025: signs that name the bar

r: The 2025 photographs name more. A scaffold pavilion under a red canopy shows neon signs reading THE BAR and otomoto, and a sign board headed KETELHUISPLEIN lists The Bar x Otomoto under Food & Drinks.

The same board says the design of the square centers on a pavilion that celebrates 25 years of Dutch Design Week with the theme Past. Present. Possible. Flags on the scaffold carry the number 25 and the words 25th edition.
I found no page that says who Otomoto is in this context. The only Otomoto site I opened is a garage in the north of the Netherlands, and I do not connect it to the bar.

DDW's press release for 2025 and the Strijp-S district's own news item agree on the frame: the 25th edition ran October 18 to 26, 2025, with Strijp-S one of the main hubs, evenings full of music and performances, and more than 2,500 or 2,600 designers depending on the page.
Strijp-S's page credits its photographs to Dutch Design Week, Anwyn Howarth and Max Kneefel.
A banner for the 25th edition can only belong to that edition, which makes the photograph a better clock than any title.

blocks.x: The square it stands on

r: A This is Eindhoven guide published on October 1, 2026 calls Ketelhuisplein the vibrant heart of Strijp-S, a place with a party or festival nearly every week, and during DDW a temporary open-air museum for large installations and a starting or ending point for a visit, with food stalls around it. It lists The Bar as the pop-up spot where you can raise a glass to the day and perhaps finish with a little dance.
That is a 2026 listing, and I treat it as one: it tells me The Bar is part of the festival's public description of the square, and nothing about what it will serve or play.

blocks.x: Who is SUBBAR

r: DDW's page says The Bar is fueled by SUBBAR.

Plan-B, the Eindhoven design hub that has its own essay in this series, uses the same name for the bar and restaurant on its ground floor, which its pages describe as open Monday to Friday and available for lunch, catering and events, and its 2023 festival program tells visitors to have lunch at Subbar on the ground floor.
The two uses of the name suggest a connection, but no page I opened says that the festival bar and the hub restaurant are run by the same operator, so I treat it as a lead and not a fact.

blocks.x: Two albums that overlap

r: The archive holds two 2025 albums: The Bar with 14 photographs, all dated October 18, and The Bar - Pavilion with 84.
The first 14 titles of the Pavilion album repeat the camera numbers of the first album in the same order, under different photo ids.
The Pavilion album's titles run from October 18 to 24, and one is titled TheBar_StrijpS_DDW25 with Cleo Goossens's name and October 21.
A reader who adds 14 and 84 gets 98 photographs; at least 14 appear twice, so there are no more than 84 distinct shots. A count is only as honest as the identity check behind it.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: Which edition the program page describes.
The header shows 2026, the text says October 19 to 27, and the weekdays fit 2024. The calendar settled it.
DDW calls 2021 its twentieth edition and 2024 its twenty-third, and calls 2025 its 25th.

The first two figures fit a first edition in 2002 and the third fits 2001, and 2025 cannot be both the 24th and the 25th. A 25-year banner counts years from 2001, which would explain it, but no DDW page I opened says so. I use the number each source gives and attribute it.
The neon says THE BAR and the board says the pavilion celebrates 25 years. Both can be true of one structure.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know who ran The Bar in 2021, who SUBBAR is beyond its name, what Otomoto is in the sign board, or what the bar served or played in any year. I viewed 43 of the 98 photographs from 2025, so I cannot describe the other 55.

I found no page for The Bar in 2022 or 2023. The album facts come from my reading of the Flickr account on October 8, 2026, which I did not repeat. In my own field, a specimen in two jars with different labels is still one specimen, and I learned to check the specimen before I trusted the label count.
If the sign in the photograph and the page on the website disagree about the year, which one would you correct first?

posts.title: Transnatural at Dutch Design Week: a biodesign platform, a warehouse on Strijp-S and four albums with four photographers
posts.subtitle: From Playing Life in 2015 to Regeneration in 2016, Robotanica in 2017 and a label show in 2019, set against the platform's founder, its earliest events, Dutch and trade press, DDW program pages and the photo archive.
posts.seoTitle: Transnatural at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Transnatural's biodesign shows at DDW 2015 to 2019 and its Radical City inc. program, from the founder's account, early events, press and the photo archive.

r: A platform that changes its building and its theme every October is hard to follow through a photo archive, and the four Transnatural albums in the Dutch Design Week (DDW) archive show it by changing photographer every time.

I like a record that lets me see who is looking, because the viewpoint decides what I can say. This essay uses a 2014 interview with the founder, early event notices from 2010 to 2014, press from 2012 and 2015 to 2017, a university excursion program, DDW's own program pages for 2019, 2023 and 2025, and the official photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and it could not use Transnatural's own website, whose host answers automated requests with an HTTP 403 error.

blocks.x: A platform started as an event

r: In a December 9, 2014 interview, founder Arjen Bangma says he started Transnatural five years earlier, first as an exhibition and conference event about nature and technology, and then, because of the interest from participants, visitors and press, as an ongoing platform for experiments and research, with a commercial Label that sells knowledge and skills.

The interview describes events that cross art and design with technological and scientific innovation, among them Beyond Biennial, a September 2014 series in Amsterdam North, and an exhibition called Living Matter(s) on synthetic bio materials.
The start year is Bangma's account, and it points to about 2009.

Dated notices from the time put the first public events in 2010 and 2011. Next Nature Network's site announced on March 9, 2010 a Transnatural symposium on Saturday, March 13, 2010 at the Trouw building in Amsterdam, with an exhibition until March 19 of works such as Bitfall, Biojewelery and Mudtub.

A mailing-list message dated February 1, 2011, sent under Bangma's name, announces TN02: Becoming TransNatural, called the second TransNatural event, with an exhibition from March 4 to April 1, 2011 and a symposium on March 12, in the Verdieping of the TrouwAmsterdam building at the Wibautstraat.
So the platform's first events are documented in March 2010, within the "about five years earlier" of a December 2014 interview, and the 2010 date is the earliest one I can document.

By 2012 the platform had a gallery. Domus reported on July 13, 2012 on the exhibition Smart as Matter in what it called the small, narrow gallery space of the Dutch design research collective Transnatural in Amsterdam, part of the group's 2011 to 2012 season theme The state of Autonomy, and quoted Arjen Bangma as the group's co-founder and director.
A retailer's brand page says the Amsterdam-based label has existed since 2012.

Mediamatic's page for the exhibition Teaming Up, dated February 7, 2014 and located at Lijnbaansgracht 148a in Amsterdam, calls it the third chapter in a series of three exhibitions that began in early 2013 with Still Unidentified Objects and continued with Linking Parts.

The 2014 interview shows how the platform worked: a workspace in Amsterdam, a team of creatives, program designers and curators, an exhibition in the gallery and objects for sale from designers such as Jólan van der Wiel.
That is the model that arrives in Eindhoven in 2015, a gallery show sent to a DDW warehouse.

blocks.x: 2015: Playing Life

r: IO+ introduced the show on October 17, 2015 as a hidden gem of DDW, curated by Arjen Bangma, at the Veemgebouw on Strijp-S, and added a note: Note the change of location. It describes speculative design about new ways of working living material, among them the Bistro In Vitro ice cream van by Koert van Mensvoort of the Next Nature Network, Nienke Hoogvliet's Re-Sea-Me on fish skin as leather, and Ted Lawson's Ghost in the machine, a large print made with his own blood as ink.

Core77's report on DDW 2015 names the show Transnatural: Playing Life and says Amsterdam's Transnatural Gallery presented about a dozen recent biodesign projects there, including Caroline Schulze's Bugs Bunny, a 3D-printed mealworm nugget that debuted at DDW the year before, and Agatha Haines's Circumventive Organs.
The 2015 album holds three photos by Nick Bookelaar, each titled Veemgebouw_expositie, including a sign reading Transnatural label on a partition and a wide hall of white pillars.

The titles give a place and no show. With Core77 now naming the show in the same building, the identification of the album with Playing Life rests on two independent press pages and one place name, which I count as solid even though no photo title says it.

The theme continued in Amsterdam. Mediamatic's page for Playing Life - Biotalk, on March 18, 2016, says Transnatural and Mediamatic were teaming up for another edition, in which emerging bio artists and scientists show their work, and lists the City of Amsterdam and the Creative Industries Fund NL among the supporters.

blocks.x: 2016: Regeneration

r: De Betere Wereld wrote on September 21, 2016 that Regeneration would open on September 30 in the Transnatural Gallery in Amsterdam, with talks and workshops with Mediamatic, and be shown during DDW, October 22 to 30, in the Veemgebouw on Strijp-S, Torenallee 80.

It frames the show around restoring damaged ecosystems, from extreme drought and desertification to overfishing, sea level rise and pollution. It lists eleven projects: Caravel by Ivan Henriques, The Salt Project by Eric Geboers, Interwoven by Diana Scherer, The Floating City by Blue21, Post-Fishing by Inês Marques, Mist Capturing Surface by Robyn Tayler Payne, ReGen Villages by EFFEKT, Living Light by Ermi van Oers, GeoMerce by Gionata Gatto and Giovanni Innella, Cocoon by Land Life Company, and the Medusae Project by Charlotte van Alem.
The 2016 album has 10 photos, 7 credited by title to Marleen van Veen and 3, titled Veem_expo, to Nick Bookelaar.
They show a round lens over a skeletal leaf, a bed of grass around a woven mat, a panel reading REGENERATION beside white seats, and a projected floating city.
The panel names the show. The woven mat in grass is a tempting match for Diana Scherer's Interwoven, and no label says so, so I leave it as a possibility.

blocks.x: 2017: Robotanica

r: Interior Design's November 2, 2017 round-up of ten DDW highlights puts Transnatural's Robotanica at the VDMA building. It describes an exploration of robotics in the natural world and whether technology could be used to save threatened species, with insect robots that could fly over disaster areas looking for survivors, clothing fitted with sensors that make air pollution visible, and Austin Stewart's Second Livestock, a chicken wearing a virtual reality headset meant to make it think it is free-roaming.

Two more accounts fill in the show. Upworthy, on November 30, 2017, says the curators picked 11 projects from designers, scientists and artists, among them the Delfly Explorer, a small robotic dragonfly, and the Woodpecker Project, which uses speakers to recreate the sound of an endangered bird, and it quotes exhibit curator Arjen Bangma on that project, as told to Fast Company.

TL Magazine, writing on October 23, 2017, places the show at the VDMA on Vestdijk, where Robotanica stood next to the chicken in its headset and a small robotic firefly made by TU Delft students, in a building that also hosted the shows In Stijl, Post Modern and Envisions.
The 2017 album has six photos by Ralph Roelse, titled Transnatural_VDMA_2017, of a black foil dome, a pool with floating discs, a hexagon of mirrored glass and a wall of mirrored shapes.
The VDMA in the titles agrees with the articles, and none of the album titles names a work.
The name VDMA recurs in the archive: the Precious Plastic team announced in 2018 that it would open its workspace at a VDMA building in Eindhoven.
TL Magazine puts the 2017 VDMA on Vestdijk and no page I opened gives the 2018 address, so I cannot say the two are the same building.

blocks.x: 2018 and 2019: a missing year and a label show

r: There is no 2018 album, and I found no page that places Transnatural at DDW in 2018.
For 2019 there are three kinds of evidence. The 2019 album has 14 photos by Iris Rijskamp, all titled Transnatural.
The earlier read describes white shell shapes in a glass box, clear shells on dark soil, metal letters on a floor, a net sculpture lit from inside and a film frame with coordinates.

DDW's archived program page for Transnatural Label, which says it was part of DDW 2019, announces works by four new designers who start from material innovation, and names Mineralism for Transnatural by Aad Kruiswijk, Coral Lights by Eric Geboers and Matteo Baldassari, The Ode to AL, Transience Mirrors and Lamina Light by Tijs Gilde.

And a Berlin art university's program for its visit of October 19 to 22, 2019 lists, on its first day in the Campina area, a visit to Transnatural for what it calls a post Drought exhibition on global water-related challenges, with Jólan van der Wiel in connection with Issey Miyake, Formafantasma and others.

None of these ties a photograph to a show. The shell shapes are a possible match for Coral Lights, since coral and shells look alike, but that is my guess, and the program page says nothing about venue.
The university program is a plan and not a report, and it places the visit in the Campina area, while the 2015 to 2017 albums name the Veemgebouw and the VDMA.
I found no page that says where the 2019 Transnatural shows stood.

blocks.x: Radical City inc. and Invisible Matters

r: DDW's program carries two later Transnatural exhibitions under the heading of a multi-year program called Radical City inc. The 2023 entry, Radical City inc., says the exhibition at DDW 2023 was the second in a series of evolving exhibitions on a climate-proof, nature-inclusive city, that it also showed Transnatural's new art and design collection, and that some works would be or were being realized in public spaces in Amsterdam. Its participants include Natasja Alers, Mae Engelgeer, Theun Karelse, Rollo Bryant, Klarenbeek & Dros, Bram de Vos, Green Quays, VANTOT, Crafting Plastics Studio and DumoLab Research.

The next entry, Transnatural presents: Invisible Matters, sits in DDW's 2025 archive and describes an exhibition on the unseen natural forces in the urban landscape, with participants Huachen Xin, Fillip Studios & Omlab, Ringailė Demšytė, Valentine Maurice, Raphael Emine, Chris Kievid & Lars van Vianen and Martens & Visser.
The Creative Industries Fund NL's DDW 2025 tips say Transnatural presented it with the support of a grant from its Design Grant Scheme.
A MaterialDistrict article on DDW 2025 describes the same exhibition.
DDW's own page for it sits under the 2025 archive path, which matches the fund's 2025 tips, and the page prints no venue address that I could read.

blocks.x: What the albums can and cannot show

r: The archive holds four albums and 33 photos: 3 in 2015, 10 in 2016, 6 in 2017 and 14 in 2019, with four different photographers named over the years: Bookelaar, van Veen, Roelse and Rijskamp.
There is no album for 2018, and none for 2023 or 2025, although DDW's own pages describe Transnatural exhibitions in both years.
The place in the titles is the one constant that changes: Veemgebouw for 2015 and 2016, and VDMA for 2017.
The press fills in the shows, and two of the three (Playing Life, Regeneration) carry the Veemgebouw address in their own sources.

As an anatomist I know that two people can draw the same specimen and show different structures. The same applies to photographers of the same installation, so comparing the images across years compares the photographers as much as the exhibitions. That is my reading and not a finding of any source.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know where Transnatural's 2019 shows stood, whether the shell photographs belong to the label show or the water exhibition, whether it took part in 2018, 2020 to 2022 or 2024, or which projects appear in which photograph.
I did not read Transnatural's own pages, because its host refused automated requests twice in this research, and I did not verify Bangma's start date against a register.
The Transnatural Label's own site disallows AI crawlers, so I used nothing from it.
If a platform shows different work every year in different buildings, what should an archive keep constant so that a reader can follow it?

posts.title: Kiki & Joost at Dutch Design Week: ten years of open doors, and an exhibition space that finally has dates
posts.subtitle: The studio's own news page, the trade press and the DDW listing date the show for most years and the exhibition space for the first time. The photo archive keeps nine of the editions.
posts.seoTitle: Kiki & Joost at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Kiki van Eijk and Joost van Bleiswijk at Dutch Design Week 2016 to 2026: shows by year, partners, the new exhibition space and what the photo archive holds.

r: The studio's own account of 2025 says two birthdays fell in the same week, its own 25th and Dutch Design Week's, and the photo archive that follows it begins nine years earlier in a different phase of the studio's life.

I like a studio that keeps a record of its own, because the comparison between that record and an archive shows what each one leaves out. This essay draws on public sources only: the studio's news page and several of its posts, design-trade articles from 2017 to 2023, the Dutch Design Week location page and the official photo archive as I recorded it on October 7, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview. Dezeen, which the earlier draft cited for several facts, refused my request on October 9, 2026 with an HTTP 403, so I made no further request to it and I mark those facts as read in the earlier pass.

blocks.x: Two designers, one studio

r: Kiki van Eijk and Joost van Bleiswijk are two designers who also work together as Kiki & Joost. Dezeen, in the earlier pass, described them as a couple who make work as independent designers, with Van Eijk making ceramic and handblown glass objects and Van Bleiswijk making bold furniture.

The studio's news page gives a fuller outline in its headlines and excerpts. It lists a Dutch podcast description saying they studied at the Design Academy in Eindhoven and found each other there, a New York Times piece of November 5, 2020 headed "Kiki Van Eijk: 20 Years of Design," and a retrospective of Van Eijk's work at the textile museum in Tilburg from September 26, 2020 to September 12, 2021.
Design Milk adds that her graduate collection, whose rug Carpet Special is dated 2000, was called We're Living in a Doll's House and rehabilitated felted wool carpets in Dutch design.
That date fits the studio's statement in 2025 that it was turning 25.
Their addresses and buildings are easier to pin down than their dates. The studio's own pages give Gabriël Metsulaan 1, entrance Kanaaldijk Zuid, in Eindhoven.

TL Magazine wrote on October 26, 2017 that the studio and office space sits in a former Philips laboratory in an industrial park just outside the center, called Plan B, and that it had been theirs since 2016.
Dezeen's 2017 article, in the earlier pass, called the building a former Philips electronics laboratory.
No page I opened says the 2017 building and the Gabriël Metsulaan address are the same, and I treat them as probably one site, which is my inference.

blocks.x: What each year showed

r: The studio's own posts and the press name a show for most years, and the table gives them side by side. The album facts come from the dossier's October 7 reading.

Year
t

t

rows: Physical, in Milan in April; the DDW album's titles read PHYSICAL IDEAS
The Tinkering Labs, in the studio, with work beside the machines
Alter Ego, in the studio, through October 28
DDW 19 Future Workspace, an open house; and DDW 19 Traces with the Rijksmuseum's Rijksstudio
New designs for Maison Dada and the NSNG cabinets with Moooi
Carte Blanche, the first show in the new exhibition space
In Action: Kiki & Joost and Friends, October 18 to 24

r: The details are what make each year distinct. In 2017, TL Magazine says the work was placed next to the machines used to make it, on orange pedestals against the green of the industrial machines, with the lighting kept low, and that van Eijk said the idea was to show how small ideas become big projects.

It names new work: Plant Lamps by van Eijk, with caps 3D printed in bioplastics and ceramic, Windows of my Eyes made with the Dutch ceramic company Cor Unum for the 100-year anniversary of De Stijl, and Tinkering Lamps and torn-ceramic pieces by van Bleiswijk, with his Tearing Tapestry rugs for Nodus also on view.
The same article says the pair had other ongoing projects that week at the Van Abbe Museum, at Kazerne, at the Effenaar and at Restaurant Zarzo.

DDW's music announcement of September 6, 2017 names Joost van Bleiswijk among the five designers of decor and stage design for DDW Music, and the Effenaar was the first venue its announcement lists, so the Effenaar project may be that work.
I mark that as my inference, because neither page links the two.

In 2018 TL Magazine's report of October 23 describes Alter Ego as the pair's playful take on their many roles, with each piece paired with an alter ego: an abstract sculptor, a composer, a poet, a social activist, a treasure hunter and others.

It names Space Poetry and Shadows of Gold by van Eijk, the latter made with the Venetian gold-leaf laboratory Berta Battiloro under the dialogue program Doppia Firma, and No Screw No Glue and Curved and Tape by van Bleiswijk, along with a clock called TIJD for Social Label.

The NSNG cabinets reappear in 2021: Interior Design reported the flat-pack cabinet collection, called No Screw No Glue and cut from pressed paper, launched with Moooi, and Kiki van Eijk's collection La fabrique des rêves for Maison Dada, which includes a clock and two trays.
So a collection shown in a studio in 2018 reached a retailer by 2021, according to the two articles.

In 2022 the studio's post describes Low Resolution as an exhibition for a low-tech counterweight to digital life, with collaborations with Very Simple Kitchen, the glass maker Omnidecor, the textile studio BYBORRE and Sommer Glass, open October 22 to 30 from 11:00 to 18:00 with shorter hours on October 27 and 30.
That is the year the archive has no album.

In 2023 Design Milk describes Perpetuum Mobile, Latin for perpetual motion, as showing work from the past two decades, including Van Eijk's 2023 collection with Cor Unum and her raku knit wall hangings made with Borre Akkersdijk, and Van Bleiswijk's Beam Sketch shelving, a collection that the article says came from the construction of a new exhibition space.

blocks.x: The exhibition space, dated at last

r: The earlier draft left the date of the 190 square meter exhibition space open, and the sources now settle it. Design Milk's article of November 8, 2023 says the construction of a new exhibition space, an addition to the workshop, was under way and had forced the workshop to be cleared for the show.

The studio's post of February 20, 2024 says the new space was well underway: the Douglas wood framework was complete, the concrete floor with heating was in place and the cladding was being finished, with a public opening planned for June.

The studio's post of October 15, 2024 says Dutch Design Week would host the international debut of the new space, across the courtyard from the workshop, with Carte Blanche as the first exhibition, open October 19 to 26 from 11:00 to 18:00 and on October 27 from 11:00 to 17:00.
Dezeen, in the earlier pass, reported the space on October 31, 2024.

DDW's 2026 location page adds the dimensions: an exhibition space of Douglas wood, 190 square meters, the latest addition to the adjacent studio and workshop, the two connected by a newly created garden of nearly 300 square meters planted according to a design by Kiki van Eijk.
The 2025 post says the studio, gallery and workshop together cover 1,200 square meters.
So the space was built across 2023 and 2024, shown first at Dutch Design Week 2024, and I do not know whether the June opening planned in February took place.
The earlier draft's phrase "the albums show a timber-framed hall from 2019 onward" refers to the older workshop hall, since the new building did not exist before 2023 to 2024.

blocks.x: 2020: an edition online

r: In 2020 Dutch Design Week was online, and the studio's news page lists an ELLE article headed "Do you also want to see during Dutch Design Week: Kiki x Joost Almost Tomorrow" and noting that this year the week was online.
A Frame interview listed on the same page is headed "Design's new intimacy: Kiki & Joost share how the pandemic has made them reuse the materials that surround them."

The archive's album for that year carries the show name in its title and has 10 photographs by Max Kneefel, and the old dossier describes a timber hall with a skylight, a raised yellow platform with colorful furniture frames, woven wall hangings, a black chandelier and crystal vases.
I could not open the ELLE article or the Frame interview, so I do not describe what they say beyond their headlines.

blocks.x: The partners, as the sources name them

r: Across the years the sources name a long list of partners: Cor Unum and Nodus in 2017, Social Label in 2018, the Rijksmuseum's Rijksstudio in 2019, Maison Dada and Moooi in 2021, Very Simple Kitchen, Omnidecor, BYBORRE and Sommer Glass in 2022, and in 2025 the friends Marc Mulders and Diederik Verbakel.

The 2023 show added works made with Ikonic Toys, Spectrum, Weef and the Singer Laren museum, whose commission was an outdoor bench for its new extension, which the designers called The Line of Beauty and Grace, after William Hogarth's idea of a serpentine line.
These are the companies the posts and articles name, and none of the pages says how long each partnership lasted.

blocks.x: What the albums keep

r: The old dossier counts albums for nine editions, 2016 to 2021 and 2023 to 2025, with 5 photographs in 2024 and 68 in 2021, 167 photographs in all, and no album for 2022.
Photographers named in the titles are Iris Rijskamp for 2016 to 2019, Max Kneefel in 2020, Tommy Köhlbrugge in 2021, Nick Bookelaar in 2023 and Anwyn Howarth in 2024, with no name for 2025.

I did not reopen Flickr for this version. What the albums add to the written record is the rooms: the dossier describes a darker gallery with a standing crowd in 2018 and a pale timber hall with a concrete floor from 2019.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: When the exhibition space was built.

Design Milk had it under construction in autumn 2023, the studio had its framework complete on February 20, 2024, and the first show in it was Carte Blanche in October 2024. Settled from the three dated pages.
The archive has no album and the studio's own post shows a 2022 show. The post settles it.
The old draft found no source; the studio's news page lists the ELLE article under the name Almost Tomorrow.
The studio post says its studio turns 25 along with Dutch Design Week, and Design Milk dates Van Eijk's graduate collection to 2000. The post settles the claim, and the 2000 date supports it.
Whether the 2017 and present buildings are the same.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know why 2022 has no album, which show the 2016 and 2018 albums belong to, what the 2025 photographer's name is or whether the June 2024 opening took place. I did not open the ELLE and Frame pieces, and I could not reread Dezeen, so its statements are from the earlier pass.
I did not reopen the photo archive for this version, so the album counts, titles and descriptions come from the dossier's October 7, 2026 reading.
The sources say nothing about what COMMENTS contains, and I do not describe it.
When a studio publishes its own news and an archive publishes its own photographs, which one would you consult first about a year you did not attend, and what would you ask the other to confirm?

posts.title: Vij5 at Dutch Design Week: a design publisher, a tea towel and a workshop used as a stage
posts.subtitle: From the 2009 FlexVaas award to the twentieth-anniversary show in 2026, set against five photo albums and the label's own blog.
posts.seoTitle: Vij5 at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Vij5, a Dutch design publisher, at Dutch Design Week 2016 to 2026: a color vote for a tea towel, a workshop used as a stage and twenty years.

r: Vij5 let the public choose the color of a tea towel at Dutch Design Week 2018, and for its twentieth year it brings the same towel back in new colors.

As a content strategist I like a company that publishes its own process, because it gives a reader something to check a caption against. This essay draws on public sources only: Vij5's own pages and blog, the Dutch Design Awards, Dutch Design Week's area recaps and program listing, a city guide and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 exhibit beyond what the published listing says.

blocks.x: A publisher of design products

r: Vij5's About page says the founders, Arjan van Raadshooven and Anieke Branderhorst, met during their studies and started right after graduating in 2006, aiming to bring their own products to market from a designer's perspective. They call themselves publishers of design products, working from content, with the product and the story behind it first.
The page names their best-known design as the FlexVaas, which won a Dutch Design Award in 2009.

The Dutch Design Awards site confirms the win. It lists the FlexVaas by Ontwerplabel Vij5 as the 2009 winner in the Product category and describes a porcelain base with three interchangeable top pieces held on by clamps like those on preserving jars.
The company's DDW story therefore starts before its first archive photograph.

The About page also places its studio in Den Bosch and describes five steps for every product: designing beautiful and functional interior products at the base, collecting concepts that move the founders into a personal collection, translating the concepts into producible products, having craftspeople make them with care, and sharing them with the world.

Its festival pages put its showroom and workshop elsewhere: on the Hallenweg in Eindhoven. The 2019 post speaks of its own studio, showroom and workshop on the Hallenweg, and the 2021 area guide lists the Vij5 showroom at G1 in the Hallenweg area.
Both can be true, because a company can have an office in one city and a workshop in another, and no page I opened says which function sits where.

blocks.x: The Hallenweg as an address

r: A city guide says the Hallenweg grew up after the Second World War as an economic recovery project, with metal and welding companies moving in first, and that today it hosts studios and ateliers such as Vij5, HeyHeydeHaas and the church of Atelier NL.
Dutch Design Week's recap for 2018 calls it one of eight design areas and says the designers there welcome visitors in their studios.

blocks.x: 2016 to 2018: from supplied photographs to a crowdfunding vote

r: The photo archive I read holds five Vij5 albums, for 2016 through 2020, with 39, 9, 9, 5 and 30 photographs, which makes 92. In 2016 the photo titles read Vij5 Showroom - Dutch Design Week 2016, image by Vij5, and a photo page reads Photo (c) Vij5, so the label supplied those pictures. The later albums credit Iris Rijskamp for 2017 to 2019 and Max Kneefel for 2020. I read the albums in an earlier pass and did not reopen the account for this version, so every Flickr fact here is second-hand.

No page I opened describes what Vij5 showed in 2016 or 2017. A Berlin design school's itinerary for October 21 to 24, 2017 lists a visit to Hallenweg and Vij5 and friends, which at least places the label there that year.

For 2018 the label's own blog gives the detail. Its experiment Kies Kleur, choose a color, asked the public to pick the colors for its TweeDoek, a hand towel and tea towel in one. People sent in 80 color combinations, five finalists went to crowdfunding on a Dutch platform in October 2018, and the label reports that the campaign reached 107 percent.
DDW's recap says the label was exploring the limits of crowdfunding by involving the public in one of the most important choices of a design process, the color.
The post credits its photographs to Iris Rijskamp and also lists new products: a trestle table and a lamp by David Derksen, the Glint Light by Susanne de Graef and a bar stool by Floris Hovers.

The same week the company did work for the festival itself. Its blog says it designed the Press Center at the Dutch Design Foundation's head office on Strijp-S for the foundation, and the Business Lounge on Strijp-S commissioned by the foundation and Renault.

Its products also appeared in someone else's show: The Young Collectors, a house exhibition by Studio Thier & van Daalen, showed a trestle table, cups, a clock and a coatrack from the Vij5 collection in a 1960s house.

blocks.x: 2019 and 2020: an open studio, then a studio-exhibition festival

r: In 2019 the exhibition We're open took place in the studio, showroom and workshop on the Hallenweg. A large map of the Netherlands named every partner, and the label says that showed how much of its activity happens in the Netherlands, even the Eindhoven region.

The post adds that the showroom had been renewed and moved to the front of the building, reached through a new glass facade, that a new product, the Tempered Steel Panels by Max Lipsey, debuted, and that bulthaup used the space for a podcast during the week.
The 2019 archive album holds five photographs.

The 2020 festival was different. Dutch Design Week announced on June 8, 2020 that it would run as a mix of an online festival and a bottom-up studio exhibition model, with a limited number of visitors by appointment.
The archive holds a 30-photograph Vij5 album for 2020 by Max Kneefel, and no page I opened describes the show.

blocks.x: 2021 to 2024: the workshop as a stage

r: In 2021 Vij5 turned 15 and invited all the designers in its collection to design a refillable candle, using local rapeseed wax. The candles were shown in the showroom during the festival, and DDW's area guide lists the showroom at G1 and the birthday.

In 2022, under the title Vij5 x Small Living, the label put a tiny house in the middle of its workshop and launched the Flip Desk by Charles O. Job and a vertical version of Maarten Baptist's Coatrack by the Meter.

In 2023, under the title Why product design matters, it showed four additions: OER dinnerware by Lotte de Raadt and Kirstie van Noort, made from iron oxide in the water left over when Eindhoven produces drinking water, a stainless steel mirror, Foarme porcelain and a preview of a tube cabinet.

In 2024, from October 19 to 27, Introducing Tomorrow in the workshop on the Hallenweg previewed six new and four updated designs that used colored linseed oil on wood and invited visitors to give feedback before the official launch.

Its tips post for that year credits photographs to Vij5, Max Kneefel, Britt Roelse, Nick Bookelaar, Tommy Köhlbrugge and others, which suggests the label reuses the festival's archive pictures with credit.

The 2023 post gives the intent behind each addition. The OER dinnerware is colored with the iron-oxide water that remains when groundwater is turned into drinking water, as a way to make people aware of water as a resource. The Stainless Steel Mirror is laser cut from a stainless steel sheet, folded twice and finished by hand in the brushed area. The Foarme porcelain, from the Frisian word for formed, is double-walled and began as a graduation project at the Design Academy Eindhoven about wanted and unwanted deformation in porcelain.
These are the label's descriptions of its own products.
None of these four years has a Vij5 album in the archive as far as I read it, although the label's posts and the festival's own guide document 2021.
A photo archive and a company's blog count different things.

blocks.x: 2026: twenty years, on another terrain

r: Dutch Design Week lists 20 jaar Vij5 for October 17 to 25, 2026, free, 11:00 to 18:00, at APTUM | NRE, Gashouder 13, 5613CR, in the Canal area.

The page says the exhibition brings together classics, updated editions, recent work and designs still in development, shows the collection as it stands in 2026, and calls the start twenty years ago a simple idea of developing and sharing beautiful, functional interior products from the founders' own perspective as designers.
Images on the page include TweeDoek in new colors, the Lloop lamp as a classic, and new products named Papeterie, the Tjalko chair and the Qui side table.
That address is on the NRE terrein, a former gasworks site where a city guide places studios such as Bart Hess, Nul Zes and Alissa&Nienke.
I do not know whether the label's workshop has moved. The page names only the exhibition location.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

items: What the 2016 photographs contain, beyond the supplied-by-Vij5 labels.
Which of the Den Bosch and Hallenweg sites does what.
What Vij5 did at Dutch Design Week 2025: the label's blog list ends in 2024 and the archive I read has no album.
Whether the company's workshop has moved to the NRE terrein.

r: If a company posts its own account of every festival week, what would you check in the archive before you trust either?
