posts.title: Vlisco showed its own prints in 2017 and other people's pictures in 2019, and kept its history in the room
posts.subtitle: Two Dutch Design Week editions of a printed-fabric house, read against the company's own history, a museum, an award jury and the official photo archive
posts.seoTitle: Vlisco at Dutch Design Week, 2017 and 2019
posts.description: Vlisco at Dutch Design Week in 2017 and 2019, set beside the company's own history, a museum page and an award jury.

r: A fabric house that was founded in 1846 spent one Dutch Design Week showing garments and another showing other people's pictures.

I like seeing a maker hand the room to someone else, and I like checking whether the archive noticed. This essay draws on public sources only: Vlisco's own pages and a history it hosts, Dutch Design Week's program entry, a museum page, an award announcement, a Nigerian culture site and the official photo archive on Flickr. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about what Vlisco shows at the 2026 festival.

blocks.x: A house with a long catalog, and a history it publishes

r: Vlisco's About page says it was founded in 1846, is known for printed fabrics made with time-honored methods, is rooted in the Indonesian wax-based batik technique, and has produced more than 350,000 unique textile designs and colorways.
The page also says the prints are designed by international teams in the Netherlands and have been embraced and redefined by African women, who gave them names and meanings.
It describes the company's history as reflecting complex cultural and historical connections.
Vlisco hosts a longer history on its site as a PDF summarizing independent research by Maarten van Riel from the company's archives.

The summary adds dates the About page leaves out. The company was established in 1846 in Helmond, and the wax technique entered its production in 1852, after a family member in the Dutch East Indies saw local batik and judged it could be industrialized.
The company did not itself export to Africa at first: around 1909 two traders, one British and one Dutch, brought its wax prints to West Africa.

Its first dedicated design department dates from 1918, and the summary calls the relationship with the artist Duco Crop likely the earliest collaboration between an artist and a manufacturer in the Netherlands.
The company was requisitioned during the German occupation to produce textiles for Germany.
The design called Angelina dates from 1962, and the Nana Benz, businesswomen of Lomé, Togo, are credited with naming designs and building distribution.
A footnote adds a detail that matters for captions: the company was long called P.F. van Vlissingen & Co., and Vlisco became its official name only in 1970.

The founding year itself has a wrinkle. Vlisco's heritage page, as captured in 2019, says that in 1844 Pieter Fentener van Vlissingen took over his father's cotton printing mill in Helmond and that two years later he renamed it P.F. van Vlissingen & Co., now known as Vlisco.
So 1846 is the year of the new name on a mill that already existed, and the About page's "founded in 1846" and the sign on the 2017 wall that reads since 1846 both use the later date.
I read these as the company's own account, supported by footnotes to published histories, and not as an outside audit. Both pages are Vlisco's.
The archive holds two albums titled Vlisco, one for 2017 and one for 2019, 20 photographs in all.

blocks.x: 2017: Day and Night

r: The 2017 album holds 9 photographs by Iris Rijskamp.

A red wall carries a small sign that reads VLISCO since 1846 and Day and Night. People in printed jackets and skirts wear pale veils over their faces, and one photograph is a detail of a skirt printed in blue, black and white, with a small grid of lit windows in the pattern.
No page I opened describes the 2017 showing. I looked for it on Vlisco's own pages, and on a 2017 capture of its campaign and lookbook pages, and found no entry called Day and Night.

The sign gives me a title and the photographs give me garments, and that is all. The veils matter to the archive as well. They make the models anonymous, so the photographs read as pictures of the cloth and not of a person.

There is a trap nearby. Vlisco's Un à Un exhibition, also called Vlisco 1:1, was shown at Kunsthal Helmond, the contemporary-art venue of Museum Helmond, from September 20, 2016 to March 12, 2017, according to the museum.

The museum describes it as developed for Vlisco's 170th anniversary, covering the company's history, its production and design processes and the use of the fabrics in fashion and art, and as part of the 2016 Mondriaan to Dutch Design year.
It won a Dutch Design Award in the Communication category for the graphic designer Michiel Schuurman, announced on October 28, 2017 during the festival.
That is a Vlisco show tied to the festival by an award, and it was in Helmond, not in the festival's Eindhoven halls, and it had closed by March.
No page I opened connects it to the red room in the album, so I keep the two apart.

The award is worth a note of its own. KABK reproduces a jury statement calling the show a majestic oeuvre exhibition, staged at a time when the industry faces challenging times, which brings the history of the Helmond-based brand, world famous in West Africa, into vibrant focus.
KABK's copy of the statement says Vlisco's colonial history, and Vlisco's own copy of the same statement leaves the word colonial out.
I cannot say which wording the jury wrote, because I did not open the awards' own report.

blocks.x: 2019: the Youth of Africa

r: Dutch Design Week's program entry for 2019, Vlisco&co presents the Youth of Africa, says Vlisco Netherlands established a new venture in 2017 named Vlisco&co, a name that speaks of Vlisco, its partners and collaboration.
It says the exhibition centers on works of fashion designers, filmmakers, photographers and graphic designers from Ghana, Ivory Coast and Nigeria.

Its image credits name a film still from the film A Beautiful Struggle by Dafe Oboro, a film still from An Alien in Town by Daniel Obasi, a research piece on heritage and storytelling by Jessica Sarkodie and a photo series called DNA by the illustrator Ngadi Smart.
The entry places the show only in Eindhoven.

The venture has a documented start outside Eindhoven. A Vlisco news page says the company launched the Vlisco&co initiative in Accra and Lagos in a month it does not name, as cultural evenings bringing together young local creative talent to interpret their own vision of Vlisco designs.

It says the Lagos edition was hosted with A White Space Creative Agency at Alara and showed works by Tokyo James, Karo Akpokiere, Daniel Obasi, Abiola Olusola, Terna Iwar and Aye!, and that the Accra edition was hosted with Nsimba Valene.
A Culture Custodian report describes the Lagos launch on a Friday, December 15, at Alara on Victoria Island, and the site shows it as published nine years before 2026, which makes the year 2017.
The Lagos report says Obasi presented his film An Alien in Town, the same title DDW credits to him in 2019.
So at least one work shown in Lagos in 2017 appears again in the Eindhoven entry two years later, which is a link between the two events that the sources support without drawing it themselves.
Culture Custodian says the aim was to reconnect the brand with a new generation of young creatives based in Nigeria.
Vlisco's news page poses the platform's questions: how tradition will merge with modernity, how the old will be improved by the new.
The 2019 album holds 11 photographs by Max Kneefel.
They show a large industrial hall with pale lattice frames hung with big portrait photographs, a table of fabric, a yellow arrow painted on the floor and a screen on a wall.

The photograph titles name no works, and none says Vlisco&co, so the link between the program entry and the album rests on what the pictures show. I think it is a fair link, and I would still call it a reading.

blocks.x: The company around the festival

r: A Vlisco news page captured in 2019 shows the platform next to other programs: the Vlisco Fashion Fund, whose 2018 winners were named from seven countries, and a meeting with the Ghana Design Network in Amsterdam.
I mention them because 2019's Ghana, Ivory Coast and Nigeria list is not a one-off. Vlisco's pages describe a pattern of working with creatives in the markets where its cloth is worn.
Vlisco's current World of Vlisco page, written for its 180th year, advertises a collaboration with six contemporary African artists to reimagine iconic designs.
I have not seen that collaboration, and it is not in the archive.

blocks.x: What changed between the years

r: In 2017 the subject is the house's own cloth, worn and lit against a red wall. In 2019 the subject is a hall of portraits by other creatives, with the house's name as the host.
The two albums are therefore two different kinds of evidence. The 2017 album shows a product, the 2019 album shows a platform, and the titles for both are the same single word.

That matters for a caption. A caption for the 2017 album can name the print and the sign. A caption for the 2019 album should name the creatives in the program entry only where a photograph can be tied to them, and the album gives me no such tie.
The photographers differ too. Iris Rijskamp is credited on all nine photographs from 2017, and Max Kneefel on all eleven from 2019.

In the photographs used in the carousel, Rijskamp works close, with a single printed skirt, a model in profile or two figures against the red wall, while Kneefel steps back and looks across the hall with visitors at mid distance. That changes what a later reader can learn. The 2017 pictures teach me about cloth and cut. The 2019 pictures teach me how people moved through a show and where the pictures hung, which is a different kind of knowledge, and it says nothing about who made any single portrait.

blocks.x: What the record cannot tell us

r: I cannot say what Vlisco showed in 2017 under the sign Day and Night, because no page I opened describes it. The titles name no works. The year comes from the album title and the album page, not from the wall, so a caption should say no more about 2017 than that.
The archive may hold more Vlisco photographs under other album titles, and I did not search for them.
I also cannot say how many people saw the Eindhoven show of 2019, or whether the Eindhoven exhibition was a full edition of the Lagos format.
The sources do not say who funded or selected the 2019 participants. The Un à Un visitor figure is called enormous by the jury and is not given as a number in any source I opened.
If a maker hands its name to a hall of other people's work, who should the label on the wall credit first? Next time you photograph a hall of pictures, write down who hung them.

posts.title: VPRO at Dutch Design Week, from a lab turned exhibition to a kick-off in an auditorium
posts.subtitle: Seven albums of talk shows and talks from 2015 to 2022, read against VPRO's own pages for 2015 to 2025 and the official photo archive.
posts.seoTitle: VPRO at Dutch Design Week, 2015 to 2025
posts.description: What VPRO's own pages say it did at Dutch Design Week each year, from the 2015 Medialab exhibition to the 2025 kick-off, and what its talk albums show.

r: VPRO has been a media partner of Dutch Design Week for years, and its own pages show the same broadcaster changing what it did there, from a lab turned into an exhibition, to talk shows, to talks made with the festival, to a kick-off event in an auditorium.

The official Dutch Design Week (DDW) photo archive holds seven albums with VPRO's name or its talk formats: two for 2015, and one each for 2016, 2017 and 2022, and two for 2020, 115 photographs in all.

VPRO is unusual among the subjects of this series because it writes down what it plans, which gives me something to set beside the photographs. This essay draws on public sources only: VPRO's own pages, two outside listings and the official photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview, and it says nothing about the 2026 festival beyond what VPRO lists.
I like a media partner for that reason: a plan on paper is something a photograph can confirm or contradict.

blocks.x: Who VPRO is, in its own words

r: VPRO describes itself as an independent media organization that traces its public broadcast heritage back to 1926, working on television, radio, a weekly magazine, websites, apps and live events, and as a media pioneer that has won Emmy Awards and Prix Europa among other prizes.

That is its own description, and I use it only to say who the partner is. The festival-specific pages call it a media partner of Dutch Design Week and say it pays attention to the festival with tips, broadcasts and interviews.

blocks.x: 2015: a lab turned inside out

r: VPRO's page of October 6, 2015 lists what it planned. It promised daily video portraits of nominees for the Dutch Design Awards from October 10, a Tegenlicht broadcast titled Gimme Shelter on Sunday, October 18 at 21:05 on NPO2 about new ideas for the growing flow of refugees, and a Tegenlicht meet-up on Thursday, October 22 at 19:00 in the Designhuis in Eindhoven.

It said VPRO Medialab and VPRO Dorst would turn the lab into an exhibition and living studio, De omroep van de toekomst, misschien, made over the previous months with St. Joost and the Design Academy, open October 17 to 25 from 13:00 to 17:00 at NatLab.

It also listed the VPRO Peepshow, a virtual reality experience from the Medialab, on Ketelhuisplein from October 17 to 25, and sessions recorded by the music program 3voor12 with artists playing at DDW Music, among them Rufus Wainwright, to be heard on 3FM from October 19 to 22.

The same page ties the documentary channel NPO Doc's NatureTech series to the festival's talk show, which it calls the Future Now talk show, theme Forward to Nature. It says the show would be live on NPO Doc on Thursday, October 22 at 20:30, with Koert van Mensvoort as the main guest and Pieter van der Wielen as presenter.

The archive calls the same series Now Future Talkshow, and a screen in the 2015 album reads Now Future Talkshow #3, what if our notion of nature changed?, and Thu 22 Oct 2015, beside the logos of VPRO and DDW.
The date on the screen matches the date on VPRO's page, which settles that the two names are one series and that the album is of that evening's stage.
Next Nature's colophon lists Koert van Mensvoort as its founder and CEO.

blocks.x: 2016: the fourth talk show

r: A trade site's copy of the 2016 program puts the Now Future Talkshow on Thursday, October 27 at 19:30 in the Klokgebouw and calls it the fourth edition, organized by DDW with VPRO, with Pieter van der Wielen talking to Bas van Abel, Luna Maurer and Robert Suarez about the research and processes behind their designs.
The count agrees with the 2015 screen, which said #3.

The same page lists a VPRO Tegenlicht broadcast on Sunday, October 23 about Bas van Abel's Fairphone, a meet-up on October 26 at Pakhuis de Zwijger in Amsterdam, a daily design program, Dagelijkse dosis design, hosted by Elfie Tromp on NPO Cultura from October 24 to 28 at 20:30, and a HoloLens mixed-reality experience from VPRO Medialab from October 22 to 30 in the VDMA building.
The HoloLens piece lets visitors live two hundred years of Maarten Baas's Tree Trunk Chair, a chair that grows inside a young tree and can be harvested in 2216, according to the page.
The archive holds 29 photographs under Now Future Talkshow for 2016, showing a stage branded The Making Of, with a screen reading Persistence is fruitful, and the audience from behind.
The trade site's own date field reads 1999, which is wrong, and I trust its text only because the dates and ambassadors it names fit the 2016 festival.

blocks.x: 2017: a debate about devices

r: A culture site's tip list of October 18, 2017 describes We Know How You Feel Tonight, an English-language debate evening organized by VPRO Medialab on Wednesday, October 25 from 19:00 to 21:30, about devices and the data they collect about us and our emotions, with executives of large organizations and writers from Stichting Gr1p, entrance five euros.
The same page says VPRO pays plenty of attention to DDW on television in the program De toekomstbouwers and on radio in Nooit Meer Slapen.
The archive has an album titled VPRO Medialab with 9 photographs whose own description names Dutch Design Week 2017.
The photographs show an installation in a dark room with visitors lying on mats inside cones of colored light, and the file titles name Design Perron.
No page I opened links the album to the debate evening, so I do not, and I cannot name the work.

blocks.x: 2019 and beyond: where the archive is silent

r: The albums this timeline uses stop after 2022, with none for 2018, 2019, 2021 or 2023 to 2025, but VPRO's pages are not silent. Its ten tips for 2019 list The Robin Who Wondered If He Was A Nightingale at Sectie-C and say the television program De toekomstbouwers, VPRO's program about DDW, would be recorded that year at Sectie-C in the studio of Collaboration O, with viewers invited to attend on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday.
For 2022, VPRO's ten tips begin with Manifestations on the eighth floor of the Veem building and mention works such as Love Letter Generator and gURL.

VPRO's DDW hub lists ten-tip articles for 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, and a Tegenlicht project in 2024 in which Medialab built an intervention to bring physical and online audiences together around an episode about new building materials.

In 2025 VPRO organized its own kick-off program on Sunday, October 19, from 10:15 to 13:00 in the Natlab auditorium, with four speakers: Pauline van Dongen on the Umbra Pavilion on Ketelhuisplein, Daan Sonnemans of Kantamanto Social Club, Eleni Soerjo of Philips on 100 years of Philips design, and Tom van Veen of Accenture on AI in the physical world. It was introduced by Miriam van der Lubbe, the Creative Head of DDW, and Tom Klaassen of VPRO, and the ticket price included a DDW ticket at 25 euros.
Its ten tips for 2025 include Designing Democracy at the Foundation We Are, Ambient Care by Plectrum at Matchbox on Strijp-S, and the Zandkorrelverspreider on Nieuwe Emmasingel.
The kick-off and the tips are VPRO's announcements, and I describe them as such.

blocks.x: 2020: three talks made with the festival

r: In 2020 VPRO says DDW and VPRO made three talks in which ambassadors, makers and designers explore the future.

The first, according to VPRO's teaser for it, has Chris Kijne in conversation with the DDW20 ambassador Lidewij Edelkoort and Lucas de Man, founder of Biobased Creations. The third, published on October 21, 2020, has Pieter van der Wielen with the ambassador Sabine Marcelis and the urban planner Winy Maas about the green future of the city, new ways for designers to exhibit digitally and why architects and filmmakers are alike.
VPRO's talk pages credit their photographs to about.today and Oscar Vinck.

The archive holds 10 and 12 photographs for the first and the third talk, showing the same studio set in a large hall, with a sign reading vpro ambassadeurs talks DDW, two or three people at a long table and camera crews at the sides.

A talk is the hardest kind of event for a caption to improve on, because the words matter and the picture shows a room. The pages above give the topics the speakers were meant to cover and not what was said, so any sentence about the content of a talk would need a recording I have not opened.

blocks.x: 2022: a program with no page

r: The archive album for 2022 is titled VPRO - De wereld van Dutch Design and holds 12 photographs of a television set with a round table, guests, a presenter standing, a seated audience and a screen reading wereld van dutch design.
No page I opened describes that program, so I give it no date. VPRO's ten tips, published on October 22, 2022, are a different thing: they point viewers to works around the city.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: VPRO's 2015 page writes Future Now talk show, while the 2016 program copy and the album screen write Now Future Talkshow. The screen's date and VPRO's date for the live broadcast match, which settles that they are one series.
The trade site says 1999 and describes the festival starting on October 22, which fits 2016.
Whether the 2017 album belongs to the debate evening.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what was said in any of the talks, what the 2022 television program was about, or who made the installation in the 2017 album. I did not find VPRO pages for 2018, 2021 or 2023 beyond the ten-tip articles listed on its hub. The album facts come from my reading of the Flickr account on October 8, 2026, which I did not repeat.
A talk leaves a speaker list, a date and a few rooms. If you caption a talk photograph, which of those three can you actually source?

posts.title: World Design Embassies at Dutch Design Week: eight Octobers of themed embassies, 24 albums and a program that closed in 2025
posts.subtitle: From the first World Design Event in 2017 to eight embassies in 2024: who ran each one, where it stood, what the Dutch Design Foundation says about its end, and what the photo archive can and cannot show.
posts.seoTitle: World Design Embassies at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: The Dutch Design Foundation's World Design Embassies, 2017 to 2024: curators, venues, the 2025 close and Coalitions, and what the DDW photo albums show.

r: A program that calls its exhibitions embassies has to explain what they represent, and the Dutch Design Foundation's World Design Embassies did it by naming a social question for each one and handing it to a curator.

This essay follows the program through the Dutch Design Week (DDW) pages that describe it, the Dutch Design Foundation's own pages for each embassy, the partners' pages, press from 2017 to 2024 and the 24 embassy albums in the official photo archive. It reports no visit and no interview. I read the embassies the way I would read a medical case series: each one is a case of a design question meeting a venue, and the useful comparison is across years.

blocks.x: What the program was

r: A DDW page about Dutch Design Foundation (DDF) says the foundation organizes DDW and the Dutch Design Awards and, throughout the year, manages programs under the flag of Design Works, among them World Design Embassies, What if Lab and Driving Dutch Design.
Design Works is described as the part of DDF that builds business relationships between designers and companies, organizations and governments.

A Dutch article for DDW 2022 says DDF started the program five years earlier, to explore how design helps with the social questions of the time, and that eight themed embassies would show the society of the future with designers and partners.

The program began as something else. On March 27, 2017, IO+ reported on the opening of DDF's year, at which the foundation announced a new festival, the World Design Event, that would run every four years alongside DDW, with eight embassies for the future as creative breeding grounds for food, care and climate, and a People's Pavilion by the design studio Overtreders W with the firm SLA.

The four-year rhythm did not last. The embassies came back every October, and in 2024 DDW's page described World Design Embassies as a year-round program that culminates during DDW, with eight embassies.

Pakhuis de Zwijger, the Amsterdam debate house, filed twenty talks under a World Design Embassies series between October 15, 2020 and March 31, 2022, and describes the program in the same year-round terms.

DDF's own pages count the years differently from the festival. The pages for the Embassies of Health, Water and Safety, written after the program ended, begin with the same sentence, that over the past seven years DDF brought designers, governments, businesses and knowledge institutions together through the program.
The Embassy of Health page lists its creative leads from 2018, which gives seven editions from 2018 to 2024, while the Safety page counts six years and the Inclusive Society page four.
The festival's own count runs from the first World Design Event in 2017 to 2024, eight Octobers.
I use both and say which I mean.

blocks.x: 2017: the first World Design Event

r: IO+ announced that the Innovation Powerhouse in Eindhoven would open to the public for the first time as the Embassy of Health, next to the new studio of the design agency VanBerlo, with the exhibition Chronic Health: Designing a Healthy Future. It named projects such as Outrospectre by Frank Kolkman, the LifeSaver CPR guidance concept by VanBerlo, the High Risk Pregnancy Toolkit by Philips and the DIY Toolkit for Dementia by Waag Society, and said Waag Society curated the exhibition.

Waag adds that the embassy was formed with VanBerlo, Philips, U CREATE and the Máxima Medical Center, that Sabine Wildevuur of its Creative Care Lab was one of the curators, and that the exhibition was open daily from 11:00 to 18:00, October 21 to 29.

The Embassy of Food stood on Ketelhuisplein. DDF's retrospective, published on September 10, 2020, says visitors saw The Future of Food, Looking Back to Now in a big greenhouse, curated by the eating designer Marije Vogelzang, with a daily dinner by the food designer Chloé Rutzerveld, a conference on food waste and the first Future Food Design Awards. It says the exhibition drew about 26,000 people and about 800 took part in the program, and that the embassy was organized by the province of Noord-Brabant with ZLTO, DDF and the Ministry of Economic Affairs.
Those are the organizer's figures, written three years afterward.

The Robot Love Embassy was a different kind of embassy. Its own page says the Niet Normaal Foundation presented it, from October 21 to 29, 2017, in the former V&D department store in the center of Eindhoven, with the Technological Universities of Delft and Eindhoven and the University of Twente, where robots learned from their interactions with humans, and it reports 63,000 visitors, which is the organizer's figure.
A 2018 press release from the same foundation repeats the number as 63,000 visits counted in nine days.
The page lists a 2018 edition at the Campina milk factory on Kanaaldijk-Zuid, September 15 to December 2, 2018.
The 2017 albums are Embassy of Food (17 photos), Embassy of Health (13), Embassy of Intimacy (7) and Embassy of Robot Love (10).

The Health album shows a DNA donation contract table, a case of medical equipment, a pregnancy simulator and visitors at a VR station, which fits the healthcare themes in the press descriptions, though no title names a project.
The Intimacy album's titles name Ketelhuisplein and the MU, not an intimacy exhibit, so I cannot say what it shows, and I found no page I could open that describes the Embassy of Intimacy.

blocks.x: 2018: six embassies, two albums

r: DDW's 2018 dossier page lists six embassy pages: Water, Mobility, Urban Transformation, Health, Circularity and Food.

The Embassy of Health returned to the Innovation Powerhouse, now described as on the Strijp-T terrain, with the exhibition Chronic Health: If not us then who?, echoing the 2018 festival title, and with the same six partners: Waag, VanBerlo, Philips, the Máxima Medical Center, DDF and U CREATE. Its curator was Sabine Wildevuur of Waag, and its examples included an artificial womb, a bicycle for elderly and insecure cyclists and a game helping teenage girls cope with the loss of a father or brother.
The other pages give each embassy a place and a person. The Embassy of Food, curated again by Marije Vogelzang, was a smaller Micro Embassy on microbes and food, in her words.

The Embassy of Water stood in AtelierNL's church on Bergmannstraat, with Anouk van der Poll, owner of vanderPolloffice, as curator and two themes, Water-Sensitive Urban Design and Nature-Based Solutions.
DDF's retrospective, published on July 25, 2019, adds that the embassy was initiated by her as a platform for water-related design and credits its photographs to Iris Rijskamp.

The Embassy of Mobility stood in the former V&D building, with the consultant Nienke Dijkstra in charge of the program and the urban developer Harm Rensink designing the exhibition and a test circuit for electric vehicles.
The Embassy of Urban Transformation was a collaboration between the Rotterdam design agency A/BZ and The Student Hotel, using Eindhoven's District E as a playground for experiments.

The Embassy of Circularity, curated by Marieke Rietbergen of Design Innovation Group, asked how to produce 2020 entirely circular apartment buildings by 2020 with partners that included ABN AMRO, DEMEEUW, CIRCO, New Horizon and the Urban Mining Collective.
The archive has two 2018 albums, Embassy of Health with 21 photos by Ruud Balk and Embassy of Water with 15 photos whose titles read AtelierNL, by Iris Rijskamp.
The Water album's title now has an explanation, since AtelierNL's church is where DDW's own page puts the embassy.
The other four 2018 embassies have no album.

blocks.x: 2019: six embassies and a change of structure

r: On October 17, 2019, IO+ listed six embassies for DDW, October 19 to 27: Safety and Circular & Biobased Building on Ketelhuisplein, Sustainable Design across Strijp-S and Strijp-T, Health in the Klokgebouw, Mobility behind Radio Royaal and Water at the Campina terrain.

The roster had changed from 2018: Safety, Sustainable Design and Circular & Biobased Building appear for the first time on the list, Circularity, Food and Urban Transformation do not, and Water moved from the church to Campina.

The Embassy of Sustainable Design was curated by Leonne Cuppen of Yksi Connect with VanBerlo, as part of DDW's theme If not now, then when, and was spread over Strijp-S and Strijp-T, the Innovation Powerhouse, Gloeilampenplantsoen and Yksi Expo. Yksi Connect names partners from IKEA Netherlands and NS to TU Delft, Design Academy Eindhoven and FrieslandCampina.
DDF's Embassy of Health page names Jetske van Oosten as creative lead from 2019 to 2022 and describes the 2019 exhibition Chronic Health: It's Only Human?.
The 2019 archive has albums for Embassy of Mobility (11 photos) and Embassy of Sustainable Design (7), both credited to Britt Roelse.

blocks.x: 2020: a virtual house and a talk series

r: DDW 2020 was virtual. On October 18, 2020, DDW TV posted a video in which Lucas De Man walks viewers through The Exploded View, a detached house rebuilt with circular methods and biobased materials.
DDF's Health page calls the 2020 edition Chronic Health: Happily Ever After?, held in a digital setting.

The year-round side shows in the Pakhuis de Zwijger series, whose livecast talks that autumn took one embassy a week: Rethinking Plastic on November 5, then Circular & Biobased Building, Water, Health, Mobility, Food and Safety, the last on December 17, 2020.
The 2020 albums are Circular & Biobased Building with 26 photos and Rethinking Plastic with 11.

blocks.x: 2021: no album and a new embassy

r: There is no embassy album for 2021, yet the program was there. The DDW article for 2022 says the Circular & Biobased Building embassy built a circular and biobased house at DDW the year before, and calls the 2022 Inclusive Society embassy the second edition.

DDF's own page for the Embassy of Inclusive Society says it was in its inaugural year at DDW 2021, asking how designers can contribute to a society in which everyone feels seen and represented, and names Jorn Konijn as creative lead for 2021 and Shay Raviv for 2022 to 2024.
Its photograph credits for the Embassies of Health, Water and Safety also list DDW21 images.

The Pakhuis de Zwijger series ran six talks in 2021, on circular thinking, a healthy environment, food and water systems, a safe and inclusive society, living with water, and mobility with livability first.

blocks.x: 2022: the largest year in the archive

r: The DDW article for 2022 shows how the roster worked. Food, with food designer Chloé Rutzerveld as curator, built three scenarios for the supermarket of 2050 in the Klokgebouw. Water, with Anouk van der Poll, argued for regenerative housing at the Designhuis Eindhoven. Urban Mobility, with Rob Adams, worked on liveable streets in the Klokgebouw. Safety, with Tabo Goudswaard, took the theme In makers we trust. Inclusive Society, with Shay Raviv, was in its second edition at the Van Abbemuseum. Health, with curator Marleen van Bergeijk, was in its sixth year in a row, in the Klokgebouw.

Two more embassies in that article mark the end of a thread. Rethinking Plastic, with Leonne Cuppen as curator, was in what the article calls its very last year, at Yksi Expo, and Circular & Biobased Building, curated by Lucas De Man and Pascal Leboucq, was building a modular exhibition on Strijp-S inspired by the circular and biobased house it had built the year before.
DDW's program page adds that Rethinking Plastic ran changing exhibitions, lectures and workshops through the year, with students from several design schools in a Rethinking Plastic Academy.
Yksi Connect lists a Rethinking Plastic exhibition at Yksi Expo from September 2, 2022 as the start of a two-year program, and a traveling version in Bucharest in June 2021.
The two statements about 2022 differ, since one calls it the last year and the other the start of a two-year program, and I do not resolve them.

The 2022 archive is the largest: eight albums for the embassies (Inclusive Society 43 photos, Urban Mobility 14, Health 17, Rethinking Plastic 48, Circular & Biobased Building 32, Safety 11, Food 40) plus a 63-photo conference album titled Ch.. Ch.. Changes.
The Water embassy, which the article places at the Designhuis, has no 2022 album, although DDF's Water page lists a DDW22 conference photograph.

blocks.x: 2023: seven embassies

r: For 2023, DDW lists seven embassies, each with a creative lead and venue. Circular & Biobased Building, led by De Man and Leboucq, stood on Ketelhuisplein. Food, led by Barbara Vos, was in the Evoluon, showing a farm of the future. Health, led by Marleen van Bergeijk, explored health as currency at Foundation We Are. Inclusive Society, led by Shay Raviv, built a spatial gym for training an inclusivity muscle at the Van Abbemuseum. Mobility, led by Joost van der Made, ran a living lab across the city with a permanent exhibition at DONNA. Safety, led by Goudswaard, had the theme Making (amends) in the Klokgebouw. Water, led by Van der Poll, built a pavilion at Stadhuisplein.
DDF's later page names the gym's designer, Gabriel Fontana, and a companion installation that visualized guidelines for inclusive and accessible presentations.
The 2023 archive has six albums, 116 photos in all, and none for Food.

blocks.x: 2024 and the end

r: DDW's program page for 2024 lists eight participating embassies, Circular & Biobased Building, Digital Futures, Food, Health, Inclusive Society, Mobility, Safety and Water, as part of the exhibition Designing Society, for October 19 to 27, 2024.
Digital Futures is the one name that does not appear in earlier years.
DDF's account of the Inclusive Society embassy says that in 2024 it took part in Designing Society and focused on turning isolated inclusive initiatives into sustained practice.
My reading of the archive stops at 2023, and I did not check Flickr for 2024 embassy albums.

The end is on record. On March 25, 2025, DDF announced that World Design Embassies and What if Lab would continue as Coalitions, a platform and structural approach that builds on both programs, with the first products called Co/Labs, collaboration trajectories in which design teams work with organizations that own a societal challenge.
DDF's pages for the individual embassies, written afterward, say it plainly: since 2025, the World Design Embassies program has come to a close, and DDF is building on its legacy with Coalitions.
DDF's current About page describes a foundation that builds coalitions with partners from business, policy and science and does not list World Design Embassies.
An earlier version of this essay said no page announced the end. DDF's own pages do, and they use the word close.

Brainport Eindhoven's article of October 11, 2024 gives the funder's view. It says that with funding from the Regio Deal Brainport Eindhoven, DDF set up programs that link designers to government and industry, that DDF's Head of Design Works, Marianne Aarnoudse, is responsible for programs such as the What if Lab and the World Design Embassies, and that in the embassies DDF acts as director, bringing the relevant parties together with designers. It also quotes the DDF leadership saying that they might make themselves redundant in the coming years, if the design world penetrates traditional markets.

blocks.x: Who led each embassy

r: DDF's embassy pages carry the creative leads by year, which makes them the best single record of who stood behind each name. Health: Sabine Wildevuur (2018), Jetske van Oosten (2019 to 2022) and Marleen van Bergeijk (2022 to 2024), with the partners Alles is Gezondheid, AMS-IX, Health Holland, Philips, the Máxima Medical Center, Waag, the province of Noord-Brabant and the Creative Industries Fund NL among others.
Water: Anouk van der Poll, with Brabant Water, the City of Eindhoven, the province of Noord-Brabant and the water board De Dommel.
Safety: Tabo Goudswaard, with the Ministry of Justice and Security, the police, the Public Prosecution Service and the Probation Service.
Inclusive Society: Jorn Konijn (2021) and Shay Raviv (2022 to 2024), with ActiZ, two ministries, the Van Abbemuseum, the Vriendenloterij and the VSB Fonds.
A reader of the albums sees the name of an embassy. The leads and partners explain why the same name looks different from year to year.

blocks.x: What the archive can and cannot show

r: The embassy albums hold 522 photos: 47 in 2017, 36 in 2018, 18 in 2019, 37 in 2020, 268 in 2022 and 116 in 2023.

There is no album for 2021, although the 2022 article says the Circular & Biobased Building embassy built a house at DDW the year before, DDF says Inclusive Society began that year, and Yksi's pages place a traveling Rethinking Plastic show in Bucharest in June 2021.

The same name appears in many years, Health in 2017, 2018, 2022 and 2023, Mobility in 2019, 2022 and 2023, Circular & Biobased Building in 2020, 2022 and 2023, and the curator, the venue and the question change under it.
A caption that says only Embassy of Health tells you the program and not the year, the room or the people.
One credit needed checking. The archive's 2017 Robot Love album credits Iris Rijskamp by title, while the Robot Love page credits a photo of the Pepper robot to Iris Rijswijk of Dutch Design Week.

DDF's own Water retrospective spells the photographer Iris Rijskamp, as the archive does, so I read the Robot Love page's spelling as a misspelling, though a printed credit should still be checked with DDW.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what the Embassy of Intimacy showed in 2017, what the 2019 Sustainable Design and Mobility albums show beyond their titles, what the Digital Futures embassy showed in 2024, or how many visitors each embassy had apart from the two organizer figures for Food and Robot Love.

I could not read DDF's public annual reports for 2021 to 2024, which are the likely place for program-level numbers, because the files returned errors at the addresses a search listed and an archive copy came back empty. I did not find the date the program was first called World Design Embassies instead of World Design Event, although the 2017 announcement already names the embassies.
Dezeen's guide to the 2017 embassies is on a host that refused my automated request, so I used nothing from it.
When one name is reused for eight Octobers, which part of the caption would you check first: the curator, the venue or the question?

posts.title: Yksi at Dutch Design Week: one name, four organizations, and an exhibition space that changed hands in 2023
posts.subtitle: The curator's own pages, two press releases and DDW's listings give themes, dates and credits for the years the photo archive labels only Yksi.
posts.seoTitle: Yksi at Dutch Design Week
posts.description: Yksi Expo on Strijp-S, 2011 to 2022: Dutch Design Week exhibitions, Rethinking Plastic, the 2023 handover to Foundation We Are, and what the photo archive holds.

r: Yksi's own record of its Dutch Design Week years is a list of curated exhibitions, and each of them has a named theme, a date and a photographer credit, which the photo archive's titles mostly do not.

I like that gap, because it shows what each kind of record is good for. This essay draws on public sources only: the pages of Yksi Expo's curator, two press releases, an exhibition announcement, a lecture listing, Dutch Design Week's program pages, a building page from Strijp-S and the official photo archive as I recorded it on October 7, 2026. It reports no visit and no interview, and it describes the 2026 week only through what a DDW location page lists.

blocks.x: One name, four organizations

r: The Yksi home page links three parts, called ontwerp, expo and connect, and in the version I could read on October 9 it carried nothing else.

The pages behind the names describe different organizations. Yksi Ontwerp says it has been active in the design world since 1991 and calls itself an initiator of Dutch Design Week, with a team of an interior designer, an industrial designer and a founder, working on interiors and products, among them a design label called JAPTH.

Yksi Expo was a foundation with a gallery. Its December 2022 press release says Yksi began in 1991 as a design studio with a foundation and gallery next to it, to give Dutch design and above all young designers a platform, that after some years in the Designhuis near the city hall the foundation settled on Strijp-S in 2011, and that the foundation was later separated from the studio by mutual agreement.
Yksi Connect is the company that Leonne Cuppen founded, in her words more than seven years ago, to connect designers with the field.
A fourth organization enters at the end of the story. Foundation We Are, founded in 2018, took over the space in 2023, as the release explains below.
I keep the four apart because the archive's albums say only Yksi.

blocks.x: The building, and what the dates do not say

r: Yksi Expo's address is Torenallee 22-04 on Strijp-S, and its 2021 press release describes the space as the ground floor of the Apparatenfabriek.

Strijp-S's building page says that in 1928 three large buildings known as the Hoge Rug rose at great speed, among them the Apparatenfabriek, formerly known as building SK, which was built as the first radio equipment factory, where the first Philips radios were produced and, after the war, television sets.
The same page says the housing corporation Trudo transformed the building in 2013 into a business center with more than 100 workspaces.

Those dates sit side by side awkwardly. Yksi's release says it settled on Strijp-S in 2011, and the building page dates the conversion to 2013, so Yksi may have been in the building before the conversion.
Neither page says so, and I do not know which part of the building Yksi used before 2013. The curator's page puts the size of the space at 600 square meters.

blocks.x: What the curator's page says about each year

r: The best written account of Yksi Expo's Dutch Design Week years comes from Leonne Cuppen's curation page, which lists her exhibitions with dates, themes and photographers.
I report what it says as her own account.

The 2017 edition is documented by an exhibition announcement posted on an architects' site under the name Yksi Ontwerp: for the 16th Dutch Design Week, October 21 to 29, 2017, Yksi Expo at Torenallee 22-04 presented twenty-five projects, presentations and products, with attention to material experiments and design for the circular economy.

It names Material Sense Lab's Bio-Boost, with a living fungus as natural black paint, paper pulp as a base for building elements and tiles and a festival token made of bioplastic, fish skins from NYVIDD, Daria Biryukova's research on reusing waste for glazes with Van Gansewinkel, the label Pour by Julie van der Boorn and the launch of the brand Zooi, which makes lifestyle articles from residual material.

It also lists craft furniture by students of the Koning Willem I College, the results of the Masters of Materials design competition organized by Baars & Bloemhoff, and an exhibition called Austrian Design Compositions as a contrast to Dutch design.

In 2018 the curator's page gives Yksi Expo's Dutch Design Week program as October 20 to 28, about twenty designers and companies, on sustainability, circular design and social design, tied to that year's festival motto, which she renders as "If not us, then who."

The same page lists two exhibitions before the festival, Like Leather, from July 4 to September 29, and Paper Generations, which she curated as a tribute to her father, and a larger show called Clean Revolution: Dutch Design for a Better World, which she lists for the Global Climate Summit in San Francisco on September 12 and 13, for Dutch Design Week October 20 to 28 in the Veemgebouw, and for Yksi Expo.
An Innovation Origins listing of the lectures on Monday, October 22, 2018, lists two lectures at "Yksi, Torenallee 22-04," at 14:00 and 16:00, both titled KVGO and Print Pakt.
The page is Innovation Origins' list, not DDW's own schedule.

For 2019 the page gives Yksi Expo's program as October 19 to 27, about sustainability and circular design, with several thematic exhibitions and some twenty presentations by designers, small and medium businesses and schools, and says Yksi Expo formed part of the Embassy of Sustainable Design, which Cuppen curated with the design agency VanBerlo.
It lists Beyond Coffee at Yksi Expo from July 19 to November 3, 2019, and a long partner list for the Embassy that includes IKEA Netherlands, Renewi, NS, FrieslandCampina and several universities.
The Embassy was a program of the World Design Event during Dutch Design Week 2019, under the theme If not now, then when.

blocks.x: 2021 and 2022: plastic

r: For 2021 the press release of September 13, 2021 describes Yksi Expo's Dutch Design Week, October 16 to 24, as entirely about plastic.

It describes a 50 square meter studio space furnished with products of recycled plastic, bioplastic or sustainable alternatives, a complete house of plastic called the Rethinking Plastic House, built with companies and institutes of the Brightlands Chemelot Campus, a Rethinking Plastic Academy for projects by students and young designers, a small recycling workshop from the foundation Sparkling Plastic, the platform Solaris with products made of ocean plastic from Thailand, and the winners of the No Waste Challenge and the Green Product Award.
It says the program had run for more than a year and that it formed the Embassy of Rethinking Plastic, part of the World Design Embassies of the Dutch Design Foundation.
The curator's page adds TNO's Torwash, a technology that dissolves bioplastic so it can be reused, and three designers' results shown at Yksi Expo during the festival.

Dutch Design Week's own program archive lists Rethinking Plastic as part of DDW 2022, presented by Yksi Expo, with a main exhibition photographed by Jeroen van der Wielen, and mentions Wint designLab and a project from the Vilnius Academy of Art.
The archive has no Yksi album for 2022.

One date does not line up. The curator's page dates the exhibition Rethinking Plastic at Yksi Expo from September 2 to December 31, 2022 and calls it the start of a two-year program, while the September 2021 press release says the program had already run for more than a year.
The most consistent reading is that the page's 2022 is a slip for an earlier year, but I cannot settle it from the pages, and the press release is the dated document.

blocks.x: The handover in 2023

r: Yksi Expo's press release of December 10, 2022 says Cuppen stops with the foundation on January 1, 2023, after more than 31 years, and hands on the baton to the younger generation.

It says that a plan for members of the Yksi Expo Young Talent team to continue the work could not be realized, and that the new tenant of the Torenallee space is the foundation We Are, founded in 2018 to bring the creative sector and experts in societal transitions together, which began on Sectie C and then sat on the former Campina site.

DDW's 2026 location page lists Foundation We Are at Torenallee 22-04, calls it a design collective that began eight years ago with eight designers and is now a young cultural organization, and lists an exhibition there for the 2026 week.
The foundation has separate albums in the archive and belongs in a different timeline.

Cuppen's own pages say she continues with Yksi Connect, and that more recently she has been curator of the materials fair MaterialDistrict and a guild master of a maker place called Nieuw Zwanenburg, which she describes as a place in the making.
I describe those as her pages' account and do not add to them.

blocks.x: The claim about Dutch Design Week itself

r: Two Yksi pages say Yksi was among the initiators of Dutch Design Week, and Cuppen says in her own words that she was one of the initiators of the Dutch Design Week and the Designhuis in Eindhoven.
That is a self-description. I found no DDW page that confirms it, so I report it only as a claim made by Yksi and leave it out of any statement about the festival's history.

blocks.x: What the albums keep

r: The old dossier counts six Yksi albums, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2021, with 11, 16, 20, 14, 17 and 6 photographs, 84 in all.

The photographers named in the titles are Patrick Meis for 10 of the 11 in 2015, Iris Rijskamp for 2016 to 2019 and Max Kneefel for 2021, while the curator's page credits Jeroen van der Wielen for exhibitions of 2018 and later and Oscar Vinck for the 2019 Embassy.

The dossier describes banners in the 2018 album that read Online Department Store of the Future and name Indigo People and Planq, and a 2019 panel on green coffee beans that fits the Beyond Coffee show.
I could not tie those to the written sources beyond that one match.
The old dossier also records that Dezeen's 2016 festival guide listed Yksi among venues with international exhibitions, a fact I did not reopen because Dezeen refused my request.

blocks.x: Where the sources disagree, and what settled it

r: The old draft called it DDW's schedule. The page is Innovation Origins' list.
2011 per Yksi, and the building's conversion is dated 2013 by Strijp-S. Not settled.
The September 2021 release says more than a year before; the curator's page says September 2022. The dated release is the stronger source.
Whether Yksi initiated Dutch Design Week.
Two Yksi pages say so; no DDW page does. Not settled.
Who the Torenallee space belongs to.
Yksi Expo until January 1, 2023, then Foundation We Are. The press release settles it.

blocks.x: What the record does not show

r: I do not know what most of the archive photographs show, because titles after 2015 do not name works, and I do not know why 2020 and 2022 have no album. I do not know what Yksi Expo showed in 2015 and 2016 beyond the album titles and a trade listing, or which part of the Apparatenfabriek it used before 2013. I did not open Yksi Expo's own website.
I did not reopen the photo archive for this version, so the album counts, titles and descriptions come from the dossier's October 7, 2026 reading.
Nothing here describes Foundation We Are's 2026 program beyond DDW's listing.

If a single address held a curator's exhibition space for thirty-one years and then a younger collective's, which name would you put on a caption for a photo from a given year, and which document would you show to prove it?
